Why u2ue

Who this is for: the evaluator deciding whether to use u2ue - what it does, what it has proved, what it costs and what is not done yet, on one page.

Port a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5, and prove it is still the same game.

What it does

u2ue is a porting toolkit behind one command line, py -m u2ue, called the facade; each of its commands is called a verb. It reads the Unity project as text (the YAML files Unity saves scenes, prefabs and materials in), with no editor running. It converts what is not game logic: particle effects, scenes, UI, materials and audio (the steps that are still manual are listed below). It measures in Unity any behaviour that has to be matched exactly. It holds the result to Unity on numbers, frame by frame and bit by bit. The game's logic is ported by an AI model following the toolkit's own skill (a written procedure the model loads as its instructions), and a reviewer judges that port by reading a generated UML model (diagrams of how the code is built and what it is for; Reading UML and use cases teaches them) instead of a diff.

What sets it apart, each with the chapter that has the details:

  • A price before you start. u2ue estimate prices the port of your Unity project on Opus 5.5 (an Anthropic AI model), in tokens (the units a model reads and writes, and is billed by) and dollars, with a band (a low and a high figure) and a confidence level, from rates measured on a real port. It needs no editor and no project file (the one JSON file that describes a game to the toolkit). What a port costs.
  • One command for the whole port. u2ue port runs every stage a verb can do, and stops with one question where a person, the AI or a Unity editor is needed. Chapter 4.
  • It reads Unity without Unity. Prefabs, variants, scenes, materials and ScriptableObjects are read from their YAML, and the textures Unity actually samples from Library/Artifacts (where Unity keeps its imported copy of each texture). Nothing steals focus or blocks the person working. Chapter 6, Chapter 11, Chapter 12.
  • Shuriken to Niagara, with evidence. The toolkit's converter turns effects made with Shuriken, Unity's particle system, into Niagara, Unreal's. Every behaviour added to the converter lands as a route (its handling of one Unity behaviour) behind a switch (an environment variable that turns that route on or off), and the switch turns ON only with an evidence row: the record of the trial (the route tried on real effects first) that proved it. What it cannot port is named per emitter (one particle system inside an effect), with the reason. Chapter 7, Chapter 11.
  • It measures Unity instead of guessing. A probe (an Editor C# script that sets up a case in Unity and records what happens) measures how Unity behaves, only while the person at the editor is idle, and each rule keeps the Unity version it was measured on. Chapter 8.
  • The same bits on every runtime. The game's rules run on .NET, on the target Unity version's own Mono (the runtime Unity runs C# on) with no editor, and in Unreal, and their answers are compared by float bits, a check called parity (u2ue digest, u2ue parity). Chapter 5, Chapter 14.
  • Data first, pictures last. Unity's own particle state is held against Niagara's read-back (Unreal's particles, recorded frame by frame) for every emitter (u2ue conform), and every miss (an emitter whose particle count or first birth disagrees with Unity's) is listed, most with a named cause. Chapter 9.
  • Checks that can fail. Every judge (a script that holds a result to a rule) must refuse a planted fault, a defect put there on purpose (u2ue judge --prove), and u2ue cycle checks every promise of the product, called a pillar, on each recurring run: a promise with no check reads ABSENT, never PASS. Chapter 14.
  • Headless on both sides. Headless means run with no window open, so nothing takes the screen's focus. Unity's Editor-folder tests (the NUnit tests Unity normally runs inside its editor) and a C# type-check run with no Unity Editor. Unreal runs headless, and u2ue host makes the game's own Unreal project. Chapter 12, Chapter 13.
  • Built for an AI porter, and checked. The toolkit's skills tell an AI model how to port a game's logic and an effect gap (an emitter Unity draws and Unreal does not). Each step of the logic skill names the command it runs and when it is done, and a gate (a check that refuses a result breaking one rule) refuses a skill that names a command the toolkit lacks. Chapter 15.
  • A model to review, not a diff. The use cases (each goal, told as numbered steps), the requirements, the class model (which classes the code holds and how they use one another) and the traceability (the chain from each requirement to the check that proves it) are generated on every build from the code and the toolkit's own documents, and every use case step cites the page it was read from. Chapter 17, Chapter 22, Appendix E.
  • Never a silent default. Every value is READ from the source, MEASURED in Unity, or ABSENT (proven missing, or unreadable), with where it came from or the reason. Chapter 1.

What it has proved

Each tile is printed on every build from the showcase record (the file in which the toolkit records its headline numbers, named under the tiles), never typed by hand. The effect, parity and conformance tiles were measured on the reference port, a commercial Unity 6 tactics game moved to Unreal Engine 5.7; the last two price a second, unrelated game.

The tiles use a few words of their own. A ULP (unit in the last place) is the smallest step between two floats, so two results one ULP apart differ by the least two floats can. A seam is an interface the game's rules call instead of an engine API, and each engine's host code fills it. Coupled lines of code use a Unity API, and the prompt cache serves the part of each AI call the model has read before, at a fraction of the price. Reading UML and use cases explains the use case tiles, What a port costs the last two, and the glossary (Appendix C) every other term.

Why the numbers can be trusted

u2ue's iron law is one principle: propose from a fixed space, verify by execution, report a measured confidence, refuse rather than invent. Applied to a port:

the principle u2ue
propose from a fixed space every value is READ from the source, with where it came from; a symbol must be one the class model holds
verify by execution a Unity behaviour is READ from source or MEASURED in Unity by a probe; every change runs a judge, and every judge has a plant it must refuse
report a measured confidence every number names its record and its denominator; a stale input prints STALE
refuse rather than invent a value that cannot be read is ABSENT, with the reason; a miss in an index (one of the toolkit's lookups of what the code holds) is UNKNOWN, never ABSENT

The same principle holds the AI porter's work. The model proposes; the class model and the index are the fixed space its proposal must land in; the gates verify by running, and each refuses a planted fabrication: the class-model gate a method name the code lacks (uml.py selftest), the manual's command gate an option the facade does not read, the use-case checker a step whose citation does not resolve. The toolkit never relies on the model not to invent; it makes an invention fail, by name, before anyone reads it. What it has not shown is a token saving: on exact-name lookups the index saved none (Chapter 15).

What it costs

The game's logic is the one part an AI writes, and that is where the model tokens go; every other stage is run by a verb. Ask for the price of your own game before you start. It opens no Unity and no Unreal, and needs no project file:

py -m u2ue estimate --unity <your Unity project> --roots <the game's code folders>

What a port costs shows estimates for two real games, the measured rates they multiply by, what the toolkit saves, and how sure the number is, with the reasons.

What is not done yet

  • The logic is not automatic. The toolkit gives the method, the runtime, the analysis and the gates. An AI model following the logic skill, or a person, moves the code and writes the Unreal hosts (Chapter 1, Chapter 5).
  • Animation and physics are not covered. The reference port had neither, so no tool is claimed.
  • Some steps are tools, not verbs yet: a scene's middle steps, between importing it into Unreal and reading the saved level back (textures, material parents, lighting, outline hulls: the extra material slot per mesh that draws the toon outline Unity's outline pass draws).
  • Not yet proven in Unreal: drawing Unity's trails and the host templates' headless smoke run. The UI capture refuses by name until it ships in the package, and the lit-material and Timeline routes sit behind switches that are still OFF.
  • Not yet a released package. The Unity package (package.json, a versioned release) and the probes as its Editor assembly (code Unity loads only in its editor) are still open, and many effect and scene tools, and the tools that queue and report effect work, still default to the reference port's folders. Each is moving onto the project file's variables, proven by its selftest (the tool's own check of itself) and an unchanged output (Chapter 18, "Converting a tool"); u2ue cycle counts the hard-wired sites (code that names one game, machine or person) left in the toolkit's core, and that count may only go down. The toolkit's parts live in two trees today: u2ue/tools.py names each part's folder once, U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT moves them as a whole, and u2ue release assembles them into one repository (Chapter 20).
  • There are a lot of switches. Chapter 21 counts them, generated. Each is a proof trail; the permanently-on ones are to be retired in one pass that whole_trace (the offline replay that proves a converter change) shows changes nothing.
  • The probes need the owner's Unity editor, and run only while it is idle. Nothing in the window protocol (the guarded session in which the probes run) depends on whose editor it is, so a team could run it on a dedicated machine.
  • The Unreal hosts depend on UnrealSharp (the plugin through which Unreal runs their C#), which had no console path and no production promise when it was last checked.
  • Two games so far: the reference port and a second, unrelated game, one short of the rule of three (a reusable part is general only once three different applications have used it).

Appendix B has the plan for every item above that is planned, and what ends it. Appendix D has the sources for the last two.

About this manual

Who this is for: every reader, on the way in - which part of the manual is yours, the path through it, and the conventions it is written in.

Edition 2026-10-17. The manual of u2ue, the Unity to Unreal porting toolkit. It assumes you know Unity and Unreal as a user, Python well enough to run a script, and C# well enough to read a MonoBehaviour.

Examples

Every example in this manual is real: its commands ran, and its output was recorded on the game named beside it.

  • A first port, start to finish - Chapter 4: a second, unrelated game (Unity 2021.3) from its project file to its first report, with what each step printed; then its code, scenes, UI, Unreal project and conformance.
  • The reference port in numbers - Appendix A: what was ported, how, and what it measured.
  • Porting one effect gap, in depth - Chapter 11, from the census (an offline count of the emitters a new route would gain) to the flip (its switch turned ON) with its evidence row.
  • A game's own Unreal project made from nothing - Chapter 13, measured step by step on the second game.
  • A test for a newly ported rule - Chapter 14, from the rule to the cycle.
  • Recipes for extending the toolkit - Chapter 18: a game adapter, a verb, a converter route, a material family, a measured rule, a selftest, a concept, and converting a tool onto the project file.
  • Every goal as a fully dressed use case - Chapter 17, each step citing the page it was read from (Reading UML and use cases explains the form).

Conventions

  • The reference port - the commercial Unity 6 tactics game moved to Unreal Engine 5.7 that the toolkit was built on. The second game - a different studio's project on Unity 2021.3, run through the same facade to show what is general.
  • READ - a value taken from the Unity source (a file, a field) with where it came from.
  • MEASURED - a Unity behaviour observed in Unity itself by a probe, judged by a judge that refuses a planted wrong answer.
  • ABSENT - a value proven not to exist, or not readable, named with the reason. There is no fourth category: the toolkit never substitutes a plausible default, and a refusal is reported by name.
  • HAVE / NOT YET - whether the toolkit itself provides something today. NOT YET is always followed by the plan that delivers it.
  • Commands run from the toolkit's root folder: py -m u2ue .... Sample output is real; a project's name is written <game> and machine paths <work>/..., <unity project>, <unreal project>.
  • "Chapter N" and "Appendix X" are links in the one-page edition.

How the manual stays true to the code

The parts that describe the code (the command reference, the facade's requirements, the use cases, the class model, the switch, tool and selftest tables, the traceability) are generated from the code and the requirements model on every build, so the manual cannot describe a toolkit that has moved on. The requirements model is the toolkit's use cases and requirements, held as facts the build reads (Chapter 15 and Appendix E say how). The build refuses a page that names a particular game, its folders or a machine path, shows a command or an option the facade does not have, or names a tool file the package does not ship.

The toolkit's earlier documents beside the code (u2ue/README.md, u2ue/GUIDE.md, u2ue/BASICS.md, u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md, u2ue/CONCEPTS.md, u2ue/USECASES.md, u2ue/PACKAGE.md, the u2ue-port and u2ue-logic skills, and four other notes, among them vfxport/README.md) are folded into this manual, so a person need not read them; the skills stay the prompts an AI model loads. u2ue/manual/coverage_gate.py checks that every section of each is here, or is named as out with the reason.

The Markdown files in u2ue/manual/ are the source. py u2ue/manual/build.py regenerates the generated parts and writes manual.html, the single-page edition; py u2ue/manual/build.py --check exits 1 when a generated part is stale, and py u2ue/manual/build.py --selftest proves the gates still refuse their plants.

Reading UML and use cases

Who this is for: every reader who has not used UML or use cases before - after it you can read every diagram and use case page in this manual. Read it before any page assumes it.

This manual shows the toolkit, and the method it gives a port, in two kinds of model: diagrams of how the code is put together, and use cases that say who wants what done and how they get it. Both come from UML, the Unified Modeling Language: a standard set of diagram kinds for describing software, kept by the Object Management Group. You do not need the standard to read this manual. This page is everything it uses, and nothing it does not.

Why a porting manual uses UML

A port is mostly moving code into a new shape: rules out of Unity's MonoBehaviours into a model that knows no engine (Chapter 5). A diagram of the shape you want is a shorter, checkable description than prose. The method is to draw the target first and then make the code match it, and an AI model doing the port is given the diagram as its instructions (Chapter 15). The generated diagrams are held to the code, so a diagram here is a checked fact, not a drawing ("The rules this manual holds its UML to", below).

The three diagram kinds

The diagrams are written in Mermaid, a text format that draws diagrams in a web page. Mermaid has no use case diagram, so this manual draws use case diagrams as flowcharts and says so where it does.

  • Class diagram: the STRUCTURE. Which things exist (classes) and how they use one another. Chapter 22's concept model (the toolkit's main ideas, each held by one class) is one.
  • Use case diagram: the GOALS. Who uses the system (actors), for what (use cases), and how the goals depend on one another. Chapter 17 has the toolkit's.
  • Activity or flow diagram: the ORDER. Steps, the arrows between them, and the checks between steps. Chapter 17 draws the epic (the whole port as one use case, explained below) this way, generated; the short version and Chapters 7 and 14 sketch a pipeline this way by hand. Chapter 5 and Chapter 22 also use the flowchart form for structure: Chapter 5's model and its hosts, Chapter 22's layers and its facade map (each verb and the tools it runs; its caption gives its legend).

A UML glossary: every symbol this manual draws

In a class diagram

The concept model in Chapter 22 uses the first three rows. The toolkit's class model is printed there as a table, because a diagram of over a hundred boxes is unreadable at page width; py u2ue/survey/design_diagram.py OUT.mmd draws it, with the last two rows.

what you see its name what it means here
a box with a name on top class one idea the code holds as one class. In the concept model the first line under the name says what it is in plain words (this manual's own habit, not standard UML), and the lines after it are its main members
name() inside a box method something the class does; a name without brackets is data it holds
a solid arrow A --> B with a label association A uses, asks or holds B, and the label says how ("Project --> Adapter : asks" reads "a Project asks its Adapter")
a dashed arrow dependency A imports B
a hollow triangle at one end generalisation the class at the plain end is a kind of the class at the triangle, its base

In a use case diagram (drawn as a flowchart)

what you see its name what it means here
a dashed box outside the boundary actor a role that wants something from the system: a person (the porter, the game's owner, a developer), the AI model, or the toolkit's own runners (the scripts that, for example, measure Unity in an idle editor). A role, not a person: one person can play several
the large box around the cases system boundary what is inside is the toolkit; what is outside uses it
a rounded shape with an id (UC-07, EPIC-1) use case one goal an actor can reach, named as a goal ("The owner checks every pillar of the product each cycle")
a plain line between an actor and a case association that actor takes part in that case
a dashed arrow labelled include include the base case always does the included case as part of itself; the arrow runs FROM the base TO the case it includes
a dashed arrow labelled extend extend the extending case runs only when a condition at one step of the base holds; the arrow runs FROM the extension TO the base, the opposite way to include

In a flow diagram

what you see what it means
a box one step, or in a structure sketch one part
a solid arrow then: the order of the steps; in a structure sketch, "uses"
a label on an arrow the command that moves from one box to the next (Chapter 7), or what passes between them (Chapter 5)
a diamond a gate: what is checked before the next step (Chapter 7)
a cylinder stored data: files one step writes and the next reads (Chapter 7); in Chapter 22's facade map, a folder of tools
a six-sided box an extension: where the step it hangs from can go wrong (Chapter 17's epic)
a circle the start or the end (Chapter 17's epic)
a dashed arrow not the main order: an input that feeds a step (the short version: measuring Unity), or a branch to an extension (Chapter 17's epic). Chapter 22's facade map uses it for a tool a verb runs, and says so
a box drawn around boxes a group: the boxes inside are one part (Chapter 5's engine-free model, Chapter 22's facade map)

The three small diagrams below are drawn the way the manual's own diagrams are, with made-up names, so each symbol can be seen once before it is met in a real one.

A class diagram. Project and Adapter are classes: the name on top, then members (a name with brackets is a method, one without is data). The solid arrow is an association, read along its label: a Project asks its Adapter. The dashed arrow is a dependency: Cli imports Project. The hollow triangle points at the base class: GameAdapter is a kind of Adapter.

What a use case is

A use case is one goal of one actor, written as a short story in numbered steps that ends with the goal reached, plus the ways the story can go wrong. It is not a feature list and not a method of the code: "The porter takes a new game from its project file to its first report" is a use case; build() is not. This manual writes use cases in the "fully dressed" form Alistair Cockburn describes in Writing Effective Use Cases, and every case in Chapter 17 is laid out the same way:

field what it holds
name the goal, as an active phrase
level how big the goal is: kite (a summary that strings several goals together - an epic), sea (one goal a user sits down to reach, the level to prefer), fish (a step inside another goal)
primary actor the role whose goal it is; supporting actors are the others it needs
stakeholders who else cares about the outcome, and what each wants
trigger what starts it
scope what the case covers
precondition what must already be true for it to start
minimal guarantee what holds even when it fails (here: nothing is dropped silently)
success guarantee what holds when it succeeds
main success scenario three to eleven numbered steps, each naming what it needs; outside that range the goal is the wrong size
extensions where it can go wrong, each numbered by its step: 3a branches from step 3, * from any step
read from the document the case was read out of
proven by the command that checks a step; that command is the test, and it must fail on a planted defect before it is trusted

An epic is the kite-level case that strings the others together: EPIC-1, "Port a Unity game to Unreal and show how identical it is", is the whole port, and each of its steps names the cases that carry it. A reviewer starts there (Chapter 22).

The chain, and the requirements it finds. Each step's result is the next step's precondition. When a step needs something no earlier step guarantees, the chain has found a requirement nobody wrote down. It is marked INFERRED and goes to the owner to confirm. A step that names code which exists is marked HAVE with the real name.

How to read a use case page

  1. Read the name and the primary actor: whose goal, and what.
  2. Read the success guarantee: what is true at the end. Then the minimal guarantee: what is true even when it fails.
  3. Walk the main success scenario. For each step ask what it needs and whether an earlier step gave it.
  4. Read the extensions. They are where a real port goes wrong; Chapter 16 is the same branches by symptom.
  5. Run a step's "proven by" command instead of taking the step on trust.

The rules this manual holds its UML to

  • Generated, then gated. Every UML view is regenerated on every build: the class model and the facade map from the code's own imports and bases, so they cannot name what the code lacks; the facade's requirements (what each verb accepts and refuses) from each verb's own code; the use case model and the traceability from the requirements model, and a use case that cites a page the manual no longer has stops the build; the concept model from u2ue/CONCEPTS.md, whose gate checks on every u2ue cycle run that each concept it calls a class exists in the code (Chapter 22).
  • Sketches are named as sketches. The flowcharts of the short version and Chapters 5, 7 and 14, and Chapter 22's layer sketch, are drawn by hand: they show an order or a shape, and no gate checks them.
  • The model comes first. A new idea is drawn as a class before the code is written, and a step of the logic port draws the target diagram before any code moves (Chapter 5, step 2 of the playbook; Chapter 18, "A concept").
  • One idea, one class. Each concept in the concept model names the class in the code that holds it. The manual's terms are defined once, in the glossary (Appendix C).

What a port costs

Who this is for: the evaluator deciding whether to use u2ue - what porting your game will cost in model tokens and in dollars on Opus 5.5, worked out before you start, and how sure that number is.

Every figure on this page comes from a record. The generated block below holds them, and the sections after it say what they mean: processed and new tokens and the rates under "What the number is made of", the bands and the leave-one-out figures under "How sure it is".

Ask it about your own game

py -m u2ue estimate --unity <your Unity project>                          every folder under Assets, each listed with its lines
py -m u2ue estimate --unity <your Unity project> --roots Assets/Game      only the folders that are the game's own code
py -m u2ue estimate --unity <your Unity project> --exclude <a folder>     leave out a vendored library, which is replaced, not ported

It reads the project's files: it opens no Unity and no Unreal, and it needs no project file. It prints five things:

  • the code to move, split into coupled lines (they use a Unity API, a lifecycle method or a Unity base class) and pure lines (plain C#);
  • the tokens for each stage;
  • how many of those tokens the prompt cache serves;
  • the cost at Opus 5.5's list price, with the cost of the same calls without caching beside it;
  • a band, and a confidence level with its reasons.

With no --roots, every folder under Assets is counted and listed, because vendor packages (third-party code copied into the project) live there too. The logic figure is then an upper bound. Name the game's own folders, leave out the libraries it vendors, and run it again: the third row below is the second row's game with its two vendored libraries excluded.

Real estimates

project coupled lines pure lines processed tokens (band) of them new Opus 5.5 list cost (band) with no prompt cache confidence
the reference port, as it was before its logic moved (Unity 6000.3) 90,777 4,888 6.5 billion (5.0 billion to 8.4 billion) 176 million $2,705 ($2,078 to $3,467) $26,680 LOW
a second game, another studio's (Unity 2021.3), every folder its project file names 125,959 56,170 10.0 billion (7.9 billion to 12.6 billion) 263 million $4,089 ($3,231 to $5,130) $40,898 LOW
the same game, its two vendored libraries excluded (a networking framework and a WebSocket client, each read by its namespace) 89,817 13,840 6.6 billion (5.1 billion to 8.4 billion) 178 million $2,738 ($2,119 to $3,488) $27,105 LOW

How big each project is, read off its files by the same census (a code line has its comments and strings blanked, and blank lines are not counted):

  • The reference port, as it was before its logic moved (Unity 6000.3): 95,665 code lines of game C# in 339 files (90,777 coupled, 4,888 pure); its own editor tools 111,014 lines in 282 files, not ported; 3,768 prefabs, 2,445 of them with a particle system; 146 scenes, 1 in the build.
  • A second game, another studio's (Unity 2021.3), every folder its project file names: 182,129 code lines of game C# in 1,932 files (125,959 coupled, 56,170 pure); its own editor tools 7,366 lines in 55 files, not ported; 3,229 prefabs, 52 of them with a particle system; 463 scenes, 24 in the build.
  • The same game, its two vendored libraries excluded (a networking framework and a WebSocket client, each read by its namespace): 103,657 code lines of game C# in 1,392 files (89,817 coupled, 13,840 pure); its own editor tools 5,333 lines in 30 files, not ported; 3,229 prefabs, 52 of them with a particle system; 463 scenes, 24 in the build; 80,505 lines of vendored libraries left out.

The rates they multiply by, each read from the reference port's records (u2ue/basis/tokens.json):

  • logic_coupled_line: 70,776 tokens per coupled code line, n=27, bootstrap band 54,112 to 91,003, one sample's actual over predicted 0.40 to 2.13 (leave-one-out, P10 to P90), all-in overhead x1.61 (all the agents of wf_341e7e76-b72 over those that moved one measured file each: verifying, gating, playing and consolidating are real cost too); 97.3 % of them cache reads, 0.6 % output. Workflow runs wf_341e7e76-b72 (81 agents): each step agent's tokens off its own transcript; each step's file measured in the pre-move copy (14469 code lines in 27 samples).
  • logic_pure_line: 19,358 tokens per pure code line, n=1, all-in overhead x1.61 (all the agents of wf_341e7e76-b72 over those that moved one measured file each: verifying, gating, playing and consolidating are real cost too); 98.0 % of them cache reads, 0.4 % output. The pure batch step of wf_341e7e76-b72: 5 moved files, 2751 code lines in the pre-move copy.
  • conductor_turn: 563,904 tokens per model call, n=13, bootstrap band 502,050 to 568,133, one sample's actual over predicted 0.25 to 0.97 (leave-one-out, P10 to P90); 99.2 % of them cache reads, 0.2 % output. 13 main-session transcripts on claude-opus-5-5 since 2026-10-01 (49148 calls), one call = one turn.

Opus 5.5's list price per million tokens: input $4, cache write $5 (5 minutes) or $8 (1 hour), cache read $0.20, output $20 - read 2026-10-17 from https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing.

  • saving effect_prefab: ABSENT - the reference port's effects were ported in main sessions and the lane's queues, not in workflow runs that count prefabs: the three effect workflow runs there are were method work, with no count of prefabs ported
  • saving scene: 859,736,921 processed tokens per scene by hand, $294 at Opus 5.5's list price (15 million new), n=1: 8 workflow runs (wf_8bb82424-fb6, wf_9e5fde94-0ab, wf_a9670ab9-cdb, wf_baf92932-d44, wf_5f097467-aa1, wf_9f5af880-73d, wf_32e26135-528, wf_3aa4fd19-2ad): every agent's transcript

A yardstick. The reference port, the game the toolkit was built on and its first row, is a medium-sized game: about 96,000 code lines of game C#, thousands of prefabs and over a hundred scenes (its size line above). Bigger than a game jam project, well short of a large studio title. The logic estimate grows with the coupled lines, so a game with half as many coupled lines costs about half as much to port.

What the number is made of

The logic is where the tokens go. Effects, scenes, UI conversion, the game's own Unreal project, parity and the acceptance page (the report of every effect, every gap and every decision left to the game's owner) are each run by a verb. u2ue port runs them and stops only where a person, the AI or a Unity editor is needed. Each stop costs one turn of the model, priced at the measured tokens per call (conductor_turn in the block above; Chapter 4 has the stops). The logic is the one part an AI writes: it moves the game's rules out of its MonoBehaviours into an engine-free model (Chapter 5, and the logic skill).

The logic's rate was measured, not modelled. The reference port moved its coupled files into an engine-free model with one agent (an AI model session given one task) per file. Each agent's tokens are read off its own transcript, with a streamed call counted once. Each file is measured in a copy of the project taken before the move, by the same classifier the estimate applies to your project. Agents that verified, gated or played the game, rather than moving one measurable file, are in the rate as overhead, so it is all-in.

Processed tokens and new tokens are different things. Every call reads its whole context again, and processed tokens count every token a call reads or writes. Claude Code (the Anthropic tool the model works in) serves most of that from the prompt cache, and a cache read costs a twentieth of an uncached input token on Opus 5.5. So most of the processed tokens are cache reads, and they cost little. That is why a total in the billions costs thousands of dollars, not tens of thousands. The column "with no prompt cache" shows the difference. The new tokens (the column "of them new") are the rest: uncached input, cache writes and output.

The prices are read, not remembered. They come from Anthropic's pricing page and are kept with the date they were read (u2ue/basis/prices.json). They are the API's list price on the standard tier. A subscription plan's usage limits are not modelled.

How sure it is

The confidence is printed for every stage, with its reasons, and every estimate above reads LOW. The number of samples, the model a rate was measured on and how far a game lies outside the measured files set it; four things to know:

  • Per file the estimate is rough; summed over a game it is steadier. The leave-one-out figure in the block above is how far one file's real cost fell from what the other files predicted for it; P10 to P90 is the range that holds the middle eight files in ten. Over many files those errors average out, which is what the bootstrap band shows: the rate recomputed over many random resamplings of the measured files, from its P10 to its P90.
  • The logic rates were measured on Opus 5 and Fable 5.1 (two other Claude models), and priced as Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5's own token count for the same work is unmeasured.
  • A game much larger than the measured files is an extrapolation. The tool prints how many times larger.
  • The pure-code rate rests on one sample, and the main session that ran the extraction (the conversation that directed its agents) is not in the logic rate, so for that part the figure is a floor.

To raise the confidence, measure your own game: port one slice with the skills, then rebuild the basis from your own runs (py u2ue/survey/token_basis.py --project <game> --write, which reads your project file's estimate_basis block). The estimate then speaks for your game and your model.

What the toolkit saves

  • Prompt caching. The block above prices the same calls with and without the cache. This is measured on the work the rates come from.
  • The stages a verb runs. The reference port brought its first level to Unreal by hand, across eight agent runs; the saving line in the block gives what that cost. A verb now runs that path (Chapter 6). The saving is claimed for one scene only, because what a second scene costs by hand was never measured.
  • Effects. No saving is claimed. The reference port's effect work was not done in runs that count prefabs, so there is no rate to claim from.
  • The logic. No saving is claimed. It is AI work with the toolkit or without it, and no port was measured without the toolkit. What the toolkit adds there is a check on every step: the gates and parity that make the model's work provable (Chapter 14, Chapter 15).

How long it takes

The estimate does not give a time, because no time per line has been measured yet. For scale: the reference port's extraction ran as one workflow (a script that runs many agents and decides what runs next) of 81 agents, and its record shows it ran for close to sixteen hours. A single session stops long before that. Chapter 15 explains how the long-run skill and a workflow keep a port going.

Porting to Unreal in a nutshell

Who this is for: the evaluator who wants the whole job on two screens before deciding - a quick start to try on your own project today, and the five problems every Unity to Unreal port meets, each with the toolkit's answer and the chapter that has the details.

Quick start

You need Windows with native PowerShell, Python with PyYAML, the .NET SDK, Unreal Engine 5.7, and your Unity project saved as text (Force Text serialization). Chapter 3 has the full list.

py -m u2ue                                          # every verb the toolkit has
py -m u2ue find <words>                             # everything it holds about a subject, as path:line

First, what it will cost. This needs no project file:

py -m u2ue estimate --unity <your Unity project> --roots <the game's code folders>

Then describe your game in one project file, u2ue/projects/<game>.json (Chapter 3 has a complete one), and run the port:

py -m u2ue --project <game> port                    # every stage, read from its records, and the next action - nothing runs
py -m u2ue --project <game> port --run              # runs every stage a verb can; stops where a person, the AI or an editor is needed

port stops in four places: the project file, which only you can write; the logic, which the u2ue-logic skill does in Claude Code with u2ue-long-run keeping the session going (Chapter 15); a Unity window, for what can only be measured or captured in your editor; and the decisions the acceptance page asks of the game's owner. Run port again after each stop: it reads where the port stands. Chapter 4 walks the stages one by one with real output, and What a port costs says what the estimate is made of and how sure it is.

The five problems every port meets

1. Unity does not behave the way its documentation reads

A converter written from the documentation is wrong in the details that show: the frame a sub-emitter's child (a particle system its parent's particles start) is born on, what a scaling mode really scales, how Mono prints a float. The toolkit measures Unity instead of reading about it. A probe case is data, run in the game's own Unity editor only while the person using it is idle, and judged by a judge that must refuse a planted wrong answer. Each rule is stored with the Unity version it was measured on, and on another version it is reported as unverified rather than trusted. Chapter 8, Chapter 12.

2. Shuriken and Niagara do not map one to one

Shuriken is a fixed set of modules; a Niagara emitter is a set of scripts, each a stack of modules (Chapter 11). A Unity setting can need several Niagara modules, and some have no equivalent at all. The toolkit reads every effect into an engine-neutral IR (an intermediate representation: one JSON file per effect, read from Unity's YAML), converts it in stages, and puts each behaviour it adds behind a switch. A switch starts OFF and is turned ON only with an evidence row that a trial proved. What cannot be ported is named per emitter on the acceptance page, never dropped. Chapter 7, Chapter 11.

3. The game's rules are tangled into MonoBehaviours

The rules live inside Update methods, coroutines, inspector values and Unity types, in an execution order nobody wrote down. The toolkit moves them into an engine-free model behind seams. The engine fills the seams (view, input, camera, effects, platform); the model is driven in Unity's frame order and runs without either engine. Its answers are proven by float bits on .NET, on that Unity version's own Mono runtime, and in Unreal. Chapter 5, Chapter 14, and the logic skill.

4. Transforms do not compose the same way

The two engines differ in axes, units and rotation order. Worse, a non-uniform scale under a rotation makes Unity draw a shear that Unreal's transform cannot hold at all. The toolkit states one conversion, in one place, and finds every node Unreal cannot place as Unity does (py -m u2ue --project <game> shear), with the error in centimetres. Such a node is named for a decision, never averaged into something that looks close. Chapter 6.

5. "It looks right" is not proof

A photo of an effect is one draw of a random process. A metric alone can lie too: on the reference port, a render whose whole scene went black scored better, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The toolkit proves the data first. It reads back every emitter frame by frame and holds it to Unity's own particle state (u2ue conform). It reports "identical" as a family of four numbers, never one. Pictures come last, with the capture's own artefacts labelled. Chapter 9, Chapter 10, Chapter 14.

The one rule under all five

Every value is READ from the source, with where it came from; or MEASURED in Unity, by a judge that can fail; or ABSENT, named with the reason. There is no fourth kind. A port that guesses looks finished long before it is. Chapter 1.

The short version

Who this is for: the evaluator who wants every aspect of a port in one sitting - one screen each, saying what happens, the command that does it, what it printed on a real game, and what it does not do yet.

The output shown here is real, from a second Unity game the toolkit was not built on (Unity 2021.3, a different studio's project), with that game's name written <game> and machine paths written <work>/... and <unreal project>. Numbers from the game the toolkit was built on - a commercial Unity 6 tactics game ported to Unreal Engine 5.7 - are called the reference port. Part II has the procedure behind each screen, and Appendix B the plan for each NOT YET.

S1. What u2ue is, in five lines

  1. A command-line facade, py -m u2ue, over the tools that move a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5.
  2. It reads the Unity project as text (YAML prefabs, scenes, materials, .meta files): no Unity editor runs to port anything.
  3. It converts what has a counterpart (particle effects, transforms, UI layout, lights, materials), and gives the game's own code a runtime and a method instead of pretending to translate it.
  4. Where Unity's behaviour is not written down, it measures Unity, once, in the game's own editor, and keeps the measurement.
  5. It proves every change before it ships and reports every difference by name, with a number and a reason.

It is not a button that makes a Unity game run in Unreal. Chapter 1 says exactly what it does and does not promise.

S2. The workflow at a glance

The default path is two commands: py -m u2ue estimate --unity <unity project> for the price, then py -m u2ue --project <game> port and port --run, which run every stage below that a verb can do and stop where a person, the AI or a Unity editor is needed (Chapter 4). The stages:

flowchart LR
  P["describe the game<br/>info"] --> C["the code<br/>inventory, data"]
  C --> X["the content<br/>extract, check"]
  X --> B["Unreal<br/>build, read, photo"]
  B --> R["the result<br/>report, metrics"]
  M["measure Unity<br/>probe + judge"] -.-> X
  M -.-> B
step command runs in
say where everything is py -m u2ue --project <game> info no editor
list the game's code and what it touches inventory no editor
read what the inspector holds data --from <asset> --script <Class> no editor
turn the effects into an engine-neutral IR extract no editor
run every selftest and gate check no editor
build, read back, photograph build, read, photo Unreal, headless
the acceptance page and the numbers report, metrics, tempo no editor
search everything the toolkit knows py -m u2ue find <words> no project

S3. Describe the game

What happens. One JSON file per game, u2ue/projects/<game>.json, names the Unity tree and version, the Unreal host, where the work goes and the game's folders. No field is defaulted: a missing one is an error, not a guess.

py -m u2ue --project <game> info
project <game> (u2ue/projects/<game>.json)
  unity.root           dir       <unity project>                     ok
  unity.assets         dir       <unity project>/Assets              ok
  work.effects         out-dir   <work>                              ok (exists)
  work.photos          out-dir   <work>/photos                       to be created (its parent exists)
  unreal.uproject      file      <unreal project>.uproject           ok
  unreal.content_root  game-path /Game/U2UE/<Game>                    ok (an Unreal content path)
  unity.editor         dir       <Unity 2021.3.21f1 install>         ok (its unity_builtin_extra exists)
  adapter: unity_project (spawn rules unity)

Every path is opened, not just printed. The last line names the game's adapter: the object that answers the few questions that differ per game, such as which prefabs are effects (Chapter 18). Limits: the project must be serialized as text (Unity's Force Text).

S4. The game's code

What happens. The toolkit does not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors. It tells you what every type touches, and gives you a method: move the rules into an engine-free model (plain C# that references no engine), let each engine run it through a thin host, and prove both engines get the same answers.

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory
u2ue inventory <game>: 1987 files, 2453 types (plain 1384, MonoBehaviour 789, ScriptableObject 160, ...); 1148 pure rules
  serialized data                  473 types   1708 sites
  platform (log, files, prefs)     365 types   1525 sites
  spawn / destroy                  311 types   1049 sites
  lookups                          275 types    661 sites
  coroutines / Invoke              273 types    997 sites
  transform                        222 types   1652 sites
  ...

The 1148 pure rules use no Unity API and move first. The inventory also lists every MonoBehaviour's script execution order with its lifecycle methods - the table Unity's frame is rebuilt from. Then:

need what the toolkit gives
inspector values, ScriptableObjects u2ue data: every serialized value, prefab overrides applied, references resolved to asset paths
Unity's frame, Time.deltaTime, coroutines the U2ue.Runtime .NET library: UnityFrame, UnityClock, Coroutines with Unity's rules, each held by tests
logging, files, PlayerPrefs, JSON, random six platform interfaces with Unity's exact semantics (Random.Range's bounds, JsonUtility's fields)
an Unreal host to start from the U2ue.Unreal templates: the frame actor, the pointer, the camera rig, the platform services
the model stays engine-free u2ue check --only model: an engine reference in the model fails
the answers agree u2ue parity: every runtime's digest (its answers to the same cases, floats written as bits) compared float bit by float bit

Limits: the toolkit does not move the code or write the hosts. Chapter 5 is the method. Measured on the reference port: three scripted battles gave byte-identical event logs in the Unity-free test run and in the Unreal host.

S5. Transforms, hierarchies and scenes

What happens. Unity is metres, y up, left handed; Unreal is centimetres, z up, left handed. One module holds the conversion, and its selftest holds it to the two other copies in use, the effect converter's and the reference port's model's, so they cannot drift apart unseen (Chapter 6 has the table).

The one thing that does not convert: a rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is sheared in Unity, and Unreal's transform cannot hold a shear. u2ue shear finds every such node and says how far off it would land, in centimetres:

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<Scene>.unity

Expect some: measured on the reference port's first battle map, 46 nodes were sheared, two of them drawn, the worst 63 cm off. Accepting, baking or fixing each is your decision, made with the number.

Whole scenes go through u2ue scene: export to glTF (an open 3D scene format) in the game's own editor, import into a new Unreal level, read the saved level back, and scene check - a gate that grades hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting and placement against the scene's own measured baseline. Limits: the steps between import and readback (textures, material parents, lighting, outline hulls) are tools, not verbs yet: Chapter 6 lists them, and Appendix B has the plan.

S6. Prefabs, and reading Unity's YAML

What happens. Effects and data are read straight from the YAML: nested prefab instances expanded with their modifications, prefab variants, removed components, the material chain through m_Parent. Each effect is counted as a key: one effect the game can spawn, usually one prefab. A file the reader cannot handle is refused by name, never half-read:

py -m u2ue --project <game> extract
u2ue extract: 60 READ key(s): 56 IR file(s) with 189 emitter(s), 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign path(s)
  REFUSED unity.prefab.5ccd...: .../Winter Door.prefab: PrefabInstance 4843689442982340616: modification target 1211823196678298638 (m...

Limits: a prefab instance's removed components and removed GameObjects are applied, but one that adds a GameObject or a component to its source is refused by name; objects inside a nested model (FBX) are not read - FBX is binary - so a scene that modifies one is refused by name.

S7. Materials and lighting

What happens. Effect materials use custom shaders. The blend mode is read as a number from the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never from the shader's name. Each shader family gets one Unreal parent material, authored once; every material of that family becomes an instance with its values read off its .mat.

Lit materials need Unity's lighting, not Unreal's. For Shader Graph materials the toolkit translates the HLSL Unity itself generated for the graph, and evaluates URP's own Lit lighting (URP is Unity's Universal Render Pipeline; the lighting is its BRDF, its spherical-harmonics ambient, its reflection decode) from the scene's measured sun, ambient probe and reflection cube.

Point lights an effect carries become Unreal point lights by a mapping read from both engines' source (Chapter 7 has it). In Unity the mapping's source side was measured on lit pixels: nine cases fit URP's own formula at a ratio of 1.0000.

Limits: the lit route is behind a switch until its trial is looked at; a graph that moves vertices in object space, or that includes custom code, is refused by name; fog, shadows and ambient occlusion on these materials are named, not drawn.

S8. Particle effects

What happens. Every Shuriken ParticleSystem becomes a Niagara emitter, written through Unreal's own converter library, in twenty stages in the order Unity runs its modules. Each Unity behaviour added to the converter is a route: it arrived behind a switch, default off, and was flipped on only with its evidence.

An emitter Unreal does not draw is a gap only if Unity draws it. What u2ue metrics prints about it (the reference port, from its record of 2026-10-15, lines shortened):

keys      674: BUILT 673, IR REFUSED 1; 673 drawn, 197 of them with a named gap
emitters  drawn 7810 | absent: gap 642 (Unity draws them, Unreal does not), 374 absent exactly as in Unity
coverage  92.4 % of the emitters Unity draws are drawn in Unreal (7810 / 8452)

Limits: VFX Graph assets and particle systems authored directly in scenes are listed, not converted. TrailRenderers: Unity's law is measured and reproduced exactly by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw; drawing it in Unreal is NOT YET (Appendix B has the plan). Chapter 7 has the rest.

S9. UI

What happens. uGUI (Unity's UI system) and UMG (Unreal's) lay out differently, so the toolkit does not rebuild screens as UMG trees. A Unity Canvas is captured (every RectTransform, anchor and component, as Unity resolved it) and laid out in Unreal by a port of uGUI's own layout solver and TextMeshPro's glyph layout, the generic library U2ue.Ui:

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test
py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture> --screen NAME --out DIR

The tests hold the library to Unity's own captures, and a planted transform defect makes them fail (Chapter 6 has the run). Limits: the capture runs in the game's Unity editor in Play mode; shipping it as the package's Editor assembly is NOT YET (Appendix B), so ui capture refuses by name until then. Which view model feeds which panel stays the game's.

S10. Audio

What happens. Authored clips (.wav, .ogg) import into Unreal as Sound Waves. Which sound plays, and how loud, should be a rule in the model, so both engines choose the same one. Sounds Unity generates at run time are rendered once to float PCM and played through a small bridge that hands the samples to Unreal's mixer unconverted. Limits: the bridge is the host template's plugin; it builds in a host and plays headless (its judge passed the captured tone on 2026-10-15). Mapping a Unity AudioSource is NOT YET (Appendix B).

S11. Measuring Unity

What happens. Much of what a port must match is not documented: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, how a trail drops its points, what a Timeline does before its clip starts. The toolkit measures it:

  1. A judge (Python) states the rule and is selftested against planted wrong answers - before any measurement exists.
  2. A probe (an Editor C# script) is dropped into the game's editor in a window: only after ten idle minutes, stopped the moment its user returns, compiled headless first, everything else's checksum compared before and after.
  3. The probe writes a bake; the judge reads the rule off it or refuses it with the numbers.

On the second game, on 2026-10-17:

py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts
  188 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       188 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters
  188 of 188 rules this project's build uses were measured on another Unity: its report must not call them measured for it

A rule measured on another Unity version is still used, but never reported as measured for this game.

S12. Proving every change

What happens. Four rules, each enforced by a gate rather than recommended:

  • Read it or name it absent - no plausible default stands in for a value.
  • A gate must be able to fail - every gate carries plants it must refuse.
  • Prove a change offline - the converter is replayed against a recording stub (a stand-in for Unreal that records every call the converter makes, in order) over every emitter of every effect: switched off, a new route must change nothing; switched on, exactly the emitters it names.
  • Verify with both - the data proves itself first; then the numbers and the pictures confirm it, each looked at.
py -m u2ue --project <game> check            # every selftest, the field gates, the measured rules' versions, the model gates
py vfxport/whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py     # a converter change: identical engine calls, or exactly the predicted set

S13. Reports and numbers

What happens. Every number comes from a record on disk, with its denominator, its definition and its date; a number that cannot be computed prints ABSENT with the record it needs; an input older than the newest build prints STALE.

py -m u2ue --project <game> report --out <game>.html      # the acceptance page: every key, every gap, every owner decision
py -m u2ue --project <game> metrics                       # coverage, measured share, read-back, photos, machine hours, routes
py -m u2ue --project <game> tempo                         # each route's first code -> verified flip, read off git

Before anything is built, the page already lists every effect the game must account for.

S14. What it does not do

  • Animation (Animator state machines, Mecanim retargeting) and physics: not covered. The reference port had neither, so no tool is claimed until a game that has them is ported and measured. One animation case is handled: an Animator that drives an effect root's scale.
  • The game's code is moved by you or by an AI model following the logic skill, with the method, the runtime and the gates (S4).
  • Anything the toolkit cannot reproduce exactly is reported on the item, with the measured size of the difference.

1. Introduction

Who this is for: the evaluator - exactly what u2ue is, what it does today, the rules it holds itself to, whom it serves and what it does not promise. It is the last page of Part I: after it you can decide, and the porting developer moves on to Part II.

What u2ue is

u2ue is a set of tools behind one facade, py -m u2ue, for porting a Unity game to Unreal Engine 5. Every tool in it was written while moving one real game - the reference port, a Unity 6 tactics game - to Unreal 5.7, and u2ue check runs the tools' selftests (Chapter 21 lists them). A second, unrelated game (a different studio's project on Unity 2021.3) runs through the same facade to keep the toolkit honest about what is general and what was one game's.

A port with u2ue has two halves:

  • The game's code. The toolkit inventories the game's C# type by type, reads its serialized data, gives the moved code a runtime that keeps Unity's frame, time and coroutine rules, gates the result so it stays engine-free, and compares its answers across the runtimes it runs on (Chapter 5).
  • The game's content. Particle effects are converted end to end - read from the prefabs, converted to Niagara, built headless, read back frame by frame, photographed beside Unity's frames, and reported (Chapter 7). Transforms, scenes, UI and audio have their own tools and methods (Chapter 6).

For the effects, the job fits in one line: every Shuriken particle effect a Unity game fires becomes a Niagara system in Unreal that draws as Unity draws it - and every place it does not is named, on the emitter, with the reason.

The problem it solves

In one sentence: a studio engineer, helped by an AI agent, uses one package with a single entry point to port a whole Unity game to Unreal - its MonoBehaviour code, its transform chain and scenes, its effects and the rest - by implementing adapters or interfaces rather than making the game generic, with an architecture a senior engineer can grasp, and with the porting speed and the percent identical measured.

The problems that fall out of that sentence are the toolkit's shape:

problem where the toolkit answers it
knowing what the toolkit already holds py -m u2ue find (Chapter 2)
knowing what a game's code needs before porting it u2ue inventory (Chapter 5)
moving game code without making the game generic the engine-free model and its adapters (Chapters 5 and 18)
the transform chain u2ue.transform, u2ue shear (Chapter 6)
proving how identical the result is parity, read-back, photos and the metrics (Chapters 5, 9 and 10)
a review that holds the use cases and the class model (Chapters 17 and 22)

What it does today

area today
The price of a port, before it starts HAVE - u2ue estimate, from rates measured on a real port (What a port costs)
The whole port as one command HAVE - u2ue port, which runs every stage a verb can and stops where a person, the AI or a Unity editor is needed (Chapter 4)
Shuriken particle effects to Niagara HAVE - extract, check, build, read, photo, report, metrics (Chapter 7)
Effect materials (custom shader families) HAVE - one parent per family, every material an instance read off its .mat (Chapter 7)
Lit (Shader Graph / URP Lit) effect materials HAVE behind a switch, default OFF until its trial's photos are looked at - the graph's generated HLSL translated, URP's lighting evaluated (Chapter 7, Appendix B)
Point lights on effects HAVE - read, mapped by both engines' source, spawned on the effect; the Unity side measured on lit pixels (Chapter 7)

Serialized data (inspector values, ScriptableObjects) HAVE - u2ue data (Chapter 5)

Audio HAVE the method and the PCM bridge plugin, which builds in a host and plays headless (judged 2026-10-15); mapping a Unity AudioSource with no human step is NOT YET (Chapter 6, Chapter 13, Appendix B)

Three principles

Every stage follows three rules. Each was earned by a failure, and the toolkit enforces them rather than recommending them.

  1. Read it, or name it absent. A value the port writes is read from the Unity source; one it cannot read is named absent with the reason. There are no defaults that stand in silently: a substituted value is a lie the acceptance report would repeat.
  2. Every rule is measured. How Unity behaves is read from its data, its source where it ships source (Unity's packages, Unreal's engine), or measured in Unity by a probe whose judge is written first and refuses a planted wrong answer. A rule measured on one Unity version is reported as unverified on another (Chapter 8).
  3. Every change is proven before it ships. A new converter route lands behind a switch, default off; the converter is replayed over every emitter of every effect and must show identical engine calls except exactly the predicted set; a trial is built, read, judged and photographed; only then does the default flip (Chapter 9).

In practice: a measured rule's bake is kept as a fact file (shared/conformance/*-facts.json) with the Unity version it was measured on, and a project on another version is told which rules are unverified for it (u2ue check --only facts). Documentation and intuition are where a rule is suspected, never where it comes from. The replay that proves a converter change, whole_trace.py, traces every engine call of every active emitter of every effect, under one converter file and then the other, and compares them.

Who it is for

  • An evaluator deciding whether to use it: Part I of this manual.
  • A porting developer - an engineer moving a Unity game to Unreal, who wants the game running the same and every difference named: Part II.
  • An AI model doing that port: the package ships skills for it (the entry skill u2ue/skill/u2ue/SKILL.md, which hands the game's logic to u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md and an effect gap to u2ue/skill/u2ue-port/SKILL.md), and every output is text a model can read (Chapter 15).
  • A toolkit developer extending it, and a reviewer - a senior engineer judging how a port is done: Part III. Chapter 22 and u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md are written for the reviewer.
  • The game's owner - who answers only the decisions that are theirs; the report lists them, each with its count.

Two systems support them: the game's Unity editor, where a Unity behaviour is measured only while the person using it is idle (Chapter 8), and the Unreal host, where one headless Unreal runs at a time (Chapter 3).

What it does not promise

u2ue does not make a Unity game run on Unreal by itself. The game's own code has to be moved into an engine-free model and given Unreal hosts, by an AI model following the logic skill or by a person - the toolkit gives the method, the runtime, the analysis and the gates, not a button. Where it cannot reproduce Unity exactly, it says so on the item, with the measured size of the difference. Appendix B lists what is not done yet.

u2ue as a product

u2ue is built to ship as a Unity package installed in the source project, which an AI model drives through the same command line a person uses (Appendix B has the package's layout and what is left to ship). How identical the result is, is measured, not claimed; so is how long each converter route took from its first code to its verified flip. How fast a whole game is ported is not measured yet (Chapter 10).

What is reusable, in five layers

The tools fall into five layers. The first three are the product and serve any game; the fourth serves any game that uses the same vendor effect packs (third-party sets of ready-made effects and their shaders); the fifth is each game's own. Not every tool reads its paths from the project file yet: a tool that still names one game's folder is converted by the recipe in Chapter 18, and Appendix B tracks the rest.

  • Unity readers, offline (no editor). Prefabs, nested, variant and legacy, read into the engine-neutral IR; Unity's own imported textures read off Library/Artifacts, every mip it samples; its built-in resources; alpha derivations; a PSD inside a PNG. Proven on two games and two Unity versions.
  • The engine-pair knowledge: Shuriken to Niagara. Every route flipped on with its evidence row, or named OFF with what it waits on; Chapter 21 counts them. Every rule in it was MEASURED in Unity or READ in an engine's source. This is the asset a second game reuses for free.
  • The proof machinery. The read-back per frame and its sweep (each check run over every emitter read back), a judge per route written before its trial with a plant that must fail, photo pairs against Unity's fixed-seed reference frames, sheets that label the capture's own artefacts, the acceptance report, and u2ue metrics.
  • Asset-pack material ports. One hand-authored Unreal parent per Unity shader of the vendor effect packs the reference port used (Chapter 18 lists them) - reusable by any game that uses those packs.
  • The game's own. Its engine-free model (the method of Chapter 5 is reusable; the code is not), its effect maps, its scenes.

2. Concepts

Who this is for: the developer porting their own game - the ideas the rest of Part II is built on (the project file, the facade, adapters, asset families, the IR, routes and switches, windows, gates, the model and the concept classes), each explained once, so no later chapter stops you on a word.

The project

A project is one JSON file, u2ue/projects/<name>.json, that names everything about one game: its Unity tree and version, its Unreal host (the Unreal project the toolkit builds and runs in), where the work goes, and the game-specific choices. A required field that is missing is an error, never a default. Chapter 3 lists the fields; py -m u2ue --project <name> info opens every path the file names.

The facade and its verbs

The facade, py -m u2ue, is the only entry point. It answers verbs (its commands) such as estimate, port, info, inventory, extract, build and parity; py -m u2ue alone lists every verb, and Chapter 20 documents each one. A verb WRAPS the tools that do the work and never rewrites them, so every tool still runs by hand, with its own selftest where it has one (the tool's check of itself, which must refuse a planted fault).

py -m u2ue find <words> searches everything the toolkit holds (concepts, verbs, adapters (below), tools, every documentation section, measured rules, converter stages, verified routes) and needs no project. Every word must match; the hits come grouped by kind, best first, each with the file:line to open next (--kind narrows the kinds, --top N shows more of each):

py -m u2ue find coroutine

Adapters: where a game plugs in

The toolkit holds no game's knowledge. The few questions whose answer depends on the game are ports (u2ue/adapters/__init__.py; here a port is a question the toolkit asks and the game answers, not the act of porting), answered by an adapter:

port the question the default (any Unity project) a game adapter (example: the reference port's)
effect_keys which prefabs are the game's effects every prefab holding a ParticleSystem the keys its battles actually fire, resolved as the game resolves them
spawn_rules what starts when the game spawns one Unity's: playOnAwake systems and their sub-emitters its effect pool's own rule
host_busy is the Unreal host free no Unreal is running and none of its own build queues is alive

Most games need no adapter of their own: the project file (u2ue/projects/<name>.json) says "adapter": "unity_project". The default adapter was proven on a second game: 60 effect keys (an effect key is one effect the game can spawn, usually one prefab), 56 IR files (the IR, below, is the form each effect is read into), 189 emitters, 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, with no game code written (Chapter 4, step 5). A game adapter subclasses UnityProject and overrides only the answers its game gets wrong (Chapter 18). extract refuses a resolve (the key list the adapter writes) whose keys disagree with the adapter's spawn rule, because the IR reader picks the rule by the key.

Asset families: what ports itself

Everything except a game's logic ports with no AI in the loop. Each kind of asset is an asset family, and every family takes the same five steps: extract it from Unity, build it in Unreal, read back what Unreal built, judge that against Unity, and photograph it. A step no command does yet is ABSENT and says why. The table is generated from u2ue/assetfamily.py and checked against the facade, so every command in it exists:

family extract build read judge photo
effects extract build read conform diff photo
scene scene export scene import scene readback scene check ABSENT
ui ui capture ui convert ABSENT ui test ABSENT

Each command runs as py -m u2ue --project <name> <command>. Where a step is ABSENT:

  • scene photo: no verb photographs a level: the scene check judges data only (hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting, placement)
  • ui read: no separate read: the converted screen is laid out headless inside ui test, the same run that judges it
  • ui photo: no verb photographs a screen

The engine-neutral IR

Effects pass through an intermediate representation: one JSON file per effect, read off the Unity YAML by u1e_ir.py (nested prefab instances expanded, overrides applied, every node's frame composed). The IR is the boundary between the engines: it is testable without either editor and diffable between runs.

The converter, its routes and switches

vfxport/build_niagara.py turns one IR emitter into Niagara stack writes, in twenty stages in the order Unity's own modules run. A route is one ported behaviour (a shape, a curve mode, a sub-emitter trigger). Each new route lands behind a switch (an environment variable, VFXPORT_<NAME>), default off, and is flipped on only after its proof (Chapter 9). Chapter 21 lists every switch, its default and its evidence.

Windows: measuring Unity

Where Unity's behaviour is not in its data, it is measured. A probe (a small Editor script) is dropped into the game's Unity editor for one run inside a window - only after ten minutes with no mouse or key input from its user, and stopped at its next step once they return - and writes a bake: raw numbers only. A judge (Python), written and selftested before the bake exists, decides what the numbers say and refuses a planted wrong answer. The bake is kept with the Unity version it was measured on (Chapter 8).

Records, reports and gates

Every build, read and photo writes a record. The acceptance page (every effect key, every gap and every decision the owner owes, written by report) and the metrics are computed from records only, each number with its definition and age. Gates refuse what must not pass: field gates (an unread Unity field is a silent gap), model gates (the code moved into the model, below, must know no engine), the converter trace (a change must touch only what it predicts), parity (the rules must agree across runtimes).

The model architecture (the game's code)

The game's rules move into an engine-free model (plain C#) behind two kinds of seam - a platform seam (logging, files, preferences, JSON, random numbers) and view seams (what the presentation asks the engine to draw) - and each engine gets one thin host (that engine's code that runs the model; not the Unreal host project above). Unity and Unreal then run the same model, which is what makes parity provable. Chapter 5 is the method.

The concept model: one class per idea

Every idea you need to follow a port is ONE class in the toolkit, with a docstring that says what it is and where its evidence lives. The product in one sentence: you point an AI agent at a Unity game; the agent ports the game's LOGIC through the u2ue-logic skill (Chapter 5), and every other asset family ports itself - each by Routes that follow measured Rules, held to Unity by Judges. py u2ue/survey/concepts_gate.py checks every concept the table below names, and a pillar (one promise of the product) of u2ue cycle requires the count that exist never to go down. The concept diagram is generated from u2ue/CONCEPTS.md: Chapter 22, "The concept model".

Where each concept lives in the code

Every concept is a class today (the source table's status column reads EXISTS on every row). The class column is the module and the class that holds it.

concept class where it lives, and what it does
Project u2ue/project.py:Project the project file and the environment it exports
Adapter u2ue/adapters/__init__.py:UnityProject the default; a game's own in u2ue/adapters/<game>.py
AssetFamily u2ue/assetfamily.py:AssetFamily effects, scene and ui: the facade command for each of the five steps, or ABSENT with why (the generated table above)
Route u2ue/routes.py:Route one switch, the files that read it, its evidence rows, and its state read off those files
Rule u2ue/facts.py:Rule one conformance bake (shared/conformance/*.json) and the Unity version it was measured on
ProbeCase u2ue/probecase.py:ProbeCase one case of the generic particle probe, as data: a real prefab placed by the game's spawn, or a SYNTHETIC system set by name. A run writes its cases file and its Unity window spec, and conform cases goes through it
Window u2ue/verbs/window.py:Window one runner; a window is a JSON spec (Chapter 8)
Capture u2ue/capture.py:Capture one photo run, judged by what it holds, never by its exit code: a system with an error, no background or no frame is NOT CAPTURED, and a frame asked for but not written by THIS run is SHORT. u2ue photo and a trial's photos step judge through it
Readback u2ue/readback.py:Readback one read of built systems and its capture summary. u2ue read and a trial's read step judge through it; systems() streams one system at a time, so a read larger than memory is judged with the same rows
Judge u2ue/judge.py:Judge each judge tool, the trials that run it and its plant, read off the trial specs (no list kept by hand); each is proven by its own --selftest or declared by a trial (u2ue judge --prove)
Trial u2ue/verbs/trial.py:Trial one runner; a trial is a JSON spec
Run u2ue/run.py:Run a run on a snapshot of the toolkit's code (pin()): u2ue trial run pins first, so an edit to the live converter mid-queue cannot change what runs; the owner can stop it gracefully
Pillar u2ue/pillars.py:Pillar the product's pillars, checked by u2ue cycle
Check u2ue/pillars.py:Check one recurring check of a pillar: held, trending, or absent
LogicPort u2ue/logic.py:LogicPort each step of the logic skill judged by its DONE WHEN (the observable that ends the step) from the records (u2ue logic); the method is the skill
Seam u2ue/seam.py:Seam every interface your model declares, sorted by who implements it: SEAM (an engine fills it), FACET (the model fills it), NONE (no implementer found by text: UNKNOWN, never absent). It gives the list of sockets a host still lacks
Gate u2ue/gates.py:Gate the field gates and the model gates that check runs; logic_diff.py (what parity runs) is still its own tool
HostProject u2ue/hostproject.py:HostProject u2ue host: the game's own .uproject made from the host template, each step judged by its proof line (Chapter 3)
Release u2ue/release.py:Release u2ue release: the package assembled as a repository by one manifest, every exclusion named with its reason; a secret refuses the whole release
PortPlan u2ue/port.py:PortPlan u2ue port: the whole port as ordered stages, in the order of the use case model's epic
Stage u2ue/port.py:Stage one step of the port, of one kind - AUTOMATIC, EDITOR, AI or OWNER - its state read from the records its own verb writes (DONE, TODO, RED, STOP, WAITS, ABSENT, UNCHECKED)
PortRun u2ue/port.py:PortRun the plan run in order: a read by default, --run runs every AUTOMATIC stage that is TODO, a RED stage holds back only its dependents, and running it again resumes
Census u2ue/estimate.py:Census u2ue estimate: what a Unity project holds, read off its files - code lines pure and coupled per folder, the build's scenes, particle prefabs, UI assets
TokenUse u2ue/estimate.py:TokenUse one model call's tokens in the five kinds a price list prices (uncached input, 5 m and 1 h cache writes, cache reads, output), a streamed call counted once
MeasuredRate u2ue/estimate.py:MeasuredRate tokens per unit read from a real port's records, with n, a bootstrap band and a leave-one-out error - or ABSENT with its reason
PriceTable u2ue/estimate.py:PriceTable per-model prices per token kind, read from Anthropic's pricing page and kept with its URL and date (u2ue/basis/prices.json)
Estimate u2ue/estimate.py:Estimate a Census times the rates: tokens per stage, the cache split, the list cost, the confidence, and the saving where one was measured (the cost page)

The table answers "where is X" without reading code; u2ue find answers it for everything else, and uml where <Name> for a class of the game's model. How a new concept becomes a class is toolkit work: Chapter 18.

3. Installation and the project file

Who this is for: the developer porting their own game - what to install, how to describe the game in one project file, how to make its Unreal host, and how to prove the install works. After it, every later chapter's commands run on your machine against your game.

Requirements

component version used what needs it
Windows 11 the Unreal runs are driven from native PowerShell
Python 3.13 every tool; the facade
PyYAML 6.0 with libyaml reading Unity YAML (libyaml is about 7x faster; measured equal output)
markdown (Python) 3.8 building this manual's HTML edition only
.NET SDK 8.0 or later (10.0 used) the runtime library and its tests; an UnrealSharp host (below)
Unreal Engine 5.7 build, read, photo: Niagara, the CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin (its FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary writes the Niagara stacks), the engine's Python scripting (UnrealEditor-Cmd -ExecutePythonScript)
UnrealSharp, the plugin that runs C# inside Unreal the host project's C# hosts for the game's model (Chapter 5)
Unity Editor the game's own only for measurement windows and reference photos, in the game's own editor; the toolkit never launches one

The Unity project must be serialized as text (Edit > Project Settings > Editor > Asset Serialization: Force Text): YAML .prefab, .unity, .mat, .asset and .meta.

Where the toolkit lives

Beside the facade (u2ue), the toolkit is a set of folders called parts: the converter (vfxport), the effect tools, the scene tools, the lane part (the queues and the report builder), the measured Unity rules and the UI converter. They are named once, in u2ue/tools.py (PARTS); set the environment variable U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT to move them as a whole. Run every command from the toolkit's root:

py -m u2ue                       # every verb
py -m u2ue find <words>          # search the toolkit

The project file

One file per game, u2ue/projects/<game>.json. A complete one, for a game whose effects are simply its particle prefabs:

{
  "name": "mygame",
  "adapter": "unity_project",
  "about": "free text, shown by info",
  "unity": {
    "root": "<unity project>",
    "assets": "<unity project>/Assets",
    "version": "2021.3.21f1",
    "editor": "<Unity 2021.3.21f1 install>"
  },
  "effects": {
    "key_source": {"kind": "particle_prefabs", "roots": ["Assets"]}
  },
  "unreal": {
    "uproject": "<unreal project>.uproject",
    "engine": "<Unreal Engine 5.7 install>",
    "content_root": "/Game/U2UE/MyGame"
  },
  "work": {
    "effects": "<work>",
    "ir": "<work>/ir",
    "guid_index": "<work>/guid_index.json",
    "resolve": "<work>/resolve.json",
    "records": "<work>/records",
    "photos": "<work>/photos",
    "inventory": "<work>/inventory"
  },
  "code": {
    "roots": ["Assets/Game", "Assets/GameShared"]
  }
}
field meaning
name the project's name
adapter unity_project (Unity's own rules) or a game adapter's name (u2ue/adapters/<name>.py, Chapter 18)
unity.root, unity.assets, unity.version the Unity project, its Assets folder, its version (measured rules are checked against it)
unity.editor (optional) that version's Editor install: its built-in shaders and materials are named off unity_builtin_extra (the Editor's file of built-in resources)
effects.key_source what the effects are: {"kind": "particle_prefabs", "roots": [...]}, or a game resolver through its adapter
unreal.uproject, unreal.engine, unreal.content_root the Unreal host, the engine, the content folder the systems are built under
work.* where the work goes: the IR, the guid index (every Unity asset GUID to its path, read off the .meta files), the key list, the records, the photos, the code inventory
code.roots the game's OWN C# folders (u2ue inventory --survey lists every folder first; vendor packages live in Assets too)
