model.root, model.layers, model.scan, model.hosting, model.unreal_links, model.hosts the engine-free model, once the game has one (scaffold, the verb that creates the model's projects, writes the first four), and where each engine's host code is (Chapter 5)
parity.dir, parity.engines where the model's per-runtime digests (one runtime's answers to the rule cases, floats as bit patterns) are written, and the runtimes parity requires (Chapter 5)
mono.faithful (optional) the Editor-recorded digest digest faithful re-measures Unity's standalone Mono against (Chapter 5)
unreal.host (optional) the game's own Unreal project for u2ue host (below, and Chapter 13)

u2ue/projects/ holds two example projects: the reference port's (a game adapter, a model, parity) and the second game's (the default adapter, nothing else).

Check it:

py -m u2ue --project <game> info       # every path OPENED; exit 1 when an input is missing

The Unreal host

The verbs that run Unreal (build, read, photo, host) need a host project with the plugins above, and run one headless Unreal at a time from native PowerShell (Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without the dotnet entry UnrealSharp looks for, and the verbs refuse such a PATH). A game builds under its own content_root (/Game/U2UE/<Game>).

u2ue host makes your game its OWN Unreal project: name it in the project file's unreal.host block, then run the steps one at a time. Each step is judged by the line in its own log that proves it, never by an exit code. Chapter 13 has the block's fields and each step in full; on a machine with no Windows SDK installed, the C++ compile needs an AutoSDK root (a folder that holds a Windows SDK and a toolchain), which the block's sdks_root hands to the build as UE_SDKS_ROOT. The managed project the steps make is the host's C# project, which UnrealSharp compiles and the engine loads.

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan        # every step: its command and the line that proves it
py -m u2ue --project <game> host create      # the .uproject from the toolkit's host template, renamed
py -m u2ue --project <game> host install     # each plugin cloned at its pinned commit; the toolkit's own copied
py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile     # the editor target (UnrealSharp generates its C# glue, the bindings to the engine's types)
py -m u2ue --project <game> host generate    # UnrealSharp's own command makes the managed project - no editor dialog
py -m u2ue --project <game> host wire        # the model, the digest cases and the host templates into it
py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish     # to both folders the engine may load from
py -m u2ue --project <game> host run         # headless: the host answers the digest; then `parity --require Unreal`
py -m u2ue --project <game> host status      # each step: proven, failed, or not run

Measured on the second game: from nothing to parity --require Unreal exit 0 in 9 minutes, the C++ compile 255 s of it.

Verifying the installation

Scope: the toolkit itself, on this machine. Precondition: the requirements above are installed and a project file exists. Minimal guarantee: a tool whose selftest fails is named. Success guarantee: every selftest passes, the runtime library's tests pass, and the manual matches the code. Trigger: the toolkit is installed or updated.

py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests     # every tool's own selftest
dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests              # the runtime library
py u2ue/manual/build.py --check                          # this manual is current

The Unreal-run tools

The install is done. The last two sections are for when your builds grow long: how the verbs launch Unreal, and how a long build and a trial share the one Unreal.

Every verb that runs Unreal launches it through ue_headless.ps1, which refuses a launch that could open a window, passes -DeterministicAudio (audio goes to Unreal's non-realtime renderer, never to the machine's sound device), and kills a runaway run at a time or log-size cap; the verbs refuse while another Unreal runs, so there is one at a time. build builds its keys in one headless run, in compile batches (--batch), and resaves only the systems it made; split a whole game into chunks by handing each chunk's key list to --keys. A texture, material parent or instance built before is reused only when nothing it came from changed. Chapter 13 has each tool the build, read and photo verbs run.

Unattended queues and the pause protocol

A whole-game build runs for hours, unattended, and there is one Unreal slot. Two rules keep a long build and a trial from spoiling each other:

  • A trial never shares the Unreal slot with a running build. The verbs that run Unreal refuse while the host is busy, and never interleave. If you script a long series of builds yourself, give it a pause point between chunks: the series waits while a pause file exists, the trial runs its whole chain (build, resave, read, every check and its plant, photos), and only then is the pause removed. Nothing removes a pause but the one who set it. No verb provides this pause; it belongs in your own queue script.
  • A trial is data, not a copied script. py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <spec.json> runs one from a spec: build, resave, read, judge (with its plant), photos. It runs alone, waits until no other Unreal runs before each Unreal step, and runs from a snapshot of the toolkit's code, so an edit to the live converter cannot change a trial half way. trial stop ends it at the next step boundary, never mid-step. A project supplies only its key lists and its work folders.

4. Tutorial: a first port, step by step

Who this is for: the developer porting their own game - the commands of a whole port in order, with real output from a game the toolkit was not built on. After it you can take your own game from its project file to its first report, and you know the command and the chapter for each stage after that.

This chapter takes a game the toolkit was not built on - a different studio's project on Unity 2021.3 - through a port. Steps 1 to 8 show what each printed on 2026-10-15; steps 9 to 18 are the rest of the port, each with its command and what it proves. The game's name is written <game> and its folder names are shortened; the numbers are as printed.

Scope: one game, from its project file to its first report. Precondition: the toolkit is installed and verified (Chapter 3). Minimal guarantee: every path the project names is opened, and every key the game must account for is listed before anything is built. Success guarantee: the acceptance page and the numbers, each number read from a record or naming the record it waits for. Trigger: a game the toolkit was not built on is to be ported.

The one command

Three lines carry the whole port: one prices it, two run it. The numbered steps after this section are what they run, one at a time.

py -m u2ue estimate --unity <unity project> --roots <the game's code folders>    what the port will cost, before you start
py -m u2ue --project <game> port                                                 every stage, read from its records; the next action
py -m u2ue --project <game> port --run                                           run every stage a verb can; stop where one cannot

estimate needs no project file (What a port costs has what it prints and how sure it is). port reads each stage's state from the records its own verb writes, so running it again resumes where the port stands. On this game, on 2026-10-17, with the paths and three long lines shortened:

py -m u2ue --project <game> port
u2ue port: <game> - reading every stage (nothing runs)
  [OWNER    ] project    DONE      describe the project (paths, code roots) - info exit 0
  [AUTOMATIC] inventory  DONE      read the game's C#, type by type - <work>/inventory/inventory.json
  [AUTOMATIC] classmodel DONE      the game's class model off its own code - <work>/inventory/uml
  [AI       ] logic      DONE      move the rules into an engine-free model - every step of u2ue-logic DONE, JUDGED or NOT RUN (9 DONE of 12)
  [AUTOMATIC] host       DONE      the game's own Unreal project, the model running in it - host status: every step PROVEN
  [AUTOMATIC] scene      ABSENT    the scenes as Unreal levels, held to Unity - the project file names no scene block
  [AUTOMATIC] extract    DONE      the effects read into the engine-neutral IR - <work>/u1e-ir.json
  [AUTOMATIC] gates      DONE      every Unity field the IR carries read or excused - check --only gates exit 0
  [AUTOMATIC] build      TODO      the Niagara systems built - no build record <work>/records/u1e-build-u2ue.json
  [AUTOMATIC] read       WAITS     the built systems read back frame by frame - waits on build
  [AUTOMATIC] photo      WAITS     the built systems photographed beside Unity's frames - waits on read
  [EDITOR   ] ui         UNCHECKED the UI screens captured, converted, rebuilt - the UI verb has no read-only status
  [AUTOMATIC] parity     DONE      the rules agree on every runtime, by the bit - parity exit 0
  [AUTOMATIC] report     DONE      the acceptance page from the records - <work>/report/<game>_acceptance.html
  [OWNER    ] owner      STOP      the owner's decisions the page asks - read the acceptance page and answer them
NEXT: build - `py -m u2ue --project <game> build`, or `port --run --with-unreal` (it launches a headless Unreal: one at a time)

Each stage is one of four kinds. AUTOMATIC: a verb does it, and --run runs it. EDITOR: it needs a free Unity editor, so port names the window and never opens one. AI: the logic, done by the u2ue-logic skill in Claude Code, with u2ue-long-run keeping the session going (Chapter 15). OWNER: a decision only the game's owner can make. A stage that launches a headless Unreal runs only with --with-unreal, one Unreal at a time.

Each stage's state is read, never assumed: DONE; TODO (an AUTOMATIC stage not done yet, which --run runs); WAITS (a stage it depends on is neither DONE nor ABSENT); STOP (it needs a person, the AI or an editor, and names the one question); RED (its check ran and failed); ABSENT (the project file names nothing for it); UNCHECKED (no read-only check exists for it yet). A RED stage never runs, and it holds back only the stages that wait on it. ABSENT and UNCHECKED stages are said, never skipped silently.

1. Describe the game and open every path

Write u2ue/projects/<game>.json (Chapter 3 has a complete one), then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> info
project <game> (u2ue/projects/<game>.json)
  unity.root           dir       <unity project>                     ok
  work.effects         out-dir   <work>                              ok (exists)
  work.photos          out-dir   <work>/photos                       to be created (its parent exists)
  unreal.uproject      file      <unreal project>.uproject           ok
  unreal.content_root  game-path /Game/U2UE/<Game>                    ok (an Unreal content path)
  adapter: unity_project (spawn rules unity)
  key source: {'kind': 'particle_prefabs', 'roots': ['Assets']}

Every path the file names is opened; an input that is missing exits 1.

2. Find the game's own code

Vendor packages live in Assets beside the game's code, so the toolkit never guesses which folders are the game's:

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory --survey
  AssetStore     4226   + 917 in Editor folders
  GameCode       1907   + 55 in Editor folders
  GameShared       25
  ...

Name the game's folders as code.roots in the project file.

3. Inventory the code

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory
u2ue inventory <game>: 1987 files, 2453 types (plain 1384, MonoBehaviour 789, ScriptableObject 160, base outside the scanned code 88,
EditorWindow 15, Editor 12, PropertyDrawer 5); 1148 pure rules; -> <work>/inventory
  serialized data                  473 types   1708 sites
  platform (log, files, prefs)     365 types   1525 sites
  spawn / destroy                  311 types   1049 sites
  lookups                          275 types    661 sites
  coroutines / Invoke              273 types    997 sites
  transform                        222 types   1652 sites
  UI                               134 types    373 sites
  time                             112 types    254 sites
  physics                           83 types    317 sites
  input                             75 types    236 sites
  animation / timeline              54 types    309 sites
  ...

<work>/inventory/inventory.md lists every type's Unity calls by family (each family names its section of u2ue/BASICS.md, whose topics are Chapter 5's "Topic by topic"), the 1148 types that use no Unity API (what moves into an engine-free model first), and every MonoBehaviour's script execution order with its lifecycle methods - the table Unity's frame order is rebuilt from in the model. Chapter 5 is what to do with it. Read the counts as a plan: this game has physics in 83 types and animation in 54, which the toolkit does not cover (Appendix B), and you know that on day one.

4. Read the data the inspector holds

py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from Assets/<data folder>/<data asset>.asset --script <DataClass> --tsv data.tsv
u2ue data <game>: 1 component(s) in Assets/<data folder>/<data asset>.asset
  None  fileID 11400000  23 fields

Every serialized value as the file stores it: 487 leaf values in the TSV for this game's ScriptableObject, with the avatar-mask reference resolved to its asset path. The values are read, never retyped into the port. (The game's own asset and class names are written <data asset> and <DataClass>.)

5. Extract the effects

py -m u2ue --project <game> extract
    - Snow_Particles   active=True  depth 0 loop=True  dur 5  life (2.2, 2.2) size (0.15, 0.3) space World ...
        render Stretch  shape Box(enabled True)  rate 500.0 bursts []  modules ['colorOverLifetime', 'rotationOverLifetime', ...]
    material .../Snow_Particles.mat
        shader Legacy Shaders/Particles/Alpha Blended (None)  blend {'_SrcBlend': 1, '_DstBlend': 0, '_ZWrite': 1}
REFUSED BY KEY: 4 of 60 READ key(s), each named above
u2ue extract: 60 READ key(s): 56 IR file(s) with 189 emitter(s), 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign path(s)
  REFUSED unity.prefab.5ccd...: .../Winter Door.prefab: PrefabInstance 4843689442982340616: modification target 1211823196678298638 ...

This writes the guid index (to work.guid_index), the effect keys (every prefab holding a ParticleSystem, by the default adapter, to work.resolve) and one IR file per key (under work.ir), and prints a one-line summary of what was read for every emitter. Four keys are refused, each with the object the reader could not follow; nothing is dropped silently. What the effects path does not cover (VFX Graph assets, particle systems authored in scenes) is listed with counts.

6. Check before building

py -m u2ue --project <game> check
...
u2ue check: the measured rules' Unity versions against project <game>
  163 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       163 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters
  163 of 163 rules this project's build uses were measured on another Unity: its report must not call them measured for it
u2ue check: PASS

check runs every tool's own selftest, the field gates over this project's IR (an unread Unity field fails here, not as a silent gap later), the measured rules' Unity versions against the project's, and the model gates (no model yet: said so). Here every rule is reported unverified for this Unity: the build still runs, and the report says so.

7. Build, read, photograph (the Unreal host)

py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry     # the plan and the host's state - always first
py -m u2ue --project <game> build
py -m u2ue --project <game> read --tag <TAG>
py -m u2ue --project <game> photo --tag <TAG>

Run from native PowerShell, one headless Unreal at a time. A build keeps its record as records/u1e-build-<TAG>.json (the tag is u2ue unless build --tag names another), and read and photo take the same tag to find the systems that build made. Appendix A has the reference port's numbers for these steps.

8. Report and measure

py -m u2ue --project <game> report --out <game>.html
py -m u2ue --project <game> metrics
u2ue metrics - <game> (every number from a record; definitions: u2ue/verbs/metrics.py)
  keys      60: NEVER BUILT 56, IR REFUSED 4; 0 drawn, 0 of them with a named gap; 0 from the acceptance rebuild
            the rules behind 'measured' were measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1 - UNVERIFIED for it
  machine   ABSENT: no per-key seconds in the chosen build records
  data      ABSENT: no <work>/records/checks_summary.json - the readback sweep has not run
  image     ABSENT: no sheets listing <work>/records/fx18_sheets.txt - the photo pass has not run

Before any build the page already lists every key the project must account for, and every number it cannot compute yet says which record it is waiting for. Chapter 10 defines every number.

Part two: the rest of the game

Steps 1 to 8 brought the effects to a first report. A port also moves the game's code, its scenes, its UI and its Unreal project. The steps below are the same port continued, in the order that keeps each step's input ready for the next. Each step names its command and what that command proves; the chapter named beside it has the full procedure, the options and the traps.

9. Draw the class model of one slice

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract
py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>

A slice is a handful of types that hold one rule of the game; the code moves one slice at a time. extract reads the class model off the game's own code roots (and its engine-free model, once there is one). mermaid --focus draws one slice with every member a real one. The diagram comes before any code moves, and a diagram that names a member the code lacks is refused. Chapter 5, and the u2ue-logic skill's step 2.

10. Make the engine-free model

py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <DIR> --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <DIR>

The first line shows what would be written, and the second writes it. You get a Core project (<Model>.Core, the model's own C# project) that references only the toolkit's runtime library, a headless test project, and the project file's model block. Then the verb builds both and runs the model gates. Exit 0 means the model exists, compiles, and no engine reaches it. A second scaffold is refused, so this never overwrites. Chapter 5, step 6.

11. Move the slice and prove it on Unity's own runtime

Move the slice's rules into the Core, each with its test, then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Class.Method> --cases <Cases.cs>
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity

digest run answers the rule's cases with no engine at all, on CoreCLR (.NET's own runtime, the one the Unreal host and the headless runs use) and on the project's Unity version's own Mono runtime, writing each runtime's answers as a digest. digest faithful proves that the no-editor Mono run gives the same rows as the Editor does. parity compares every runtime the rules run on by float bits, and names each row that differs. Chapter 5, step 7, and Chapter 14.

12. See where the logic port stands

py -m u2ue --project <game> logic

Each step of the u2ue-logic skill is judged by its own DONE WHEN, read from the project's records, and the verb names the step to take next. An AI model doing the port starts every session here instead of working out the state again. Chapter 5.

13. Find what Unreal cannot place as Unity does

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<scene>.unity

This lists every node whose transform chain Unity can draw and Unreal's transform cannot hold (a non-uniform scale under a rotation shears), with the error in centimetres and whether the node draws. Whether to accept, bake or fix each error is your call, made with its number. Chapter 6.

14. Bring a scene across

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene export
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene import
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene readback
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check

--dry opens the scene's paths and shows the Unreal host's state. export runs in the game's own Unity Editor, in a window: the verb itself never touches an editor, and prints the trigger the window drops (.RUN_SCENE_EXPORT, the file that starts the export). import brings the glTF into a new Unreal level through the engine's own scene pipeline, and readback reads the saved level back headless. check is the fidelity gate: hierarchy, materials, textures, lighting and placement, held to Unity's files and to the scene's own measured baseline. Chapter 6.

15. Convert the UI

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture dir> --screen <NAME>
py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test

convert turns one captured screen into a folder Unreal reads: the capture, its sprites, and each TextMeshPro font's TTF, proven by identical glyph indices. test runs the generic uGUI and TextMeshPro library's own tests headless. The capture itself runs in the game's Unity Editor in Play mode. The package does not ship that capture as an Editor assembly yet (Appendix B), so ui capture refuses and says why. Chapter 6.

16. Make the game's own Unreal project

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan
py -m u2ue --project <game> host create
py -m u2ue --project <game> host status

plan lists every step (create, install, compile, generate, wire, publish, run) with the command it runs and the log line that proves it. Run the steps one at a time, from native PowerShell, and status shows each one as proven, failed, or not run. The run step is proven only when the model's digest file is written after the run started. Chapter 13.

17. Hold the effects to Unity on numbers

py -m u2ue --project <game> conform cases --name <run>
py -m u2ue --project <game> conform diff --unity <particle-cases record> --unreal <readback record> --report <FILE>
py -m u2ue --project <game> conform latest --run <run>

cases writes one probe case per effect key, plus the Unity window and the Unreal read that measure them. After both have run, diff judges every emitter of every key on its live count and its first birth, paired by file id. latest prints the share that holds, from the newest stamped report. Chapter 9.

18. Check every pillar

py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --dry
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle

Every promise of the toolkit is checked: PASS, FAIL, HELD by a named decision, or ABSENT where no check exists yet. Red stops the cycle. Run it before any report. Chapter 14.

Where to go next

  • The game's code, in full: Chapter 5, with each part of a Unity game in its "Topic by topic".
  • A behaviour that must match exactly: Chapter 8, and the tools that run it: Chapter 12.
  • An effect family the converter refuses: Chapter 7's route protocol, then Chapter 11.
  • Something went wrong: Chapter 16.

5. Porting the game code

Who this is for: the developer porting their own game - how its code moves into one engine-free model that both engines run, what the toolkit gives at each step, and how to prove the answers agree. After the method and the playbook you can move one slice of your game's rules and prove it on every runtime; the later sections are reference to come back to.

The particle effects are content; the game itself is code: MonoBehaviours, coroutines, inspector values, the transform chain. The chapter's parts:

  • The method (steps 1 to 8): the order of work, what the toolkit gives at each step, and its real output.
  • Topic by topic: each part of a Unity game - what Unity does, what Unreal offers, the route that worked, what the toolkit gives.
  • What the field says about the model: what published engines and authors say about the model's choices, and what a port should take from it.
  • The logic playbook: the method as the u2ue-logic skill (u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md) an AI agent follows, each step with its command and the observable that ends it.
  • The model in depth, then its recipe, gates and traps: the seams, the event contract and the checks your model needs.
  • The model's tools and the effect ledger: what the package ships around the model.

Scope: the game's code - its rules, its per-frame order, its data. Precondition: a project file names the game and its code folders. Minimal guarantee: what the toolkit cannot do for a rule is said, and the model's gates stop an engine reference. Success guarantee: one engine-free model both engines run, with the same answers by the bit. Trigger: the game's rules live in MonoBehaviours, which Unreal cannot run.

The decision everything follows from

Do not translate MonoBehaviours into Actors one by one. Move the game's rules into an engine-free model - plain C# that references no engine - and write one thin host per engine. Unity and Unreal then run the same model, and the only differences left are the hosts', which is what makes the port provable. It splits into two layers: the rules (state and seed in, state out) and the presentation (the per-frame look: camera, popups, motion). The toolkit's Unreal hosts are UnrealSharp C#, with C++ only where UnrealSharp cannot reach.

flowchart LR
  subgraph model["engine-free model (plain C#)"]
    R["rules: state + seed -> state"] --> PR["presentation: what to show, frame by frame"]
  end
  PR -->|view seams| UH["Unity host: MonoBehaviours"]
  PR -->|view seams| EH["Unreal host: UnrealSharp actors"]
  PR -->|view seams| TH["headless test host"]
  RT["U2ue.Runtime: Unity's frame, clock, coroutines, platform"] --> model

The method, step by step

1. Inventory the code

py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory --survey     # every top folder under Assets with its .cs count: name the game's own as code.roots
py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory

Per type: MonoBehaviour / ScriptableObject / plain, its lifecycle methods, every Unity call by family, and the pure rules - types that use no Unity API, which move into the model first. Partial classes are merged across their files. The reader is lexical (comments and strings blanked, a brace stack per type): a call through an alias or reflection is not seen, so a miss is unknown, never "does not use". Chapter 4 shows a full run.

A rule does value-type maths (Vector3, Mathf, Color). The inventory counts Unity's value types as a family of their own, so such a rule is not pure: its arithmetic is UnityEngine's. It does not move as written: where those types live in an engine-free model is the owner's decision, made once for the whole model ("Floats across runtimes" below has the two answers), and the rule waits for it. Branches from step 1.

Then draw the class model of the first slice before moving anything - the diagram is the plan a person reviews:

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract                        # the class model off the game's code roots (its own index)
py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus TypeA TypeB    # a slice's class diagram, every member a real one

2. Read the frame order

The same inventory lists every MonoBehaviour's script execution order (its .cs.meta executionOrder, from the file named after the class - the script Unity orders) with its lifecycle methods. Unity's frame is: Update in that order, then the coroutine phase (yield return null resumes after every Update), then LateUpdate. The order between scripts is behaviour: measured on the reference port, re-making it by hand across several engine ticks made its first Unreal host draw things a frame late.

3. Give the model Unity's runtime rules

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime (netstandard2.1 and net8.0, no engine reference):

type Unity's rule
UnityClock Time.deltaTime = the real step clamped to the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, times timeScale; the unscaled step is not clamped. The maximum is the project's own: py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5 (5 is the TimeManager's YAML type id; Unity's default is 0.33333334).
Coroutines Start runs to the first yield; a coroutine started during a frame resumes after the next frame's Updates; yield return <IEnumerator> runs nested and stops with its parent; yield return <Handle> waits and resumes the same frame its target ends; Wait.Scaled / Wait.Unscaled.
UnityFrame one frame in Unity's order: Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, LateUpdate. A host calls Tick once per engine frame.
Platform.* the six platform services (below) and SeededRandom.
FloatBits float bit patterns and ULP distance (how many representable floats apart two values are), for parity digests.
PlaybackQueue<TEvent> the model resolves an action at once and appends ordered events; the host shows one per frame, only when its presenter (IPresenter<TEvent>) is idle, and takes input only when IsCaughtUp. A history that shrinks is refused.
Digest one runtime's answers to the rule cases: digestVersion=N, then key=value rows in ordinal order, floats as bits - the file u2ue parity reads.
TrailLaw Unity's TrailRenderer as measured: the points it holds each frame (TrailLaw.Point) and the drawn vertices (TrailLaw.Vertex) with the fraction width, colour and U run on. Its test replays Unity's own play-mode bake.

What a host does with it - one frame object, the game's former MonoBehaviours registered by their execution order, one call per engine frame:

using System.Collections;
using U2ue.Runtime;

var clock = new UnityClock(0.33333334f);      // the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, READ with `u2ue data` (above)
var coroutines = new Coroutines(clock);
var frame = new UnityFrame(clock);
frame.Add("CameraRig", -100, update: rig.Update, lateUpdate: rig.LateUpdate);   // -100: its .cs.meta executionOrder
frame.Add("HudPresenter", 0, update: hud.Update);
frame.AddCoroutines(coroutines);

IEnumerator Flash() { hud.Show(); yield return Wait.Scaled(0.5f); hud.Hide(); }
coroutines.Start(Flash());

// the host's tick, once per engine frame, with the real elapsed seconds:
frame.Tick(deltaSeconds);    // clock -> every Update by order -> coroutines -> every LateUpdate

Run with two frames of 0.3 s (the snippet compiled against the library as printed, with the rig and HUD writing a line each):

show            <- Start: the coroutine runs to its first yield at once
rig update      <- frame 1: every Update, by execution order
hud update
rig late        <- 0.3 s < 0.5 s: the coroutine waits; LateUpdate
rig update      <- frame 2
hud update
hide            <- 0.6 s >= 0.5 s: resumed in the coroutine phase, after every Update
rig late

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests holds every rule and builds on any machine. dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.OriginTests runs a set of coroutine scripts on the reference port's measured runner and on the library and requires identical step logs; it needs that port's code on disk, so it is a separate test project that runs only where that code is.

4. Put the engine behind seams

  • The platform seam: six interfaces, one engine call per member - ILog (Debug.Log), ITextAssets (Resources.Load of text), IKeyValueStore (PlayerPrefs), IFileStore (the save file), IJsonCodec<T> (JsonUtility), IRandomSource (UnityEngine.Random). "The platform seam" below has every member and the trap each one taught.
  • View seams: what the presentation asks the engine to show - for a board game, IEntityView, IHudView, ICameraDirector, IEffectPlayer and IInputSource ("The view seam" below). The model says what happened; the host decides how it looks.

5. Read the data, never retype it

py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <scene|prefab|asset> --script <ClassName>    # or --class <id> for a built-in

Every serialized value of the matching components (nested prefab instances expanded, overrides applied, references resolved to asset paths), as JSON or a dotted TSV. "Unity serialization beats the C# initializer": the scene's value is what plays. Measured on the reference port's camera rig: it equals the hand-written reader it replaced on all 152 fields and 32 curve values.

6. Cut the model, then gate it

py -m u2ue --project <game> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <a folder outside Assets>
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model

scaffold writes <Model>.Core (netstandard2.1 + net8.0, referencing only U2ue.Runtime) and <Model>.Core.Tests, adds the project file's model block, builds both and runs the gates on the empty model; it never overwrites.

layer_gate refuses an engine namespace in the model and any reference outside each layer's allowed set (model.layers, inner layer first); host_gate refuses a platform member declared anywhere but the hosting folder (model.hosting: the one folder that may declare platform services, <Model>.Core/Hosting as scaffold writes it). Both run on the folders the project names (model.root, and the projects model.scan lists); layer_gate checks the model's Unreal-facing references only when model.unreal_links is set. A project with no model yet is told so.

7. Prove the rules agree across runtimes

Each runtime the model runs on (Unity on Mono, the Unreal host on CoreCLR, a headless test runner) writes a digest, <parity.dir>/logic-<Engine>.txt: a digestVersion=N line, then one key=value row per case with every float as its 8-hex-digit bit pattern. Unity's side needs no editor: u2ue digest run compiles the rule cases (a static method returning a Digest) twice - for CoreCLR (logic-Headless.txt) and with the project's Unity version's own Mono compiler and runtime (logic-UnityMono.txt):

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs>
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful      # standalone Mono vs a digest the Editor wrote: on Unity 6000.3, 383 of 383 rows equal

faithful reads the project's mono.faithful block: the Unity editor whose Mono it runs, the entry point and the case sources the Editor's own runner compiled, the assemblies they reference (mono.faithful.refs), and the digest that Editor wrote (reference).

Make the cases' inputs exact on every runtime (integer arithmetic, each input written to the digest): a driver that makes its own inputs with float maths measures its own drift - on the second test game it produced 177 false differences where the rule had 2. Then:

py -m u2ue --project <game> parity
game-logic comparison - digest v1
  Headless    383 rows
  Unity       383 rows
  Unreal      383 rows
  per rule group (differing / total):
    damage_base                    27 /  144  <<<
    ...
    fpmode_fused                    8 /   36  <<<
    fpmode_stepped                  0 /   36
    ...
  DIFFERING ROWS (first 20):
    damage_base_009              Headless=40400001  Unity=40400000  Unreal=40400001
    ...
  ODD ONE OUT: Unity on 35 of 35 differing row(s)
  DIAGNOSIS: fpmode_fused differs and fpmode_stepped does NOT: an intermediate precision difference ...
  CHARACTERISED AND ALLOWED: 35 row(s), each pinned to its exact bits and to 1 ULP.
    ...
VERDICT: Headless / Unity / Unreal agree on all 383 rows except 35 characterised 1-ULP row(s), which are
         unchanged since they were measured.

That is real output, from the reference port. Every row across every runtime is compared; a difference is red unless the characterised allowance pins that exact row to its exact bits and to one ULP. Here Unity's Mono is the odd one out on every differing row - it may keep float intermediates wider than float32, which ECMA-334 (the C# language standard) permits - and the two fpmode groups prove it: the same expression written with explicit float locals agrees everywhere. Applying that fix moves Unity's own values by one ULP, so it is the game owner's call.

8. Write the hosts

One thin host per engine implements the seams and drives the frame. The toolkit's Unreal templates (u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal, taken from the reference port's hosts with the game removed) are the starting point; copy them into the host's managed project (its C# project, Chapter 3):

template what it is
AU2ueFrameActor the actor that owns the frame: each tick hands the real step to UnityFrame (clamped by the project's own maximum step, which a subclass must supply - the default refuses). Summon it with -ExecCmds="summon /Script/UnrealSharp.<Name>_C"
UnrealPointer the cursor, its position in Unity's frame (origin bottom left), its world ray, and keys pressed or released this frame - polled before the frame runs
UnrealCameraRig one camera actor made the view target; the model's pose copied onto it, with Unity's vertical field of view converted to Unreal's horizontal one
UnrealPlatform.cs the six platform services on Unreal: the log, a manifest-backed text folder, a save-folder file store, PlayerPrefs as one file, System.Text.Json with fields, a random source with Unity's bounds

dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal compiles them against a real UnrealSharp install (set U2UE_UNREALSHARP to the host's Plugins/UnrealSharp), so a template that no longer matches the engine's bindings fails there.

What the toolkit does not do here

It does not move the code for you, decide the seams, or write the hosts. It tells you what each type touches, gives the moved code Unity's runtime rules, reads the data, gates the boundary and proves the answers agree.

Topic by topic: the rest of a Unity game

The method above is the order of work; this is the map by topic: for each part of a Unity game, what Unity does, what Unreal offers, the route that was proven (on the reference port, unless the topic says otherwise; here a route is the approach that worked, not a converter route behind a switch), and what the toolkit gives today. NOT YET means the toolkit has nothing for it yet and the route is the only worked example. py -m u2ue find <words> searches this manual, the tools and the converter together; in the toolkit's own tree it also searches shared/PORTING_ANOTHER_PROJECT.md, the long form this chapter was written from, which the package does not ship.

The one decision everything else follows from

The decision at the top of this chapter. Toolkit: HAVE. py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model runs layer_gate.py (the model references no engine - not UnityEngine, not UnrealSharp) and host_gate.py (logging, files, JSON and random numbers go through the platform seam, never a host interface) on the folders the project file names (model.root, model.layers, model.scan, model.hosting); a project with no model yet is told so. Step 6 has what each gate refuses.

The lifecycle: Awake, Start, Update, LateUpdate, OnDestroy

  • Unity: Awake and OnEnable on load, Start before the first Update, then every frame Update, the coroutines, LateUpdate, in script execution order; OnDisable and OnDestroy at teardown.
  • Unreal: an Actor's constructor, BeginPlay, Tick(deltaSeconds), EndPlay(reason). There is no LateUpdate and no coroutine phase; tick groups exist but do not mirror Unity's order.
  • Route: one actor owns the game screen. BeginPlay builds the world, Tick runs one frame object once per engine frame, EndPlay tears it down. The frame object is Unity's frame order written once - the clock, each former MonoBehaviour's Update in its order, the coroutine pass, LateUpdate - each entry citing the executionOrder it stands for, read from the .cs.meta files. Not one actor per MonoBehaviour: the order between them is the behaviour (step 2).
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue inventory lists every MonoBehaviour's execution order and lifecycle methods; U2ue.Runtime.UnityFrame is the frame object (step 3).

Coroutines, WaitForSeconds, Invoke

  • Unity: StartCoroutine(IEnumerator), yield return null / WaitForSeconds, resumed after Update.
  • Unreal: latent actions, timers or async tasks. None of them resumes at Unity's point in the frame.
  • Route: keep the iterators. A small runner steps them - Start, Stop, StopAll, and Resume (the yield-null pass) - with a scaled and an unscaled wait for WaitForSeconds and WaitForSecondsRealtime. The model never waits: a rule that waited in Unity becomes a step the host advances. Do not make the model await either: that inverts control into every coroutine site, and the reference port had 833 of them.
  • ABSENT: Invoke / InvokeRepeating and FixedUpdate. The reference port uses none of them, so there is no worked example, and UnityFrame has no fixed-step phase.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.Coroutines (Wait.Scaled / Wait.Unscaled), held to a measured runner by dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.OriginTests (step 3); u2ue inventory counts every type that uses coroutines.

Time

  • Unity: Time.deltaTime (scaled, and clamped by the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep), unscaledDeltaTime, timeScale.
  • Unreal: Tick's deltaSeconds, and global time dilation.
  • Route: one clock for the whole frame takes the engine's unscaled seconds each frame and derives Unity's: DeltaTime = Min(unscaled, MaximumDeltaTime) * TimeScale.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.UnityClock takes the project's own maximum step (read it with u2ue data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5, field Maximum Allowed Timestep; Unity's default is 0.33333334).

Random numbers

  • Unity: UnityEngine.Random, one global, unseeded stream.
  • Unreal: FMath::Rand, and random streams.
  • Route: the model asks IRandomSource. Unity's adapter (the Unity-side class that implements the seam; "The layers, as they are on disk" below calls these engine adapters) keeps the global stream, so the sequence the player sees is unchanged; headless and parity runs use a seeded System.Random. A presentation-only noise (a UI sound's samples) draws from the host's own stream, never the rules' stream.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. U2ue.Runtime.Platform.IRandomSource and SeededRandom, with Unity's bounds (int upper-exclusive, float both-inclusive); u2ue parity compares the rules' answers across runtimes.

Floats across runtimes

  • Unity runs C# on Mono; the Unreal hosts and the headless runs use CoreCLR, and the same float expression can round differently. Measured on the reference port: 35 rows, every one 1 ULP, all in one damage formula, Mono the odd one out on every row (step 7 has the run and the fix; the header of logic_diff.py records it). A second game's first slice met the same cause: its PID formula (a proportional-integral-derivative controller that steers a turn) differs by 1 ULP on 2 of 641 rows.
  • Compare floats by bit pattern, never by printed text: Mono prints 9 digits and .NET prints the shortest (FloatBits.Hex; the text difference alone once produced 230 false mismatches). Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue parity (wrapping logic_diff.py) compares every runtime's digest by float bits against a characterised allowance; U2ue.Runtime.FloatBits writes and measures bit patterns.
  • Unity's side with no Editor: u2ue digest run compiles the cases for CoreCLR and with the project's Unity version's own Mono (<editor>/Editor/Data/MonoBleedingEdge: its csc.exe and mono-bdwgc.exe). u2ue digest faithful measured that Mono run equal to the digest the Editor wrote, 383 of 383 rows on Unity 6000.3.16f1; another Unity version is UNMEASURED until its own Editor-recorded digest is compared.
  • Unity's value types in a model (Vector3, Mathf, Color; u2ue inventory counts them as their own family): where they live is one decision for the whole model, with two answers - copy each member the rules use into the model, measured bit-exact against Unity (the reference port's route), or allow a value-type library as the model's one reference, which is only as exact as its measurement (the reference port's shim UnityCompat.Core, its own copy of Unity's value types ("The shim route" below), is bit-exact on 101 of 105 members). It is the owner's call; port the float-only rules first.

Spawning and destroying: Instantiate, Destroy

  • Unity: Instantiate(prefab), Destroy(go).
  • Unreal: SpawnActor, DestroyActor; Niagara systems through UNiagaraFunctionLibrary.
  • Route: the model never spawns. It states what happened ("The event stream contract" below) and the view adapter makes or removes the engine objects: AActor.Spawn for an entity, SpawnSystemAtLocation for an effect, DestroyActor to remove one. Ask the engine whether an actor is still alive: the managed wrapper outlives DestroyActor.
  • Toolkit: effects HAVE (the converter builds the systems the player spawns). Actors: a TEMPLATE, AU2ueFrameActor in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal (step 8); its headless smoke run is NOT YET (Appendix B).

Finding things: GetComponent, FindObjectOfType, singletons

  • Unity: components found at run time, often through a static Instance.
  • Unreal: components and subsystems; GetActorOfClass.
  • Route: the model is handed what it needs through host interfaces (I*Host, one per question the rules ask), so nothing searches a scene. The hosts hold their references directly.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue inventory lists, type by type, every Unity call by family (lookups among them) and the pure-rule types that use none - what moves into the model first (Chapter 4 shows the second game's run).

The transform: axes, units, rotation

  • Unity: metres; x right, y up, z forward; left-handed. Euler angles apply Z, then X, then Y.
  • Unreal: centimetres; x forward, y right, z up; also left-handed.
  • The conversion, one line each way: ue.X = -x*100, ue.Y = z*100, ue.Z = y*100, with its exact inverse. Directions: u2ue_dir(v) = (-x, z, y); rotations: u2ue_quat(q) = (-qx, qz, qy, qw) (both functions in vfxport/build_niagara.py). The ZXY Euler order was MEASURED on Unity 6000.3, not assumed. Chapter 6 has the full table.
  • A trap: a scene imported through glTF arrives in a frame the pipeline chose (Chapter 6), so a level and a hand-placed actor need not share a frame. Measure the imported level's frame once and convert every hand-placed actor through it.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue/transform.py holds every convention above, held by its selftest to the converter's own functions; its Unreal composition is READ from the engine (TransformVectorized.cpp:295-323).

The transform chain: hierarchy, scale, shear

  • Unity: a Transform composes as a 4x4 matrix, so a rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is sheared.
  • Unreal: a SceneComponent holds translation, quaternion and scale. It cannot hold a shear.
  • Route: measure, do not average. Compose every node both ways and push each drawn mesh's corners through both; whether to accept, bake or fix the error is decided with its number, then pinned by a gate (Chapter 6 has the numbers). The effect converter refuses a sheared particle node and names it.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue shear --gltf <export> (or --from <scene>, which expands nested prefab instances by the effect reader's rules) lists every sheared node, whether it draws, and the error in cm under Unreal's own composition rule; on the reference port's first map it finds the same 46 nodes that were measured by hand.

Scenes and prefabs

  • Unity: .unity and .prefab YAML, .meta GUIDs, nested prefabs and overrides.
  • Unreal: levels (.umap) and Blueprint or C# actor classes.
  • Route: geometry, materials and textures go through the standard pipeline - exported from Unity with glTFast (a glTF exporter run as an Editor script), imported with Interchange (Unreal's own scene import pipeline). Inactive subtrees are skipped and listed; every value not carried is named ABSENT. scene_fidelity_gate.py re-measures hierarchy, materials, textures and placement against Unity's own files without opening either editor.
  • Toolkit: HAVE - u2ue scene (Chapter 6). The notes on reading prefab YAML (nested instances, variants, legacy prefab records) apply to any scene reader.

Inspector values, ScriptableObjects, data files

  • Unity: serialized fields on MonoBehaviours and ScriptableObjects, Resources.Load, JsonUtility.
  • Unreal: UPROPERTY defaults, data assets, data tables.
  • Route: the values are read, never retyped. JSON goes through IJsonCodec<T>; on Unreal that is System.Text.Json with IncludeFields = true, without which public fields serialise as nothing. Text assets go through ITextAssets.
  • Toolkit: HAVE. u2ue data --from <scene|prefab|asset> --script <Class> (or --class <id>) writes any component's or ScriptableObject's serialized values as JSON or TSV, nested prefab overrides applied (step 5 has its measured check).

Input

  • Unity: Input.GetKeyDown, the mouse position, Camera.ScreenPointToRay.
  • Unreal: Enhanced Input, or polling the player controller.
  • Route: polled. The IInputSource implementation uses APlayerController.WasInputKeyJustPressed and UGameplayStatics.DeprojectScreenToWorld; the pick itself is a rule of the model, not an engine trace, so both engines pick the same cell. Enhanced Input is not needed.
  • Toolkit: a TEMPLATE - UnrealPointer in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal (step 8); its headless smoke run is NOT YET.

Logging, files, preferences: the platform seam

The six interfaces of step 4 - ILog, ITextAssets, IKeyValueStore, IFileStore, IJsonCodec<T>, IRandomSource - which your game implements the same way any game does; "The platform seam" below has their members and the rule each one taught. Toolkit: HAVE - the six in U2ue.Runtime.Platform, their Unreal implementations as a template (UnrealPlatform.cs in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal), and u2ue check --only model refuses a platform member declared outside the hosting folder.

Camera

  • Unity: a Camera component, often driven by a controller script; Cinemachine.
  • Unreal: a CameraActor or CameraComponent made the view target.
  • Route: the camera's rules are the model's, fed the rig's serialized values (read as data, above). Unreal places a camera actor and makes it the view target with SetViewTargetWithBlend; a director class on the host carries the shots.
  • Toolkit: a TEMPLATE - UnrealCameraRig in u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal (step 8); its headless smoke run is NOT YET.

UI

  • Unity: a uGUI Canvas, RectTransforms, layout groups, TextMeshPro.
  • Unreal: UMG widgets, or Slate.
  • Route: not a UMG tree. The Canvas is captured, laid out by a port of uGUI's own solver and painted in one UUserWidget.OnPaint, because UnrealSharp's UWidgetTree.RootWidget is read-only and a UMG tree cannot be assembled from C#.
  • Toolkit: HAVE the layout side - U2ue.Ui, the generic uGUI / TextMeshPro library with its own tests (u2ue ui test), and u2ue ui convert. The capture needs the package's Editor assembly (Appendix B). Chapter 6 has the whole route.

Audio

  • Unity: AudioSource pools, procedural clips through AudioClip.SetData.
  • Unreal: Sound Waves, Sound Cues, MetaSounds.
  • Route: a presentation rule picks the voice and the gain as Unity's audio manager did; Unity's procedural clips are rendered to float PCM once and played through a small C++ bridge that hands the samples to the mixer unconverted, as a 2D one-shot.
  • Toolkit: the bridge as a plugin of the host template, u2ue/templates/unreal/Plugins/U2ueAudio, with a judge for its selftest's rendered tone. Its build in a host and its headless play are proven (2026-10-15); an AudioSource mapping is NOT YET (Appendix B).

Animation and physics

There is no worked example for an Animator, Animation Blueprints, Sequencer, or physics simulation: the reference port's units are painted cards whose motion is a rule of the model. ABSENT, said here so nobody reads silence as a recipe (Appendix B).

What none of this proves

A host that compiles is not a port. It is proven by the same model run on both engines and compared - py -m u2ue --project <name> parity, which wraps logic_diff.py (step 7) - and by pixels for the look.

What the field says about the model

What published engines, frameworks and their authors say about the choices this chapter makes: who owns the state, how the core tells the view what happened, and how many interfaces a boundary needs. Each claim is linked to its source, with how sure it is.

Who owns the state

The simulation owns it

The field's answer is not split.

  • Photon Quantum. The Frame is the game state. The Unity view holds none of it and uses the Frame API only to read, because writing from Unity would be non-deterministic; the view polls the frame's generated structs (link).
  • Forge. The framework owns attributes, tags, effect lifecycles, ability grants and cooldowns; engines keep no parallel state.
  • Unity's own guidance. Its testing articles and its ScriptableObject guidance push logic out of MonoBehaviour into plain C#, because a MonoBehaviour cannot be created with new, so it cannot be constructed or mocked in a test (unit testing, data and logic).

Confidence HIGH: three independent sources, one of them the engine vendor a port leaves. None has the model reading state back out of the engine object.

Role interfaces and header interfaces

Cutting a model out of engine classes tends to leave many narrow interfaces, each naming the members one collaboration needs, all implemented by the one engine-side class. Martin Fowler recommends exactly that: it is his RoleInterface, argued for against the HeaderInterface (one interface that mirrors the class), and the only cost he names is the effort of forming each role (RoleInterface). Confidence HIGH on what the page says.

So the case for collapsing them cannot be "role interfaces are bad". Two arguments survive. One is a measurement: with one production implementor nothing is segregated, and every forwarding member and generic parameter pays for a substitutability nobody uses (the reference port's first extraction, 2026-09-30: 130 interfaces, 128 of them with one implementor, and 141 members that only forwarded). The other is the sharper name: when dozens of role interfaces together enumerate the class's whole public surface, member for member, with no transformation, they add up to a header interface split many ways, which Fowler defines and recommends against (HeaderInterface). Role interfaces in construction, one header interface in aggregate explains why each decision looked right and the whole did not.

Names for the fix

Three traditions point the same way:

  • Aggregate (Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design): one object owns a consistency boundary; outside code holds it, not its parts.
  • Humble Object: the hard-to-test environment object becomes a thin shell over a testable core. Its primary page, xunitpatterns.com, refused the connection on 2026-09-30, so it is named here, not quoted.
  • Plain-data components (Quantum's DSL, a domain-specific language; Overwatch's ECS, an entity component system; data-oriented design generally): the state is a struct, there is no interface at all, and systems run over filtered sets of structs.

The third is what the field ships: Quantum did not fix many facets with a better interface; it removed interfaces from the state model. Justify one sealed aggregate with the measured cost (generic parameters and forwarding members that serve one class), not the interface count: on count alone the literature is against you.

Plain data and systems, not interfaces

Quantum declares its game state in a DSL (.qtn files) that generates plain C# structs, attached to entities and used to filter them, for memory layout and generated serialisation and checksums, not polymorphism. There are no per-rule interfaces anywhere in its state model. Confidence HIGH, vendor documentation read directly (link).

Overwatch arrived at the same place independently: strict ECS, server-authoritative, prediction on top (Tim Ford, GDC 2017, "Overwatch Gameplay Architecture and Netcode", video, vault). Confidence MEDIUM: known from several secondary descriptions; the talk was not watched, so it is not quoted.

One aggregate interface and a cue stream

Forge (gamesmiths-guild), an engine-agnostic C# gameplay framework modelled on Unreal's Gameplay Ability System (netstandard2.1 and .NET 8, claiming Unity, Godot and other C# engines), integrates through ONE interface, IForgeEntity (attributes, tags, effects, abilities, events, shared variables), and presents through a "Cues" event system. The framework owns the state; the engine reads it (link). Confidence LOW as proof (32 stars, a README that calls it a work in progress, no multiplayer), HIGH as a data point about shape: someone solving the same problem arrived at one aggregate interface and a cue stream.

How the core tells the view what happened

"The simulation emits events and the view interprets them" is the standard answer, but the field never uses events alone. Two independent shipped systems - one commercial middleware, the other Epic's own framework inside the engine a port moves to - describe the same three-part split.

Poll, events, commands

Poll anything continuous. Quantum's guidance is that polling the simulation from Unity is generally preferable for ongoing visuals, and events are for one-off occurrences. Polling suits values that change often, and a late joiner gets everything it needs from the game state.

Events for one-off occurrences, with their unreliability documented. Quantum events are fire-and-forget, flow from the simulation to the view, and must never change game state; a late joiner does not receive events raised before it joined, and the entity view an event targets may already be destroyed. Epic says the same of Gameplay Cues (the Gameplay Ability System documentation for UE 5.8, read 2026-09-30): they run visual and sound effects and do not use reliable replication, so a client may never receive one, and tying gameplay code to them causes desyncs (link).

Address effects by tag, not by call. This is the part worth copying. A Gameplay Cue is not called: it is associated with Gameplay Tags, and any Gameplay Effect that matches those tags applies it. The simulation applies an effect carrying a tag; the presentation registers handlers against tags; no simulation code names a presentation function.

Commands for the direction that needs an answer, and never synchronous. Quantum Commands carry input from the view into the simulation as DeterministicCommand objects, consumed by the simulation on a later tick that a remote client cannot predict (link). The view asks; the simulation acts on a later frame; nothing blocks.

Confidence HIGH: two independent vendors, both primary documentation, read verbatim, saying the same three things.

Where events break

  • Rollback duplicates events. A frame simulated more than once (prediction, rollback) raises its events more than once. Quantum drops duplicates by a hash over the event's data (nothashed marks the members left out of it) and offers a synced keyword that holds an event until the server confirms the frame.
  • Anything built from events cannot be rebuilt on a late join, a reconnect, a save and load, or a replay scrub.
  • The general form. Fowler, on Event Sourcing: events that send updates to external systems go wrong on replay, because those systems cannot tell replay from real processing; his fix is a Gateway that checks for replay mode before passing a call out (link).

Confidence HIGH on Fowler (primary, read directly) and on Quantum (vendor documentation, read verbatim). A callback from the model into the engine is this general form: a call to an external system that a replay will repeat.

What really needs a synchronous answer

As far as the research could find evidence, fewer things than it seems, and they split two ways:

  • "Can this move?" is a QUERY on the model, not a call into the view. It is a callback only while the state still lives in the engine object; moving the state into the model dissolves it. Keeping queries apart from state-changing commands is CQRS (link), cited as a name, not as game-specific evidence.
  • "Did the player confirm?" is a COMMAND that arrives later, as Quantum's do, processed on a later tick. A playback queue between the model and the host is what makes that possible.

The line for a port: everything shaped "something happened, show it" becomes a tagged event with handlers registered by tag on each engine, which is Epic's own answer inside Unreal; everything continuous is polled off the model; and the residue that truly needs an answer is counted only after the state has moved into the model.

How many ports

Alistair Cockburn calls what is and is not a port in a hexagonal architecture largely a matter of taste: one port per use case would give hundreds, merging them all would give two, and his own choice tends to two, three or four. In the same paragraph he adds that there seems to be no particular damage in choosing the "wrong" number (link). He does not say a high port count is harmful.

Count ports properly: a port is a boundary to an external technology. A model's view seams and platform services ("The model in depth" below) are ports; interfaces the model uses to read its own state are a coupling problem, not a port count. Counted that way, a presentation seam of a few interfaces sits inside his range, and the overshoot is the callbacks from the model into the engine. Confidence VERY HIGH on Cockburn's words, read on the day; the recount is the research's analysis.

One implementor per interface

  • The Reused Abstractions Principle (Jason Gorman): an interface with only one implementation is a code smell. Gorman's own posts returned HTTP 500 on every attempt and were not read. The verified anchor is Mark Seemann, "Interfaces are not abstractions" (2010-12-02), which credits the principle and describes header interfaces as stating the same thing twice (link).
  • The honest counter: Ted Kaminski defends single-implementation interfaces because they cut off transitive dependencies, a benefit that disappears when the interface and its only implementation share a module (link).

So look at where they live. Interfaces in the model's assembly whose one implementor - a MonoBehaviour - lives in the Unity assembly cut a real assembly boundary, which is exactly why the model need not reference UnityEngine. The case for one aggregate is not that they do nothing; it is that one interface cuts the same boundary for a fraction of the price. Confidence HIGH on Seemann and Kaminski (both read directly), MEDIUM on the principle itself (its primary text was not reachable).

Pass-through layers

  • Architecture Sinkhole antipattern (Mark Richards and Neal Ford, Fundamentals of Software Architecture): requests that pass through layers with no business logic applied; Richards' rule of thumb tolerates about 20 % pass-through traffic. The O'Reilly chapter returned 403 and was not read; this is a secondary restatement that cites them (link). A layer that is 100 % pass-through (the reference port's 141 of 141 forwarding members) is five times the tolerated ratio.
  • Middle Man, and its fix Remove Middle Man (Fowler), are the class-level names (link), with the catalogue's own caveat: a middle man made on purpose to cut dependencies, or a Proxy or Decorator, is legitimate.
  • Speculative Generality (Fowler and Beck) is the name for the motive.
  • The sharpest operational test is Aleksey Kladov's "Concrete Abstraction" (2020-08-15): if every call site uses a concrete type, you do not need the abstraction; his case study deleted 124 lines (link). Measure it: count how many of the model's generic type parameters are ever instantiated, outside test doubles, with anything but the one engine-side class. Zero is the whole argument.

Abstraction as speculation

Robert Nystrom, Game Programming Patterns: every layer of abstraction is a bet that the flexibility will be needed; abstractions everywhere make code slow to trace; and modularity that does not turn out useful becomes actively harmful (link). Sandi Metz, "The Wrong Abstraction" (2016): duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction (link). Confidence HIGH that these are the arguments and their sources; both are qualitative, with no measurements.

The performance argument does not apply

Casey Muratori's "Clean Code, Horrible Performance" measures roughly 1.5x from dropping polymorphism and up to about 15x with table-driven rewrites (link), and Mike Acton's CppCon 2014 keynote (video) is a console-engine performance argument. A turn-based rules core that resolves a whole turn at once is not a hot loop: these are bad reasons to collapse a model's interfaces, and should be called bad rather than accepted as a free win.

What the prior art says to do in a port

The lessons above, and Chapter 14's on determinism, as one list in the order to act on them:

  • Settle the motive in writing first (Appendix D, "Test the motive"). It is the only finding that can invalidate a plan rather than adjust it: if the second engine came off the roadmap tomorrow, would the extraction still be worth finishing? If not, the plan rests on one community plugin, tried in one application, with no published case of an engine-free core making a real port cheap.
  • Make byte identity a tripwire, and name the real contract. Neither ECMA-334 nor ECMA-335 promises it, and two JITs are two compilers (Chapter 14, "What the standards allow"). Make the contract the same ordered events with the same identities and values, floats compared to a stated tolerance, and keep the bit-for-bit checksum as the strict check that fires first.
  • Run the explicit-cast experiment before spending anything else on drift: (float)((float)(a * b) / c) against a * b / c, since conv.r4 (the explicit conversion a float cast compiles to) must discard extra precision. Expect it to rule out fused multiply-add, because RyuJIT (.NET's just-in-time compiler) refuses to contract a*b+c and .NET has no fast-math mode; Mono's float32-as-double arithmetic is the better suspect (Chapter 14, "Fused multiply-add, and Mono's float32"; step 7's two fpmode groups are this experiment).
  • Audit the model for the two known non-rounding divergences: any float-to-int cast (undefined on Mono) and any System.Math or MathF call other than Sqrt (measured to differ between operating systems on one .NET build). Both are likelier, larger and cheaper to find than a ULP (Chapter 14, "Two divergences that are not rounding").
  • Guard against what actually desynced shipped games: ambiguous sort comparators, iteration order over hash containers, random-call-count discipline, and number-to-string formatting inside the model (1e-05 against 1e-005). A checksum catches these after the fact; a guard names them (Chapter 14, "What desynced shipped games").
  • Address presentation events by tag, not by method name (Gameplay Cues, above). Events that carry an identifier give a third engine a registry to fill rather than a list of members to implement; converting N callbacks into N named event types moves the problem without solving it.
  • Give those events the three properties the field says they need: cosmetic only, droppable, and rebuildable from state ("Where events break"). The late-joiner rule and the replay rule are the same rule, and it bites on save and load and on scrubbing a replay even in a game with no multiplayer.
  • Sort the callbacks by shape before converting any: punctual (an event), continuous (the view polls it off the model), and needs-an-answer (a query on the model, or a command answered on a later tick). Count the needs-an-answer residue only after the state has moved into the model; counted earlier, callbacks look more necessary than they are.
  • Argue an interface collapse with the sharper names: a header interface in aggregate, the sinkhole ratio, and the count of generic instantiations - and keep Kaminski's defence in view, so the refactor does not throw away interfaces that cut a real assembly boundary.
  • Write the presentation gaps on the second engine down as a feature matrix, as the READMEs of Spine (animation middleware with a Unity and an Unreal runtime, Appendix D) do, not as a to-do list.
  • Decide whether consoles are in scope, because it has an architectural consequence today (Appendix D, "Platforms").

The logic playbook: the u2ue-logic skill in full

Everything that is not logic ports itself: the effects through the u2ue-port skill, scenes through u2ue scene, screens through u2ue ui, data through u2ue data. Logic is the one part a person or an AI model ports by hand. This section is the method above as the skill file u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md holds it, one slice at a time: each step with the command that runs it and the observable that says it is done, pointing back to the method or a topic for the background. Chapter 15 covers running it with an AI agent over a long port.

The acceptance test: the game's rules run in ONE engine-free model; Unity, the Unreal host and a headless runner give the same bits for every case (u2ue parity exits 0); and the game as the owner plays it still works.

Scope: a Unity game's C# - its MonoBehaviours, coroutines and frame order - and the engine-free model it moves into. Precondition: the game's Unity project is on disk serialized as text, and a project file names it. Stakeholders: the porter wants the game running on Unreal, the same; the owner wants only their decisions asked; a reviewer wants the design reviewable from its class model, not line by line. Minimal guarantee: nothing is invented - a rule that cannot move is named with its reason, and a red gate stops the step. Success guarantee: the rules run in one model, Unity's runtime and the Unreal host give the same bits, and the game still plays.

Kickoff prompt

The owner pastes this to an agent, with the two names filled in:

Port the logic of the Unity game at <UNITY PROJECT ROOT> with u2ue, project name <name>. Follow the u2ue-logic skill step by step. One slice at a time, smallest first. Do every step's RUN, and do not start the next step until its DONE WHEN is true. Draw the class model before moving code. Ask me only for the decisions the skill names as the owner's.

The bones: each concept one thing

The analogy is the handle; the class is the truth.

  • Project (u2ue/projects/<name>.json) - the game's address book: every path, named once.
  • Inventory (u2ue inventory) - the survey of the house before the move: every type, what it touches in Unity, which are already furniture that moves as it is (pure rules), and the order the rooms are walked in each frame.
  • Core (<Model>.Core, made by u2ue scaffold) - the rulebook: what happens, never how it looks. No engine in it.
  • Aggregate - ONE class per entity holds its state (a unit, a card, a board); the engine's object HOLDS one and forwards to it. Never forty little interfaces over one MonoBehaviour: the shape adds code and makes nothing testable ("What a second game writes" has the measurement).
  • Seam - the plug sockets: the platform seam (logging, files, preferences, JSON, random numbers - U2ue.Runtime.Platform), the view seam (what draws), the capability seam (optional extras on top of the view seam, "The interface set" below). An engine implements a seam; the Core declares it.
  • Event stream - the referee's call sheet: rules resolve a whole action INSTANTLY and append ordered events. The model never waits.
  • PlaybackQueue (U2ue.Runtime.PlaybackQueue<TEvent>) - the replay operator: one event per frame, only when the view is idle; input waits for IsCaughtUp.
  • UnityFrame (U2ue.Runtime.UnityFrame with Coroutines and UnityClock) - Unity's frame order (Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, LateUpdate) as one object an engine ticks once per frame.
  • Digest (U2ue.Runtime.Digest) - one engine's answer sheet; parity (u2ue parity) marks the sheets against each other, bit for bit.
  • Host - the engine's side: a Unity MonoBehaviour or an Unreal actor that holds the aggregate, feeds input and presents events.

The law of the playbook

It overrides speed and tidiness:

  • READ or ABSENT - a value in the model comes from the game's code or data, with where it came from; never a plausible constant.
  • No fallbacks - a rule that cannot resolve throws and names what is missing; catch {} and a default are the same lie.
  • Move, do not rewrite - the rule's code moves into the Core as it is; a behaviour change is a separate, named decision.
  • The model knows no engine - u2ue check --only model after every move; a red gate stops the move.
  • A check that has only passed proves nothing - every gate here has a plant it must fail (--selftest); run it once.
  • The owner's editors are the owner's - never the Unity Test Runner; Unity runs only in a window the owner allows; one headless Unreal at a time; never a modal answered for them.

The playbook's steps

Each step has a DO (what to do), a RUN (the command; every one exists and runs, and skill_gate.py checks that) and a DONE WHEN (the observable that ends it). py -m u2ue --project <name> logic judges each step's DONE WHEN from the records and says where a port stands.

Before you start: name the project

  • Do: write u2ue/projects/<name>.json from the complete example in Chapter 3, and fill in the Unity root, its version and the work folders. For a port already under way, ask where it stands first and resume at the step it names next - never re-derive the state from the files.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> info, then py -m u2ue --project <name> logic.
  • Done when: info exits 0 - every path it names opened.

Step 1. Read the game before touching it

  • Do: survey the Assets folders, name the game's OWN code folders as code.roots (vendor packages live in Assets too - never guess which are the game's), then inventory them. Read inventory.md: the pure-rule types, each MonoBehaviour's Unity families, the frame-order table.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory --survey, then py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory.
  • Done when: inventory.json lists every type with its kind, and you can name the ten purest types and the five heaviest Unity users.
  • Trap: the reader is lexical - a call through reflection or a helper is not seen; a miss is UNKNOWN, never "does not use".
  • Trap: "pure" means no Unity API AND no Unity value type: a rule that does Vector3 maths cannot move as written (the method's step 1).

Step 2. Draw the class model of ONE slice before moving anything

  • Do: pick the first slice - one feature whose rules use the fewest Unity families (a damage formula, a scoring rule, an inventory stack). Extract the class model over the game's code roots, draw the slice's types, and write the TARGET diagram: which types become the aggregate, which stay hosts, which seams appear. The diagram is the plan a person reviews; the code follows it.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> uml extract, then py -m u2ue --project <name> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>.
  • Done when: the slice's current and target diagrams exist, and every name in them resolves (uml where <Name>).

Step 3. Sort the slice's types and members

  • Do: give every type in the slice ONE destination - CORE (a pure rule: it moves as it is), AGGREGATE (the state and rules inside a MonoBehaviour: they move into one Core class the MonoBehaviour then holds), HOST (what only an engine can do: draw, play, read input) or SEAM (a platform chore). Label each member the host keeps by its kind - PUNCTUAL, ONGOING, MUTATION, ANSWER or CONTROL (the table in "What a second game writes" says what each one is and what it costs an engine).
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory.
  • Done when: the target diagram carries every type's destination and every kept host member's kind.
  • Absent: a host-kind census for any game's model. Label by hand by the rule above: a non-void member is an ANSWER.

Step 4. Cut the Core

  • Do: create the engine-free model OUTSIDE the Unity Assets tree, declared in the project file.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> scaffold --name <Model> --dir <folder>.
  • Done when: scaffold exits 0 - both projects build and the model gates PASS on the empty Core.

Step 5. Put the platform seam in first

  • Do: every log line, file read, preference, JSON document and random draw the slice makes goes through U2ue.Runtime.Platform (ILog, ITextAssets, IKeyValueStore, IFileStore, IJsonCodec<T>, IRandomSource / SeededRandom) - never re-declared on a rule's host. The reference port found a log line declared on five hosts and a random draw on seven before it did this.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model, then dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests.
  • Done when: host_gate PASSES and no rule in the slice calls Debug.Log, Random, PlayerPrefs, File or JsonUtility directly.

Step 6. Move the slice's rules into the Core

  • Do: move the code (do not rewrite it) into the aggregate; the MonoBehaviour now holds one aggregate and forwards its properties to it, so state has one home. A rule that waited (a coroutine, WaitForSeconds) becomes a step the host advances - the model never awaits. A rule doing Unity value-type maths (Vector3, Mathf) waits for the owner's one decision ("Floats across runtimes" above); take the float-only rules first. Write one test per moved rule in <Model>.Core.Tests, with the value the Unity build gives.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model, then dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests.
  • Done when: both gates PASS, the slice's tests pass, and the Unity project still compiles with the MonoBehaviour holding the aggregate.

Step 7. Emit events; replay them

  • Do: each rule that changes what the player sees appends an event to an ordered, append-only list instead of calling the view. The host replays the list through PlaybackQueue<TEvent> with a presenter that is idle when its animation ends; input is taken only when IsCaughtUp.
  • Run: dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests, then dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests.
  • Done when: a test runs the slice's action headlessly and asserts the event list, in order.

Step 8. Keep Unity's frame order

  • Do: per-frame code the slice keeps (Update, LateUpdate, coroutines) registers with ONE UnityFrame in its script execution order (the inventory's frame-order table, read from the .cs.meta files); coroutines run on U2ue.Runtime.Coroutines. Never one engine tick per former MonoBehaviour - the order between them IS the behaviour.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> inventory, then dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests.
  • Done when: every kept per-frame method is registered with the order the inventory lists for its type.

Step 9. Prove it: the same answers, by the bit

  • Do: write the slice's cases ONCE, as a static method returning a Digest (no NUnit in that file), driving the moved rules the way the game drives them (its own constants, READ with file and line). u2ue digest run compiles them twice - for CoreCLR (Headless: what an Unreal host runs) and for the project's Unity version's OWN Mono (UnityMono: no Editor opens) - and writes both sheets into parity.dir. Bump the digest's version whenever the case set changes.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs>, then py -m u2ue --project <name> parity.
  • Done when: parity exits 0 across Headless and UnityMono, and any characterised row (parity --characterise) carries its measured cause.
  • Trap: the cases' INPUTS must be exact on every runtime - make them by integer arithmetic and write each one to the sheet (_in rows). Measured on the second game's first slice: a driver that made its own target angles with float maths produced 177 false differences in 321 rows; with exact inputs the rule's true difference was 2 rows.
