  • Trap: UnityMono is Unity's runtime, not the Editor. u2ue digest faithful measures one against the other on an Editor-recorded digest (Unity 6000.3: 383 of 383 rows identical); a Unity version without that measurement is labelled UNMEASURED in the provenance, and its Mono answer is not called the Editor's.

Step 10. The Unreal host

  • Do: the game gets its OWN .uproject, made by u2ue host the way a customer makes one: name it in the project file's unreal.host block (the template, each plugin with its source and pinned commit, the AutoSDK root, the digest's entry and cases), then run the steps in order from native PowerShell - the Unreal steps refuse while an Unreal runs, and each step is judged by its proof line, never by an exit code. wire references <Model>.Core, compiles the digest cases in, COPIES the toolkit's Unreal templates into the managed project (u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal: AU2ueFrameActor, which ticks UnityFrame, UnrealPointer, UnrealCameraRig and UnrealPlatform.cs; the method's step 8) and writes the module that answers the digest; run starts the host headless, and it writes logic-Unreal.txt from the same cases. Grow the host from there: it holds the aggregate and presents events through PlaybackQueue.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> host plan; py -m u2ue --project <name> host create (then install, compile, generate, wire, publish, run, one at a time); py -m u2ue --project <name> host status; dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal.
  • Run: py -m u2ue.seam --project <name> --list names every seam the model declares that no model type fills and the Unreal host does not fill yet (the project's model.hosts says where each engine's host code is) - each a socket to implement, or one the host says it leaves out, and why.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> parity --require Unreal.
  • Done when: parity exits 0 across Headless, Unity and Unreal.
  • Measured: a second game's host was made this way from nothing in 9 minutes (the compile 255 s), and its digest equalled the headless CoreCLR one byte for byte. Absent: a generic publish proof by the loaded assembly's MVID (the module version id in a .NET assembly's metadata, G6 below); until it lands, run proves the host ran THIS publish only by the digest it wrote after the start.

Step 11. Record the slice and take the next one

  • Do: write the slice's record to <work.effects>/slices/slice-<N>.json (logic reads it there) - the slice, its first commit and its parity commit (the tempo), and the gates' output - and take the next slice, bigger. Each slice's diagram joins the game's model.
  • Run: py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only model.
  • Done when: the record names both commits and the parity verdict, and the next slice is chosen.

When to stop and ask the owner

A behaviour change a rule would need (a bug the port would fix), where Unity's value types live for the Core, where the game's Unreal host lives, anything that would run in the owner's live editor, and anything outward-facing. Ask one precise question, and take the next slice meanwhile.

The model in depth: what a second game implements

This section is the architecture your game's model implements - the layers, the seams and the contract between them - as rules, each with the reference port's version as its worked example. Implementing the adapters is your work; a port is not finished until a person PLAYS the Unreal build, attended.

Three things to read before the rest:

  • Read the gates (below) before the recipe. A green summary that was not measured is the exact failure the gates exist to catch: byte-identical means cmp exit 0, quoted, never a summary.
  • The event stream is half the seam. The interfaces say what an engine must implement; the stream says what the model must tell it. Measured on the reference port: most early drawing faults were the model leaving something unsaid, or saying it twice, while every interface was implemented correctly and the picture was still wrong.
  • The shim is not the architecture. Emulating namespace UnityEngine (a shim such as the reference port's UnityCompat.Core and UnityCompat.Engine) lets Unity-shaped code compile anywhere, but your game should not build its model on it ("The shim route" below says why).

The layers, as they are on disk

  • The Core is the engine-free model. Its project file holds no Reference, ProjectReference or PackageReference that leads to an engine - scaffold makes one whose only reference is U2ue.Runtime, itself engine-free - and that emptiness is the whole design: there is nothing for an engine to arrive through. It is multi-targeted for every host (scaffold writes netstandard2.1;net8.0), so one assembly serves Unity as a managed plugin, the headless suites and UnrealSharp. The model is (state, seed) -> state. It never waits: a grep for yield return or yield break over its sources must count 0 (an IEnumerator in a comment is prose). Check that with a search, not memory.
  • The platform seam is the six interfaces of U2ue.Runtime.Platform, declared once ("The platform seam" below); a domain host (one of the I*Host interfaces of "Finding things" above) declares only domain callbacks.
  • The presentation layer is the view seam: the view interfaces plus the replay that drives them (PlaybackQueue, the board as shown, one format for view calls). It references the Core and never the reverse. Every method is a GAME VERB (Place(id, cell)), never an engine primitive.
  • The engine adapters, one set per engine: the entity view, camera director, effect player and input source, and the six platform services (on Unreal, the template's UnrealPlatform.cs).

The interface set

The BASE set your game implements is five view interfaces (the four a board needs, plus IHudView) and six platform services. On top sits the optional capability seam: interfaces an engine implements when it draws more of the game than the base calls say. Every other interface in a model is a domain host or a facet of that game's rules, and your game declares its own, because they are its rules.

The view seam

The reference port's view interfaces are the worked example; the rules they follow are what transfers.

  • IEntityView draws the world. Every call is a statement about what the player should now see, never a question: spawn, place (no travel), move (the view owns the duration and the path's shape), show a health change with the HP remaining, kill, despawn (removal with no death), and an IsIdle. There is deliberately no IUnitView and no ITileView: Unity spawns a GameObject per entity while Unreal can draw tiles as instanced meshes, both satisfy one interface, and the model never learns which. If a new entity kind forces a new method, the abstraction has drifted and the fix belongs in this interface, not in another.
  • ICameraDirector frames the action: play a beat on a focus entity, and an IsIdle. The model NEVER mentions a beat: the presentation derives beats from the event stream, which is what frees Unreal to use Sequencer and look nothing like Unity.
  • IEffectPlayer is effects and sound together, because an impact is a flash AND a thud, and splitting them makes every caller coordinate two things that always fire together. Its effectKey names the effect in the GAME's vocabulary, never an engine asset path; the adapter maps it to a Shuriken system or a Niagara asset, and that mapping is the one place the two engines may disagree about what an effect looks like.
  • IInputSource is the only way anything reaches the model, and it is pull-based on purpose: a push callback would run the model from inside an engine's input handler, the inversion the event stream exists to avoid. Its commands are GAME verbs, and the command type lives in the Core, because a command the model consumes cannot live above the model. A verb like "select cell" or "confirm" describes a mouse, not the game.
  • One object is all an adapter hands over (the reference port's PresentationHost): the entities, camera, effects and input views, an optional HUD (none for a headless run), and an IsIdle that ANDs the idling views. One object beats five constructor parameters threaded everywhere.
  • IHudView draws the HUD from the board AS SHOWN (the reference port's ShownState), and is handed nothing else. The replay (there, its PlaybackQueue) calls it after the initial board and after every event it shows, at the pace of the view calls, so the HUD is never ahead of the animation. It cannot show the verdict while the killing blow is still in flight - which is exactly what a HUD bound to the model would do, because the model resolves a whole turn instantly. The HUD is not part of IsIdle: it owes no animation, so the replay never waits on it.
  • One recorder both engines and the headless suite use: a view double that writes one line per view call. Beats are derived in the replay itself; there is no separate beat-policy interface.

The capability seam

The base calls say WHAT happened; they cannot say how Unity paces and frames it (a settle before an effect, a zoom on a target, a cutscene's flight, a banner's wait). Porting those rules engine-free leaves three decisions:

  • The replay (PlaybackQueue) stays ONE switch. It never forks per engine. For each optional surface it tests the host's view with is against that surface's interface; a view that is not one gets the BASE call instead (a PlayBeat, a Play), exactly what it got before the capability existed.
  • The recorder (the reference port's RecordingView) records "the base call it replaces, or nothing". Alone (the headless suite) it answers as a view WITHOUT the capability; wrapped around a drawing view it forwards, and a drawing view that LACKS a capability makes it THROW - never a silent skip. So a run shown through the capability path records line for line what the base path records, and no recorded stream moves when a capability lands.
  • One frame object owns the one-tick order and ONE clock (Unity's frame, as UnityFrame holds it), so an adapter is a per-tick COPIER of engine-free state plus a click source.

A capability extends one base view (the entity view, the camera director, the effect player or IHudView) and records what its base call records. A new surface gets its own READ record (one data file per surface), never new lines in an existing slice, so a recording made before the surface existed stays valid.

The platform seam

These six are what any game implements the SAME WAY; that is the test for belonging here. The toolkit ships them as U2ue.Runtime.Platform:

interface members the rule its implementations taught
ILog void Info(string), void Warn(string), void Error(string) a three-level log is the smallest complete logging seam, even before anything calls ILog.Error
ITextAssets string LoadText(string resourcePath) NULL is the ABSENT signal and the only one; an existing but empty asset returns "" and parses as zero rows. On Unreal, resolve a carried text through the copy's manifest, never by guessing an extension
IKeyValueStore int GetInt(string,int), void SetInt(string,int), string GetString(string,string), void SetString(string,string), void DeleteKey(string), void Save() PlayerPrefs' own flush semantics: Set changes memory, Save writes the file
IFileStore string RootPath { get; }, bool DirectoryExists(string), void CreateDirectory(string), bool FileExists(string), string ReadAllText(string), void WriteAllText(string,string) a platform seam must not name a Unity folder (RootPath, not StreamingAssetsPath). Shipped data and save data are two stores, because one root cannot be both
IJsonCodec<T> string ToJson(T), T FromJson(string) on Unreal, System.Text.Json with IncludeFields = true - that option is the whole implementation: without it a game's fields serialise to {}
IRandomSource float Value(), int Range(int minInclusive, int maxExclusive), float Range(float minInclusive, float maxInclusive) the two Range overloads have DIFFERENT bounds, as Unity's do (int upper-exclusive, float both-inclusive), and getting that wrong compiles perfectly

Three more rules from the random source:

  • A seeded System.Random was measured bit-identical across Mono 6.13, .NET 8.0.22 and .NET 10.0.12 (the reference port, 2026-09-27), which is why one seed is one game on all three runtimes.
  • Keep the game rules' stream private to the model's own SeededRandom, and give the host's random service only to what is NOT the rules; handing the rules a host stream would end the byte-identical event log. A Value() meant to reach the float overload's inclusive maximum cannot be built on NextDouble(), which is [0, 1); the template's UnrealRandomSource returns Next(0, 1 << 24) / (float)((1 << 24) - 1). Unreal's own FMath::Rand is not in UnrealSharp's managed glue, so System.Random is the runtime's own there.
  • IRandomSource is the member that proves the seam is worth having: before the seam, the reference port declared the same draw on several domain hosts under different names (step 5's count). host_gate.py refuses every one of those names outside the hosting folder, so the leak cannot come back under a new spelling.

The event stream contract: what the model must SAY

The view interfaces are the engine's half of the seam. The other half is the model's event list: ordered, append-only, written through one sink, read by PlaybackQueue, which turns it into view calls at the view's pace. An engine draws ONLY what the stream says, so everything a player must see has to be said, once, with what a view needs to draw it. On the reference port a headless suite that plays every authored action on a test board went looking for violations and found eleven classes of them - every one the model's, not an adapter's. These rules fixed them, and your model should be held to them from its first event:

  • Every HP change is announced, with the HP LEFT - the delta and the remainder, because a health bar needs both. Silent writes are the trap (damage over time, reflected damage, an aura's victims, an action's own HP price). The check: every step's HP difference must be the stream's last word on it.
  • A status's tick is ONE announcement, its only HP event; the damage inside it says nothing more, or the same HP drops twice. A tick that moved no HP shows no number.
  • Every effect event names the square its effect plays on. An event left at the default cell asks for its effect at the board's origin and nothing else fails, so it is invisible until someone looks. That happened four separate times.
  • What a HUD shows is announced, not inferred: an action-point change with its delta and total, from ONE sweep in the flow, not from each place that writes it; a status leaving, one event per entry, from the one method entries leave through.
  • A unit an action moves is announced like a walk. A move the stream never states leaves the unit's view on the wrong square until its next walk.
  • Say each fact in ONE layer, and choose that layer on day one. A fact said in two layers makes the presenter tell the copies apart; a model that says each once needs no dedupe rules.
  • Durations are what the entry was GIVEN after every rule that touched it, not the authored number.
  • An end-of-turn tick of an action is its own event, and names the action. Whether a tick SHOWS anything is the presentation's decision, never the model's.

What it costs to check: the suite turns each rule into an expectation over every case, and each is proven able to fail by a planted fault. One was VACUOUS until a case existed that moves a unit - a gate that has only ever passed cannot be told from one switched off. Copy the suite's shape, not just the rules.

The recipe a second game follows

The playbook above is the order of work for one slice; this recipe is the order for the adapters around the model, with what each step guards against.

Step 1 - write the Core (the playbook's step 4): model state and rules only, no engine reference. Do not trust yourself about a stray using UnityEngine or using UnrealSharp, or an engine build that source-links .cs files out of another engine's tree: layer_gate.py checks both (G1 below), and its --selftest must FAIL on a planted using and a planted <Compile Include> before a PASS means anything.

Step 2 - cut the platform seam FIRST, not last (the playbook's step 5). Every log line, file, preference, JSON document or random draw declared on a domain host is surface a second engine has to implement again. Give host_gate.py your member names.

Step 3 - the engine class PRESENTS events; it never sequences a turn. This is the step that most looks like the old code and most must not be. The flow is INSTANT: it takes state and a seed, runs the whole action, and appends an ordered, immutable event list. The ENGINE ADAPTER owns a PlaybackQueue: the queue accepts the list (Accept), shows one event per frame into the views (Tick()), and exposes its Backlog and IsCaughtUp. Input is GATED on IsCaughtUp, so a player cannot act into an animation they have not seen; the adapter's IInputSource builds the commands, and the queue asks for one only once the views are idle. Three measured reasons this is not negotiable: a (state, seed) -> state model is why the reference port's Unreal side could run a whole game with no world at all; awaiting inverts control into every coroutine site; and different effect lengths per engine would otherwise take different code paths per engine.

Step 4 - write ONE adapter and prove it headlessly before writing a second. A view double prints one line per view call; that printed slice is the artifact everything else diffs against, so write it before any engine is involved.

Step 5 - write the second adapter and diff the slices byte for byte. Not "looks the same": cmp exit 0.

Step 6 - keep the model as a compiled artifact both engines LOAD, and prove the artifact is the one they loaded. This catches the failure nobody sees: an engine running a two-day-old model and producing a beautiful, stale, byte-identical artifact. Measured on the reference port, both engines did it with nothing saying so - Unity's plugin DLLs left stale, and Unreal's made stale minutes after a clean publish by an edit to the model's source. G4 (plugin_sync_gate.py) and G6 below catch it. Run G4 at the start of every session as well: a model source newer than the DLL an engine loads is the stale state, found before anything is built on it.

Step 7 - know what your reference checksum does NOT cover. A byte-identical reference run proves the MODEL on every engine. It does not exercise the engine's own game object at all if that object is not what the reference run plays on - on the reference port, every engine's reference run used the model's aggregate while the game as played ran a Unity MonoBehaviour. A refactor of the engine object therefore needs the engine's OWN game played as its gate, before and after, beside the checksum: a real game driven in Play, every exception attributed. That driver walks one game's own flow, so the package does not ship one: write yours against your game.

What a second game writes

  • Its own Core, all of it. The reference port's interfaces are its own rules (a damage formula, a type chart, and so on); your game declares its own. Nothing here is a framework to inherit from. What transfers is the SHAPE: domain hosts for "a question the model needs answered, or an announcement only the game can render", and nothing else on them.
  • One engine-free aggregate per entity - not a header interface split into facets. Measured on the reference port: one MonoBehaviour implemented 40 facets through 144 explicit pass-through members, one property was declared by seven of them, and exactly one production type implemented all 40, so nothing was segregated where it ships. Give the rules one aggregate per entity, let the engine's object HOLD one and forward its properties, and cut an interface only where a second implementor supplies it differently.
  • The host seam sorted into five kinds before it is ported, because they cost a second engine very different amounts:
kind what it says what it costs an engine
PUNCTUAL "a thing happened" one KEY-ADDRESSED registry per engine, not one implementation per member
ONGOING "a value is now X" one polling loop: the view reads the value each frame
MUTATION the model asking the engine to change state it owns nothing, eventually: it is model state living in the engine object, and it goes away with the aggregate
ANSWER returns a value real work per engine while the value lives outside the model
CONTROL menus, the AI's turn, the camera real work per engine, and honest

Only the last two are irreducible. Measured on the reference port (435 host members, 141 of them ANSWER or CONTROL), most ANSWERs existed only because the entity's state lived in the MonoBehaviour, so the aggregate removes them. - Art addressed by a KEY the model owns and a TABLE each engine owns. The model's own resolver turns an entity into a file name, a test runs it over the disk to write a table (READ or ABSENT per row, never a guess), and each engine resolves the same key to its own imported asset and FAILS LOUDLY, naming the path, when it is missing. Effects already work this way (IEffectPlayer takes a string key). Give your adapters a gate that refuses a placeholder primitive (a cube, a sphere) in a missing asset's place: a plausible frame with the wrong geometry is the failure that hides longest. - Six platform service implementations - every member is one engine call. - The view adapters per engine - the real work, and bounded: the reference port's are 16 methods and 4 properties in all. - Nothing else. No serialisation format, no message bus, no scripting layer. A JSON bridge between the engines loses to event-log replay, because a bridge makes every value cross a wire and a replay makes every value a diff.

The model's gates, G1 to G7

Copy these. Each exists because something passed every other instrument while broken; what transfers is what each checks and the trap that made it. u2ue check --only model runs G1 and the platform-seam gate from the project file.

  • G1 the layer boundary - py layer_gate.py, and its --selftest. No banned namespace in the model's projects, no unaccounted source link out of another engine's tree, and the accounted links kept on a ratchet file that must empty. Its selftest plants a <Compile Include> under the Unity tree and must report FAIL before a PASS means anything.
  • G2 the model's own suite - dotnet test of the model's tests, no engine in the process. Keep in it the tests that assert the cross-engine claim (the Unity build's native run equals the headless reference): they go red after every model change until the Unity side is re-recorded against the new model, as they should. The cure is the plugin sync (G4) and a re-record, never an edit to the test. Beside it, a second suite that plays every authored action headlessly, every expectation READ from the game's data with its provenance or ABSENT with the reason.
  • G3 it compiles on every host - py typecheck.py (the Unity side, headless Roslyn, no editor) and dotnet build of the engine's managed project.
  • G4 the artifact both engines load is the current source - py plugin_sync_gate.py hashes every plugin DLL against what the source builds now; --sync copies them. The order after a sync is: recompile, wait for the domain reload to SETTLE (not compiling, three times running), console_check (the Unity console gate, "The model's tools" below), then the native re-run. A fresh recording timestamp is NOT proof of a fresh assembly: an editor whose compile fails keeps the old one and records against it happily. Run this gate BEFORE any cross-engine diff, never after, because a stale plugin makes every later comparison one of two different games, and nothing in a diff says which side is stale.
  • G5 the slice is byte-identical across engines - cmp, exit 0, on the printed view-call slice and on the event log, and the exit code quoted; not a diff summary, not an md5 quoted in prose. A slice of 31 lines against one of 55 is a DIFFERENT GAME, not a near miss, and the entity ids give it away. An exit 2 (no such file) is the honest row: that side was never produced.
  • G6 the publish proof - before believing ANY artifact an engine produced: sha256sum every DLL in the engine's managed output; read the MVID from the #GUID heap of the CLI metadata of the model DLL there and of the one the current source just built; compare them; and compare each artifact's mtime against the DLL's. A mismatch, or an artifact OLDER than the DLL, means the engine ran a stale model and every artifact since the last publish is not proven. Reading the MVID is about 40 lines of Python, and it is the only thing that tells a fresh byte-identical run from a stale one. The reference port's gate for this names its own DLLs and is not in the package; write yours from this description. Make the run write its own run-manifest.txt naming the assembly it bound (by a type's assembly, not by searching for a name), written on arming so a crashed run still leaves one. The publish recipe, each part a trap met:
  • RunUAT.bat BuildUserSolution -ScriptsForProject=<uproject> -Project=<uproject> -OutputPath=<dir> ONCE PER PATH (Binaries/Managed and Binaries/Managed/net10.0), in Release. Its success line on Unreal 5.7 is AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success); Result: Succeeded is the C++ compile's line, which a publish never prints, so a grep for it finds nothing.
  • The proof run goes through one launcher (the package's scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1, as -game -RenderOffScreen -unattended), with the run's trigger file dropped FIRST; without it the module's startup digest does not run, and a stale logic-Unreal.txt is refused as older than the DLLs.
  • Launch from native PowerShell: UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the literal Program Files\dotnet\ on the PATH.
  • A publish does NOT need the editor closed, because UnrealSharp hot-reloads the DLLs. What must not happen while the owner's editor is open is WRITING the model's sources: a hot reload that lands mid-write fails to compile and can wedge the editor (Chapter 16).
  • Removing a reference does not remove the DLL. A runtime that probes a directory can still bind what the build no longer names; the publish gate fails if an old DLL comes back, and its selftest plants one to prove it.
  • G7 the game actually plays - enter play on the real scene, drive it to a verdict, and capture BOTH a JSON outcome and a PNG; then read the PNG. A gate that reads only the JSON cannot tell a played game from a black screen (Chapter 9 has the measured case). Its second half is easy to skip: console_check with --reset BEFORE the run and again after, and the count of new console errors (consoleNewErrors) is part of the verdict - one new error is RED, not "passed with a note". Three traps in how a result reads on disk: a JSON that exists is not a run, and ok:true is about the HTTP call, not the game (one such file said "ok":true with "turnsTaken":0: it had held a menu and never played); a run that hits a turn cap (TURN_CAP) proves the loop keeps running, not that the rules can end a game; only a real verdict row ("outcome":"DEFEAT", or a win) proves that. And a Unity run driven by a script writes to a scratch folder, never to the folder that holds the reference recording. Give your recorder no default output folder: the reference port's defaulted to the reference directory, so one forgotten option overwrote the recording.

The headless UI capture trap. On Unreal, HighResShot does NOT capture UMG or Slate: a magenta rect painted at FLinearColor(1,0,1,1) over 30720 known pixels read rgb(12,4,1) in a HighResShot frame, identical to a control frame with no widget at all, while the engine's own screenshot showui captured it exactly, 30720 of 30720 pixels at rgb(255,0,255) (the reference port, 2026-09-29). Every HUD capture uses screenshot showui. Finding that before writing a HUD is the point of a probe.

What stays engine-specific, and why

What a port keeps engine-specific, and the rule each item teaches (measured on the reference port, 2026-09-30):

  • Find a moved file's closure with the compiler, in passes. When an engine project stops source-linking game files out of the Unity tree, most links turn out to be needed only by other linked files; the compiler names the rest, and they MOVE into the model byte for byte, keeping their global namespace so no Unity call site needs a using. It takes several builds: a CS0246 on one type stops the binder from naming what the next expression would have needed. The links that remain are deliberate: the measurement pair (float bits, the digest writer) compiled identically into every host, source-linked so there is ONE spelling.
  • Exercise every platform service on real data at start-up, and write what it answered beside the run's artifacts (the reference port's Unreal side writes platform-Unreal.txt), because a host that compiles and answers null for everything cannot be told from a game that ships no data.
  • A behaviour with no equivalent is REFUSED with its reason, not faked. The conformance oracle (conformance_diff --require Unity Unreal) records one failure on the reference port - forward after a 90-degree yaw read (2.220446E-16, 1, 0) where (1, 0, 0) was expected, an axis convention, not rounding - and two skips: Unity's 32 named layers (Unreal uses collision channels and traces) and the screen size (a rendering concern out of parity scope; inventing 1920x1080 would be a fabricated value). A SKIP is an honest gap, recorded apart from a PASS.
  • The float difference is characterised, not waved through (step 7). Every differing row is pinned in logic-allowance.json to its exact bits AND to 1 ULP, so a new row, a moved value or a wider gap is still red; an allowance that let every float difference through would be a fallback, not a gate (logic_diff.py's header records the measurement). The difference is latent in a game's own arithmetic, not caused by the port: any game meets it the moment it runs the same code on two runtimes.
  • Count the seam honestly; do not go looking for a kernel. Your game's seam is the interface set above plus its own domain hosts; a single board interface or a shared kernel package is not the goal. The HUD contract (IHudView, drawn from the board as shown) is the one to copy rather than invent.
  • Expect the Unity side to keep its old shape for a long time. The Unreal side is written once, against the seam; on the reference port the Unity side still nested random sources privately in game files and called JsonUtility directly.
  • A logic gate's captures are greybox, and a capture manifest must be able to fail. Conformance-harness renders (cubes and grey tiles) are right for a logic gate and not to be read as the game. Record an md5 and a byte size per frame on every engine: a manifest that records only a label cannot detect a repeated frame. A capture gate opens the PNG - one effect capture on the reference port caught a loading screen at 0 percent instead of the effect.
  • A test that re-implements the rule it tests passes when the product is wrong. The reference port's Unity-side suite declared simulation types in 48 files, and at least fourteen were static classes holding a SECOND copy of a game rule; a green suite of that shape is not by itself evidence about the model.
  • Decide the logic port's scope, and say it. Logic parity and rendering parity are separate questions; the owner decides whether rendering parity is in the logic port's scope, and nothing above is a rendering complaint.

Traps the model work met

Each was met on the reference port and still bites:

  • Read every engine member from metadata, never from memory. UnrealLogger.Log(logName, message, verbosity) takes the CATEGORY first and the message second; both are strings, so the wrong order compiles perfectly and logs nonsense. Keep a seam map re-verified on every run, with an impossible sentinel row that must report STALE, so the verdicts cannot be assumed.
  • UnrealSharp conventions the compiler is the right oracle for: [UClass] types must be partial (its source generator writes the other half), and AActor.BeginPlay is public virtual, not protected.
  • AStaticMeshActor's root is Static, and a Static component refuses every move in a game world. Set Mobility to Movable and READ IT BACK at spawn, and use the move FUNCTIONS rather than the RelativeLocation UPROPERTY, which never updates ComponentToWorld.
  • AActor.GetAttachedActors returns children REVERSED. Record the order SetParent was asked for and cross-check the count with the engine's.
  • The Unreal editor world never ticks actors outside Simulate or PIE (Play In Editor): -run=pythonscript asserts and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. A host that must tick has to be IN a world; run it headless as UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <uproject> <Map> -game -nullrhi -unattended -nosplash.
  • A configured value says so where it is declared. An engine backend that needs a value the engine does not have names where its value came from: a FrameCount kept as its own tick count (Unreal exposes no frame counter to managed code), a FixedDeltaTime set to Unity's 0.02 default (Unreal has no fixed timestep). Naming the provenance is the difference between a configured constant and a fabricated one.
  • A managed reference does not keep an Unreal asset alive. Unreal's garbage collector sees only what the ENGINE holds (UPROPERTYs, the root set, strong pointers); a C# field, a Dictionary cache or a plain C# property on a managed [UClass] is invisible to it. A cache of StaticLoadObject textures handed back a texture the collector was purging (it purges over several frames, and UnrealSharp zeroes the managed wrapper only at the final free, so IsValid does not save you in between): the renderer died with Texture not valid! UE-23902! and then an access violation, six minutes into a long run. Root every asset a cache keeps with UnrealSharp's TStrongObjectPtr<T>, and assert liveness on every cache hit. Make a GC bug deterministic before fixing it: -ExecCmds="gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects 0.5" (a collection every half second) turned the six-minute crash into one in 32 seconds, every time. Run long runs under that pressure, and fail a run whose log shows the default rate.
  • Move a rule into the model without touching a single call site. When the game's scripts live in the global namespace, C# resolves a global type before one a using imports, so a rule can be added to the model while the Unity copy still exists, the plugin synced, and only THEN the Unity copy deleted: every call site resolves to the model's copy unchanged. Two traps on the way: an alias such as using X = Rule.Nested; cannot see the file's other using lines, so spell its namespace out; and every test project that linked the old file must stop linking it in the same step.
  • A second implementation of an engine type silently wins. A private copy of a shim's Mathf shadowed the bit-verified one (UnityCompat.Core), and thousands of tests ran against the unverified copy with nothing in the build to say so. If you keep a shim, gate it: a second declaration of any type the shim declares fails the build.

The shim route, and why a new port should not take it

A shim declares Unity's value types in namespace UnityEngine (the reference port's UnityCompat.Core, differentially tested against the real UnityEngine at float32 BIT equality) and an engine backend seam (UnityCompat.Engine: an IEngineBackend seam, a static facade, a LifecycleScheduler, a FakeBackend). A project's existing call sites then compile untouched; in a Unity build the real UnityEngine wins and the shim is not referenced. It is not part of this toolkit's package.

It is a good first move for an EXISTING codebase: it is how the reference port's Unreal side ran a game byte-identically before any adapter existed, and it stays useful as the PARITY ORACLE during a migration (the reference port's backend tests are 38 scenarios every backend must pass). But it keeps a game Unity-shaped for as long as it is load-bearing. A game starting its port today writes its Core engine-free from the beginning and never grows a shim. Reach for one only to get an existing Unity codebase moving before the extraction is done, and treat every day it survives after that as debt.

The shim's tooling is not in the package either. If you build a shim anyway, it needs four instruments, each measured on the reference port's: a gap compiler (compile the scripts against the shim and rank what is missing; the ranked list is the worklist), a surface census of the Unity API by call site, an oracle of which UnityEngine members are callable headlessly, and a differential test of the value types against the real UnityEngine, bit for bit. The census is also why the seam should be small: on the reference port Vector2 alone was 15.9 percent of call sites, the top 5 symbols 48.3 percent and the top 30 83.4 percent. The package's nearest instrument is py -m u2ue --project <game> inventory, which lists every Unity API family each type uses (by family, not by call site).

The model's tools

These are the tools the package ships around the model. They sit at the toolkit root unless the part says otherwise; "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

tool part what it does check
layer_gate.py root the model layer knows no engine (G1); u2ue check --only model runs it from the project file yes
host_gate.py root the platform-seam gate: a platform member declared only in the hosting folder yes
typecheck.py root does the game's C# compile - no Unity, no window, no focus stolen (G3) -
plugin_sync_gate.py root the model's plugin DLLs that Unity loads are built from the current source (G4) not run: its selftest corrupts and restores the plugin DLL an open editor loads
logic_diff.py root the game's logic digest compared across engines - what u2ue parity runs yes
console_check.py root the Unity console gate: did the thing just done put NEW errors in the log yes
u1e_publish.ps1 effects_tools the managed project rebuilt and published to BOTH managed paths, then a run started headless -
publish_verify.ps1 scene_tools proves a managed publish actually RUNS, not just that it built -

The reference port also ran gates written for its own model - a gate that refuses a stand-in drawn where the game's own asset belongs, one that proves the game's own effect calls still happen once and in order, a finder for code that compiles on Unreal but never runs, a census of its host interfaces. They are not in the package: each is the shape of a gate your game's model may need, written against your own model's names.

Your game supplies its own model projects and banned-namespace list (layer_gate.py), its host member names (host_gate.py), its plugin folder, its reference run, and the slice files the engines diff byte for byte.

Game integration: the effect ledger

The Unreal adapter reads an effect ledger: one row per effect key, naming its built system, joined from the three stages' own outputs (the key's verdict, its IR timing with provenance, what was built) and CHECKED against the disk, so the ledger and the assets cannot disagree. The reference run, played headless on Unreal, proves the game fires what was built.

tool part what it does
u1e_ledger.py effects_tools writes the effect ledger the Unreal adapter reads, checked against the disk
u1e_battle.ps1 effects_tools runs the game's reference run headless on the ALREADY-PUBLISHED DLLs and says which frame is which moment, so a frame is always opened knowing what it should show; for asset-only changes
u1e_run.ps1 effects_tools builds the reference run's effect systems, headless

Your game supplies its adapter's effect hook (the model asks IEffectPlayer for a key; the ledger turns the key into a system) and its reference run.

6. Transforms, scenes, UI, audio

Who this is for: the porting developer - after this chapter you can convert any transform between the engines, find the nodes Unreal cannot place, import a level and a UI screen and hold each to Unity, and bring the game's sound across. The first half is the method; from "What the UI capture measured" on, the chapter is the measured lessons and the tools behind each step.

The conventions, in one place

u2ue/transform.py holds every transform convention the port uses. Use it rather than writing your own: its selftest holds it to the effect converter's own functions (200 random cases), so the two cannot drift apart.

Unity Unreal
units metres centimetres
axes x right, y up, z forward x forward, y right, z up
handedness left left
position (x, y, z) (-x, z, y) x 100 - transform.position
direction (x, y, z) (-x, z, y) - transform.direction
rotation quaternion (qx, qy, qz, qw) (-qx, qz, qy, qw) - transform.rotation
scale (sx, sy, sz) (sx, sz, sy) - transform.scale
Euler angles Quaternion.Euler(x, y, z) turns Z, then X, then Y, about the fixed axes (MEASURED, Unity 6000.3) -

From Python:

>>> from u2ue import transform as T
>>> T.position((1.0, 2.0, 3.0))                      # Unity metres -> Unreal centimetres
(-100.0, 300.0, 200.0)
>>> T.rotation((0.0, 0.7071068, 0.0, 0.7071068))     # Unity's 90 degrees about y (up) -> Unreal's 90 degrees about z (up)
(-0.0, 0.0, 0.7071068, 0.7071068)

How each engine composes a hierarchy

  • Unity composes a Transform chain as matrices: each level's rotation times scale applies to everything below it. A rotated child under a non-uniformly scaled parent is therefore sheared.
  • Unreal stores a component's world transform as rotation, scale and translation. Its rule for composing a child with its parent is READ from the engine (Engine/Source/Runtime/Core/Private/Math/TransformVectorized.cpp:295-323): with no negative scale on either side, rotations multiply, scales multiply componentwise, and the child's offset is turned and scaled by the parent; with a negative scale, it multiplies the full matrices, normalises the axes and re-applies the signs (TransformVectorized.h:1552-1587). Neither branch can hold a shear.

transform.compose_matrix and transform.compose_trs reproduce both; transform.shear_of and the corner errors measure the gap.

Finding the nodes Unreal cannot place: u2ue shear

py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --gltf <scene export>.gltf --json shear.json
py -m u2ue --project <game> shear --from Assets/<Scene>.unity

The verb reads a scene either as the glTF file the scene pipeline exports (below) or straight from the Unity scene file, with no export. It composes every node both ways and lists each sheared node: its axes' worst non-orthogonality, how far the corners (+-1, +-1, +-1) land apart (unitCornerCm), whether it draws, and, for a drawn glTF mesh, its bounds' corner error. Measured on the reference port's first battle map: 46 sheared nodes, 2 of them drawing (a rope bridge's meshes, 63.46 and 55.89 cm off at their box corners). A sheared node that draws nothing still moves its children. Whether such an error is accepted, baked into the mesh, or fixed in the Unity scene is the owner's decision, made with the number. Then pin it with a gate, so a later change that makes it worse fails: the scene's fidelity gate (below) holds the world bounds' residual to the scene's own baseline.

Scenes: u2ue scene

Scope: one Unity scene, imported into Unreal as a new level. Precondition: the project file names the scene and its work folder, and the scene's own fidelity baseline exists. Minimal guarantee: a scene with no baseline is refused, never graded against another scene's numbers, and a sheared node's error is a number the owner decides on. Success guarantee: the imported level passes the scene's fidelity gate, every leg at or better than its baseline. Trigger: one of the game's scenes is to run in Unreal.

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene --dry          # the scene's paths, opened; the host's state
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene export         # REFUSED here: runs in the owner's editor, in a window - prints the trigger
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene import         # the glTF into a NEW level through Interchange (Unreal, headless)
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene readback       # the saved level read back (Unreal, headless)
py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check          # the fidelity gate against the scene's own baseline (no editor)

The project file names the scene: "scene": {"unity": "Assets/<Scene>.unity", "name": "<Name>", "dir": "<scene work folder>", "content": "/Game/.../<Name>"}. Until it does, port reports the scene stage ABSENT (Chapter 4). The gate grades the level against that scene's own measured baseline, <scene dir>/fidelity-baseline.json (scene.dir, the work folder above): the counts and residuals every leg holds, and the materials and actors the scene expects by name. It exits 0 when every leg holds, 1 when one moved, 2 when an input or the baseline is missing. The reference port's first battle map, graded against an earlier readback of its level:

py -m u2ue --project <game> scene check
SCENE FIDELITY GATE - <Name>, Unity scene against the imported Unreal level
...
  PASS world AABB residual has not regressed     1037 row(s) (baseline 1037) worst centre 1.431278 / extents 1.453828
CHECKS 45, FAIL 0
VERDICT PASS

Re-read after the level's lighting was changed on purpose, the same gate reads 3 FAIL (the sun, the sky light and one colour): it grades Unity's numbers, so a deliberate departure stays red until the owner accepts it by name.

The verbs wrap the generic legs of the pipeline below. A real level also needs steps between import and readback (textures, material parents, lighting, outline hulls, effect actors). Those are not verbs yet; their tools are under "The scene tools" below. The gate grades the finished level.

  1. Export from Unity with glTFast (an Editor script in the game's project): meshes, materials and textures one to one; inactive subtrees skipped and listed; every value not carried named ABSENT; the terrain baked from its TerrainData, the asset where Unity keeps a terrain's shape and painted layers (heights, the splat layers' albedo: the colour of each painted layer).
  2. Import into Unreal with Interchange, the engine's own import pipeline (an editor Python script in the host).
  3. Check with scene_fidelity_gate.py: hierarchy, materials (slot by slot against the .mat), textures, lighting and placement against Unity's own files, through a headless readback of the saved level.

A trap: a scene imported through glTF arrives in a frame the pipeline chose (glTFast negates x; Unreal's importer takes glTF's y-up as z-up), so a level and a hand-placed actor need not share a frame. Measure the imported level's frame once (one small class is enough) and convert every hand-placed actor through it.

Prefab YAML: what a reader must handle

The effect reader (u1e_ir.py with u1e_nested.py) handles nested prefab instances with their modifications (a nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's), prefab variants, legacy prefab records, m_RemovedComponents, m_RemovedGameObjects (the removed object leaves the instance with its child subtree and their components), and nested MODEL instances (left out and named). m_AddedGameObjects and m_AddedComponents are not ported yet: a prefab that uses either is refused by name. Unity's YAML writes booleans as 0 and 1, so the loader keeps the words On, Off, Yes, No as strings.

UI

Unity's uGUI (Canvas, RectTransforms, layout groups, TextMeshPro) has no one-to-one Unreal counterpart: UMG and Slate lay out differently. So the toolkit does not rebuild a screen as a UMG tree. It captures the Unity Canvas as Unity resolved it in Play mode, lays it out in Unreal with a port of uGUI's own solver, and paints it in one widget's paint pass (UUserWidget.OnPaint), because UnrealSharp's UWidgetTree.RootWidget is read-only and a UMG tree cannot be assembled from C#. Each captured state is held to Unity's own pixels.

The generic part ships as the library U2ue.Ui (u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Ui): uGUI's layout, meshes, raycast and selectables, and TextMeshPro's layout, with no game reference. Its own tests hold it to Unity's captures, and a planted transform defect fails 264 of them:

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test
Passed!  - Failed:     0, Passed:   398, Skipped:     9, Total:   407, Duration: 3 m 28 s - U2ue.Ui.Tests.dll (net10.0)

Not in the package yet: the capture. Today it is the reference port's Editor script; shipping it as the package's Editor assembly is on the roadmap (Appendix B), and until then a second game supplies its own editor's capture route ("The UI tools", below). The bindings, which view model feeds which panel, stay the game's. port lists the UI as an EDITOR stage: it needs a free Unity editor, so port never opens one (Chapter 4).

Scope: one game's uGUI screens, laid out in Unreal by a port of uGUI's own solver. Precondition: each screen can be reached in Play mode in the game's own editor. Minimal guarantee: a font whose glyph indices differ is refused, and a panel with no view model and binding is not drawn. Success guarantee: each captured screen is laid out in Unreal as Unity resolved it. Trigger: a screen of the game is to run in Unreal.

The UI port, in order:

  1. Capture the Canvas in the game's own Unity Editor in Play mode: every RectTransform, its anchors and its components, as Unity resolved them.
  2. Hold the library to Unity: py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test runs U2ue.Ui's tests against Unity's captures.
  3. Convert each capture into a folder Unreal reads: py -m u2ue --project <game> ui convert <capture dir> --screen NAME [--out DIR] (--out defaults under the project's work.ui). It finds each TextMeshPro font's TTF by the GUID its font asset recorded, and refuses a font whose glyph indices differ.
  4. Bind each panel to its view model in the game's own host; only a panel with a view model and a binding is drawn.
  5. Paint the bound panels in one UUserWidget.OnPaint, laid out by the solver from the converted folder.

Audio

Authored clips (.wav, .ogg) import into Unreal as Sound Waves directly. Which sound plays, and how loud, should be a rule in the model (one presentation class is enough), so both engines pick the same sound. Clips Unity generates at run time are rendered once to float PCM and played through a small C++ bridge that hands the samples to Unreal's mixer unconverted, as a 2D one-shot (played once, with no position in the level, like Unity's 2D voices). The bridge ships as the host template's U2ueAudio plugin (Chapter 13). It builds in a host and plays headless: the self test's tone, captured from a headless run on 2026-10-15, passes its judge. A Unity AudioSource still maps by hand (Appendix B). Headless runs pass -DeterministicAudio so nothing reaches a device (Chapter 16).

Animation and physics

Not covered (Chapter 5): no tool is claimed for Animator controllers, Mecanim retargeting or physics simulation. What a port of either needs, and what to measure in Unity first, is in Appendix B. The effects path ports one animation case: an Animator on an effect's root that drives its scale (Chapter 7).

What the UI capture measured

The capture (the reference port's Editor script, served on its editor bridge as /ui/capture) records the live uGUI subtree in Play: the RectTransforms AND their resolved rects, the layout components and LayoutUtility's answers (each element's minimum, preferred and flexible size, as uGUI's layout reads them), sprites with their pixels, mesh effects, selectables, and TextMeshPro's own per-glyph layout. Rebuilding from what Unity resolved, rather than from the authored values, surfaced these rules, each measured on the reference port:

  • The look is not in Image.color. uGUI's Outline draws FOUR offset copies behind the graphic, with alpha = the effect's alpha x the vertex alpha / 255, in bytes; under a translucent fill they tint the whole interior. A panel authored navy was teal on screen because of it.
  • Unity (linear colour space) blends in LINEAR space; Slate blends in GAMMA space. The same layers came out (55,147,165) in Unity and (41,99,117) on Slate. The fix is exact where the UI covers itself: composite the layers under each translucent graphic in linear, then solve its colour for the gamma blender (U2ue.Ui's UiMesh.SolveForGammaBlending). Glyph edges keep a residual (text about 0.85 of the ink).
  • Unity evaluates TextMeshPro's float maths in double, rounding only on a store: in float32, TextMeshPro's preferred-size rounding lands 0.01 off (14.41 where Unity gives 14.40). The port matches at float32 bit equality once it does the same (TmpF32 in U2ue.Ui).
  • uGUI's layout is a rebuild of ROOTS in depth order, four passes each (horizontal sizes bottom-up, horizontal control top-down, then the same vertically). An Image's preferred size is its sprite's MIN size when sliced, not its rect: a real Unity behaviour the rebuild must reproduce.
  • HighResShot never captures UMG or Slate; screenshot showui does. A UI frame taken with the former shows the level and no UI while the log says the widget painted (Chapter 5 has the measurement).
  • Slate pixel-snaps DrawBox and DrawText vertices (there is no NoPixelSnapping through UMG's paint helpers) and puts a text baseline at the draw position + round(face height x ppem / upem) + round(descender x ppem / upem), where ppem is the font size in pixels per em and upem the font's design units per em. Place glyphs ONE BY ONE at Unity's origins: a string drawn by Slate drifts (1.7 px over 12 characters), because its hinted advances are not TextMeshPro's.
  • Putting the owner's editor into Play steals focus, so a capture runs only while the editor is free (Chapter 8's window rules).

The effect readers: the IR extraction tools

What extract runs (Chapter 7 has the pipeline): every effect the game can fire, resolved from the game's own data to a prefab, then each prefab's ParticleSystems READ into the engine-neutral IR, with nested prefabs expanded, the game's rules that switch emitters off applied, and missing assets named. The column "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest (Chapter 21 lists them all).

The scene tools

The level steps that u2ue scene (above) does not wrap yet: the scene's own particle systems, its ambient light and exposure, and its material parents. Each is a script with its own log, written for the reference port's first battle level.

The UI tools

The tools behind the UI port above. The UI part has its own README in its folder. A HUD is drawn by the model's IHudView from the board as shown (Chapter 5); its gate is written against your own HUD, so the package has none.

tool part what it does
