The oracle is the instrument to copy: redrawing Unity's own draw data on Unreal separates "the layout is wrong" from "the renderer draws the same mesh differently". A second game supplies its screens (the capture list), its editor's capture route, and its fonts' TextMeshPro assets.

Meshes, textures and sprite art: the tools

Binary FBX and Unity text-asset meshes are read without an editor, EXR frames (images stored as half floats) turned into Unity's reference PNGs, and saved Unreal assets read without Unreal.

tool part what it does check
u1e_fbx.py effects_tools the few facts the build needs out of a BINARY FBX, read off the file with no SDK -
u1e_objmesh.py effects_tools a Wavefront .obj mesh read into the shape the FBX writer takes yes
u1e_unitymesh.py effects_tools a Unity Mesh saved as a TEXT .asset (YAML, the vertex and index buffers as hex) read into the same shape yes
u1e_exr.py effects_tools a frame exported as EXR turned into the 8-bit sRGB PNG Unity's reference camera writes; standard library only yes
uasset.py scene_tools a saved Unreal 5.7 editor .uasset read without an editor and without Unreal's Python -

The sprite and tile art steps are written per game, so the package does not ship them. Follow this method, in this order; each step is a lesson from the reference port:

  1. Create everything a sprite unit needs headlessly: its texture, its card mesh (the flat plane the sprite is drawn on) and its material, in one headless run.
  2. Read which properties the engine build exposes before you set one. A texture (UTexture2D) property named in the documentation did not exist in Unreal 5.7.1. List the properties; never guess a second name.
  3. Give every imported texture the settings Unity's own importer recorded for it (its .meta), and prove each one took.
  4. Render one card on its own, away from the level's lighting, with its material and texture measured. "Invisible in the level" then becomes one cause instead of three guesses.
  5. Export an imported texture back out and compare it with the PNG it came from.
  6. Make a card two-sided only from the rule that says so, and keep the source of that rule beside it.
  7. Rebuild the material the game draws with, which may not be the one the prefab serializes. On the reference port the game built its card material at run time. Read the code that builds a material, not only the asset.
  8. Read a debug material's blend mode, shading model and outputs before a mesh wears it.
  9. Give a sprite card Unity's depth of field the way Unity's card takes it, through its own depth pass.
  10. Import the textures the game loads at run time (highlights, overlays) headlessly too: nothing in a scene names them.

7. Effects

Who this is for: the porting developer - after this chapter you can run the effects pipeline that turns the game's Shuriken particle effects into Niagara systems, tell a real gap from an emitter Unity does not draw either, and close a gap with the route protocol.

Shuriken particle effects are converted end to end. This chapter is the shape of the route; Chapter 11 gives the reasons behind each step, and the traps.

The pipeline

flowchart TB
  U["Unity project: prefabs, materials, .meta"] -->|extract| IR[("IR: one JSON per effect")]
  IR -->|check| G{"selftests + field gates"}
  G -->|build| N["Niagara systems + build record"]
  N -->|read| R[("particles per frame")]
  N -->|photo| P["Unreal frames beside Unity's"]
  R -->|judge| J{"read-back checks, each with a plant"}
  J --> REP["acceptance page"]
  P -->|LOOK| REP
  REP --> M["metrics + tempo"]
step runs in tool what proves it
extract no editor u1e_ir.py over shuriken_ir.py every key an IR file or a named refusal; every path it names exists
check no editor u2ue check every tool's own selftest; every IR field read or excused with its values
build Unreal, headless u1e_build.py running build_niagara.py the build record: per key its verdict, every module written, every absent emitter with its reason
read Unreal, headless u1e_color_size_readback.py read-back checks per 1/60 s frame, each refusing its plant
photo Unreal, headless u1e_fx_photo.py, u1e_photo_sheet.py the pair sheets (each effect's Unity frames above its Unreal frames), LOOKED at; capture artefacts (frames the capture itself spoiled) labelled, never counted
report no editor report_build.py every number from a record, with its denominator and its age

py -m u2ue --project <game> port --run runs these steps in order (its check stage is check --only gates). build, read and photo launch a headless Unreal, so port runs them only with --with-unreal, one Unreal at a time (Chapter 4).

The IR

One JSON file per effect key, read off the Unity YAML. Every value carries how it was read (readAs: the fields it came from and the mode Unity serialized it in, its minMaxState), so a reader of the IR can tell a constant from a curve from a range, and a value that was not read from one that was zero. An excerpt (a snow emitter, from the second game):

{
 "key": "unity.prefab.4ca04dc9501451e498e3f029e625ccaf",
 "lifetimeSeconds": null,
 "naturalLengthWhy": "LOOPING emitter(s) Snow_Particles: no natural end",
 "emitters": [{
   "name": "Snow_Particles", "duration": 5, "looping": true, "simulationSpace": "World", "maxParticles": 900,
   "startLifetime": {"mode": "constant", "scalar": 2.2, "value": 2.2, "readAs": "scalar (minMaxState 0)"},
   "startSize": {"mode": "randomConstants", "scalar": 0.3, "min": 0.15, "max": 0.3,
                 "readAs": "minScalar..scalar (minMaxState 3, serializedVersion 2)"},
   "emission": {"enabled": true, "rateOverTime": {"mode": "constant", "scalar": 500, "value": 500, "readAs": "scalar (minMaxState 0)"},
                "bursts": []},
   "shape": {"enabled": true, "type": "Box", "scale": {"x": 30, "y": 1, "z": 30}, "...": "28 fields in all"}
 }]
}

lifetimeSeconds is null, not a number: a looping emitter has no natural end, and what ends a spawn of it is the game's code, so the IR says so instead of inventing a length.

The converter

vfxport/build_niagara.py writes Niagara stacks (each of an emitter's scripts is a stack of modules, run top to bottom) through Unreal's FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary. build_emitter is a loop over twenty stages in the order Unity's own modules run: setup, emitter state, spawning, particle spawn, shape, start speed, update, colour / size / rotation over lifetime, gravity, force, noise, velocity over lifetime, collision, renderer, flipbook (texture sheet animation), sub-emitter roles and trails, inherit velocity, and the modules not ported (named per emitter). A rule measured in Unity is re-derived from its bake at build time by its judge (Chapter 8): a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly.

What a gap is, and what it is not

An absent emitter is a GAP only when Unity draws it. The report counts apart, each by a measured or read rule, what Unity does not draw either: a sub-emitter (a child system that a parent's particles start at their birth, death or collision) Unity never fires, one the game never starts, one whose renderer draws nothing, one Unity measured at zero particles. Measured on the reference port: 348 emitters that its first acceptance pages counted as gaps were of these kinds.

The reverse is a gap too: an emitter the port DRAWS where Unity never does. Coverage counts it as drawn, so nothing flags it unless a probe looks. The reference port had one: a "spawner" particle living a ten-thousandth of a second, whose three Birth children (sub-emitters started as each particle is born) Unity never fired while the port drew them for a few frames. When a probe measures zero particles at every moment a parent could fire a child, that fact goes in a list derived from the probe record (never typed), the converter refuses the child by name, and the report counts it absent, as in Unity. That is data for one effect, not a rule taken from one case.

The worst gap is a silent one

Most Shuriken fields are min-max values: a constant, a curve, a random value between two constants, or one between two curves (Chapter 11, "Two models of one effect"). A reader that reduces a value it cannot port (a curve to its first key, two curves to one) and writes no note makes a gap the report cannot see: the emitter counts as drawn. The reference port found this class twice, the second time by auditing for it after the first:

  • an emission rate authored as a curve was built as its first key: a constant rate, or no spawn at all where the curve starts at 0 (52 emitters, not one named);
  • start size, start speed, start lifetime and gravity authored as curves read the same way (46 emitters).

The rule: every reader of a min-max value either ports its mode or writes a SUBSTITUTED note, which the report counts as a stand-in. When one silent reader is found, audit every reader of the same kind of value before calling it fixed.

What the measurements say: a rate curve is the scalar times the curve at the LOOP's normalized time (the time into the loop over the duration), the k-th particle born where its integral reaches k. A start size or lifetime (one curve or two) reads the curve at the END OF THE STEP that emitted the particle; a start speed reads it at the particle's own emission time inside that step. Gravity reads its curve at the emitter's normalized time on every step, and with two curves each particle keeps one fixed fraction between them. All of them run on the EMITTER's clock, which starts after its start delay and wraps when the system loops. Which Niagara parameter gives each of those instants is in Chapter 11 ("Two clocks"): read the engine before you trust a parameter's name.

When a rule fits most of the data but not all of it, record the variable you are missing before modelling around the gap. The first probe of these rules recorded only each particle's age, and a size read one step late looked like a rule that held for 4 particles in 19. The second probe recorded the step each particle first appeared on, and the same data then fitted one rule exactly.

A companion emitter needs its parent's lifecycle rule. A trail is drawn in Niagara as a ribbon (a strip through a list of points), which runs as its own emitter on its own loop. A sub-emitter child's emitter already lived until its parents' last trigger, but its trail's loop was timed from the system's start: the trail closed while the fired particles were still alive, and sooner still in an emitter whose time was rescaled. When an emitter gains a lifecycle rule, every emitter that exists only to follow it needs the same rule.

Porting a gap: the route protocol

  1. Find the root: the report lists absent emitters by root (the emitter a gap is charged to: see gap root), and what porting each root would bring back.
  2. Read or measure the Unity behaviour (Chapter 8): a judge first, its plant, then the bake.
  3. Write the route behind a VFXPORT_<NAME> switch, default off.
  4. Prove it offline with vfxport/whole_trace.py (Chapter 9, "Proving a route offline"): off, identical engine calls on every emitter; on, exactly the emitters --expect-only names change.
  5. Trial: build the affected keys with the switch on, in a content root of its own (an Unreal content folder apart from the project's content_root) so the trial cannot touch the accepted build; then read, judge (with the plant), photograph, LOOK.
  6. Flip with its evidence row in patch_flip_defaults.py.

A change to a tool a running build loads is written as a patch script with its proof (--prove on a copy) and applied (--land) after the build: a build that changes behaviour half way through is two builds, and neither is the one that was proven.

Materials

Unity effect materials use custom shaders. The blend mode is a NUMBER in the material (_DstBlend == 1 means additive), never the shader's name; each distinct shader family needs one hand-authored Unreal parent material, after which every material of that family is an instance with its values read off the .mat (a material variant's values come through its parent, m_Parent). Built-in shaders and materials are named off the Editor's unity_builtin_extra (set unity.editor). A family with no parent yet is refused by name.

Lit materials

A lit (URP Lit or Shader Graph) material cannot use Unreal's lighting and look the same: the BRDF, the ambient and the reflection decode differ. The toolkit evaluates URP's own lighting inside the Unreal material:

  1. The surface comes from the HLSL Unity generated for the Shader Graph (the translator u1e_sgport.py): texture samples with their tiling, keywords as scalars, Unity's frame for positions and normals. A graph that moves vertices in object space, or that includes custom HLSL, is refused by name.
  2. The lighting is URP 17's Lit, transcribed from its source (u1e_urplit.py): the metallic and specular workflows, the main light, per-pixel spherical-harmonics ambient, the reflection probe's mip and decode, emission added raw.
  3. The inputs are measured, not assumed: one window reads the scene's sun (colour, intensity, direction), its 27 ambient coefficients and its default reflection cube (every face of every mip), which are baked into the parent material.

The route is behind VFXPORT_URPLIT until its trial's photos are looked at against Unity's frames taken under the same lighting (the photo probe's lit option opens the scene and copies its sun). Named, not drawn: fog, shadows, screen-space ambient occlusion, and lighting that changes at run time.

Lights on effects

Point lights an effect prefab carries are read with the rule that turns each on (on at every play; on when a pooled instance is reused; never) and spawned on the played effect as Unreal point lights, attached so they follow it. The mapping, READ from both engines' source (d is the distance to the light, r its range, and saturate clamps to 0..1, so the saturate term is a window that fades the light to zero at its range):

Unity (URP) Unreal
1 / d^2 x saturate(1 - (d^2 / r^2)^2)^2 inverse-squared falloff, AttenuationRadius = 100 x r (the same range window)
intensity I, diffuse with no 1 / pi pi x I candelas (Unreal's Lambert divides by pi)
color.linear x I the colour's sRGB bytes, through the engine's own sRGB round trip
shadows CastShadows = false, the light made movable. The reference game turns its effect lights' shadows off at spawn, so the mapping never casts shadows: a game that keeps them on gets lights without them

The Unity side was measured on lit pixels: a probe renders each light on a lit plane, light on and off, and a judge holds the difference to URP's formula; on the clean bake all ten cases fit at a ratio of 1.0000 (Chapter 8). The named residuals: URP's diffuse carries a 0.96 that Unreal's does not, and Unreal's distance term is 1 / (d^2 + 1 cm^2).

Beyond particles

Effect prefabs carry more than ParticleSystems. The toolkit inventories them and treats each as its own class:

what today
an Animator on the effect's root driving its scale ported
point lights ported (above)
a Timeline (PlayableDirector) starting groups at their clip times the law measured (Chapter 8); the route written and proven offline behind VFXPORT_TIMELINE, default OFF; its trial is NOT YET
TrailRenderers the law measured and reproduced exactly by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw (72 of 72 frames, 15 of 15 meshes); the Unreal draw is NOT YET
audio sources listed

Appendix B has the plan for each NOT YET.

8. Measuring Unity

Who this is for: the porting developer - after this chapter you can measure a Unity behaviour the port must reproduce exactly: write its judge first, run its probe in the game's own editor without costing the owner anything, and make the build rely on the measurement.

Unity's documentation does not state most of the rules a port has to reproduce exactly: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, how a TrailRenderer drops its points, what a Timeline does to a ParticleSystem before its clip starts. A port that guesses at them looks right in a screenshot and wrong in the game. So when no file states a rule the port relies on, the rule is MEASURED in Unity itself and kept with the run that measured it. Chapter 9 gives the rule behind this: every value is READ, MEASURED or named ABSENT, never a plausible number.

A rule is measured with a probe, a judge, a bake, and a window in the game's own editor.

The parts

part what it is where
probe an Editor C# script that sets up a case in Unity, steps it, and writes every value it observed to a JSON fact file. It is triggered by a file, so nothing has to click vfxport/unity_probe/*.cs
judge a Python script that states the rule a port will rely on, and READS it off a fact file or REFUSES it with the numbers. Written and selftested before the bake vfxport/unity_probe/*_judge.py, *_check.py
fact file the bake: what Unity did, with the Unity version it ran on shared/conformance/*.json
window a short, guarded session in the game's own editor that puts a probe in, runs it, and takes it out again u2ue window (u2ue/verbs/window.py); a window is a JSON spec

Write the judge first

A judge names the rule in terms a port can use ("a point is dropped once its age on Time.time passes time", where Time.time is Unity's game clock and time the TrailRenderer's own Time setting), and the evidence it needs to READ it ("every removed point was still present at its last age at or below time plus one frame, and gone at its first age above time less one frame, with at least 10 removals seen"). Its --selftest builds synthetic facts that obey the rule, and planted defects that each break it one way; the judge must accept the first and refuse every plant. Only then is the probe run.

The order matters. A judge written after the bake is fitted to the bake, and passes whatever Unity happened to do. A judge written first can be wrong: then the bake refuses it, the numbers say why, and the rule is restated and re-planted. Where you do not know the answer, the judge must not assume one: the TrailRenderer judge's HOLD case reads FROZEN, DRAINED or CHANGED off the facts, and the bake answered FROZEN (a still trail neither adds nor drops a point; points expire only while it moves).

py vfxport/unity_probe/trailrend3_judge.py --selftest      # the plants bite
py vfxport/unity_probe/trailrend3_judge.py                 # the bake: exit 0 READ, 1 refused, 2 no input

When the judge refuses the bake

A refusal is information, never a reason to loosen the judge. The point-light bake is the worked example. Its probe renders each case with the light ON and with it OFF, and the judge holds the difference to URP's formula (Chapter 7, "Lights on effects"). Its first judgement refused cases for two causes, each found in the facts before anything changed.

  • white_diffuse was wrong by a ratio that grew toward blue. Its OFF render, the first after setup, was all zero where every later OFF render held the scene's ambient, so the ambient was read as light. The probe now throws two renders away first, and the judge refuses, by name, a case whose OFF render disagrees with its surface's other OFF renders.
  • Every other failing sample sat on row 272, where the game camera's full-screen pass (which samples the frame in blocks of pixels) computes floor(272.5 / 720 x 330.275) = floor(125.0003): on an exact block edge the GPU's float can land either side. The judge now accepts either block on an edge, and counts how many samples it did that for.

Re-judged: nine cases at a ratio of 1.0000 with every sample inside its rounding bound, and white_diffuse refused by name; the clean re-bake passed all ten. Both fixes went into the judge's selftest as plants, and a plant must be strong enough. The first consistency check only asked that the bad case fail: it passed its plant, then refused every case of the real bake, because one black render pooled with the rest made every case look inconsistent. The plant now requires the bad case to be refused alone, and the check compares each case with the per-texel median of its surface's OFF renders.

The window protocol

Scope: one Unity behaviour, measured in the owner's own editor. Precondition: a probe and its judge are written, and a window spec names the probe, its inputs and its outputs. Minimal guarantee: the owner's editor is left as it was - every record and guard file md5-held, the probes removed, nothing replaced. Success guarantee: the fact file is written with the Unity version it was measured on. Trigger: a rule the conversion needs is not measured.

The probe runs in the game owner's own editor, which is in use. A window is built so it cannot cost the owner anything:

  1. Idle gate. Start only after 600 s with no cursor movement and no key or button (wait_quiet.ps1); a launcher whose wait was killed does not start.
  2. Presence watch. A watcher writes one line the moment the owner returns; every later step checks it and stops.
  3. The editor lock. One file (.opus-tools/.locks/unity-editor.lock) names who holds the editor; a window refuses to start while anyone else holds it.
  4. Compile headless first. The probe is type-checked against the project's editor assemblies (typecheck.py --editor --extra) before it is dropped in. A probe that does not compile never enters the project.
  5. Nothing is replaced. A window refuses to start when its fact file or trigger already exists, and records the md5 of every existing fact file before and after: a bake that touched another rule's evidence is visible.
  6. Wait for the real compile. The editor assembly's timestamp must change and Unity's isCompiling flag read false; the probe's name must be in the rebuilt DLL.
  7. Trigger, wait, collect. A trigger file starts the probe; the window waits for the fact file with a timeout.
  8. Play mode only when it must. One short Play, entered and left by the window, with isPlaying checked inside the probe (edit mode never ages a TrailRenderer, so that law needed Play).
  9. Take it out. The probe and its .meta are deleted and the editor recompiles until no trace of its name is left in the DLL.
  10. Read the console. console_check.py --reset before, console_check.py after: new errors stop the work.

A window never answers a dialog it did not open.

The owner comes back. At any step the window leaves Play first, then takes the probes out (step 9); nothing else runs. Branches from step 2.

All of this is one runner, and a window is a data file - the probes, the inputs copied in, the trigger and the outputs expected, never a script cloned from the last window:

py -m u2ue --project <game> window check <spec.json>    # every refusal judged now; nothing touched
py -m u2ue --project <game> window run <spec.json>      # waits for the quiet, then runs steps 1-7 and 9-10 above

{"label": "x6", "probes": ["EffectPhotoProbe"],
 "inputs": [{"from": "<lane>/x6/effect-photo-list-x6.tsv", "to": "effect-photo-list-x6.tsv"}],
 "trigger": {"file": ".RUN_EFFECT_PHOTO", "lines": ["list:effect-photo-list-x6.tsv", "record:effect-photo-unity-x6.json"]},
 "outputs": ["effect-photo-unity-x6.json"], "wait_seconds": 900}

The project names the Editor folder a probe is dropped into (unity.probe_dir) and the files whose md5 must hold (unity.guard). A probe places a real prefab only through ProbeSpawn (the game's own spawn composition, or the prefab as authored, named), which the runner drops in with it; probe_spawn_gate.py refuses a probe that instantiates one itself. The runner's selftest drives the whole flow against a simulated editor, including the owner returning after the compile, and a mutation run on it killed all 8 of its mutants (copies of the runner with one deliberate fault each, every one of which the selftest must fail; Chapter 14 has the method). Play mode (step 8) is not in the runner yet: a probe that needs it still has its own script.

From a bake to the build

A measured rule is not copied into the converter as a constant. At build time the converter re-derives it from the bake through the same judge (for example, the sub-emitter frame rule through vfxport/subframe_rule.py), so a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly. u2ue check --only facts lists every bake with the Unity version it was measured on, against the project's unity.version (the second game, on 2026-10-15; the count grows with every bake):

py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts
  163 measured Unity bakes; this project is Unity 2021.3.21f1
       163 measured on Unity 6000.3.16f1    UNVERIFIED for Unity 2021.3 - re-measure where it matters
  163 of 163 rules this project's build uses were measured on another Unity: its report must not call them measured for it

A rule measured on another Unity is still used (the build runs), but the report must not call it measured for your project. Whether to re-measure is your decision; the probes and judges are the means.

The laws measured so far

Every row is a fact file in shared/conformance with its judge. A selection, to show the kind of rule that has to be measured; check here before you measure one again:

law what Unity does judge
sub-emitter frame the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in and the position it inherits vfxport/subframe_rule.py, sub_frame_rule_check.py
node shear the order a turning mesh or billboard (a camera-facing quad) particle's rotation and a non-uniform node scale are applied nodeshear_rule_check.py, nodeshear2_rule_check.py
shape scale what the Shape module's own scale does to a particle's birth point and direction shape_scale_judge.py
non-uniform motion a local particle moves unscaled and is drawn through the node's whole transform, scale included nonuniform_motion_judge.py, nonuniform_world_judge.py
ring buffer past its lifetime a ring-buffered particle lives on, its age held, until it is replaced ringbuffer_check.py
mesh alignment a mesh particle's drawn frame under each render alignment, and the frame a view-aligned rotation turns in meshalign_judge.py, alignview_judge.py, alignspin_judge.py
TrailRenderer width, colour and U (the texture coordinate along the trail) run on the distance fraction from a head vertex at the transform; on a moving frame the oldest point is dropped while the NEXT point's age exceeds time, then a point is added; a still trail freezes; the tail is drawn at the position time ago, clamped to the oldest segment trailrend_judge.py, trailrend2_judge.py, trailrend3_judge.py; the whole law replayed by U2ue.Runtime.TrailLaw's test (72 / 72 frames, 15 / 15 meshes)
Timeline control a controlled object is off before its clip, simulated at the clip's time less its start delay, off after timeline_judge.py
point light a URP point light's term on a lit surface is URP's formula exactly (the 0.96 diffuse, the sRGB decode, the range window), through the game camera's full-screen pass lights_judge.py (ten of ten cases at a ratio of 1.0000 on the clean bake)
scene lighting the sun, the 27 ambient coefficients and the default reflection cube (every face of every mip) URP lights a scene with litinputs_judge.py
Quaternion.Euler turns Z, then X, then Y, about the fixed axes u2ue/transform.py selftest

Writing a new probe

  1. Copy the nearest probe in vfxport/unity_probe/. Keep its shape: an [InitializeOnLoadMethod] that hooks EditorApplication.update to poll for its trigger file, one fact file out, and an error field in that file rather than an exception.
  2. Record what you will judge, not what is convenient: every frame's raw positions rather than a summary.
  3. Write the judge and its plants; run --selftest.
  4. Run the window. Commit the fact file, the probe, the judge and the window spec together.
  5. Make the converter re-derive the rule from the bake, and register the judge's selftest (Chapter 18).

The measurement tools

Two kinds of measurement feed the converter: what Unity ACTUALLY draws (the bakes above, under shared/conformance), and what Niagara actually does with a module input, measured in headless Unreal. Every converter rule cites one of them. "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

The window plumbing. u2ue window run <spec.json> (above) waits on two gates, both PowerShell scripts in the lane part:

tool part what it does
wait_quiet.ps1 lane waits until nobody has touched the mouse or keyboard for the quiet period: the cursor has not moved and no key or button went down
wait_presence.ps1 lane waits until someone touches the machine: the cursor moves, or a key or button goes down. The Windows idle timer (GetLastInputInfo) cannot answer this where injected input resets it constantly, so the gate polls the cursor position and the key states itself

The Unity-side judges (in vfxport/unity_probe/, beside their probes), each reading a bake. The rows use Shuriken's own settings: a system simulates in Local or World space, and its scaling mode (Hierarchy, Local or Shape) decides which scale reaches its particles; Chapter 11, "Space, scale and the transform chain", explains both.

tool what it reads off its bake check
particle_facts.py the particle facts a general probe measured -
cube_facts_check.py which texel Unity samples along a direction, on a cube texture -
shapes4_facts_check.py where real emitters' shapes put their particles, and with what velocity, as Unity emits them -
nodeshear_rule_check.py the ORDER Unity applies a turning mesh or billboard particle's rotation and a non-uniform node scale in -
nodeshear2_rule_check.py the second node-shear bakes, holding the rule on more cases yes
viewshear_rule_check.py the view-aligned shear rule, against measured quads -
trailscale_check.py a trail's WIDTH under a uniform Hierarchy node scale: whether the node scale reaches the width yes
sub_frame_rule_check.py a Birth or Death sub-emitter child's emission frame, against every measured case yes
shape_scale_judge.py particle by particle, what Unity does with the Shape module's own scale yes
force_scale_judge.py which rule a force, or a World-space velocity over lifetime, on a LOCAL system follows under scale -
wstretch50_judge.py a World stretched billboard and a Local-scaling child under a scaled root -

The Unreal-side probes: what Niagara does, read before the converter relies on it.

tool part what it measures check
v4_module_inputs.py scene_tools a Niagara module's own input names, types and DEFAULT values, READ off the engine yes
v4_probe2.py scene_tools which write route a colour curve takes -
u1e_shape_probe.py effects_tools how Niagara's cylinder location composes "Non Uniform Scale" with "Cylinder Axis" -
u1e_trail_probe.py effects_tools how Niagara carries a trail, before the converter writes one -
u1e_trail_real_probe.py effects_tools real trail emitters built through the converter's own code, read back -
u1e_trail_diag.py effects_tools why a probe's ribbon got no particle -
u1e_random_probe.py effects_tools whether two of the converter's per-particle randoms are INDEPENDENT of each other in one particle -
u1e_burstp_trial.py effects_tools what a BUILT system's probability burst does over many plays -
u1e_burstp_judge.py effects_tools judges those plays and writes what Niagara did as facts yes
u1e_bursttrain_probe.py effects_tools whether a burst train is written the way the converter predicts -

A second game supplies nothing here: the probes measure the ENGINES. It re-runs the windows for the features its effects use that no bake covers yet, and for any rule that matters on its own Unity version (each bake records the version it ran on, above).

9. Verification and gates

Who this is for: the porting developer - after this chapter you know the four rules every check in a port follows and which gate applies each, and you can prove a converter route offline and hold a whole build to Unity on numbers with u2ue conform.

Four rules

  1. Read or absent, nothing else. Every value is READ (from a file, with where it came from), MEASURED (Chapter 8), or named ABSENT with the reason. A tool that cannot read a value stops and names it. It does not substitute a default and carry on: a build that silently drops a value is worse than one that fails, because the failure is invisible and later reasoning builds on it.
  2. A gate must be able to fail. Every gate carries planted defects (its --selftest) and must refuse each. A gate that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off. When a gate's scope is widened, its plants are run again.
  3. Verify with both. Numbers and pictures each lie in their own way. On the reference port a render where the whole scene went black scored better on a pixel metric, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The data must prove itself first; then the metric and the image confirm it. Neither one diagnoses on its own.
  4. A miss is unknown. The toolkit's code readers are lexical: they match the code's text, not its compiled meaning. A call through an interface, a delegate, reflection or a UnityEvent is invisible to them, so "no caller found" means unknown, never unused.

The gates

gate what it refuses run by
every tool's own selftest the tool's planted defects u2ue check --only selftests
vfxport/yaml_field_gate.py a Unity field, in a module this project enables, that the reader neither reads nor excuses with the values it may take u2ue check --only gates
vfxport/ir_field_gate.py an IR field the converter neither uses nor lists in DELIBERATELY_UNREAD with its reason u2ue check --only gates
the measured rules' versions a rule measured on another Unity, reported as measured (it is named UNVERIFIED) u2ue check --only facts
layer_gate.py, host_gate.py an engine reference in the model; a platform member outside the hosting folder u2ue check --only model
vfxport/converter_trace_gate.py a converter change that alters what an existing route writes (every engine call recorded against a stub unreal, working copy against a commit) by hand, before a converter change lands
vfxport/whole_trace.py a new route that changes more, or less, than the emitters it names by hand, per route (Chapter 7)
v4_msg_gate.py a write the engine refused: Niagara's SetParameter logs an unknown name or a wrong type as an error and returns false, and the message is saved inside the package (the system's saved asset file) per trial, over the built packages
the read-back judges a built system whose particles, per 1/60 s frame, do not match the rule they were built from u2ue read
u2ue parity a model row that differs between runtimes beyond its characterised allowance Chapter 5
scene_fidelity_gate.py a moved hierarchy, material, texture, light or placement in an imported level Chapter 6

Proving a route offline

The converter writes through Unreal's Python API, so a route can be proved without an engine: run the converter against a recording stub (a stand-in for the unreal module that records every call and its arguments), once at a reference commit and once with the change, and compare every call.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tool whole_trace.py <ref> <work>                # switch off: identical calls on every emitter
py -m u2ue --project <game> tool whole_trace.py <ref> <work> --on VFXPORT_<NAME> --expect-only KEY:PSFILEID
                                                                            # switch on: exactly the named emitters change

<ref> and <work> are the full paths of two copies of the converter (build_niagara.py): tool runs the tool in its own folder, and the tool refuses to start outside the facade because it reads the project's paths. Each KEY:PSFILEID names one emitter: an effect key and the file id of its ParticleSystem (the id that object carries inside its prefab file), which every later record pairs emitters by.

This is what lets a route land behind a switch while other builds are running: it is proved to change nothing until it is turned on.

Conformance over every key, data first

Scope: every effect key of a project at once, Unity's particle state against what the built Niagara systems compute. Precondition: the keys are built in Unreal, and the owner allows a Unity window. Minimal guarantee: an emitter one side does not have is named UNPAIRED, never dropped. Success guarantee: every emitter OK, or its verdict named with its numbers. Trigger: a build is to be held to Unity on numbers before its photos are looked at.

Photos compare one draw at a time. This compares every emitter of every key on numbers, in one pass:

  1. Write the cases: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform cases --name <run> writes, from the project's IR, one probe case per key (its prefab placed by the game's own spawn, the seed pinned, read from a restart at each time), the Unity window that runs them, and the Unreal read of the same keys.
  2. Read Unity: py -m u2ue --project <game> window run <run window spec> runs the one generic probe in the owner's idle editor (Chapter 8).
  3. Read Unreal: py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <run read spec> reads the keys' built systems at the probe's own step, 0.02 s, with no new build.
  4. Compare: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform diff --unity <record> --unreal <record> --report <file> pairs each emitter by its system's file id and reads BOTH sides at Unity's sample times only. The Unreal read has every frame and Unity only its few samples, so otherwise a particle born and gone between two samples would be counted against the port. A first birth is compared by the frame it is first drawn on, and Unity's ages are put in real time by the emitter's simulation speed (the converter rescales each emitter to real time). Each emitter reads OK, LATE or EARLY (first drawn on a later or an earlier frame), COUNT (the live counts apart at a sample by more than 1 or 5 %, whichever is larger), BIRTH UNREAD (no age can be read: an infinite lifetime), UNPAIRED, or NO DATA (neither side drew a particle at the times read). The report is stamped with the judge's own id.
  5. Keep the score: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform latest reads the newest stamped report of the run the project names in conform.standing_run, and refuses one that another judge made (re-run the diff). u2ue cycle (the recurring check of every pillar) trends its share of OK emitters, so a converter change that loses some goes red; a denser run is another measurement, made the score only by changing that field.
  6. Name each miss: py -m u2ue --project <game> conform classes --report <file> names a LATE, EARLY or COUNT row only when the converter's own build note on that emitter (joined by file id), or a measured signature (a miss already measured and named, such as one warm-up tick late), agrees with it in direction AND size. Every other row is listed as the work, never passed. A class names the WHOLE row: the judge records every sample of a COUNT row, and a class reads them all, never the first difference alone. Some misses are the probe's own: Unity's emission covers the half-open step (from its start up to, but not including, its end), so a burst due exactly on a sample time is drawn one step later than the port draws it. That is a capture artefact, never a game frame; the reference port measured it on every such sample of two runs before naming it. A particle at its exact end on a sample is the same instant from the other side, and is named only when each side's own particles say so (Unity's remaining lifetime, the port's age, both at the end). A probe can be blind. The reference port's case probe, restarting the simulation for each sample, never drew a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter (0 of 284). Stepped at its 0.02 s default, it drew 15 the PORT does not draw, which the restart read had hidden as no data, while seven the port draws stayed empty; stepped at the game's own frame step (1/60 s, conform cases --step 1/60), those drew too, their counts matching the port's. Check a class built on a probe's silence against a second way of looking, with the probe stepping the way the game steps, before calling the port right or wrong.
  7. Follow the class, not the key. A verdict a whole class of emitters shares is one rule to measure or one route to fix: the reference port's first such read found every non-prewarmed burst (one whose emitter does not start as if it had already run a loop) born one warm-up tick late, 121 of 121. That first read of every key also found the judge's own faults before the port's: a first birth taken from every Unreal frame against four Unity samples, and infinite lifetimes passing as OK because an undefined age compared as no difference. Make the judge prove itself with plants before believing what it says about the port.

Looking at the result

Photos are checked by eye, and the toolkit makes that part of the process instead of a courtesy:

  • u2ue photo renders Unreal frames at Unity's sample times; u1e_photo_sheet.py lays each effect's Unity and Unreal frames side by side.
  • A sheet is LOOKED at before a route is called done. A frame where the capture itself failed (a black frame, a missing texture stream) is labelled as a capture artefact and never counted for or against the port.
  • A screenshot route returning ok proves bytes were written. Open the file.

When a gate goes red

Three rules, each with its measured case in Chapter 14 ("Rules that keep tests honest"): check that the thing moved before believing it broke (a gate that walks one folder reports what the port moved as ABSENT); never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green; re-run a test that another worker changed minutes ago before investigating it.

10. Metrics and reports

Who this is for: the porting developer - after this chapter you can build the acceptance page, read each number it prints by its definition, quote it honestly, and find the tool behind each read-back, photo and report.

Every number the toolkit prints is computed from a record on disk, with its denominator and its definition. A number it cannot compute is printed ABSENT with the record it needs. An input older than the newest build is marked STALE, because it describes builds that no longer exist.

The acceptance page: u2ue report

py -m u2ue --project <name> report [--out FILE]

One HTML page per project, built from that project's records: the IR summary, every key's build verdict, the read-back sweep (every read-back check run over every built system's read), the photo sheets, the gap roots, and the decisions only the owner can make, each with its evidence. It reads what is there: a key never built reads "never built", and a pass not yet run reads absent. A project's first report, before any build, already lists every key it will have to account for. In port, the report is the last automatic stage; port then stops for the owner's decisions the page asks (Chapter 4).

The numbers: u2ue metrics

py -m u2ue --project <name> metrics [--json FILE]
number definition
keys the project's effect keys (its IR summary), each with the verdict of the record the page chose for it
drawn an emitter whose build log carries modules: it draws in Unreal
absent, as Unity absent exactly as in Unity, each by a measured or read rule: the game never starts it, Unity never fires it, Unity draws or emits nothing there itself, or Unity has no particle to draw it on
absent, gap every other absent emitter: Unity draws it and Unreal does not. Charged to its root (an absent parent's children to the ancestor absent for its own reason), so a root's count is what porting it brings back
coverage drawn / (drawn + gap): of the emitters Unity draws, the share Unreal draws
measured drawn emitters with no SUBSTITUTED note: drawn by a rule measured against Unity, not a named stand-in
data the read-back sweep: per check, emitters checked and failures, summed
image the photo screen: pairs compared, pairs flagged, and of those how many are labelled capture artefacts
machine the chosen records' own build seconds per key, summed and as a median
routes the converter's switches flipped default ON with their evidence, and those deliberately OFF with what each waits on

The emitter numbers are the acceptance page's; the metrics verb never recounts them, because two programs that count the same records will not agree. Measured on the reference port: three drafts of the coverage figure were wrong before the one quoted (99.4 %, 91.3 % and 91.8 %), from reading a stand-in's "draws nothing" as Unity's, counting skipped logs as drawn, and missing the measured sub-emitter chain rule. So the definitions are part of the claim: a number quoted without its definition is not one.

Sample output, from the reference port on 2026-10-17 (the gap roots cut to the first; the page lists every one). The figures move as builds land: Appendix A reads the records of 2026-10-15, two days earlier. A number that cannot be trusted says why on its own line: data reads STALE (older than the newest build ...) when a build is newer than the read-back sweep, and image reads ABSENT: no sheets listing ... - the photo pass has not run.

keys      674: BUILT 673, IR REFUSED 1; 673 drawn, 197 of them with a named gap; 514 from the acceptance rebuild
emitters  drawn 7810 | absent: gap 641 (Unity draws them, Unreal does not), 375 absent exactly as in Unity (Unity NEVER fires it
          267, not started when the game spawns it 58, Unity draws nothing here itself 25, which the game never starts 14, Unity
          emits nothing here itself 7, so Unity has no particle to draw it on 4)
coverage  92.4 % of the emitters Unity draws are drawn in Unreal (7810 / 8451)
measured  86.4 % of the drawn emitters carry no stand-in (6745 of 7810; 1065 drawn with a named SUBSTITUTED note)
          800 named parts absent on drawn emitters (a module or field each, on the page)
gap roots (what porting each brings back - emitters, keys, the root's reason):
            31   20  non-uniform scale (..) on an ENABLED shape; the location modules take one radius, so it is REFUSED rather than
machine   32.8 h of build time over 673 keys, median 100 s a key (the chosen records' delete..finalize seconds)
data      26973 emitter-checks over 26 checks, 8 FAIL (99.97 % hold)
image     673 sheets, 164 flagged for a big difference (24 of them ONE DRAW, 34 GRIDTICK - the capture, not the port); 75.6 % unflagged
routes    98 verified switches read default ON today, each with its evidence row (111 TABLE rows - a switch read in two files has
          two; 3 switches with a row still read OFF: VFXPORT_FX35_ORBIT, VFXPORT_FX35_WORLD, VFXPORT_SUBSHAPEPOS); 11 switches
          deliberately OFF, each with what it waits on (toolkit-wide, not per project)

In image, ONE DRAW marks a key whose look hangs on a few random particles, and GRIDTICK a burst born exactly on a photo time: frames where a difference is the capture, not the port (Chapter 11, "Photos are draws; their dates mix").

Porting speed: u2ue tempo

py -m u2ue --project <name> tempo [--json FILE] [--since YYYY-MM-DD]

How long each converter route took from its first line of code to its verified flip, read off git. A route is one switch; first code is the earliest commit whose added lines carry the switch's name; flipped is the earliest commit in which every file that reads it reads it default ON. Read the median with the batch lines beside it: in the sample below (the reference port, 2026-10-18), the routes flipped alone or in a commit of fewer than five routes took a median of 2.9 h, and the 58 flipped together in batch releases 40.9 h. That wait was the release's, not the route's, so tempo reports the two apart.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tempo
u2ue tempo - the toolkit's verified routes, first code -> verified flip, from git (definitions: u2ue/verbs/tempo.py)
  VFXPORT_AMESH                  first code 2026-10-10T17:41 (c369e881)  flipped 2026-10-12T13:47 (70ee5858)     44.1 h
  VFXPORT_BILLMESH               first code 2026-10-10T17:45 (e9e0addb)  flipped 2026-10-12T13:47 (70ee5858)     44.0 h
  ...
  VFXPORT_BUILTINMIPS            first code 2026-10-14T11:30 (83a9ce50)  flipped 2026-10-14T17:30 (74aa80ed)      6.0 h
  ...
  97 routes: first code -> flipped, median 28.4 h (quartiles 3.5 / 43.5 h); flipped per day: 2026-10-12 50, 2026-10-13 22, 2026-10-14 14, 2026-10-16 11
    flipped alone or in a commit of fewer than 5 routes: 39 routes, median 2.9 h
    flipped in a batch release (one commit flipping 5+ routes): 58 routes, median 40.9 h - the wait is the release's
  1 switches carry no OFF stage on record (first code already reads them default ON): VFXPORT_CULLFRONT
  NOT FLIPPED / ABSENT VFXPORT_FX35_ORBIT: vfxport/build_niagara.py (reads it default OFF today)
  NOT FLIPPED / ABSENT VFXPORT_FX35_WORLD: vfxport/build_niagara.py (reads it default OFF today)
  NOT FLIPPED / ABSENT VFXPORT_SUBSHAPEPOS: vfxport/build_niagara.py (reads it default OFF today)

Routes are the toolkit's, so tempo reads the same git history for every project; a switch with an evidence row that still reads OFF is listed, never counted as flipped.

What tempo does not measure, so that it is never implied: the time from finding a defect to its first code, the agent's tokens, and the machine's build hours (those are metrics).

Reading the numbers honestly

  • Quote a number with its denominator and its date: "92.4 % coverage" in the sample above means 7810 of the 8451 emitters Unity draws, on 2026-10-17.
  • Coverage is not fidelity. An emitter that draws can still draw wrongly; measured, data and image are the numbers that speak to fidelity, and image needs the photos to have been looked at.
  • A gap is a named, owned item, not a failure to hide. The report lists every gap root with the reason the converter gave.
  • A check that ends without a result is UNCOUNTED, never clean. u2ue metrics and the check sweep list such runs apart; on the reference port a crash once went into the sum as zero failures and hid a real one.
  • Expect a long tail of gap roots. In the 2026-10-17 run sampled above (Appendix A names the same root), the biggest root brings back 31 of the 641 gap emitters (a non-uniform scale on an enabled shape, over 20 keys). No single route closes the gap: work down the report's list of roots.

What the numbers do not measure yet

"Percent identical" is never one number. It is a family of four, each answering its own question: coverage (does it draw), measured (is it drawn by a measured rule), data (do its particles follow Unity's numbers), image (do the frames agree, capture artefacts excluded and counted). One combined "identical" figure would hide which of the four moved.

Not measured yet, and how it will be:

  • Porting speed on a fresh game. The second game's run, timed from extract to its first report and on to each coverage milestone, with the agent's own wall-clock and token count beside the machine hours. Today u2ue tempo times routes, not a game, and py -m u2ue --project <name> metrics [--json FILE] sums build hours, not a porter's.

Read-back and checks: the tools

What a BUILT system really holds (renderers, module inputs, the particles of a simulated frame, mesh properties), read back and held to the IR's prediction, emitter by emitter. Every check names what it could not judge, and every check has a PLANT that must make it FAIL. A plant that depends on a read (--plant on the read-back checks) needs that trial's OWN read pair, never an older one: a check once paired with the newest build FAILED for that reason alone. "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest.

v4_write_gate.py is the example of a static check that knows its own reach: it can type only the writes its table covers (92 of the converter's 383 on 2026-10-13, u2ue/README.md), so its selftest passes while the gate itself exits 1 for that coverage. The authority it defers to is v4_msg_gate.py, which reads what the engine actually refused. A second game supplies nothing here beyond its build records.

Photos and contact sheets: the tools

A frame of each built effect beside Unity's, one contact sheet per effect, and a screen for the pairs that differ most: the image half of "verify with both" (Chapter 9), because a metric alone has lied.

The acceptance report: the tools

The acceptance sentence is the game owner's to write. The reference port's was: every effect the game fires draws in the Unreal build as Unity draws it, and every gap is named. One report holds it: per key the verdict, the named gaps, which absences Unity shares (never fires, draws nothing itself), and the decisions only the owner can make.

A second game supplies its own acceptance sentence.

11. Shuriken to Niagara, in depth

Who this is for: the porting developer working on effects - after this chapter you can say why an effect draws differently in Unreal, read what the converter writes for each Shuriken module, and close a gap yourself, from the census to the flip.

Chapter 7 gives the effects pipeline and the route protocol as steps; this chapter gives the reasons behind each step. Read Chapter 7 first, and come back here when an effect does not draw as Unity draws it, or before you write a route of your own.

Why a purpose-built converter

No tool converted Unity particle systems to Niagara when the toolkit was started (searched 2026-08-22; Appendix D gives the search and what it found). The toolkit borrows one thing from Epic: the CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin (built to convert Unreal's own older Cascade particle systems to Niagara), whose Python API writes a Niagara stack module by module.

One finding frames the work: an effect's STRUCTURE ports automatically, its LOOK does not (the look lives in materials and shaders, "Materials and textures" below). shuriken_ir.py reads prefab YAML into the engine-neutral IR with no Unity running, and build_niagara.py runs inside Unreal and writes the systems, materials and textures; the verbs run every stage for any project ("The verbs, underneath", below).

The rules, before any command

Chapter 9 states the toolkit's rules. Effects give each one a reason of its own:

  1. READ or ABSENT, never a guess. A rule measured at one value is not known at another: a ring-buffered particle is held past its lifetime at 1/60 s and longer, and NOT at 0.005 s or under (measured 2026-10-13). A route that had extrapolated from a 1 s measurement drew a glow Unity never draws.
  2. No fallbacks. log + continue, except: pass and a default substituted on failure are the same lie, made invisible. A refusal names the emitter by its system name (the name the build logs): an IR name does not match an emitter Niagara de-duplicated.
  3. Verify with both. A read-back check can pass while the frame is wrong. LOOK at the pair sheets before calling anything done.
  4. A check that has only ever passed proves nothing. Every check has a plant, a deliberately broken input it must FAIL.
  5. A converter change is proven before it builds anything: vfxport/whole_trace.py over the whole IR, a Niagara probe where the stubbed trace is blind (compile errors, run-time kills), a trial that is read, judged and looked at, then the flip with its evidence row in patch_flip_defaults.py and a clean flip_audit (no switch a trial set still reads default OFF, unless it is named deliberately OFF: "Routes and switches", below). A new route goes behind a VFXPORT_* switch, default OFF, until its trial.
  6. One headless Unreal at a time, from native PowerShell. UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with its trailing backslash, which a PowerShell started from Git Bash loses (Chapter 13). The Unreal verbs refuse that shell up front, and refuse while the host is busy.
  7. The owner's Unity editor is the owner's. A measurement window starts after 600 s of idle (wait_quiet.ps1 600), stops the moment the owner returns (wait_presence.ps1), leaves every fact file it did not write untouched (md5 before and after) and never answers a modal. The Unity Test Runner is never used (Chapter 12).

Why it is hard

Two models of one effect

A Shuriken ParticleSystem is one component with a fixed set of modules, each with an enabled flag and a fixed list of fields. Most fields are a MinMaxCurve or MinMaxGradient in one of four modes: a constant, a curve, a random value between two constants, or one between two curves. Unity runs the modules in its own fixed order inside its own particle step.

A Niagara emitter is a set of scripts (emitter spawn and update, particle spawn and update, event handlers), each a stack of modules, plus renderers kept apart. Each module is a graph with declared inputs, and an input can belong to one version of the module and not another, sit behind a static switch (an option fixed when the script compiles) or an inline edit condition (a flag that must be on for the input to apply), or take a dynamic input (a small graph that computes the value) or a data interface (a curve is one) instead of a value. So one Unity field becomes a module, an input name, a type, a version and sometimes a switch, and the API reports a failure at any of those by returning False rather than raising (see the traps). Niagara runs a stack top to bottom, so the converter writes modules in the order Unity runs its own.

Space, scale and the transform chain

  • Simulation space. A Local system simulates in its node's frame and the transform carries the result into the world; a World system's particles stay where they were born.
  • Scaling mode (scalingMode: Hierarchy 0, Local 1, Shape 2). Under Hierarchy Unity multiplies a particle's size by the node's whole lossy scale (its scale in the world, lossyScale), under Local by the system's own scale, under Shape by neither. A Niagara sprite's size is absolute: it is laid along unit tangents and never passes through the component's transform (NiagaraSpriteVertexFactory.ush:993, read in UE 5.7). So the converter folds the scale into the size. Without the fold every sprite draws wrong by exactly one over its lossy scale (on the reference port's first scene, 3.571 times too large under a lossy scale of 0.28).
  • Motion under a scaled chain. MEASURED (2026-10-07): a Local system moves in UNSCALED local units (start speed, velocity over lifetime, radial push, limit, drag) and the transform scales the result into the world, but gravity acts in world units. The port's frame carries the chain's turn and place, not its scale, so without a correction a scaled emitter moves at the unscaled speed (2.5 times too fast at 0.4); motion_scale in vfxport/build_niagara.py scales each local-unit input. A World system under a scaled chain takes different factors per part (the WSCALE route).

The transform chain is composed up m_Father (each Transform's link to its parent in the YAML) to the prefab root, the root's rotation included, and carried into Unreal by one fixed frame: Unreal (X, Y, Z) = (-100 x, 100 z, 100 y) in centimetres. That matrix has determinant +1, so a quaternion maps as (-qx, qz, qy, qw). Unity's Quaternion.Euler turns Z, then X, then Y about the fixed axes.

A NON-uniform node scale shears a facing quad in Unity (measured: a View-aligned billboard takes the node's lossy scale along the WORLD axes after facing the camera), which no Niagara sprite draws; the VIEWSHEAR route reproduces it in the parent material's World Position Offset. The IR's ownerScale, the axis-aligned product of the local scales, is not Unity's lossy scale diag(R^T M) where a non-uniform scale sits above a turn, so the IR also carries lossyScale and nodeMatrix. And a spawn scale on the Unreal component reaches a Local emitter's positions and a mesh but never a sprite's size (NiagaraSpriteVertexFactory.ush:923-1003): the SPAWNSCALE route writes it into the size every frame, and only a photo at the game's own spawn scale can see the rule.

Two clocks

Unity's particle clock adds each step up in float32 and tests a burst against it half-open. A Unity probe that steps Simulate on the fixed timestep runs at the project's own step (0.02 s on the reference project) while the Unreal read steps 1/60 s: the two share ages only at multiples of 0.1 s, so compare at the particles' own ages and read the step off the data.

With interpolated spawning (the converter's empty template has it), Niagara's spawn script reads every float emitter parameter LERPED by the particle's spawn fraction, so Emitter.Age read at spawn is the emission instant; integers and a short list of engine constants are not lerped (read: NiagaraHlslTranslator.cpp:5113-5153; Chapter 7 gives what this means for start values). Pick the clock to match Unity's: the lerped parameter for a start speed (read at the emission instant), the frame's end rebuilt from values that are never lerped for a start size or lifetime (read at the END of the emitting step).

Random draws

The toolkit's Unity probes pin the seed (useAutoRandomSeed = false), so a Unity frame is reproducible. Niagara's VM (the virtual machine that runs its scripts on the CPU) seeds its randoms per batch off the CPU cycle counter (VectorVMRuntime.cpp:444-446); determinism is a compile-time emitter flag the converter does not set and Python cannot reach. So no random value is compared particle for particle: the port matches the DISTRIBUTION Unity draws, measured. A random-constants start size is uniform and independent of the start rotation, speed and lifetime (a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, KS, of 0.018 from uniform, 2026-10-06); a TwoColors start colour draws ONE fraction for all four channels; two RandomRangeFloat inputs in one particle are independent (correlation 0.006); a value Unity holds per particle is a spawn-only random in Niagara.

The IR: reading Shuriken offline

The reader is effects_tools/u1e_ir.py over vfxport/shuriken_ir.py, with effects_tools/u1e_nested.py for nested prefabs. It reads the YAML of a project serialized as text, with no Unity running. Chapter 7 shows an IR excerpt, Chapter 21 its format.

Per effect key it holds: every emitter's modules, each value with its mode and a readAs saying how it was read; the renderer (mode, alignment, rendererEnabled, meshes, pivot, sort); the material, its shader resolved by guid and its blend READ as numbers; the emitter's place in the prefab (prefabPos, prefabRot), ownerScale, lossyScale and nodeMatrix; the system's file id (_psFileID), by which every later record pairs it; the sub-emitter links; and the natural length, or null with the reason.

Reading MinMax values

At serializedVersion 2 the constant modes do not use the curves: minMaxState 0 is scalar, minMaxState 3 the range [minScalar, scalar], and the curves stored beside them are stale (a random-constants range's order is in the traps, below). Unity writes a float field holding 0 as 0, which a YAML loader returns as an integer: type a value by the field it replaces.

File ids

Every object in a Unity YAML file carries a file id, the number after & on its header line, by which other objects reference it (a negative file id is one of the traps, below).

  • Nested prefab instances. An object inside a nested instance has, in the outer file, the id (instance id XOR source object id) AND 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, and references inside the expanded objects re-key the same way (measured 2026-10-07 on every placeholder of 15 expanded prefabs). The outer file's "stripped" placeholders, read as objects, look like extra root transforms. u1e_nested.py expands each instance, applies its modifications, checks every placeholder against the formula and drops it. A prefab variant's root is an instance of its base, so the same expansion reads it.
  • Legacy records. Class 1001, the YAML class of a nested prefab instance (!u!1001), is also a pre-2018.3 prefab's own "Prefab" record (&100100000, m_RootGameObject or m_IsPrefabParent, no source); Unity 2018.1 and 2018.2 wrote it as m_SourcePrefab {fileID: 0} with m_IsPrefabAsset. It is kept, never expanded.
  • Removed and added objects. The effect reader applies m_RemovedComponents and m_RemovedGameObjects (the scene reader is Chapter 6's); added GameObjects and components are refused by name. A nested MODEL instance (an FBX) has no YAML: it is left out and named unless the IR depends on it.
  • Shader Graph shaders are cited with a NEGATIVE file id (a sub-asset of the .shadergraph file). A regex expecting a positive integer reported "no shader" for 1,930 of the reference port's 1,999 effect materials (read 2026-09-29).
  • Built-ins. The guid 0000000000000000f000000000000000 is the Editor's unity_builtin_extra, whose names are read off that file (set unity.editor). The built-in Default-Particle material is file id 10301, its texture 10300 (64 x 64 RGBA32, 7 mips).

What the game decides, not the prefab

What starts when an effect spawns is the game's rule. Unity's own rule plays a system whose Play On Awake is on; a game's pool may do more (the reference port's pool also plays the first system's whole subtree). The adapter names the rule (Chapter 18), the IR records each emitter's spawn start, and an emitter the game never starts is absent in both engines.

The field gates, and what they cannot see

yaml_field_gate holds every key of every ENABLED module (and the ParticleSystem and renderer) to the reader: named by shuriken_ir.py, or excused with the reason and the values it may take, re-checked on every run. ir_field_gate holds every IR field to the converter: named there, or listed in DELIBERATELY_UNREAD with its reason. Both run in u2ue check --only gates.

One hole, READ on 2026-10-17: the reader reads no Color by Speed, Size by Speed or Rotation by Speed module, and yaml_field_gate matches a field by its NAME. Every field those modules serialize (enabled, gradient, curve, range, separateAxes, x, y, z) is a name the reader reads for another module, so the gate passes an enabled by-speed module. (The Trigger module's inside and outside are named nowhere, so an enabled Trigger module fails the gate as it should.) Until the gate keys on the module too, list a project's enabled by-speed modules yourself before trusting a build.

Module by module

"Measured" means a Unity probe baked the rule (Chapter 8) and the converter re-derives it at build time; SUBSTITUTED is a stand-in the acceptance report counts; ABSENT is not drawn, with its reason.

Unity module Niagara state
Main: duration, loop, delay, prewarm, max particles EmitterState (Life Cycle Mode Self), loop delay, system warm-up, a cap route measured; the cap SUBSTITUTED (one frame late)
Emission: rate, bursts, rate over distance SpawnRate (a curve where authored), SpawnBurst_Instantaneous per burst, SpawnPerUnit measured; a random rate over distance ABSENT
Shape SphereLocation V1 / V2, BoxLocation, CylinderLocation, spawn assignments per shape measured per shape; the rest named
Main: start values InitializeParticle, AddVelocity, AddVelocityFromPoint measured, with the instant each is read
Colour / Size / Rotation over Lifetime ScaleColor (RGB and alpha separately), ScaleSpriteSize / ScaleMeshSize, SpriteRotationRate or mesh orientation measured
Colour / Size / Rotation by Speed none not read (see the field gates)
Velocity over Lifetime, Force, Limit, Gravity update assignments, AccelerationForce, VortexForce, Drag, GravityForce, SolveForcesAndVelocity measured where planned; the rest named
Noise CurlNoiseForce SUBSTITUTED: Unity's noise is not measured
Collision its own route on the measured subset, else CollisionQuery measured, else SUBSTITUTED
Renderer sprite renderer (alignment, facing, pivot), mesh renderer, sort hints measured per mode; allowRoll SUBSTITUTED
Texture Sheet Animation SubImageIndex per the measured frame rule Grid, whole sheet, lifetime and FPS modes
Trails a ribbon emitter fed by a location event measured
Sub Emitters event generators on the parent, handlers on the child Birth and Death measured; the rest named
Custom Data Dynamic Material Parameters measured per stream layout
Lights point lights on the effect (Chapter 7) per-particle Lights module ABSENT
External Forces none SUBSTITUTED (wind zones are the scene's)

Emitter state and the loop

EmitterState's "Life Cycle Mode" defaults to System, under which an emitter IGNORES its own loop behaviour, duration and delay while every write reports success: the converter sets Self, and writes the loop delay with its inline edit condition on. Unity prewarms an EMITTER; Niagara warms the whole SYSTEM and floors the warm-up to whole ticks. The port warms the system by the longest prewarmed loop, written half a step over, and delays every other emitter to start where Unity starts it. Unity's run-once window is half-open while Niagara's loop runs one frame long, so a run-once rate emitter grows one extra particle (67 of 93 on the reference port, 2026-10-07): the converter kills a birth at or after the window's end inside the spawn script. Niagara's ParticleState kills a particle a hair before its lifetime where Unity still draws it: the converter kills on Age > Lifetime. A start lifetime of Infinity becomes float32's largest finite value, named.

maxParticles is a cap Unity refills in the step a particle dies. Niagara takes its spawn counts from the count at the frame's START (NiagaraEmitterInstanceImpl.cpp:1300-1313), so the port refills one frame late: exact where nothing is replaced, a named substitute elsewhere. Without the route nothing holds the cap at all (one emitter kept about 50 alive where Unity keeps 1). Its room and frame-start count are INTEGER parameters, because a float one reaches the spawn script lerped. Named, not ported: cullingMode, stopAction (the host decides), useUnscaledTime, and the ring-buffer modes outside their measured range.

Rate, bursts and rate over distance

A rate curve is the scalar times the curve at the loop's normalized time (Chapter 7). Niagara's first tick after activation adds nothing to SpawnRate, so the converter preloads the spawn remainder with rate x DeltaTime at emitter spawn: k / rate at any frame rate. Each burst is its own SpawnBurst_Instantaneous with an Int32 count (how Niagara names the second is a trap, below). A repeating burst is one module per cycle or a burst train; one that repeats forever is refused; a probability fires the whole burst, one roll per firing. A burst exactly on a step's end in Unity's half-open float32 clock fires on the NEXT step (0.25 s ends step 15 at 1/60 and fires on 16; 0.5 s stays on 30): the BURSTLAG route puts every off-grid burst's first frame on Unity's step. Under a system warm-up every non-prewarmed burst is born one warm-up tick late (178 of 178 on the reference port), which the WARMBURST route corrects. Chapter 21's switch table gives each route's default.

Rate over distance is particles per unit the SYSTEM travels, one at each crossing (measured). SpawnPerUnit takes the spacing exactly, places each particle up to one frame of travel AHEAD of Unity and at large steps misses the first and last crossings (named). A random rate over distance is ABSENT: Unity draws a new rate every step. A sub-emitter child's distance emission is its PARENT's travel.

Shapes

  • Cone. Unity's Cone emits from its BASE, a disc of radius r (radiusThickness 0 is the rim), along the generator through each point, tilted atan(u tan a) at fraction u of the radius (measured). ConeLocation fills from its apex and has a Cone Length and no radius, so the converter uses CylinderLocation at height 0, at its latest version, turned to the axis, and writes the direction.
  • Sphere and Hemisphere. SphereLocation V1 adds its Offset in simulation space, unturned; V2 with "Offset Coordinate Space" Local turns it with the component. Both sample uniformly in volume (measured).
  • Circle, Donut, Arc. A Random-mode arc spread snaps particles to multiples of spread x 360 degrees; a Loop arc or donut moves at 360 x speed x birth time, wrapped at the arc; a BurstSpread burst of N sits at i / (N - 1) of an arc, i / N of a full 360.
  • Edge. A BurstSpread burst of N lies at i / (N - 1) along [-r, r]; a Loop edge moves at u = Frac(speed t / r), which only a bake at a radius other than 1 could tell.
  • Mesh. Particles start on Unity's own vertices, P = T + R (S . v), the start speed along the turned vertex normal.
  • Rectangle. A moving Rectangle's start velocity is along the shape's turned +Z (measured within 6e-8).

A disabled Shape module's transform does nothing in Unity (measured); an enabled one's rotation turns the emission axis, not the particles, and its position is composed under Hierarchy scaling and refused under the others. Named where unmeasured: randomPositionAmount outside its measured case, a Random radius spread on a shape other than a Circle, animated radius modes.

Start values, colour, size and rotation

InitializeParticle carries the start lifetime, size, colour and rotation ("Sprite Rotation Angle" does nothing unless "Sprite Rotation Mode" is "Direct Angle (Degrees)"); AddVelocity the start speed along the shape's direction; AddVelocityFromPoint a radial push. A start size or lifetime curve is read at the END of the emitting step, a start speed curve at the emission instant (Chapter 7).

Colour over lifetime goes through ScaleColor's "RGB and Alpha Separately" arm, Scale RGB from a VectorFromCurve and Scale Alpha from a FloatFromCurve: the only arm Python can build, and the closer mapping, since Unity authors RGB and alpha as separate gradients. Keys built in Python get automatic tangents unless they go through unreal.InterpCurvePointFloat with CIM_CURVE_BREAK and FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary.keys_from_interp_curve_float; a curve data interface defaults to a 128-sample lookup table, and use_lut False evaluates it exactly. Size over lifetime is ScaleSpriteSize or ScaleMeshSize, each rebuilt from the spawn size so nothing compounds. Rotation is SpriteRotationRate on a sprite; a mesh renderer reads only its mesh orientation, so a mesh's spin goes there.

Motion, collision and noise

Velocity over lifetime (linear, orbital, radial, speed modifier) is written as ordered update assignments where its plan is measured; otherwise a stand-in (a constant acceleration, one vortex) is SUBSTITUTED and every part it leaves out ABSENT. A pasted module can land BEFORE the solver (Niagara fixes up dependencies on paste), hence the assignments. Gravity falls world-down even in a Local emitter, velocity first, as in Unity; limit and drag use the unscaled size and local speed (measured). The VM's vector length uses an ESTIMATED reciprocal (VectorVMRuntime.cpp:1912: 999.875 for 1000), so a rule that depends on a length uses a dot product and a power of 0.5. Noise is a CurlNoiseForce of the same strength and frequency, SUBSTITUTED.

A Planes collision with every slot unassigned collides with nothing in Unity, so nothing is written. Where the measured subset holds (the touch at radiusScale x size / 2, the bounce, the slide, a lifetime loss of 1, World behaving as Planes, a Collision child's burst on the touching step) the converter writes its own route; any other collision is a CollisionQuery, SUBSTITUTED. GenerateCollisionEvent drops a touch slower than its "Velocity Threshold" (1 cm/s by default) unless the threshold is written -1.

Renderers

  • Billboard. Unity drops the camera's ROLL; Niagara's facing modes keep it, and no stock dynamic input gives the per-particle camera forward that would drop it: allowRoll is SUBSTITUTED.
  • Stretched billboard. The long axis is size x lengthScale. The legacy pivot moves the quad 2 x pivot.y x size forward whatever the length (measured at lengthScale 1 and -1, after a bake at 2 could not tell the rules apart). A negative Niagara sprite size mirrors the IMAGE, never the quad. Velocity alignment zeroes the sprite rotation; custom alignment faces the camera POSITION, not its plane.
  • Horizontal and Vertical. A Horizontal billboard's DIAGONAL is the particle size (side size / sqrt 2) and Niagara's custom facing needs a facing vector written. A Vertical billboard draws the same upright quad under View, World, Local and Facing alignment (measured), side size / sqrt 2.
  • Mesh. The import is REFUSED unless it matches the file per corner: position, UV and winding (an FBX's axis signs turn Unreal's import and not Unity's mesh; a box check cannot see a 180-degree turn). Unity multiplies a mesh's vertex colour into the particle colour (measured); Niagara's VertexColor is the mesh's own colour and 1 on sprites and ribbons, so Particle Color x VertexColor is exact on all three. Niagara corrects culling for the COMPONENT's determinant only: a mirrored mesh is safe only two-sided.
  • Render mode None draws no particle (a trail-only emitter draws its trail); m_Enabled 0 draws nothing. The descending sort is spelled CUSTOM_DECENDING in 5.7's Python.

Texture sheet animation

Measured, re-derived at build time: frame = floor(N x frac(f + s)), N = tilesX x tilesY, f the frame over time (a constant, a random held per particle, scalar x curve(frac(cycles x normalized age)), or fps x age / N in FPS mode) and s the start frame. The converter writes Particles.SubImageIndex itself (SubUVAnimation has no start-frame override). Named where unmeasured: Speed mode, a Sprites-list or single-row sheet, flipped sheets, a partial UV channel mask.

Trails

A trail is a Niagara RIBBON emitter beside its parent, on the route Epic's Cascade converter uses: a location event generator on the parent and a handler on the ribbon spawning one point per event. Measured in Unity: the head vertex IS the particle; each point lives the lifetime fraction x the particle's lifetime; width and colour run from head 0 to tail 1; the trail's colour over lifetime is taken at the particle's CURRENT age and tints the whole trail. A ribbon point cannot read its parent, so each carries its parent's normalized age, lifetime and draws in the event payload, on slots the receive module actually applies. Niagara never scales a ribbon's width (NiagaraRibbonVertexFactory.ush:862) while Unity scales a Hierarchy trail under a scaled parent: the TRAILSPAWN route writes it. A textureScale other than 1 is SUBSTITUTED.

Sub-emitters

The frame a Birth or Death child emits in, MEASURED on 117 cases (vfxport/subframe_rule.py, judged by vfxport/unity_probe/sub_frame_rule_check.py):

R = Cw . LookRotation(u, up = (0, |u.z|, 1 - |u.z|)) . Cl . S     the parent particle moving at the trigger
R = Cl . S  (world-fixed)                                         the parent particle still

Cw is the child system's world rotation, Cl its OWN local rotation (so its local turn counts twice), S its shape rotation, and u the parent particle's total velocity at the trigger in the child's frame (Birth after the parent's first step, Death as it died, Collision after the bounce). A rule fitted on axis-aligned cases alone fitted a WRONG rule exactly; oblique, rotated and grandchild cases broke it. A child's own GameObject position plays no part. In Niagara the child is an event-spawned emitter. A Birth child of a Birth- or Collision-spawned middle NEVER fires in Unity (measured) and is counted apart; an unported child is EMITTER-ABSENT with its reason, never drawn as an ordinary emitter. The event traps are listed below.

Custom data and vertex streams

Custom Data reaches a Unity shader only through the renderer's Custom Vertex Streams. Measured: a Custom1.xyzw list packs uv0.zw = Custom1.xy and uv1.xy = Custom1.zw, default streams give uv0.zw = (0, 1), and Custom Data curves run ONE simulation step behind the particle's age. The converter writes Dynamic Material Parameters above ParticleState, which keeps that lag, and supports a layout only where a control case read it. STREAM_SLOTS_READ names the slots each shader reads, and a read slot on an unmeasured layout is refused; a shader not listed is taken to read none, so each newly ported shader adds its row.

What Niagara has no equivalent for
