Each is a named stand-in, an emulation or a refusal: refilling a cap in the step a particle dies; a billboard that drops the camera's roll; a 4-channel colour curve from Python; per-emitter prewarm (emulated); Unity's sheared quad (emulated in the parent material); deterministic random draws from Python; a single-particle event mode (5.7 has Every Particle and Spawned Particles); an event-spawned child whose curves are not applied twice (the console variable that stops it breaks trails); and what an asset pack's custom shader does beyond blending, which needs a hand-authored parent per shader family. Unity's noise field, external forces, culling modes and unscaled time are named for another reason: their Unity rule is not measured yet.

The converter's machinery

vfxport/build_niagara.py writes Niagara stacks through FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary in a real Unreal editor process, one stage per Unity module in the order Unity runs them (Chapter 7 lists the twenty stages, Chapter 18 shows their code). A route of your own lands in one stage, behind its switch. What follows is what a route meets when it writes.

Writing one value

  • add_mod refuses a module asset that is not there: create_asset_data on a missing path still returns an asset.
  • setp tries each candidate input name and returns whether one TOOK, honouring set_parameter's boolean, and records every miss in the build report's param_misses.
  • VERSION pins a module's script version per module; some modules answer differently at 1.0 and at their latest graph.
  • Propagated static switches. UNiagaraGraph::FindStaticSwitchInputs (NiagaraGraph.cpp:2143-2166) returns the module graph's own static switch nodes AND every function call node's PropagatedStaticSwitchParameters, renamed to their propagated name when set; SetParameter accepts both. A reader that walks only the switch nodes calls the second kind "not declared" while the engine takes it: ShapeLocation V2's "Rotation Mode" lives on a function call node, and one build wrote it on 57 emitters with 0 refusals. scene_tools/v4_module_inputs.py lists a module's declared inputs off the shipped .uasset, propagated switches included; read it before calling such a write wrong.
  • Module names. A module is found by NAME anywhere in the stack, so every extra instance a route adds gets its own name (the traps, "Events, sub-emitters and trails").
  • One input object, one parent. A script input handed to two parents is lost from one; build a fresh input per use.

Names, rules and notes

Niagara renames a clashing emitter handle, and every event names its source by the REAL handle (the rule is in the traps). vfxport/niagara_names.py reproduces the engine's naming (59 of 59 systems exact against a full build, 2026-10-06), assigns every name before the emitter is added, and avoids the reserved namespace names (an emitter called "Particles" stops the system compiling).

A measured rule is not a constant in the converter. cap_rule, trail_rule, flipbook_rule, sub_emitter_rule and their siblings read the bake (shared/conformance/color-size-facts.json and others) at build time and re-derive the rule from the case's own control; a rule that stops holding makes its route refuse by name.

vfxport/shuriken_size.py holds the size arithmetic with no engine in it, so the converter inside Unreal and a measurement in plain Python import one rule (two copies is how the first scene's size bug survived). It folds the scaling mode in (size_scale returns None to REFUSE when the scale it needs is absent), applies the measured side of a Horizontal or Vertical billboard, the stretch length, the non-uniform arm (a 188 x 1476 cm shaft written as a 200 cm square was the bug it fixed) and the VIEWSHEAR plan. py vfxport/shuriken_size.py runs its selftest.

The acceptance page (lane/report_build.py) counts a stand-in only when its field note contains SUBSTITUTED, so a runtime gap is written "SUBSTITUTED : ...". An absent emitter carries its reason in the record's absentEmitters.

Routes and switches

A route is one Unity behaviour the converter ports, behind a switch named VFXPORT_* (the converter's) or U1E_* (the effect tools'). A new switch is read os.environ.get("VFXPORT_<NAME>", "0") == "1": OFF unless set. extract, build, read and photo remove every VFXPORT_ and U1E_ variable inherited from the shell and name them, so an ordinary build is the defaults and nothing else; a trial sets its route's switches for its build step only.

The evidence table and the flip

vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py holds the evidence once, in TABLE: per row the file that reads the switch, the switch, and the evidence that it may flip (the trial, its read, its judge and plant, the sheets looked at). A flip rewrites the read to os.environ.get("VFXPORT_<NAME>", "1") != "0" (still switchable off with =0) and marks the line with the date and a pointer to its row; it adds no line. A switch read in two files flips in both or not at all: the tool refuses, exit 2, while any read of a flipped switch still defaults OFF anywhere in the code trees.

py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py --list              every row: its switch, its file, its evidence
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py --dry <ROW> ...     what the flip would change; nothing written
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py <ROW> ...           the flip: atomic per file, compiled before it replaces the file

Chapter 21's converter switch table is generated from that table and the code, with each switch's state today.

flip_audit and the state of a route

lane/flip_audit.py compares every switch a trial set with its default in the code as it stands, and flags a trial switch read default OFF anywhere (unless DELIBERATE_OFF names why) and a switch whose read sites disagree. DELIBERATE_OFF is evidence too: a route measured SLOWER (a data-processing conversion context made the finalize 1.5 times slower), a route that waits on another (an arc placement exact at the frame's end while every later burst cycle is born a tick late), a route measured DIFFERENT from Unity, a switch for probe builds only.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tool flip_audit.py

A route is ON when EVERY file that reads its switch reads it default on, DELIBERATELY OFF when flip_audit names what it waits on, and OFF otherwise. A table row is evidence that a switch MAY flip, not proof that it did: u2ue metrics counts a route as flipped only when every file reads it on today, and counts switches, not rows.

The route protocol, from evidence to flip

Take the next gap from the acceptance page's absent emitters by root, ordered by what porting each brings back:

  1. Census with today's converter, offline, over the whole IR: which emitters the route would gain, and what refuses them NEXT. Check that Unity draws them at all (never fired, never started, renderer off, emission measured 0 are not gaps).
  2. Find the measurement you already have: the cases of every shared/conformance/*-facts.json that names the module. If the rule is not measured, measure it in one window the owner allows (Chapter 8), never from documentation.
  3. Write the route behind its switch, default OFF, and prove it with whole_trace.py: off, the same engine calls on every emitter of every IR; on, exactly the predicted set changes. Add a Niagara probe where the stub is blind.
  4. Trial: a data file (keys, the route's switches, a content root of its own, the steps), run from native PowerShell. Build the gained keys, resave, read, run the route's judge AND its plant, photograph, LOOK. A photo difference counts only past two draws' spread.
  5. Flip with its evidence row, then a clean flip_audit.py. Keys built before the flip are rebuilt as a delta.
  6. Write it down: the route's numbers and its commit in your work list, and any new trap.
py -m u2ue --project <game> tool whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py --on VFXPORT_<NAME> --expect-only <key>:<psFileID>,...
py -m u2ue --project <game> trial plan <spec.json>       every command each step would run; nothing runs
py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <spec.json>        one Unreal at a time; the code parts run from a snapshot
py -m u2ue --project <game> trial stop                   stop at the next step boundary
py -m u2ue --project <game> judge --prove                every judge a trial runs; exit 1 when one has no plant that refuses

A trial runs from a SNAPSHOT of the code parts, so an edit to the live converter while it runs cannot change what it runs. A change to a tool that a running build loads is a patch script, proven on a copy and landed after the build (Chapter 7).

When an agent stops and asks the game's owner: a product decision (a shader family with no Unreal port: port it or name it; an effect that differs by design), anything that would run in their live editor, a second project's Unreal host, and anything outward-facing. Ask one precise question, then take the next gap.

Porting a gap, in depth

Census first, and count what the NEXT gate refuses

A refusal family ranked by its FIRST reason misleads: a plan function returns at its first failing condition, so a label covering 27 emitters looked like one route; lifted, all 18 targets hit the next blocker and the route drew nothing. Lift the one gate in a COPY, run the whole trace, count what passes the next gate. A build record's reason is the converter's of its day: census with today's converter. A parked route's reach moves when other routes land: re-measure it after each.

Measure before you write

A probe in vfxport/unity_probe/ builds each case as a fresh ParticleSystem, steps it with Simulate at 1/60 s and bakes what it reads to shared/conformance/<name>-facts.json. When particle data cannot answer, read what the RENDERER draws: ParticleSystemRenderer.BakeMesh gives a sheet frame, whether a particle is drawn at all, and a mesh particle's drawn extent. The judge (<name>_judge.py) is written BEFORE the bake, derives every rule from the case's own control, and its --selftest refuses a planted bake. The window is a data file run by u2ue window (Chapter 8), with console_check before and after. Wait on the file the probe ACTUALLY writes, and never let a measurement write a file the converter reads while a build runs: give it its own output name (a trigger's out: line). When the judge disagrees with the real bake, suspect the judge first. Then the rule goes into a checker the converter calls at build time: ringbuffer_check.rules() raises when a rule stops deriving from its bake.

Before measuring, do step 2 of the route protocol (list the cases of every shared/conformance/*-facts.json that names the shape or module): an edge burst of 5 had been baked while a converter note still called it unmeasured. Fold measurements into one window, since each costs the owner's editor two recompiles, and check every asset path its trigger names.

Measure at more than one value, and read the drawn result

A bake at a parameter's unit value cannot tell a law that scales with it from one that does not: an edge loop at radius 1 could not tell Frac(speed t) from Frac(speed t / r), and the game's edge had radius 4. Measure at two values of everything a law could depend on.

What Unity reports is not always what it draws. An aligned particle's rotation3D (alignToDirection) is start + E(d) per axis, drawn by Quaternion.Euler(-rotation3D), where an unaligned one is drawn by Euler(+rotation3D) (measured). Read a drawn turn off BakeMesh of an asymmetric mesh, never off the particle's fields. When the judge's candidate rules all fail, say so, read the rule off the columns it printed, and confirm it on bakes made before the rule was seen.

Find WHICH emitter, then read the shader

When an emitter draws but its colour or brightness is wrong, isolate it first (u1e_fx_photo.py with U1E_PHOTO_ISOLATE=<handle>, about 30 s an emitter): three explanations of one dim effect were each tested on an emitter named by eye, the wrong one. Then compare the port's material body with Unity's GENERATED shader line by line (shared/conformance/generated-shaders/<name>.shader, written by the facts probe's sg: line from the Shader Graph importer), and prove a suspected slip offline: evaluate both formulas over the material's own texture, decoded as the engine samples it. One ramp branch with the wrong remap hid in 337 emitters wherever two ramp colours were close; one dim effect found it. And read what Unity samples, not the source file: its imported texture is in Library/Artifacts, found through Library/ArtifactDB (Chapter 12).

Photos are draws; their dates mix

An Unreal photo is ONE random draw; Unity's is a fixed seed (useAutoRandomSeed = false). A key whose look hangs on a few random particles reads lit or dark by luck: a route was nearly reverted for a "regression" that a second draw of the SAME build reproduced. An A/B on photos needs its noise floor: two draws of each side, and a move is real only past both sides' spread and 0.5 % of the light. u1e_randdraw_census names the one-draw keys from the IR alone (one to three births before 1 s with a wide spread, or a burst probability below 1); the sheets print ONE DRAW on them. A burst born exactly at a photo time is the capture's: Unity's float32 clock reaches 0.1 exactly at step 6 but 0.9999997 at step 60, so a burst at 1.0 s fires a step later in Unity, and the sheet marks the frame GRIDTICK. A sheet pairs each Unity time with the NEWEST Unreal photo at that time, so a trial that photographed 0.1 to 1.0 s keeps an older build's later frames; the sheet marks a frame older than its asset STALE.

Hold Unity's times as float32; read summaries

A judge that compared a double time put a 0.1 s burst a step early, and Unity's fixed-step Simulate ran on 0.02f, not on the timestep it reported (0.0199999921): read the step off the data. whole_trace.py prints at most six DIFF records, and an ON set of 14 read as 6 until --expect-only was run: read a tool's summary line, never count its rows. Quote numbers from the page: u2ue metrics runs the page's builder and prints ITS summary (a recount once printed 91.3 % where the page said 92.3 %). u2ue tempo reads each route's first code to its flip off git.

Materials and textures

Blend is a number

Blend mode decides most of an effect's look, and it is NOT in the shader name. Asset-pack effect shaders (UberFXSG, HS_Blend_CG, HS_Distortion and their kin) carry blending as numeric material floats. In a first sample of 51 materials: 19 src=One dst=One (additive), 16 src=SrcAlpha dst=One (additive, non-premultiplied), 14 src=One dst=OneMinusSrcAlpha (premultiplied) and 2 src=SrcAlpha dst=OneMinusSrcAlpha (classic alpha). A name-based guess got 14 of 51; the numeric read gets all of them. The rule: DstBlend == 1 (One) is additive; SrcBlend == 1 (One) is already premultiplied, so the emissive is NOT multiplied by alpha again. Across the reference port's 1,999 fired effect materials (read 2026-09-29): 969 additive, 904 classic alpha, 41 opaque, 13 premultiplied and 61 with no numeric blend, which are refused rather than guessed. A converter that assumed additive would get about half wrong and still produce something that looks like particles: the failure that survives a screenshot.

The largest family's author (scene_tools/vm1_author.py) keys its blend table on (src, dst): (5, 1) additive, (5, 10) alpha blend, (1, 0) opaque, (1, 10) premultiplied; any other pair is refused by name. Unreal 5.7's additive blend DOES weight the emissive by Opacity (BasePassPixelShader.usf:2261): an instance that multiplies by alpha as well squares it, and low-alpha glows go near invisible.

One parent per shader family

What a custom shader does beyond blending (soft-particle depth fade, distortion, camera-facing tweaks, ramps) has no Unreal equivalent, so the bill is one hand-authored Unreal parent per distinct Unity shader, not per material; every material of the family is then an instance with its values read off the .mat. On the reference port one family was behind 593 of the 724 effect prefabs the game fires (81.9 %, read 2026-09-29) and the next three took it into the high nineties. The parents' authors are scene_tools/vm1_author.py (the largest family) and one module per family in effects_tools/ (legacy alpha-blended particles, matcap, two-sided, blend-distort, dissolve, toon, electricity). Verify a new parent before any frame: the largest family's was held to an independent evaluation of the same shader, at a repeat floor measured from two separate editor processes, with a plant that broke one character of its HLSL. A family with no parent yet is refused by name, its emitter absent, the rest of the effect built.

Reads a picture would have got wrong, each found in shader source:

  • URP's Unlit pass never reads Emission (UnlitPass.hlsl:85); a shader driving BaseColor and Emission from one node would have doubled in brightness had both been ported.
  • A branch reading TEXCOORD1 reads a Unity custom vertex stream, not a second copy of TEXCOORD0.
  • HDR colour properties (m_ColorMode 1) are already linear in the .mat.
  • Unity samples every texture through its _ST (uv x _ST.xy + _ST.zw); a port that reads the tiling and never applies it drops it silently.
  • _Cull 1 culls FRONT faces in Unity when the shader lets the material override culling; built one-sided in Unreal it drew the faces Unity culls (the CULLFRONT route builds it as Unity draws it).

Variants and built-ins

A material VARIANT (m_Parent) serializes only what it overrides; the rest is its parent's, recursively. Read alone, a (0, 0, 0, 0) alpha channel selector picks no alpha and the emitter draws nothing while every check passes. scene_tools/vm1_read_materials.py resolves the chain, and the build refuses any input still unset: a property absent from the .mat is never evidence that the shader default applies. A built-in texture is a texture, not "no texture": a reader that treats a texture not on disk as an unassigned slot samples white (one such material drew as a 20 m orange square). Built-ins are read offline off unity_builtin_extra.

Unity's imported texture

Unity samples its IMPORTED texture: it fills RGB under alpha 0 (alpha is transparency), averages mips as an unweighted LINEAR box (Unreal's TMGS_SimpleAverage), resamples a non-power-of-two source to a power of two, and caps the size. effects_tools/unity_tex_artifact.py reads that import offline and validates every decode against the source (Chapter 12 gives how, and the trap it guards). Unreal's embedded Python has no PIL or numpy: such reads run in system Python and hand the build a derived file and a manifest. Two routes use them: the mips and mip bias of each .meta (an Unreal import is mip-less unless the route is on; a grainy look where Unity's is smooth is minification aliasing, which the .meta answers before any shader term) and Unity's stored RGB under transparent texels.

Proof

Read back every frame

u2ue read simulates each built system headless and reads its particles per frame through Niagara's sim cache (a recording of a system's particles, frame by frame; Chapter 13 gives how): position, velocity, colour, size and age every 1/60 s, or at Unity's probe step for a like-for-like read of positions. Three rules:

  • Built is not compiled, and compiled is not simulating. BUILT means saved with no converter error; a system never resaved in a fresh process reads nothing ("No valid simulation data"; Chapter 13 gives why). u2ue build and the trials resave, and effects_tools/u1e_simulates_check.py fails a system that never simulates, which no other check can.
  • NOT JUDGED is not a pass. A 90-frame read cannot see a child that fires at 2.28 s; read that system longer.
  • The record is not the asset. A caller can ignore a refusal function's False, so the record says "absent" while the asset draws. effects_tools/u1e_renderers_read.py reads what a saved system carries.

Checks on the saved asset, and judges with plants

Five checks, each with its plant: scene_tools/v4_write_gate.py refuses, before a build, a write no module declares; the other four read the SAVED package. scene_tools/v4_msg_gate.py refuses a package the engine logged a refused write into; scene_tools/v0_readback.py compares the saved fields with the IR; v4_curve_check.py compares the colour and size curves key for key; scene_tools/v2_dup_gate.py refuses a module or renderer added twice. effects_tools/u1e_names_gate.py proves the emitter names held, and effects_tools/u1e_material_errors.py tells a material's wiring-time compile messages from a real error.

Each read-back check in effects_tools/u1e_*_check.py holds one measured rule against the read and carries a plant. A check of the bound alone passes a route that does nothing: a cap check ("never above the cap, and the cap reached") passed a route that kept one particle and never spawned another, until it required Unity's refill. Ask what a route that does NOTHING would score, and plant the property the route changes. u2ue judge --prove fails a judge with no plant that refuses.

Photos

u2ue photo takes Unreal frames at Unity's sample times (0.1, 0.3, 0.6 and 1.0 s by default) for the pair sheets (Chapter 13 gives how the capture is made like for like). Unity's reference frames come from a float target (the unity_hdr photos): an 8-bit target clamps each draw before blending and under-draws HDR-boosted materials. Calibrate the Unreal capture like any instrument: an 8-bit sRGB target loses everything under about 1/510 linear, so the pair captures half floats to EXR and encodes them as Unity's target does (effects_tools/u1e_exr.py; a known constant must come back 255 / 188 / 137). A photo at an emitter's own start delay or lifetime is a step-edge frame in both engines: compare just off the edge.

Conformance against Unity's particle state

u2ue conform compares every emitter of every key on numbers (the procedure is Chapter 9). Its Shuriken specifics: Unity has no age field, so an age is startLifetime - remainingLifetime, undefined for an infinite lifetime (the first judge passed those as OK because NaN compares false). Unity's clock at a sample is the probe's own: Simulate at a simulation speed takes whole fixed steps in float32 and drops the rest (measured on 860 of 860 samples). Emitters are paired by file id, never by name, and both sides read at Unity's sample times only. A probe can be blind: one that restarted the simulation for each sample never drew a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter, which stepping at the game's own 1/60 s did.

The verbs, underneath

The effects route covers Shuriken ParticleSystem prefabs; extract lists VFX Graph assets and scene-authored particle systems by name as NOT COVERED. The game's code is Chapter 5, scenes and UI Chapter 6.

A project is one file, u2ue/projects/<name>.json (Chapter 3): the Unity project (serialized as TEXT), optionally its Editor (unity.editor), what the effects are, the Unreal host and content root, and where the work goes. py -m u2ue --project <game> info (u2ue info) opens every path and exits 1 when an input is missing: fix the project file before any other verb.

The adapter's three answers

With "adapter": "unity_project" the toolkit answers the game questions itself: every prefab holding a ParticleSystem is an effect, Unity's own rule decides what starts at spawn, and the Unreal host is busy only while an Unreal runs. Write an adapter in u2ue/adapters/ (subclass UnityProject, override ONE method) only when the game's code changes one of those answers, for example when its effects are the ones an ability table names (Chapter 18). py -m u2ue find <words> searches every document, tool, rule and route at once.

extract and check

extract builds the guid index in order - Assets/..., the project's embedded Packages/, then Library/PackageCache (package shaders resolve there) - then the keys, then one IR file per key. It exits 1 unless every key came out as an IR file or a NAMED refusal, every IR parses, and every Assets/... path an IR names exists in this project's tree. What a second project hits: legacy Prefab records (m_SourcePrefab {fileID: 0}), nested MODEL instances, m_RemovedComponents, package shaders, built-in shaders named off the Editor's unity_builtin_extra (set unity.editor). Measured on a second, unrelated game (2026-10-13): 60 keys gave 56 IR files (189 emitters) and 4 refusals, each by name.

check runs the toolkit's selftests and your project file's own, then yaml_field_gate and ir_field_gate, the measured rules' Unity versions and the engine-free model's gates. Exit 1 means do not build: a red field gate is an unread Unity field, and it will be a silent gap. check --only facts names the Unity version each measured rule was measured on against the project's unity.version; on another major.minor the rules are UNVERIFIED for this project, the build still runs, and metrics says so.

build, read and photo

build --dry first: the plan and the host's state. Then the asset-name table (two Unity files of one stem must not land on one Unreal asset), fx17_build.ps1 running u1e_build headless in batches, and a resave of only the systems THIS build made (U1E_RESAVE_ONLY). The record is <records>/u1e-build-<TAG>.json: per key its verdict, every emitter's modules and field notes, every absent emitter with its reason. Chapter 13 gives each of the three verbs' options and how it runs.

read writes <records>/rb_<TAG>_<N>.json, the input of every read-back check (effects_tools/u1e_*_check.py); a system that captured no frame is named, and the usual cause is a build never resaved. photo takes the frames, then u1e_photo_sheet pairs them with Unity's frames of the same times (<photos>/unity_hdr, taken by the effect photo probe in the project's own Editor, the owner's call). Read what differs against the record's notes first: a TwoColors start colour draws a different random colour in each engine, and a burst on the photo's own frame shows a step early or late. The verb is judged by its capture record, never the tool's exit.

report, metrics, tempo

report writes the acceptance page: every key's verdict, every absent emitter by reason and by ROOT, every stand-in, the read's sweep, the photo screen, and the owner's decisions. metrics prints the numbers, each from a record with its definition and age: coverage, measured, data, image - a FAMILY, never one "percent identical". tempo reads each route's first code to its flip off git. Quote metrics, never a recount, and treat a first number that looks too good as a bug until shown otherwise (a first coverage draft said 99.4 %: a stand-in's "draws nothing" had been read as Unity's).

Where things are

The converter is vfxport/build_niagara.py with shuriken_size.py, its proofs whole_trace.py and converter_trace_gate.py; the build, read, photo and check tools are in effects_tools/; the queues, trials and report builder in lane/; the material parents in scene_tools/; the Unity probes and judges in vfxport/unity_probe/, their bakes in shared/conformance/. The facade is u2ue/ (Chapter 18 gives how it finds each part).

The traps

Each was hit for real: the trap, then its fix. The timing traps (Life Cycle Mode, the edit condition, prewarm, the run-once end, the first tick, the lerped float, the cap) are explained under "Module by module" and not repeated here.

Unreal's Python API

  • The CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin must be ENABLED in the .uproject, or FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary and NiagaraEmitterConversionContext do not exist.
  • The conversion API asserts without Slate (-run=pythonscript dies with Assertion failed: CurrentBaseApplication.IsValid()), and -ExecutePythonScript quits when the script returns, before the tick loop runs. Use a Content/Python/init_unreal.py startup hook in a real editor, guarded by an environment variable so opening the project by hand stays inert.
  • The editor world does not tick actors (a stock system as the control drew nothing either). Enter Simulate (editor_play_simulate(), then get_game_world()) or advance the system yourself, as the sim cache read does.
  • print() does not reach stdout: write results to a JSON file.
  • Copy Epic's call patterns from Engine/Plugins/FX/CascadeToNiagaraConverter/Content/Python: Paths.py has the module and enum asset paths, every ModuleConversionScripts/*.py the exact input names.
  • Arity. CreateScriptContextArgs(assetData, [1,0]) is positional; find_or_add_module_script(name, args, category) RETURNS the script context; add_renderer(name, propsInstance) wants an instance; show_only_component(comp) takes one argument; the pool enum is NCPoolMethod, not PSCPoolMethod; unreal.Rotator is positional (roll, pitch, yaw), so use keywords (unreal.Rotator(pitch=p, yaw=y, roll=r)).
  • set_parameter reports a failed write by RETURNING FALSE. UNiagaraScriptConversionContext::SetParameter logs ENiagaraMessageSeverity::Error and returns false for an unknown name or a wrong type. A setp that ignored the bool lost 80 writes over 19 systems from 8 causes, each reported as applied (2026-09-29). The failures are INSIDE the saved asset as UNiagaraMessageDataText exports, and scene_tools/v4_msg_gate.py prints them and exits 1 on any error.
  • Read the module's declared inputs; never guess (v4_module_inputs.py, off the shipped .uasset). Guessing got wrong: the non-uniform size is Sprite Size; ScaleColor has no Scale Color; ConeLocation has Cone Length and no radius; SubUVAnimation has Number Of Frames; VortexForce has Vortex Force Amount; Spawn Count is an Int32 and Scale Factor a Vector2f.
  • A module can be VERSIONED, and CreateScriptContextArgs(ad, [1,0]) pins the OLD graph: Init builds its name map from the graph of the version handed to it. ScaleSpriteSize (bVersioningEnabled True, two graphs) refuses Uniform Scale Factor and Scale Sprite Size Mode at 1.0 and takes both at latest; ScaleColor takes Scale Mode at 1.0 and refuses it at latest. Pin the version per module; a file read that merges a package's graphs is WEAKER than the engine.
  • No 4-channel colour curve from Python: unreal.NiagaraDataInterfaceColorCurve does not exist in 5.7's Python, the factories stop at CreateVec4CurveDI (a Vector4Curve the engine refuses by name), and ColorFromCurve and Vector4FromCurve want the missing class. Use Scale RGB from a VectorFromCurve (its curve is create_vec3_curve_di's class) and Scale Alpha from a FloatFromCurve. The keys are readable after all: v4_curve_check.py compares FRichCurve.Keys with the IR.
  • The finalize pastes twice: the emitter and the system context each paste every staged module and renderer and empty neither list, so calling both built every emitter TWICE. Finalize at the system only.
  • A conversion context alive at exit asserts (call unreal.SystemLibrary.collect_garbage() at the end; never save a throwaway probe system), and a headless editor can crash in its embedded browser (launch with -nocef).

Reading Unity's files

  • Constant MinMax modes do not use the curves (scalar, [minScalar, scalar]). shuriken_ir.minmax multiplied the scalar by the first key: a tornado whose start rotation was exactly pi / 2 lay on its side, flares read 24 to 30 m/s against Unity's 30 to 70, a 0.3 s delay read 0. Every IR constant carries readAs, saying how it was read.
  • A signed file id breaks the split: --- !u!95 &-745123763528618581 did not match &(\d+); the pattern takes -?.
  • A renderer can be off: m_Enabled 0 draws nothing; the IR carries rendererEnabled, and no renderer is added.
  • A prefab's emitters have places: each emitter's transform in the prefab, root rotation included, goes into the emitter (prefab_frame, when the IR carries prefabRot).
  • Unity names an FBX mesh after its MODEL node, not its geometry; and Unreal imports through Interchange (not the legacy importer), whose unit conversion is on by default, so a metre file imports at 100 times its raw numbers. Check every import per corner.

Shapes, bursts and lifetimes

  • Unity's Cone emits from its BASE; ConeLocation fills from its apex, its axis +X by default. CylinderLocation 1.0 has no "Cylinder Axis" (refused inside the package): ask for the latest graph (location_cylinder_u1).
  • Two bursts are two SpawnBurst modules: Niagara names the second SpawnBurst_Instantaneous001, and the duplicate gate's --expect-build u1e-build.json accepts a twin only when the system holds exactly the burst modules the build asked for.
  • An INFINITE lifetime left the whole system dead in a game run, nothing in the log; a report of each system's active flag and bounds found it.
  • A random-constants range is serialized min > max as often as not: mm_range(...) returns the pair as serialized; take max() for the longest.
  • Compare counts over TIME, not only per frame: on the reference port 72 of 130 measured rows were off while every per-frame check passed (2026-10-07). Compare at Unity's sample times.
  • A named stand-in is still a stand-in (an unported child drawn at the origin), and the shot must not wait for the effect to END (photograph each effect at its peak).

Events, sub-emitters and trails

  • Niagara RENAMES a clashing emitter handle, comparing names with the FName number stripped: X_2 clashes with X, as does a distinct name such as ArcaneNoise_Lazy_Disco_1, and 001, 002 are appended. A renamed parent was never found by its events and the system read back empty. niagara_names.py names every emitter as the engine will, u1e_names_gate.py proves the names held, and every check maps names through u1e_names.table(ir).
  • find_or_add_module_script finds by NAME: two writers asking for "EventGenerator" share one module, and a parent has ONE location event. Register every generator a parent has (_parent_gens) before naming a new one.
  • ReceiveLocationEvent's Float 1 -> NormalizedAge apply also writes Age = Float 1 x Lifetime: send 0 there.
  • A dying particle moves once more before GenerateDeathEvent takes its position: keep it in an update assignment and send it through "Vector to Send as Vector 1 (Position)".
  • A spawn-stage assignment runs before InitializeParticle ("read before being set", and the system runs nothing). An event-spawned particle needs InitializeParticle, or it is born with lifetime 0; it reads Age = DeltaTime / 2 on its first frame.
  • A location generator in an event script fires nothing: route a birth child of a one-point-per-event middle to the grandparent. Use Event Probability does not gate an Every Frame location event.
  • A parent's last tick's events are read twice (the converter's guard kills the stale ones); an event-spawned child's curves apply twice; a particle killed in its first update still fires its generators (gate generation on the lifetime).
  • Deleting an if line can leave its block nested after the previous branch's return, never run and never reported. py unreachable_gate.py (in vfxport/) refuses it. A stand-in dry run counts calls on the EMITTER context (sysctx.add_empty_emitter.return_value), not the system context.
  • A ported child changes its whole family: whole_trace.py --with-parents widens the expected set to the parents the children name.

Frames, textures and capture

  • A polygon's first three corners are not its normal (a concave quad): judge winding by corner ORDER. A material's "Local" space is the particle's own transform for a mesh particle, the primitive's for a sprite.
  • A texture's platform data builds ASYNCHRONOUSLY; a draw before it finishes samples EXACTLY 0, and blueprint_get_size_x/y reads 32 x 32. unreal.AssetCompilingManager, unreal.TextureCompilingManager and UTexture.update_resource do not exist in 5.7's Python; the only reachable flush is unreal.SystemLibrary.execute_console_command(None, "Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll"), before EVERY draw. -NoTextureStreaming and never_stream do not help (13 of 13 textures, 2026-09-29).
  • Never use a WHITE texture as a binding's control: Runtime/Engine/Private/Materials/MaterialUniformExpressions.cpp:1396-1401 binds GWhiteTexture for an invalid binding, so success and failure look alike.
  • Unreal reads gamma off the IMAGE, Unity off the importer flag: Editor/UnrealEd/Private/Factories/EditorFactories.cpp:2941 sets bSRGB from LoadedImage.GammaSpace != EGammaSpace::Linear, and a 16-bit source is linear. Texture.srgb cannot fix it; SourceColorSettings.EncodingOverride = TSE_S_RGB can, on 16-bit sources only (on an 8-bit source maxTextureSize downscales it is worse). The member is TSE_S_RGB, not TSE_SRGB.
  • Unreal DISCARDS a BLEND_MASKED pixel below the clip value: a reference compositing opaque charged the material 41.1705 for an instrument gap (the true residual 0.0219).
  • The filmic tonemapper sends display values under about 16 / 255 to 0 (compare faint halos untonemapped), and an isolate photo can leak bursts at time 0 (read its live counts).

Harness and gates

  • A gate's input format is part of the gate: an audit that read one way of setting a switch missed six trial switches. Widen it, then watch it fail.
  • A check that judges a stand-in, or an emitter Unity never emits, fails emitters that are right; a raw-name match against the absent list flags a built twin. Judge by the build's notes, the IR's flags and the file id.
  • A log gate written without the known noise misfires, and a value found anywhere is vacuous ("1.0" is in "-1.0").
  • A queue's FAIL branch acts on the check's verdict: run a new check that guards an automatic restore by hand first.
  • Preflight every headless Unreal launch (effects_tools/u1e_preflight.py), and grep the checks that execute a converter function before giving it a new dependency.
  • PowerShell names are case-insensitive: a loop over $s overwrote $S, and a queue skipped its read and checks yet wrote its done marker. A step whose output is missing prints FAILED.
  • A watchdog sized by a smaller run kills a bigger one: compare the key count built with the keys asked, after every build.

12. The Unity tools: headless, driving an editor, several agents

Who this is for: the porting developer who needs Unity's answers. After it you can pick the tool that gets each answer with no editor, drive an editor someone is working in without disturbing them, and recognise the traps each tool guards against.

A port is held to Unity, so it needs Unity's answers: what a file stores, whether the C# still compiles, whether a test passes, and what the engine actually does at a given frame.

One rule runs through all of it. The Unity editor on your machine belongs to the person working in it, its owner. A tool that can answer without an editor never starts one. A tool that needs an editor waits until the owner is away, and leaves the editor exactly as it found it.

The three ways to work with Unity

way what runs what it can answer what it costs the owner pick it when
No editor Python and .NET reading Unity's files; Unity's own compiler and Mono; NUnit, the .NET test framework Unity's tests are written in what a file stores, what Unity imported, whether the C# compiles, whether a logic test passes, a rule's answer on Unity's own runtime nothing: no window, no focus always first
Driving a live editor an HTTP server inside the owner's editor, and the idle-gated window runner what the running engine does: a probe's measurements, the console, a screenshot, Play the editor itself: a recompile, a probe dropped in and taken out the answer exists only inside Unity, and the owner is away
A second editor instance a full Unity Editor on a clone of the project, on its own port the Unity Test Runner, editor tools, anything the live editor could do, without touching it a second full GUI editor on the owner's desktop, taking focus on every assembly reload the owner has allowed it and its kill switch is off (below)

The order is the order of preference. A question moves down a row only when the row above cannot answer it, and the reason is written down. "The test lives in an Editor/ folder" is not a reason: the headless NUnit runner runs those. "The test opens a scene through AssetDatabase" (the editor's own asset API) is.

No editor: reading Unity's files

Unity serialises scenes, prefabs, materials, ScriptableObjects and .meta files as YAML text. What the inspector shows is what the file stores (serialisation beats the C# initialiser), so the toolkit reads values there and never retypes them.

verb or tool what it reads where it is described
u2ue extract every effect prefab, into one IR file per key Chapter 7
u2ue data one component's or ScriptableObject's serialized values below
u2ue inventory, u2ue uml the game's C#, type by type, and its class model Chapter 5
u2ue shear, u2ue scene scene nodes Unreal cannot place; a scene's import and its fidelity gate (its export runs in a window) Chapter 6
vfxport/yaml_field_gate.py a Unity field a reader neither reads nor excuses, refused by name Chapter 9

u2ue data finds every matching component, expands nested prefab instances with their modifications applied (a value an override changed is the override's), and writes each component's GameObject path, its fileID (the object's id inside its file) and every field as the file stores it; a reference {fileID, guid} (an object in the file that guid names) carries the asset path it names.

py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <Assets/...prefab> --script <ClassName> --tsv <out.tsv>
py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <Assets/...unity> --class Light --no-expand

--script matches a MonoBehaviour by its script's guid, never a line number (a re-saved file moves its lines); --class takes a class id (20 Camera, 108 Light) or a YAML type name; --tsv writes one <dotted path> <TAB> <value> row per leaf, which two readers' outputs can be diffed in. The traps a reader must handle (the nested-object fileID, material variants, the blend mode as a number) are in Chapter 6 and Chapter 16.

Unity's imported textures, off Library/Artifacts

Unity samples its imported texture, not the source file. Each import is a SerializedFile (Unity's binary file of serialized objects) under Library/Artifacts/<hh>/<hash>, so "what does Unity actually sample here" needs no window. effects_tools/unity_tex_artifact.py finds the texture's GUID in Library/ArtifactDB (an LMDB key-value database; the GUID's bytes are nibble-swapped), reads the Texture2D fields by value, and refuses unless all agree: the size against the .meta's cap, the image size equal to the format's whole mip chain to the byte, a decoded format (DXT1, DXT5, RGBA32), the mip count, the mip bias. Validate every match against the source: the index's neighbourhood holds other assets' hashes, and 3 of 414 textures first matched a wrong image (measured 2026-10-14: a real match's 4x4 block means sat within about 6 of 255, a wrong image's read 73 to 148).

What the reads show: Unity fills the colour under alpha 0 for alpha-is-transparency textures, averages mips unweighted in linear light, and resamples a non-power-of-two source (512 x 520 became 512 x 512). None of that is in the source PNG.

No editor: the headless C# typecheck

typecheck.py answers the question asked most often, "does the C# still compile", without an editor and with Unity's own answer. Unity has already written its complete compiler command lines to disk, one .rsp per assembly under Library/Bee/artifacts/<dag>/. The tool reuses them with the Roslyn compiler inside that Unity version (Editor/Data/DotNetSdkRoslyn/csc.dll, run by the editor's bundled dotnet), so defines, references and language version are Unity's. It compiles Assembly-CSharp (the assembly Unity builds the game's scripts into), then Assembly-CSharp-Editor (its Editor/ folder scripts) against the fresh runtime assembly.

py typecheck.py                                # both assemblies
py typecheck.py --editor                       # the editor assembly only
py typecheck.py --extra <Probe.cs>             # also compile a file that is not in the project into the editor assembly
py typecheck.py --platform osx                 # with another editor platform's defines (win, osx, linux)
py typecheck.py --as-head [--keep <path>]      # what a fresh checkout of the version-control head compiles
py typecheck.py --model-from-source            # against the engine-free model built from source, not the installed DLLs

Exit 0 is clean, 1 prints the errors, 2 means the check could not run, which it says is not a pass. It proves the code builds, not that it behaves. The traps, each handled in the code:

  • The -out: line is project-relative. A rewrite that misses it lets the compiler write over Unity's own artifact; the tool refuses to compile unless exactly one -out: line was redirected.
  • The editor .rsp references Assembly-CSharp.ref.dll from Unity's last compile; the tool points it at the fresh build, or a changed signature is checked against the stale one.
  • The .rsp is a snapshot. A file created since is appended (else a new file with errors passes, and a new file without errors breaks every file that uses it); a file deleted since is dropped (else CS2001, "Source file could not be found", reads like a broken build). Both are counted.
  • There is one .dag folder per build configuration (the editor's, a development player's). The tool takes the newest holding both command lines: two assemblies from two snapshots compile against two source lists and invent errors.
  • A folder with an .asmdef or an .asmref belongs to another assembly. Without the .asmref rule a package's folder is swept into Assembly-CSharp and produces CS0433 errors (a type that exists in both assemblies) in third-party files. A false failure in innocent code is worse than a missing check: its obvious fix breaks a working project.
  • --as-head reads pending changes from Unity Version Control through its command line, cm (cm status), and compiles each edited file at its head revision, fetched with cm getfile: cm cat re-encodes non-ASCII through the console code page. A precompiled DLL that is not checked in is left out unless --keep names it, as a fresh checkout would.
  • --platform exists because a macOS editor compiles the #else side of every #if UNITY_EDITOR_WIN.
  • It never compiles a player (Unity's build of the game itself, outside the editor), so runtime code calling a member inside #if UNITY_EDITOR passes here and fails in a player build. No tool does that compile yet.

A known gap: typecheck.py has no planted selftest (--selftest-head-has proves only its head listing; it reads no --selftest flag). u2ue cycle, the toolkit's recurring self-check (Chapter 14), runs it under pillar 4 (a pillar is one promise the product makes), so that row proves the project compiled that day, not that the typecheck can fail.

No editor: the headless NUnit runner

Tests that live in a Unity project's Editor/ folder but only exercise data and logic need no editor. headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py runs them under plain NUnit with no Unity process. It exists because the alternative, the Unity Test Runner, starts a full editor (the second instance, below), which can make the owner's machine unusable.

py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <Assets/.../Editor/SomeTests.cs>
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test A.cs --test B.cs --filter "FullyQualifiedName~Resolver"
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test A.cs --typecheck-editor     # also compile the Editor assembly
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test A.cs --no-compile           # reuse the last compile
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --selftest

--define adds a define and --out names the work directory. Exit 0 means every test passed, 1 a test failed, 2 nothing ran (a filter that matches nothing is a failure, never an empty pass), 3 an environment or compile failure, or a stale build.

How it works

  1. Compile Assembly-CSharp.dll from Unity's own Bee .rsp (the newest Library/Bee/artifacts/*.dag/Assembly-CSharp.rsp) with the bundled Roslyn (Editor/Data/DotNetSdkRoslyn/csc.dll). -out is redirected to the work directory, -refout dropped, every edit guarded, and the rsp's source list reconciled with the files on disk (a brand-new .cs appended, a deleted one dropped). Nothing under Library/ is written. The result is named AC.dll.
  2. Generate a net10 NUnit project that compiles the given test file(s) with UNITY_EDITOR defined, references the fresh AC.dll, and swaps UnityEngine.CoreModule for UnityShimCore/, the shim: a purely managed replacement (Debug, Mathf, Random, Resources, the Vector and Color structs, the Object / Component / MonoBehaviour chain); Resources.Load answers null. It also references the game's own asmdef assemblies at their real implementations in Library/ScriptAssemblies (a Bee .ref.dll holds metadata only and throws when loaded) and the managed plugins under Assets/Plugins.
  3. dotnet test it. HeadlessBoot.cs prints which AC.dll actually ran (its path and MVID, the build id in its metadata), and the tool checks its md5 against step 1's compile, so a stale build can never pass quietly.

Measured on 2026-09-01: a file of 4 tests whose static constructors build the game's whole data tables compiled in 4 s and ran in 15 s, and a mutation run (the code under test deliberately broken, to see whether the tests notice; Chapter 14) failed 3 of 4 with 196 named mismatches.

Expect a minority of a project's editor test files to run as they stand. Of the reference port's 133 (headless_nunit/census_2026-09-07.json), 31 ran clean (340 tests) and 9 more with a helper file passed as a second --test (129 tests); 69 were bound to the editor (66 by their own text, 3 through a file they use) and not run, 22 failed to compile against the shim or failed at run time, and 2 held no tests.

The selftest drives the real runner on the cached compile: a planted passing test must exit 0, a failing one 1, an empty filter 2.

What it cannot run

Anything touching UnityEditor.*, AssetDatabase, real components or scenes, or a UnityEngine member the shim lacks. These fail loudly: TypeLoadException, MissingMethodException or FileNotFoundException, naming the member or the assembly. If the member is pure, add it to UnityShimCore/Shim.cs; if not, the test needs an editor, and the honest report is that it was not run.

  • Copy Unity's declaration kind, not just its name. The code under test calls a property as get_text(), so a shim field of that name throws MissingMethodException (measured on a text asset's text and on Object.name).
  • A CS0103 or CS0246 naming a type is not "cannot run headless". The runner compiles only Assembly-CSharp and the files it is given; pass the file that defines the type as another --test.
  • When a test "needs Unity", usually only its plumbing does. Moved into its own class, the arithmetic of one editor-bound fix ran its 12 tests headless in 1.4 s, and a mutation run failed exactly the 4 relevant ones. Push the logic out, leave the plumbing untested, and say so.

Traps the runner absorbs

  • The bin keeps the SOURCE file name. The reference is AC.dll, so MSBuild copies it as bin/.../AC.dll, not Assembly-CSharp.dll. A mutation run that swaps bin/Assembly-CSharp.dll swaps a file nobody loads, and "passes". Swap bin/AC.dll, and read the LOADED Assembly-CSharp: ... MVID= line every time.
  • NUnit 3.14, not 4. Unity's NUnit is 3.x; NUnit 4 moved Assert.IsNotNull and its relatives to ClassicAssert, so the same test source stops compiling.
  • -out: in the rsp is project-relative, as in the typecheck: the tool rewrites it by line prefix and re-reads the file to verify.
  • A test file changed after the rsp was written is compiled directly (the test project compiles it), but a NEW runtime file only gets in through the reconcile step: watch the "appended" line.
  • Right after a player build, the newest rsp is the player's. The runner takes the newest .dag by time, so it would build AC.dll without UNITY_EDITOR; use --no-compile until the editor compiles again.
  • The Windows console is not UTF-8. Without forcing it, a failure message quoting non-ASCII source died inside the print loop and hid the run's totals.

The game's own plain .NET test project for its engine-free rules (dotnet test <tests project>) needs neither this runner nor Unity. Report what actually ran: "compile-verified headlessly, suite not run" is an honest report.

No editor: Unity's own Mono

A float rule's answer depends on the runtime that compiles and runs it, and Unity's Mono can land one ULP (the smallest step between two floats) from CoreCLR, the runtime of modern .NET. u2ue digest answers a game's rule cases on both with no editor: once for CoreCLR (logic-Headless.txt), once compiled by that Unity version's own csc.exe and run on its mono-bdwgc.exe, the editor's own runtime build (logic-UnityMono.txt).

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs>
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful

faithful re-measures that the standalone Mono stands in for the editor: on Unity 6000.3.16f1 (2026-10-16) the digest computed this way equalled the one the editor wrote, 383 rows of 383, including the 35 where Mono and CoreCLR differ. A Unity version with no such measurement is labelled UNMEASURED. Chapter 5, step 7 is the method.

Driving a live editor: the HTTP bridge

When the answer exists only inside a running editor, an agent drives it through an HTTP server inside the editor: the bridge. That server does not ship yet ("What ships, and what does not yet", below), so until it does your project needs its own. What follows is how the reference port's bridge serves: the behaviour the toolkit's tools rely on, and the design to copy.

How it serves

  • It starts with every domain load ([InitializeOnLoad]; a domain load is Unity reloading the scripts' assemblies, as after every compile), and refuses to in a process no person drives: batch mode, an asset-import worker, an editor that is not human-controlled. Those run the same script, and before this rule they bound ports with listeners whose main thread never ticked.
  • A listener on a background thread, bound to both localhost and 127.0.0.1 (the Windows listener treats them separately, and a client may call either), on the first free port of four starting at 7860.
  • The port file. The bound port is written to bridge_port.txt at the project root and under ProjectSettings/; read it every time, since the port moves across restarts. A real stop writes 0, but a domain reload does not: if the reload hangs, a 0 would say "bridge dead" when the truth is "reload stuck".
  • Interruptible accept. The listener waits in 250 ms slices (BeginGetContext, WaitOne(250)), never in one native GetContext(): Mono cannot abort a thread parked in native code, and the old loop froze Unity on "Reloading Domain". Stopping calls Close() as well as Stop(), since only Close() releases the socket.
  • Main-thread dispatch. Unity's API is main-thread only, so requests are queued and EditorApplication.update drains up to four per tick, dropping any older than 10 s (its caller has given up).
  • What answers when the main thread cannot. /ping, /status, /capabilities, /recompile, /play, /stop and /focus are answered on the listener thread from state cached every tick, so they answer during a compile and behind a modal dialog, when an agent needs them most.

/status carries isPlaying, isPaused, isCompiling, compileTick (finished compiles), autoRefreshMode, mainThreadResponsive, mainThreadTickAgeMs, port and hotReload; mainThreadResponsive is true while the last tick is at most 4,000 ms old. /capabilities adds the advertised routes and the edit-mode-only and play-mode-only lists.

A health signal must be stamped after the work it vouches for. On a macOS editor a Windows-only user32.dll call threw on every tick and the dispatch after it never ran, while /status reported a tick stamped above the throw: healthy-looking, and serving nothing. Off Windows, window handles are ABSENT with the reason, and /focus answers 501.

The reference bridge also has a monitor window (its state and last 128 requests) and a menu command that restarts the listener.

The route families

family routes what it does
health /ping, /status, /capabilities alive; editor state; self-description
focus /focus brings the editor's window to the front (a disturbance, below)
compile /recompile a refresh that picks up changed scripts; answers 202, polled through /status
play /play, /stop enter or leave Play; concurrent requests coalesce and the latest intent wins
console /console/entries the Console's own rows, read-only (the console section, below)
events and profiler /events, /events/last, /profiler, /profiler/deep events the game posts; frame time, memory, and Unity's profiler counters averaged over 60 frames
screenshots /screenshot/game-view, /screenshot/scene-view, /sceneview/info, /sceneview/frame a PNG of the Game or Scene view (the Game view's answer carries the file's byte count and md5); the Scene view camera's facts
scenes /scene/save, /scene/reload save the open scenes; reload one from disk on an explicit path (discarding unsaved changes, edit mode only)
prefabs and materials /prefab/measure, /prefab/preview, /prefabs/audit, /materials/remap-urp-lit measure, preview or audit prefabs; re-target a material to URP Lit
imports and shaders /assets/reimport-all, /shaders/check a forced refresh and shader reimport (synchronous and slow); every shader asset's compile state
UI state /ugui/dump, /panel-gallery/* the UI's structured state; a catalogue that spawns any UI panel and captures it alone
tests /test/* in-editor suites run by the bridge and answered as JSON; /test/bridge runs the bridge's own stability tests

Read the picture, and the hash. A screenshot route answering ok with a path proves bytes were written; open the file. Two captures that should differ but share one md5 show a stale frame: with the editor in the background the Game view route returned one md5 twice, 2.5 minutes apart.

Dump the UI's state before iterating on its screenshot. A PNG loses the anchors, the computed rect, the parent canvas, the alpha. /ugui/dump?type=<Panel> first forces the layout to rebuild (LayoutRebuilder.ForceRebuildLayoutImmediate, then Canvas.ForceUpdateCanvases), since a rect read in the frame a layout changed is stale, then returns each panel's rects, parent canvas, alpha and anomalies (alpha 0 while active, Unity's default 100 x 100 never set, and others). The panel catalogue finds every class implementing the game's panel interface by reflection; /panel-gallery/headshot captures one panel alone.

Most routes are the game's own. On the reference bridge the families above are a small part of what it answers; the rest run the game's own suites and set up its levels, cameras, menus and content. Keep the families and bring your game's own.

The advertised list drifts. /capabilities lists routes from a hand-kept array beside the dispatch, so a working route left out of it is invisible to an agent that learns its tools there (read 2026-10-17, the reference bridge answered 13 routes it did not list). A new route can also fail to load when a compile error elsewhere stops the reload, so verify a new route through /capabilities, knowing the advert is a second list. The fix is a dispatch table whose keys are the advert ("What ships", below).

Guards and refusals

A route declares what it needs, and a call that lacks it is refused before any work:

refusal status
the route needs Play and the editor is not playing 400
the route is edit-mode only and the editor is playing 409
the editor is compiling 409, with compileTick
the main thread's last tick is more than 4,000 ms old 503, with mainThreadTickAgeMs

/recompile also refuses while a compile or import is in flight (in_flight) and debounces calls within 2 s (debounced). Without them, an agent retrying faster than Unity could settle scheduled one forced refresh after another, each a domain reload of 13 to 30 s by the bridge's own note, and its wait never converged because it caused the next compile. About 30 ticks after a refresh with no compile, the bridge logs "NO compile started after Refresh": a locked reload, Auto Refresh off, or nothing to compile (a byte-identical file is the last case, and a pass).

Driving a live editor: the measurement window

A probe (the probes, below) must run inside the owner's editor, which is in use. u2ue window runs one probe session from a data file, built so it cannot cost the owner anything; Chapter 8 gives the protocol step by step.

py -m u2ue --project <game> window check <spec.json>    # every refusal judged now; nothing touched
py -m u2ue --project <game> window run <spec.json>      # wait for the owner to be away, then run it
py -m u2ue.verbs.window --selftest                      # the whole flow against a simulated editor

It waits for the owner's quiet and stops at its next step when the owner returns (the gates are under "Never disturb the owner", below). It refuses to start with no bridge, in Play, under another's editor lock, over an existing output, or with a probe that does not compile headless. It removes the probes only while the editor is idle twice 5 s apart (one was once deleted mid-import). It never answers a modal, never enters Play, and never runs the Test Runner.

check exits 0 when the window would start and 2 with its refusals. run writes window-<label>.json into a windows folder under the project's records directory (work.records); PASS exits 0, STOPPED and FAIL 1, a refusal 2. The runner reaches the editor through one small interface, so its selftest swaps in a simulated editor for 11 cases, each of which must leave no probe, trigger or lock. The quiet and presence gates are Windows PowerShell scripts today.

A second editor instance: my_unity.py

Some questions need a real editor that is not the owner's: the Unity Test Runner, an editor tool. my_unity.py gives an agent a full Unity Editor on a clone of the project, on a port the owner's editor never uses, driven through the open-source Unity MCP package's client unity-mcp-cli. That package is an MCP server (MCP: the Model Context Protocol, through which an AI model calls outside tools): it runs inside a Unity editor and lets an AI model call the editor's tools (compared below). my_unity.py is the recipe for doing that safely.

py my_unity.py status                                 # is the clone's server up
py my_unity.py down                                   # close the clone's editor
py my_unity.py test                                   # sync the scripts, run every EditMode test, diff against the baseline
py my_unity.py test --no-sync                         # run against what is already in the clone
py my_unity.py test --method "Fixture.TestName"       # one test
py my_unity.py test --namespace "Some.Namespace"      # one namespace
py my_unity.py up                                     # launch the clone and wait until it serves
py my_unity.py tool <name> --input '{...}'            # one tool of the server
py my_unity.py baseline                               # record a full run as the accepted baseline

An EditMode test is one the Test Runner runs in the editor without entering Play. Exit 0 is verified green, 1 a named problem (a regression, a new failing test, a test that stopped running), 2 an UNKNOWN outcome, 3 blocked by the kill switch.

What it does for the agent

  • Its own port. The clone serves on 58447 and a second clone on 58448, so parallel agents need not queue on one editor; the owner's editor's port (58446 in the reference setup) is never a target.
  • A sync that refuses to destroy work. test mirrors the scripts live to clone (robocopy /MIR, which deletes what only the clone has), but first compares every clone script with its live copy by content and aborts, naming the files, when the clone holds edits live does not. Without that check a sync wiped an agent's work in the clone, and the run reported "no regressions" against code that no longer held it.
  • Assets do not sync into a running editor. Unity owns Assets/ while it runs: an asset copied in was rewritten by the clone from its loaded copy a minute later. Scripts are fine, since they compile from disk; a run that must see a changed asset restarts the clone cold.
  • A tree that stood still. The script tree is hashed before and after; if it moved, the outcome is UNKNOWN. Four runs "on the same tree" reported 31, 29, 23 and 32 failures because other agents were editing the clone mid-run; two runs with the tree frozen shared 33 of 34.
  • Every test named. The server's test tool withholds passing tests unless asked, so a missing name could mean "passed" or "never ran"; the script asks for all (includePassingTests: true). Without it, 1,323 tests came back as 43 rows.
  • A baseline with both sides of the ledger: the total, every test that ran, and the accepted non-passing set. test reports only what the change moved, says which coverage it proved (per name, count only, or UNVERIFIED), and reports a baseline test missing from a complete reply as STOPPED-RUNNING. Names are compared whole (shortened, Apply(Hover,0.7f,"Tex") splits on the dot in 0.7f). A subset run never touches the baseline.
  • A lost reply recovered from the run's own file. A test call can time out while the run carries on; the script waits for a TestResults.xml written after the run started and parses it once its size holds across a poll (parsed the moment it was fresh, it was caught half-written).
  • The clone's own startup modals closed, by name only. A native modal blocks the main thread, so the server never starts (a migration prompt held a clone over 10 minutes). Only the clone's own popups whose titles name a known blocking dialog are closed: closing every owned titled popup also closed a torn-off Scene view.
  • The client's traps absorbed (listed under the MCP server, below): a 20-minute call timeout, a busy runner retried every 30 s up to 20 times, and UTF-8 output forced (its box-drawing characters on a cp1252 console produced no output at all, which read as a hang).

What it costs, and the kill switch

The cost is not CPU. The clone is a full GUI editor on the owner's desktop:

  • It takes window focus on every assembly reload, and a full run reloads many times. Its modal dialogs take system focus too: a startup prompt raised three times in one session broke /focus on the owner's editor each time.
  • Measured on the reference project (2026-08-29 and 2026-09-01): a full EditMode run took about 7.5 minutes, a --method run about 8 s, a --namespace run about 12 s, and a cold clone sat at about 15 s of CPU per 5 s of wall time for about 30 minutes.
  • Left on top of the owner's editor holding a modal, it kept that editor in the background, and the owner's editor did not rebuild its scripts for a day; closing the dialog and minimising the clone made it compile within seconds.

So the second instance is opt-in, behind a kill switch, added after an agent looped a test command that launched the clone on every run until the owner could not use the machine. While .opus-tools/.UNITY_TESTS_DISABLED exists, my_unity.py exits 3 for test, up, tool and baseline, printing the file's reason; status and down still work, because they are how an agent inspects and cleans up. Only the owner removes the file. A message does not stop a loop that is already running; refusing to start does. Launching the editor another way (the MCP client directly, its test tool, Unity.exe) is the same act, not a workaround: an agent that cannot proceed without an editor reports itself blocked and asks.

When the owner allows a run, one approval covers one run, a subset's approval is not a full run's, runs are never stacked or put in an unattended retry loop, and my_unity.py down ends every session.

Several agents at once

One driver per editor

An editor is single-tenant. The bridge serialises each route call on the main thread, but a logical operation is several calls - hide every panel, show one, capture it - and nothing makes the sequence atomic: two agents interleave and each captures the other's state. The bridge protects single calls (concurrent /play and /stop coalesce to the latest intent; /recompile debounces), never sequences. So:

  • One Unity-driver agent per editor. Every route call, recompile, Play and window for that editor goes through it.
  • Every other agent works headless (the code index, version control, requirements, the readers, the typecheck, the headless tests) and asks the driver for any editor action.
  • Never two agents on one editor. An agent that needs its own editor gets the second instance, when the owner allows it, or waits.
  • Read-only diagnosis is always safe: the body of /capabilities, the tail of the editor log, unity_recovery.py --check. Before mutating, check for another live session: several sessions have been found on one editor at once.

The editor lock, .opus-tools/.locks/unity-editor.lock, is a text file naming who holds the editor, why, and since when. The window runner refuses while anyone else holds it and holds it for its whole life; any tool that changes editor state should do the same.

An MCP server on a default port is reachable by every default-configured client. One was found running inside an owner's live editor after a full EditMode session had run there and discarded an unsaved scene (the server the prime suspect, not proven). Never call the test tool or the MCP client without an explicit port.

The mail channel

Agents coordinate through files, with no server: agent_mail.py appends to .agent-mail/messages.jsonl and keeps read state in .agent-mail/read.json. Each agent keeps one stable name (--from / --as, or AGENT_MAIL_NAME); AGENT_MAIL_ROOT points every command at a sandbox.

py agent_mail.py send --from <me> --to <them> --subject S --body TEXT       # body "-" reads stdin
py agent_mail.py inbox --as <me>
py agent_mail.py ask --from <me> --to unity-driver --subject S --body TEXT --timeout 60
py agent_mail.py broadcast --from <me> --to "*" --subject S --body TEXT
py agent_mail.py watch --as <me> --seconds 60

read, mark-read, thread and agents complete the set. ask exits 0 when a reply to its message lands and 3 on timeout. bot is an auto-responder for tests (modes ack, echo, silent, error).

tool what it does
agent_super.py watch a long-lived inbox tail with a subject filter, so a supervisor sees only what matters (--as supervisor --filter HELP)
agent_super.py fanout sends each task of a JSON list to its worker, collects every reply within a timeout, and reports each reply's latency and the tasks that got none
agent_boot.py up --config harness.json starts a worker pool as background processes; status, down, logs --name; PIDs in .opus-tools/.harness-state.json, logs in .opus-tools/.harness-logs/
agent_harness.py the channel's own tests, each scenario in its own sandbox with an explicit pass criterion (from send and inbox to concurrent writes with no loss). Exit 0 only when all pass; --only T4,T5 runs a subset

The pattern that encodes the driver rule: one worker named unity-driver beside the analysis workers, and a supervisor that sends only editor tasks to it through agent_super.py fanout.

Never disturb the owner

Is the owner at the machine?

Windows' GetLastInputInfo cannot be trusted to say. Measured on the reference machine (2026-10-03): its idle time read 0.00 to 0.02 s on every sample while the cursor sat on one pixel and nothing was pressed, resetting about every 16 ms as if something injected zero-move input. Presence is read from the inputs themselves: the cursor (GetCursorPos) and every key and button (GetAsyncKeyState over 1 to 254). lane/wait_quiet.ps1 samples them every 250 ms and returns only after 600 s with the cursor unmoved and nothing pressed, printing QUIET; lane/wait_presence.ps1 samples them every second (its default) and prints one PRESENT line when either changes. A gate that never says QUIET has refused.

Focus

  • Entering Play focuses the Game view, and the owner's keystrokes land in the game (input that was not a capture's once played a turn during one). Before any Play: the owner away, the editor lock held, one short session, and a capture that checks isPlaying and a sane screen size or is discarded.
  • /focus is a disturbance. Windows does not let a background process take the foreground, so the bridge briefly attaches its input to the foreground thread's (AttachThreadInput) and reports ok: false with the reason when that fails. Restoring the window unconditionally un-maximises a maximised one (an owner's editor was found shrunk to 890 x 474). Taking focus is not permission to resize.
  • Whether a background editor compiles has been measured both ways: one behind another window did not rebuild until it came forward, and another time /recompile compiled and reloaded a background editor twice, in 30 to 60 s each. Assume neither: the editor assembly in Library/ScriptAssemblies being newer than the edited source is the only honest compile signal.

Work queued on delayCall never runs in the background

EditorApplication.delayCall does not fire while the editor is unfocused; EditorApplication.update keeps ticking. Measured twice (2026-08-28 and 2026-10-07): /recompile and /play scheduled through delayCall never ran in the background, so the bridge acts on them from its update tick; and an import watcher's delayCall body ran zero times over six imports while /status showed a tick every 39 ms. Anything that must run after an import or a route call goes on a pending list drained by the next update tick, each step in its own try / catch so one failure is red and the rest still run. delayCall is safe only as a redundant second path.

Recompile, then Play

Unity defers an assembly reload while in Play, so a /play sent too soon after /recompile runs the old assembly for minutes while /status says isPlaying: true, isCompiling: true. The symptom: an A/B run's "after" reproduces the "before" numbers exactly, because it measured the pre-edit build. The safe order:

  1. Edit, then /recompile: it answers 202 with the current compileTick.
  2. Poll /status until isCompiling is false on three consecutive polls, then wait about 20 s: the compile and its reload are done.
  3. Check that the editor assembly in Library/ScriptAssemblies is newer than the edited .cs: the running code is the edit.
  4. Then /play. If isCompiling stays true through Play, or the run reproduces the old numbers exactly, it measured the old build.

Modal dialogs

A native modal dialog runs its own message pump on the main thread. The dialog stays clickable, but EditorApplication.update never ticks: windows stop repainting (an unrelated tool window seemed to "disappear"), queued routes never run, a probe never sees its trigger. The listener thread keeps answering, so an HTTP 200 proves nothing; the honest signal is mainThreadResponsive: false with mainThreadTickAgeMs climbing.

  • Enumerate the windows and their owning processes before calling an editor hung. An editor taken for hung was healthy: a second editor's modal sat on top of it. The editor log (%LOCALAPPDATA%/Unity/Editor/Editor.log) is shared by every editor on the machine; a window enumeration says which is which. Read titles with InternalGetWindowText: GetWindowTextW blocks while Unity's main thread is busy.
  • After an unclean exit Unity asks to recover its scene backups and does not start until someone answers: the title "Recovering Scene Backups", about 72 MB and no CPU, where a real start passes 900 MB within seconds. The dialog is the owner's: answer it only when the owner has said to, otherwise say in one line what the editor waits on.

Recovery: unity_recovery.py and bridge_wake.py

py unity_recovery.py --check       # read-only diagnosis
py unity_recovery.py --wait        # poll until the bridge answers (--timeout, default 300 s)
py unity_recovery.py --auto        # diagnose, then apply the matching recovery and wait
py unity_recovery.py --kill        # end every Unity.exe
py unity_recovery.py --restart     # kill, then relaunch

--check reads the Unity.exe processes, the port file with a TCP connect and a GET of /capabilities, and the editor log's age and last reload lines, and names the first state that matches:

state what it saw recovery
crashed no editor process, no bridge relaunch
hung_in_reload an editor, no bridge, a reload begun and not finished kill and relaunch
hung_unresponsive an editor, no bridge, the log untouched for over 90 s kill and relaunch
bridge_down an editor, a fresh log, no bridge (between a stop and a start) wait, then relaunch if it does not recover
ok an editor and a bridge answering 200 none

A relaunch starts the version in ProjectSettings/ProjectVersion.txt directly with -no-safe-mode (a Hub already running sent the project to its picker instead) and dismisses the post-crash safe-mode prompt. Exit 0 is healthy or recovered, 1 anything else. The traps, each measured:

  • Unity 6 never logs "End MonoManager ReloadAssembly": 55 begins, 0 ends and 55 "Domain Reload Profiling" lines (measured 2026-10-01). The tool counts the Profiling line as the end; on the End marker alone, a bridge hiccup on a healthy idle editor reads as hung_in_reload and the editor is killed.
  • A fresh log does not prove a live main thread: a hot-reload watcher process kept writing while the main thread sat dead, and an 18-minute hang read as bridge_down. The tool filters watcher lines.
  • --check is blind to a modal: it reads the HTTP status of /capabilities, never the body. Read mainThreadResponsive yourself.
  • --kill, --restart and --auto act on every Unity.exe, found by image name: with the owner's editor and a clone open, a kill ends both. Never run them near the owner's editor without the owner's word.
  • After --auto kills an editor, "the bridge did not come up within 180 s" usually means the recovery dialog is waiting.

bridge_wake.py calls /focus, then polls /status until mainThreadResponsive (exit 0; --timeout, default 30 s; --port; --quiet); --recover runs unity_recovery.py --auto on a timeout and polls again. Exit 1 is a usage or port-file error, 3 a timeout. Since it starts with /focus, it is for an editor the agent owns, or for when the owner is away.

The console as the headless test

A compiler proves the code builds; the console is the cheap thing that proves it ran. On the reference port three faults in one session passed every other instrument (the typecheck clean, 4,104 of 4,104 .NET tests green, a player compile with 0 errors) and were obvious in the console within one frame: a tool opened a scene with broken prefabs (79 errors blamed on the tool's own file, which read from outside as "it does not compile"); a row of the level's grid lost its tiles and an exception emptied the board; a render pass bound the back buffer's depth (4,020 errors, nothing rendered).

So console_check.py is a gate, not a glance:

py console_check.py --reset                          # mark everything now in the console as seen
<the action>
py console_check.py --label "what I just did"        # exit 1 = NEW errors appeared
  • One HTTP call to /console/entries, which reads the Console itself (UnityEditor.LogEntries, by reflection), not the editor log: the Console retires rows when an asset reimports cleanly or a reload succeeds, and knows each row's severity. The route is read-only (it never clears the Console or changes its filter, and reports the active filter), and it fails loudly when the internal API changes shape, because a silent empty list would read as "no errors".
  • A watermark in .opus-tools/.console-watermark.json makes each call report only what is NEW; the backlog is never re-read.
