  • Identical rows collapse with a count. A row's identity is its kind, file and message with every number masked, so an error repeated 4,020 times with a changing frame number prints as one row.
  • Noise is counted apart, never hidden. Unity's search-index and LMDB lock messages, Unity packages' own messages, asset unloading and licensing lines are totalled separately: they can neither mask a regression nor trip the exit code.
  • --all ignores the watermark, --quiet prints only news, --label names the action. Exit 0 is clean, 1 new errors (new warnings are reported but do not fail), 2 the bridge unreachable or the route refused, which is not a pass.
  • --selftest plants rows through the gate's own function (a seen backlog, a new error, 4,020 per-frame errors, noise, a warning, the same console twice), each judged as above, and never touches the real watermark.

New errors mean stop and fix. When the change touches rendering, pair the check with a short Play: many faults exist only in a frame.

Known gap, NOT YET fixed (read from both sources, 2026-10-17). console_check.py asks for limit rows, but the route reads a parameter named max (default 200) and lists the Console's rows in order from its first. On a console holding more than 200 rows, a new error after the 200th is counted in the totals line the gate prints but is not in the list, so it is not reported as new and the exit code stays 0. Until the two agree, compare the totals line too, or start from a console under 200 rows.

Compared with the open-source Unity MCP server

The open-source Unity MCP server package (measured at version 0.87.0) exposes the editor to AI agents as tools, the Unity Test Runner included (its tests-run tool). The second instance (my_unity.py) drives it on a clone. Its client needs no MCP wiring: unity-mcp-cli run-tool <name> --input '{...}' and run-system-tool call a tool directly, unity-mcp-cli status proves the server is up, and unity-mcp-cli install-plugin --path <project> installs it (a package resolve and a domain reload, so never into an editor in use). Its narrow test filters, testMethod and testNamespace, work (the timings above).

What was measured against it

  • testClass does not filter: it answers "No tests found matching class ..." for a bare and a fully qualified class name.
  • The client's default timeout is 60 s, shorter than a real test run, so the first call reports a bogus failure.
  • A timed-out call leaves the run in flight, and the retry answers 500, "another test run is already in progress". Wait it out; do not relaunch Unity over it.
  • Every call needs an open editor, because the server lives in one: the owner's, or a second instance with the costs above. Its connection was seen to drop while the editor was in the background (null replies, "not connected").
  • A configured server that is not running still lists its tool names: a project carried the tool descriptions (86 at that version) with no package installed, advertising a toolbox no server could serve. "Listed" never means "available".
  • On a default port it is reachable by any default-configured client (the finding above).

What ships, and what does not yet

Ships in the toolkit's tree today: every toolkit verb and tool this chapter names. The bridge and the editor scripts behind its routes do not. Several of the tools still default to the reference project's folder instead of reading it from the project file; moving each one is the "No absolute paths" item of Appendix B.

The bridge does NOT ship yet. It lives inside the reference project, with the game's routes in the same file as the server. Until its generic core is in the package, a window, the console gate and the recovery tools need a bridge in your project, and a new project has none (Chapter 22 lists "a Unity measurement in another studio's editor without the reference port's bridge" as OPEN). Write yours to the behaviour above, with your game's routes registered in a table whose keys /capabilities lists, so the advert cannot drift from the dispatch.

What the package's own tools call on that server today, read from their source:

tool what it calls
u2ue window bridge_port.txt at the project root; /status (isPlaying, isCompiling); /recompile
console_check.py /console/entries, answering ok, totals (errors, warnings, logs) and entries (each kind, file, message)
unity_recovery.py /capabilities answering 200
bridge_wake.py /focus; /status (mainThreadResponsive, mainThreadTickAgeMs)

Appendix B carries the related item: the probes and the window driver as the package's Editor assembly, triggered by a file, with no dependency on the reference port's bridge.

The probes

A probe is an editor script that sets up one Unity behaviour, steps it, and writes what it observed to a fact file; its judge states the rule a port relies on and reads it off the facts or refuses it with the numbers (Chapter 8: the judge is written and planted first). Probes live in the toolkit, not the game: vfxport/unity_probe/ holds the probes, the shared placement helper ProbeSpawn.cs, and their *_judge.py and *_check.py files. A probe is copied into the project's editor folder (unity.probe_dir) for one window and taken out again.

The shape of a probe

  • Triggered by a file. An [InitializeOnLoadMethod] hooks EditorApplication.update (never delayCall) to poll for its trigger in the conformance part (the toolkit's folder of measured Unity rules, Chapter 3). The generic case probe skips every tick while the editor plays or compiles; when its trigger appears it deletes it, reads the lines the window wrote (a spec and a record name), and runs. Nothing has to click.
  • Edit mode, in a preview scene. The case probe and the photo probe place their systems in a preview scene (EditorSceneManager.NewPreviewScene), so the owner's active scene is never touched; its dirty flag is recorded before and after.
  • One record out, never over another. The case probe refuses to write a record that exists (and the runner refuses to start any probe whose output exists); a probe reports an error inside its record rather than throwing.
  • Compiled headless before it enters the project (typecheck.py --editor --extra <probe.cs>).
  • Real prefabs are placed only through ProbeSpawn, which names the placement measured (the game's effect spawn, its projectile spawn, or the prefab as authored). One probe that placed prefabs its own way dropped the root's authored rotation and made 36 reference frames wrong. vfxport/probe_spawn_gate.py refuses a probe that sets an instantiated prefab's transform itself, and the runner drops ProbeSpawn.cs in with any probe that calls it.
  • A query that can crash Unity is guarded. ParticleSystem.Particle.GetMeshIndex on a renderer without meshes kills the editor in native code, which no managed try / catch sees (Chapter 16).

A probe case is data

Hand-written probes grow: ColorSizeFactsProbe.cs reached 5,915 lines of hand-written cases. ParticleCaseProbe.cs is one generic probe for every particle question, the question given as data, and u2ue/probecase.py writes that data:

  • ProbeCase.prefab(name, path, times, spawn=...): a real prefab placed by the game's spawn (effect, projectile, authored), listing the systems the game never starts so they are cleared after every step.
  • ProbeCase.synthetic(name, modules, times): one system whose module properties are set by name ({"main": {...}, "emission": {...}}): a rule question with no new C#.
  • Every case pins the random seed on every system (two runs are identical), lists its read times and per-particle fields, and caps the particles written (the count is always whole).
  • Restart or step. Without a step, each time is simulated from a restart; with one, the probe restarts once and steps the way the game does, so the times must ascend. The restart read is blind to a sub-emitter of a sub-emitter: it drew 0 of 284, and a read stepped at the game's own 1/60 s drew 12 of 12 (Chapter 9).
  • CaseRun(name, cases, why) writes <name>-cases.json in the conformance part and the window spec <name>.json under the lane part's windows/, refusing to replace either; the window writes <name>-unity.json.
py -m u2ue.probecase --selftest      # a prefab case, a synthetic case, bad cases and runs refused, nothing replaced

u2ue conform cases builds a run of every IR key this way (Chapter 9). A rule question needs no new probe file: the simulation-speed rule was measured from 24 synthetic cases (simspeed-cases.json).

13. The Unreal tools: headless runs, the host, publishing

Who this is for: the porting developer who runs Unreal. After it you can launch Unreal headless safely, make the game's own Unreal project, publish its managed C# (the .NET code UnrealSharp runs) and prove the build that runs is yours.

Every Unreal step of a port runs the same way: headless, from native PowerShell, one engine at a time, through one runner that refuses an unsafe launch, and judged by what the run wrote, never by its exit code. This chapter is each Unreal-side tool, why it is built that way, and the traps it catches; Chapter 16's "Unreal runs" entries are the short form, by symptom.

tool what it is
scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 the one place an Unreal executable is named: six launch rules, a watchdog, the argument builders
scene_tools/ue_headless_selftest.ps1 the six rules made to refuse
u2ue/ue_py.ps1, u2ue/ue_game.ps1 one headless Python script (scene import, readback); one headless game start (host run)
effects_tools/u1e_py.ps1, effects_tools/fx17_build.ps1 one effect instrument; one chunk of effect keys built (build, read, photo, trial)
u2ue/verbs/_ue.py what the Unreal verbs share: the host guard, the PATH check, the runner, the build record
u2ue/hostproject.py, u2ue/verbs/host.py, u2ue/templates/unreal the game's own Unreal project, made from the toolkit's template
u2ue/runtime the engine-free libraries the port links

Headless Unreal runs

Native PowerShell, never a shell that rewrote the PATH

UnrealSharp, the plugin that runs C# in Unreal, finds the .NET SDK by scanning PATH for an existing directory entry that contains Program Files\dotnet\, trailing backslash included (read from the plugin's source). Native PowerShell's PATH has it. A PowerShell started from Git Bash, even indirectly (Bash runs Python, Python runs pwsh), inherits a PATH that MSYS (Git Bash's Unix layer) converted, where the entry reads /c/Program Files/dotnet or has lost its backslash. UnrealSharp then reports the SDK missing and raises a modal dialog, which under -unattended (the flag for a run with no one there to answer a prompt; rule R2, below) is answered and raised again forever: the run never ends and its log never stops growing. Measured on the reference port: one such run reached 14.5 GB resident and a 3 GB log before anyone looked (2026-09-29); another raised 265 497 dialogs in a 634 MB log and never did its work (2026-10-02).

So it is checked twice before anything starts: every verb that starts Unreal asks native_path_ok (u2ue/verbs/_ue.py) and refuses with "run from native PowerShell", and the runner's rule R6 refuses the launch, asking UnrealSharp's own question, backslash included. Open a PowerShell window and type the facade command there.

One headless Unreal at a time

The Unreal host - the machine's capacity to run Unreal, as Chapter 2's host_busy row names it, and not the host project of u2ue host below - is one machine-wide resource: two engines contend for memory, the derived-data cache (where Unreal keeps what it derives from assets, such as compiled shaders) and the project's packages (its asset files), and an open editor locks packages another process needs to save (below). So every verb that starts Unreal asks the adapter's host_busy and refuses, naming what holds the host, instead of waiting:

  • the default adapter (unity_project) answers busy while any process whose name starts with UnrealEditor runs - an editor you have open counts;
  • a game adapter may add its own build queues (Chapter 18).

build, read and photo exit 1 on that refusal, host and scene exit 2. build, read, photo and scene print the host's state with --dry, and run nothing. fx17_build.ps1 also refuses on its own (exit 9 while any UnrealEditor runs), so a tool run by hand keeps the guard. The verbs start Unreal below normal priority, so the person using the machine keeps it.

The runner and its six rules

scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 is dot-sourced by every launcher (loaded into the launcher's own scope, . ue_headless.ps1), and every launch goes through its Invoke-UeHeadless, which first calls Assert-UeHeadless on the exact argument list. Each rule is a throw that names itself:

rule refuses measured or read
R1 EXE any executable but UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe, or one not on disk the GUI editor puts windows on the desktop
R2 UNATTENDED a launch without -unattended read from the engine source: it changes how a prompt acts, not whether a window is made
R3 OFFSCREEN a launch without -RenderOffScreen 2026-09-28: an -unattended Python run put two visible windows on the desktop, one the "Executing Python Script..." notification; with -RenderOffScreen, none, and a byte-identical answer. The engine then creates its null platform application: there is no OS window to draw into
R4 ABSLOG a launch without -ABSLOG=<file> a run writes its own log, never Saved/Logs, which an open editor also writes
R5 NO GUI PY -ExecutePythonScript together with -game
R6 DOTNET a PATH with no existing entry containing Program Files\dotnet\ above

The watchdog. A plain wait cannot notice a runaway, so the runner polls every 1.5 s and kills the run with a named reason at its time cap ($script:UeHeadlessMaxSeconds, 1800 s unless the launcher sets one: ue_game.ps1 900, ue_py.ps1 3600) or when the log passes $script:UeHeadlessMaxLogMB (600 MB) - almost always one modal or one error repeated: read the log's last lines. A capped run fails; it never passes. ue_game.ps1, ue_py.ps1 and u1e_py.ps1 end with one line, exit=<code> seconds=<s> logMB=<mb> killed=<reason> log=<path>; a clean host run prints exit=0 seconds=38 logMB=0 killed= log=<work>/host/host-run.log.

The argument builders. New-UePythonArgs makes an editor Python run (-ExecutePythonScript=<script> -unattended -nosplash -stdout -DeterministicAudio -nocef -RenderOffScreen -AllowCommandletRendering -nosourcecontrol -ABSLOG=<log>); New-UeGameArgs a game run. The command line a host run logs, its log path shortened:

/Engine/Maps/Entry -game -RenderOffScreen -unattended -nosplash -stdout -DeterministicAudio
  -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 -ResX=1280 -ResY=720 -ForceRes -ABSLOG=<work>/host/host-run.log -ExecCmds=quit

-nocef keeps the editor's embedded Chromium unloaded: an effect build crashed 45 s in with an access violation whose every frame was in that library, which loads because -RenderOffScreen still lets the engine render (2026-10-09).

The gate, not in the package yet. The reference port runs a gate beside the runner, and its folders are still that port's, so it does not ship. Write the same one over your own tooling: refuse any file that names an Unreal executable by path outside the runner (except, by name and with its reason, a probe whose job is to measure the window), any launchable reference to UnrealEditor.exe, a file naming an executable without both -unattended and -RenderOffScreen, and a runner that has lost a rule id (exit 0 clean, 1 refused with file and line, 2 could not run). A launcher that named the executable itself would route around every rule above; the gate makes that a failure.

The selftest.

py -m u2ue --project <game> tool ue_headless_selftest.ps1

Nothing launches: Assert-UeHeadless reads only its arguments and the PATH. A clean launch must pass, and R1 to R6 must each throw its own rule (R6 on a Git Bash PATH); each case sets its own PATH, so the result does not depend on the shell that started it.

Audio: no speakers, and no silent mix

A headless game run opens the machine's real audio device unless told otherwise. Measured on the reference port (2026-10-05): a run's sounds played into the headset of the person working at the machine, and a recording of the master submix (the mixer's final output) caught 0.77 s of a 23 s run. -DeterministicAudio loads the non-realtime renderer: each tick renders its own delta, nothing reaches a speaker, a recording follows the game clock. The second trap is inside the mixer: the engine's BaseEngine.ini sets [Audio] UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=0.0, a headless run is never focused, so it mixes at volume 0 (the port's voices captured at a peak of 0.000000). -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 fixes it. A third: the engine's own submix recording stops when a silent submix disables itself, so the toolkit's audio plugin captures through a listener that keeps it rendering (below). Add -UseFixedTimeStep -FPS=60 when a capture's timeline must follow the game clock, and leave -DeterministicAudio out of an attended run. A silent run's log says Using Audio Hardware Device Non-realtime Renderer.

Detached launches and the shell's timeout

A shell tool - an agent's, a CI runner's - usually has a timeout, and stopping a task stops its whole process tree. Measured on the reference port (2026-10-06): an effect build of about 70 minutes, run under a 60-minute tool limit, was stopped at 60 minutes with its UnrealEditor-Cmd child, its record never finalised and its resave (each built system saved again in a fresh process; "Built, compiled, simulating", below) never run. The runner's watchdog was never the limit; the tool's timeout was. So:

  • Compare the two limits before any long launch, and give the shell tool the larger one.
  • Cut long work into chunks that fit. The effect build builds a chunk of keys per run (fx17_build.ps1 -MaxSeconds, 6600 s by default) and keeps each chunk's record. It keeps a key's previous system aside until the new one is saved, and puts back any that a killed run never replaced, so no key is left with no asset.
  • Check that a run finished. A build killed by its own watchdog can still look finished (58 of 68 keys, the resave then saving the ten stale systems as current, 2026-10-06). Compare the record's key count with the keys asked for; u2ue trial names every key not built and calls the trial PARTIAL.

Two PowerShell traps hide a stage that never ran. Select-Object -First N stops every upstream command once it has N objects: a build piped into Select-Object -First 1 printed its result, exit 0, and the resave after it never ran (2026-10-06). And every uncaptured expression in a function is output, so $rec = Build swallows its log lines; print through Write-Host.

What a headless run cannot prove

A script never moves a mouse: on the reference port every scripted run passed while a click in the attended editor picked nothing. A -game run never stops Play-In-Editor (PIE, the game played inside the editor): an object kept alive past a session crashed the editor on Stop while every headless proof was green ("UnrealSharp traps", below). Attended play stays part of acceptance.

Editor scripting limits

The converter and the effect instruments are Python scripts run inside the editor (UnrealEditor-Cmd <project> -ExecutePythonScript=<script>, through the runner). Four limits shape all of them, each with its fix in Chapter 11's traps ("Unreal's Python API"): -run=pythonscript asserts without Slate, -ExecutePythonScript quits when the script returns, the editor world does not tick actors (Niagara simulates only in Simulate, Play-In-Editor or when advanced explicitly), and the CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin must be enabled or FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary does not exist.

Every instrument writes its answer to a JSON record beside its log, and the verb judges that record.

How the read-back advances a system

effects_tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py (run by u2ue read and a trial's read step) needs no tick loop. For each built system it finishes every pending compile (Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll), spawns a fresh component in the editor world (NiagaraFunctionLibrary.spawn_system_at_location, at (0, 0, 100000) unless U1E_RB_XF moves and turns it) and activates it once, the game's path. Then, per frame, it captures the system into a Niagara sim cache (a recording of its particles' attributes) with NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary.capture_niagara_sim_cache_immediate(cache, params, component, True, dt) - the True advances the simulation by dt (1/60 s, unless U1E_RB_DT names the step Unity's probe took) before the capture - and reads every particle's attributes off the cache: position, velocity, colour, size, age, ids and the converter's own.

Each frame records whether its capture succeeded, because a system can be built and never simulate. Measured on the reference port (2026-10-10): 19 built systems read 0 of 90 frames ("SimCache Error: No valid simulation data") and no check flagged them, because every check judges the emitters that produced data; and a read of 0 frames exited 0 while two judges reported "0 judged" as if they had looked (2026-10-16). So the tool writes a capture summary beside its record, and u2ue read names every system that captured nothing or fewer frames than asked, and exits 1. The record is written one system at a time, because a single json.dump of a 673-key, 181-frame read held 55 GB of a 64 GB machine (2026-10-16); u2ue/readback.py parses it a system at a time.

U1E_RB_SPAWNSCALE is refused by name: fx.NiagaraGlobalSpawnCountScale exists in Unreal 5.7 only as a tooltip string, so setting it was a silent no-op (2026-10-13). Grep for a console variable's registration, never for its name in prose.

Built, compiled, simulating

  • Built: the converter saved the asset and reported no error (the record's BUILT). That says nothing about the Niagara compile, whose status is not reachable from Python.
  • Compiled for a game: finalize() only requests a compile, so run Editor.AsyncAssetCompilationFinishAll before the save. Even then a system built through a conversion context is saved with an EDIT compile, whose id differs from the one any process without an editor on it computes: every fresh process recompiled it on load, and the effect was blank at its first spawn. effects_tools/u1e_resave.py loads and saves each built system again in a fresh process, where the save waits for the non-edit compile, and reports one that still needs a compile after it. u2ue build runs it on what it built.
  • Simulating: only a read-back proves it; effects_tools/u1e_simulates_check.py is the gate.

Other measured limits of editor Python

Chapter 11's traps give four more with their fixes: a texture drawn before its platform data is built, unreal.Rotator's positional order, set_parameter's false on a failed write, and a conversion context alive at exit. The rest:

  • Failure by return value is general. LevelEditorSubsystem.new_level returns false when the map exists, and does not raise. Check every return.
  • An open editor locks existing packages. Re-saving an existing Niagara system returned false and a map could not be opened for writing, while a NEW package saved fine (2026-09-29). Re-test such a constraint per operation: the managed publish, assumed blocked by the same lock, ran with the editor open (below).
  • A preflight before the engine. u1e_py.ps1 runs effects_tools/u1e_preflight.py on the script and its local imports: a syntax error or an undefined name refuses the run (killed=PREFLIGHT) before minutes of Unreal start. It exists because two faults once reached Unreal that a two-second read finds: a truncated \u escape in a docstring (a syntax error at import, the run dead 30 s in) and a name written before it was bound. It refuses only what is a fault at run time - a syntax error and the undefined-name classes - and nothing about style.
  • Through the facade only. The effect tools refuse to run without the facade's U2UE_* variables, so a tool never runs with another project's paths. By hand: py -m u2ue --project <game> tool <file>.

The launchers

Every verb that starts Unreal checks the host and the PATH first (u2ue/verbs/_ue.py), runs its tool below normal priority with the project's environment, and removes and names every inherited U1E_* and VFXPORT_* variable, so a verb runs the project's defaults, never a switch left over in the shell.

u2ue/ue_py.ps1 (-ScriptPath -UProject -Log -Headless [-MaxSeconds]) runs one Unreal Python script; u2ue/ue_game.ps1 (-UProject -Map -Log -Headless [-MaxSeconds]) one game start with -ExecCmds=quit, since the host's managed module works at StartupModule. Each prints exit=4 with a reason when the runner is missing, or its script (ue_py.ps1) or its project (ue_game.ps1), and passes its environment on to the engine.

The effect build's own tools, which the build, read and photo verbs run:

tool part what it does check
u1e_build.py effects_tools builds one Niagara system per effect key, inside Unreal, through build_niagara.py -
fx17_chunks.py effects_tools cuts the keys into chunks by ESTIMATED build time, most-used effects first; the cost model is measured on a real chunk's per-phase timers -
fx18_chunks.py effects_tools the same for a whole-game rebuild, time-budgeted, so a series that is stopped has built what the game shows most -
u1e_reuse.py effects_tools the build reuses a texture, a material parent or an instance only when nothing it was built from changed -
u1e_reuse_selftest.py effects_tools u1e_reuse.py driven with fakes of Unreal and the material author, outside Unreal yes
u1e_py_introspect.py effects_tools what a few Unreal Python types actually expose - the names READ, not assumed -
u1e_compile_report.py effects_tools WHY a built system does not simulate, in the engine's own words -

The game's own Unreal project: u2ue host

u2ue host makes your game its own .uproject in steps anyone can re-run, the way you would make one by hand: project creation, the plugin install and the host template, touching no other game's project. Here host means the game's host project: the Unreal project whose C# host classes run the model (Chapter 5), not the machine's running Unreal that the verbs guard (above). Each step is the command it runs and the line in its output that proves it.

The project file's block

"unreal": {
  "uproject": "<work>/unreal/<Name>/<Name>.uproject",
  "engine": "<Unreal Engine 5.7 install>",
  "content_root": "/Game/U2UE/<Game>",
  "host": {
    "template": "U2ueHost",
    "plugins": [{"name": "UnrealSharp", "source": "<git url or local clone>", "commit": "<sha>"}],
    "toolkit_plugins": ["U2ueAudio"],
    "sdks_root": "<AutoSDK root, or null>",
    "digest": {"entry": "<Ns>.<Class>.<Method>", "cases": ["<model>/<Model>.Core.Tests/DigestCases.cs"]}
  }
}

Every field is named, never defaulted. The .uproject sits in a folder of its own name, as a new Unreal project does. sdks_root is an AutoSDK root for a machine with no Windows SDK installed (below), null otherwise. digest.entry is a static method returning the digest's text (or an object with a Text() method), and cases the files that define it - the entry and cases u2ue digest runs on CoreCLR and on Unity's Mono (Chapter 5).

The template

u2ue/templates/unreal holds host/U2ueHost - the smallest C++ project a plugin builds in: a .uproject for engine 5.7 with the toolkit's audio plugin, one primary game module that does nothing else, the game and editor targets (BuildSettingsVersion.V6: the installed engine was built with those defaults, and a target that shares its build products may not differ), and a Config/DefaultEngine.ini naming /Engine/Maps/Entry as the game's default map and the editor's startup map - plus Plugins/U2ueAudio and the host classes U2ue.Unreal (both below). Once the game has its own level, point EditorStartupMap at it: a project that opens on an engine template map shows an empty world, and the game cannot be started without hunting for its map.

The steps

py -m u2ue --project <game> host plan prints every step with its command and proof line, host status each step's record (PROVEN, NOT PROVEN, NOT RUN), and host <step> [--dry] runs one.

  1. create - py -m u2ue --project <game> host create writes the project from the template, the template's name replaced by the host's in every path and text file, the block's plugins added to the .uproject. Proves the files are written. Refused when the folder exists: create never overwrites.
  2. install - py -m u2ue --project <game> host install clones each external plugin (git clone --no-checkout, then the pinned commit) and copies each toolkit plugin without build products. Proves each .uplugin on disk and the clone's HEAD at the pin. The source must be a git repository; a local clone downloads nothing.
  3. compile - py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile runs Build.bat <Name>Editor Win64 Development -Project=<uproject> -WaitMutex, with UE_SDKS_ROOT from sdks_root. UnrealSharp's header-tool exporter writes the C# glue (the generated C# bindings to the engine's types) on the way, builds the plugin's managed bindings and generates an empty user solution. Proves Result: Succeeded.
  4. generate - py -m u2ue --project <game> host generate runs UnrealSharp's own command through RunUAT, Unreal's automation tool: RunUAT GenerateProject -ScriptDir=<plugin>/Build/Scripts -Project=<uproject> -ProjectFolder=<root>/Script/Managed<Name> -ProjectName=Managed<Name> -CreateModuleClass -GenerateSolution - what the editor's new C# project dialog runs, read off the plugin - with no editor and no dialog. (Without a managed project, a GUI editor raises a "No C# projects were found" modal at start.) Proves AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success).
  5. wire - py -m u2ue --project <game> host wire adds the model's layers and U2ue.Runtime as project references, the digest cases and three settings to Managed<Name>.csproj, copies the host classes in, and rewrites the module class to answer the digest. Proves each is written (the record counts them). Refused before generate, and a second time.
  6. publish - py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish runs RunUAT BuildUserSolution -ScriptsForProject=<uproject> -Project=<uproject> -OutputPath=<out> to Binaries/Managed, then to Binaries/Managed/net10.0 (steps publish, publish2). Proves, per output, the success line AND a log line ending in Managed<Name> -> <that output>/.
  7. run - py -m u2ue --project <game> host run starts the game once, headless, on the host's GameDefaultMap through u2ue/ue_game.ps1, U2UE_DIGEST_OUT naming <parity.dir>/logic-Unreal.txt. Proves U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN in its log AND the digest written after the run started. Then py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal compares the runtimes (Chapter 5).

Each step writes <work.effects>/host/host-<step>.json (command, proof line, seconds, ok, evidence, time) with its log beside it. Exit 0 = the step proved itself, 1 = it ran and did not, 2 = refused before it ran. The Unreal steps (compile, generate, publish, run) are refused while the host is busy or the PATH fails the dotnet check; --dry prints the command (for create, every file) and runs nothing.

Judged by a line, never by an exit code

An exit code has lied, so the host's selftest requires a compile with Result: Succeeded to pass though it exited 1, and one that exited 0 without the line to fail. A success line alone can pass the wrong result too: BuildUserSolution's says nothing about where the assembly went (2026-10-16), so a publish also needs Managed<Name> -> <its output>/ to END a log line - a substring test passes Binaries/Managed/ on a publish to Binaries/Managed/net10.0/, which the selftest caught. The run is judged by its line and by the digest's time, so a digest left by an earlier run is never this run's.

What wire writes, and why

  • EnableSourceControlManagerQueries false: an assembly that depends on git's HEAD changes its MVID on every commit (measured on the reference port), and the MVID is what proves a publish (below).
  • ShouldUnsetParentConfigurationAndPlatform false: without it a Release publish builds references from outside the solution in Debug (measured, the same project).
  • Nullable disable: the host classes are written with nullable annotations off and the generated project turns them on - measured on a fresh host (2026-10-16), 16 nullable warnings and nothing else; 0 after.
  • The module class: at StartupModule, only when U2UE_DIGEST_OUT names a file, it calls the digest entry, writes the text and logs U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN <path> (<n> lines); an editor session that names no file is untouched. Pure C# there needs no world, but nothing that spawns may run there: managed classes are registered later (a measured crash on the reference port).

Measured: the second game's host

What to expect, as a worked example: the second example project's host, made with these steps from nothing on 2026-10-16. From its records:

step seconds evidence
create 0.0 6 files written
install 0.9 UnrealSharp at its pinned commit; the audio plugin copied
compile 254.6 Result: Succeeded
generate 3.1 AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0 (Success)
wire 0.0 2 references (the model's one layer, U2ue.Runtime), 1 case file, 4 host classes, the module class
publish 4.8 the success line and Managed<Name> -> .../Binaries/Managed/
publish2 4.4 the success line and Managed<Name> -> .../Binaries/Managed/net10.0/
run 38.6 U2UE DIGEST WRITTEN .../logic-Unreal.txt (642 lines)

About nine minutes from create to the end of run, most of it the C++ compile. parity --require Unreal then exited 0, the Unreal digest byte for byte the headless CoreCLR digest (both runtimes are CoreCLR), and the four host classes had compiled against that host's own UnrealSharp - the template's proof.

py -m u2ue.verbs.host --selftest runs create, install and wire for real in a temporary folder (the real template, a local git plugin with two commits so the pin can be told from the head, the real model's projects) and the Unreal steps through a fake launcher: every judgement and refusal checked, no engine started.

Managed C# in Unreal (UnrealSharp)

UnrealSharp runs the game's model and the host classes as C# inside Unreal. The managed project is Script/Managed<Name>/; the engine loads the published assemblies from Binaries/Managed or Binaries/Managed/net10.0.

Publish to both folders, and prove what runs

Both folders were populated on the reference port and the engine may load either; a publish to one left the other holding the old assemblies (2026-09-29). So every publish runs twice, once per folder. -ScriptsForProject is required, or RunUAT answers "Failed to find command BuildUserSolution", and BuildUserSolution publishes Release (2026-09-30: the published assembly was byte-identical to bin/Release/net10.0 and to no other configuration).

A file's size and time prove nothing about an assembly: both drift between configurations while the code is identical. The witness is the assembly's MVID, from its PE metadata. The reference port's publish gate builds the published configuration fresh and compares, per assembly, the fresh MVID with the published one on each path, requires both paths identical, reads markers from the shipped file itself (an edit never published cannot satisfy it), and checks the run's own witness. Its checks name the reference port's assemblies, so it is the method to copy, and u2ue check does not run it (its selftest launches Unreal).

A matching hash is not evidence that the run ran your build. Measured on the reference port (2026-09-30): an artifact with a new time and a hash equal to its headless reference read exactly like a proof arriving, and came from an attended editor session on the OLD assembly. So the reference port's run writes a manifest when it arms, naming the assembly it is bound to, and the gate proves an artifact only against that. host run applies the smaller form: the digest must be written by this run.

Then prove it runs, not only that it built - host run, or a headless run of the game whose logs match the headless reference byte for byte. Freeze the managed sources from the publish until that proof passes: the MVID check rebuilds the current source, so an edit made during the proving run fails it, correctly, and costs a whole republish.

Automatic hot reload OFF

UnrealSharp's editor watches the managed C# and by default (OnScriptSave) recompiles the moment a file changes. A tool that writes managed code continuously - a model extraction, a code generator - lands a reload in a mid-write instant: the compile fails, and the editor can wedge. Measured on the reference port (2026-09-29): the editor stopped responding and grew from 14.6 GB to 19.9 GB, and the game could not be started. The compile errors were a lie about the code: a type reported missing dozens of times sat in its file, and dotnet build reported 0 errors minutes later. The fix, in the host's Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini:

[/Script/UnrealSharpEditor.CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings]
AutomaticHotReloading=Off

Its values are OnScriptSave, OnEditorFocus and Off (the plugin's CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings.h). Tested (2026-09-29): a managed file touched with the editor up, 0 hot reloads in 40 s, the editor responding. Hot reload still works when asked for; a half-written file just cannot take the editor down. With it back on OnScriptSave the rule is absolute: an open editor or a tool writing managed C#, never both. The safe-operation pillar of u2ue cycle reads this file in the project's host and goes red without the line. The host template writes it (u2ue/templates/unreal/host/U2ueHost/Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini), and host create refuses to make a host whose Config lacks it (u2ue/hostproject.py; the host selftest plants a template without it). A host made by hand or by an older toolkit may have only DefaultEngine.ini: add the file before its editor is opened while any tool writes managed code.

The editor watches only folders holding a .csproj under Script/ (read from the plugin's source), so a model outside Script/ can be edited and tested with the editor open; on save a file is only parsed, and only a SYNTAX error opens the blocking "C# Hot Reload Error" dialog. Measured with hot reload off (2026-09-30): three managed files written and both publishes run with the editor open logged "Processed dirty file" three times, with no reload, no dialog and no assembly locked. Restart the editor afterwards: its startup builds the solution from the current source, while a manual hot reload would compile against the model loaded at start, and fail. The facade is stricter than the engine: host publish refuses while any Unreal runs, an open editor included.

When an editor wedged: the recovery order

In this order and no other:

  1. Stop the writer and close the editor - the tool's own stop (a trial: py -m u2ue --project <game> trial stop). Proves nothing writes any more: no file under Script/ or the model changes time. The editor must close, since the Unreal steps refuse while it runs.
  2. Test - dotnet test on the model's tests. Proves the code the editor will load is green.
  3. Build - dotnet build Script/Managed<Name>/Managed<Name>.csproj. Proves 0 errors, whatever the wedged editor said.
  4. Republish - py -m u2ue --project <game> host publish. Proves both outputs, each by its own line.
  5. Prove it runs - py -m u2ue --project <game> host run. Proves the digest written by this run.
  6. Restart the editor - only now, on the published build.

UnrealSharp traps

  • USTRUCT fields start zeroed from C#. A USTRUCT is a struct declared to Unreal's reflection. The generated glue is a plain struct, so a C++ default (= -1) is documentation only: built from managed code the field arrives as 0 unless set. On the reference port every UI draw silently changed its colour decode that way (2026-10-02).
  • Glue names. A bool bFoo becomes Foo; when that collides with another property the generator skips one of them, with no error.
  • A missing binding is not proven by a document grep. UnrealSharp.xml lists member names but not return types, and missed whole classes the glue has (347 key names, 0 matches, 2026-09-30). Reflect over copies of the published assemblies (never the live Binaries), or compile a scratch project against the plugin's UnrealSharp.Shared.props - as dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal does for the host classes - and prove the check fails on a planted wrong call.
  • The garbage collector sees only engine-side references. A texture kept in a C# dictionary was purged over several frames and the run crashed reading it; IsValid() does not help in that window (2026-10-01). Hold every asset a managed cache keeps across frames through a strong object pointer (the engine's TStrongObjectPtr); a plain C# property on a managed class is invisible to the collector too. Add -ExecCmds="gc.TimeBetweenPurgingPendingKillObjects 0.5" -LogCmds="LogGarbage Verbose" to a headless run to reproduce such faults on demand: a 6-minute intermittent crash became a 32-second deterministic one.
  • Never root a world object. Rooting marks an object so the garbage collector never frees it. A widget rooted for the life of the process crashed the editor when Play-In-Editor stopped (the engine asserts on a session object that survives teardown), 2026-10-01. Root only assets; tear views down in EndPlay.
  • Noise. Property generator is not initialized at shutdown is logged when no managed class declares a [UProperty] (the plugin's source). It matters only before the run's verdict, or once a class has a [UProperty].

UnrealSharp's open issues (read 2026-09-30)

The recent open issues are almost all interop lifetime and marshalling (converting values as they cross between C# and C++) - what you would predict of a managed layer over UObject (Unreal's base object class) memory, and a class of bug a logic-parity test does not see:

  • TArrayReadOnly<T> is a live view into native memory with no lifetime tracking. If the owning native object is garbage collected while managed code holds the view, a later access reads freed memory, which surfaces as a NullReferenceException or as silently wrong data (#740).
  • TextMarshaller.ToNative writes a null TSharedRef for a null managed FText, which corrupts a C#-defined struct's cached defaults and crashes FText::IsEmpty() (#738).
  • An exception escaping an async void method in game code aborts the whole editor.
  • A crash in UCancellableAsyncAction's "Disregard for GC" object class.
  • "Missing dependency / Create Export" errors in a packaged game: a bug on the shipping path.
  • [UFunction] on a C# local function is silently inert.

From the FAQ: UnrealSharp reaches only what is exposed to reflection, the same restriction Blueprint has, so anything else needs C++ written by you; and a UObject class is made with NewObject<T>(), never new T(). The traps a port meets with it, and their fixes, are above, and in Chapter 16.

C++ builds and the SDK root

UnrealBuildTool needs a Windows SDK and a toolchain. A machine with neither fails at once with Platform Win64 is not a valid platform to build (2.5 s on the reference machine, which had no Windows SDK installed at all; 2026-10-03). An AutoSDK folder holds both: set UE_SDKS_ROOT to it in the process that runs Build.bat only - never as a machine or user variable, never by installing an SDK, which needs elevation. host compile sets it from unreal.host.sdks_root. Before reporting an SDK gone, read UnrealBuildTool's backup logs (Log-backup-*.txt, in its folder under the user's local application data) for where the last good build found one.

A project copy of an engine plugin cannot see the engine's Internal headers, which are shown only to modules of their own scope or marked as engine modules (C1083 Cannot open include file, 2026-10-09): add the one Internal folder to the copy's PrivateIncludePaths, checking every include first so one build finds them all.

The runtime libraries the port links

U2ue.Runtime

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime targets netstandard2.1 (Unity 2021 and later can load it) and net8.0 (the tests and the hosts), and references nothing engine-shaped. Chapter 5 shows a host using it; what each type stands in for:

type in place of
UnityClock Time.deltaTime (the real step clamped to the project's Maximum Allowed Timestep, times TimeScale), unscaledDeltaTime (unclamped), frameCount, Time.time
Coroutines, Handle, Wait StartCoroutine, StopCoroutine, StopAllCoroutines, WaitForSeconds, WaitForSecondsRealtime
UnityFrame the player loop's order: every Update by execution order, the coroutine phase, every LateUpdate
Platform (ILog, ITextAssets, IKeyValueStore, IFileStore, IJsonCodec<T>, IRandomSource, SeededRandom) Debug.Log, Resources.Load<TextAsset>, PlayerPrefs, the save file, JsonUtility, UnityEngine.Random with its bounds
PlaybackQueue<TEvent>, IPresenter<TEvent> no Unity type: an instant model's events shown one per tick, only while the view is idle
Digest, FloatBits no Unity type: one runtime's answers as u2ue parity reads them, floats as bit patterns
TrailLaw TrailRenderer's points and drawn vertices, as measured

UnityClock's maximum step is a constructor argument, never a constant: it is the project's own (py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from ProjectSettings/TimeManager.asset --class 5). PlaybackQueue refuses a history that shrinks, where the code it was extracted from skipped one silently: a shorter history is a different model or a reset.

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests runs headless: the clock, coroutine, frame, random, bit, digest and queue rules, the trail law replayed against Unity 6000.3's own play-mode bake (a wrong trail time must fail it). It references only the toolkit, so it builds on any machine. Hold your game to the library the same way the reference port did: step the game's own measured runner and the library through one set of coroutine scripts (a stall past the maximum step, a hit-stop, a waiter, a nested routine, a stop) and require identical logs. The reference port's version of that test references its own presentation project, so the release leaves it out.

U2ue.Ui

u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Ui (net10.0) is the generic part of the UI converter, compiled from the ui/ part's sources with no game reference. It stands in for uGUI and TextMesh Pro on a converted screen, ported line for line from the packages' source and held to Unity's captures, so the Unreal side only loads the textures and submits the frame: UiLayout (the anchor solve, the layout groups, ContentSizeFitter; a grid layout or an aspect-ratio fitter refused), UguiMesh (the vertex stream uGUI hands a CanvasRenderer), UiFrameBuilder (one draw per CanvasRenderer, in Unity's order), UiRaycaster and UiSelectables (the hit order, the colour transitions and the click), and TmpLayout (TextMesh Pro's layout, held to TMP's own output at float32 bit equality on every captured text), among others.

py -m u2ue --project <game> ui test runs U2ue.Ui.Tests, the converter's tests that touch no game type, compiled against the library alone. Measured (2026-10-15): 398 pass alone, and a planted transform defect fails 264. A known gap: no captured screen holds a rotated node, so a planted rotation defect fails none of them.

U2ue.Unreal and U2ueAudio

u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal holds the host classes AU2ueFrameActor, UnrealPointer, UnrealCameraRig and UnrealPlatform.cs (Chapter 5 says what each does). dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal compiles them against a real UnrealSharp (U2UE_UNREALSHARP): measured (2026-10-15), 0 warnings, 0 errors, and a planted wrong binding fails with CS1061.

u2ue/templates/unreal/Plugins/U2ueAudio plays the PCM a port renders at run time (Unity's AudioClip.Create and SetData) as 2D voices, the float samples unconverted (UU2ueAudioBridge.PlayPcm), and captures what the mixer rendered into a float WAV through a listener that keeps the main submix rendering. Its self test is the console command u2ue.audio.selftest <wav> (a 440 Hz tone), judged by selftest_judge.py (correlation, pitch and length on every channel; its own --selftest makes a wrong pitch, silence, a truncated tone and noise each fail). selftest_run.ps1 builds the minimal host with the plugin and runs it headless: both were proven on 2026-10-15 (the build in 95 s; the headless -game capture passes the judge on both channels), and pillar 1 of u2ue cycle re-judges that capture.

Build, read, photo

The three Unreal verbs of the effects pipeline (Chapter 7). Each refuses while the host is busy, removes and names inherited U1E_* and VFXPORT_* variables, runs its tools from native PowerShell below normal priority, and is judged by what its run wrote.

u2ue build

py -m u2ue --project <game> build [--keys FILE] [--tag TAG] [--batch N] [--no-resave] [--dry]

The keys are every READ key of the project's resolve that has an IR file, or the list in FILE. Then:

  • effects_tools/fx17_asset_names.py writes the asset-name table (names two different Unity files would share) to records/asset_names.json; a failure stops the build.
  • fx17_build.ps1 builds the keys in one headless run with batched compiles (--batch 12 by default; the cap 450 s a key, at least 2400 s), keeping records/u1e-build-<TAG>.json with each key's verdict. No record is exit 1.
  • Unless --no-resave, the fresh-process resave of only the systems this build made (U1E_RESAVE_ONLY) into <work.effects>/u1e-resave.json - not the build script's own -Resave, which resaves the whole content root (measured on the reference port: about 70 minutes for 672 systems).

Exit 0 only when the build exited 0 and (unless --no-resave) every built system was resaved without error.

u2ue read

py -m u2ue --project <game> read [--tag TAG] [--frames N] [--dry]

Every BUILT system of records/u1e-build-<TAG>.json is read frame by frame (above; 90 frames at 1/60 s by default) into records/rb_<TAG>_<N>.json with its capture summary; a system that captured no frame (a build never resaved reads nothing) or fewer than asked is named, and the verb exits 1. Only the systems and the frame count are passed: a read at another step, moved or repeated, is a trial's (u2ue trial's read step takes dt).

u2ue photo

py -m u2ue --project <game> photo [--tag TAG] [--times 0.1,0.3,0.6,1.0] [--dry]
  • effects_tools/u1e_fx_photo.py draws each BUILT system at each time into photos/unreal/<leaf>_t<ms>.png: spawned in the editor world, advanced by the same sim-cache capture the read uses, photographed by a scene capture that renders only that component from a fixed pose, sky, fog and clouds off. Each system first gets a background frame with nothing in it, which must be black - that is what makes a frame comparable - and warm-up passes come first, because a translucent material still compiling draws nothing.
  • effects_tools/u1e_photo_sheet.py lays each system's Unity frames above its Unreal frames into photos/sheets/<leaf>.png, printing beside each only what the frame is (lit pixel count, the lit area's centre and extent), so an empty or displaced frame is named before anyone opens the sheet.

The run is judged by its capture (u2ue/capture.py), never by the tool's exit: a system with no judgeable frame, or a frame asked for and not written by THIS run, is named, and a system never captured fails the verb. The selftest fakes runs whose exit is 0 every time and requires exit 1 for a system that raised, a frame never written and a run that wrote no result.

The pairing. Unity's frames come from vfxport/unity_probe/EffectPhotoProbe.cs, run in the game's own editor in a measurement window (Chapter 8): the prefab at the origin in a preview scene, every top-level system's automatic random seed off so each draws from its own fixed seed, stepped at 1/60 s (the game's frame) to each time, rendered from (0, 4, -7) looking at (0, 0.5, 0), vertical field of view 50, 512 x 512, on black. u1e_fx_photo.py converts that pose with the port's own axis map. The sheet pairs Unity's float-target frames (photos/unity_hdr) when they exist.

Like for like. Unity's reference camera renders no post-processing, so the Unreal capture leaves the tonemapper off: Unreal's filmic curve sends every display value under about 16/255 to 0, a faint halo's whole outer ring (2026-10-07). The frame must then be encoded as Unity's is: a render target made at run time is linear, so an 8-bit target held linear values as display bytes and every dim pixel read 5 to 13 times too dark. The capture renders to a half-float target, encoded as Unity's target encodes (clamp, sRGB, round).

A photo is one draw (Chapter 11, "Photos are draws; their dates mix"): a frame confirms what the read-back data holds and decides nothing. Open every sheet: a run that says ok has proved only that bytes were written.

A converter route is tried with py -m u2ue --project <game> trial run <spec.json>: the same steps from a data file, built into the trial's own content root with the route's switch on, one Unreal at a time, stoppable between steps (Chapter 7, Chapter 9).

First time on a new machine

Every item names the check that proves it.

  1. The engine is where the runner looks. $script:UeHeadlessExe at the top of scene_tools/ue_headless.ps1 is the one place an executable is named: point it at your install's Engine/Binaries/Win64/UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe. Check: Test-Path on it is True.
  2. Native PowerShell's PATH carries UnrealSharp's marker. In the PowerShell you will run the facade from, $env:PATH -split ';' | Where-Object { $_.Contains('Program Files\dotnet\') -and (Test-Path $_) } prints one entry.
  3. The .NET SDK. dotnet --list-sdks lists a 10.0 SDK: the managed project targets net10.0 (Chapter 3 lists the rest).
  4. The runner refuses each rule. py -m u2ue --project <game> tool ue_headless_selftest.ps1 prints PASS and exits 0.
  5. The Unreal-side selftests pass with no engine. py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests passes; it runs the host, photo, read-back, capture and trial selftests among the rest (Chapter 21 lists them). The host selftest builds its cases from the second example project in u2ue/projects/, so that project's model must be on disk.
  6. The host is free. After extract (Chapter 4), py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry prints the Unreal host: free.
  7. A Windows SDK, or an AutoSDK. py -m u2ue --project <game> host compile proves Result: Succeeded, or its log says Platform Win64 is not a valid platform to build: then name an AutoSDK root in unreal.host.sdks_root and run it again.
  8. The host, end to end. host plan, then each step from create to run. Check: py -m u2ue --project <game> host status shows every step PROVEN, and py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal exits 0.
  9. The host classes match this UnrealSharp. With U2UE_UNREALSHARP set to the host's Plugins/UnrealSharp, dotnet build u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal reports 0 errors.
  10. Hot reload is off before the host's editor is opened while any tool writes managed code. Check: the host's Config/DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini holds AutomaticHotReloading=Off under [/Script/UnrealSharpEditor.CSUnrealSharpEditorSettings].
  11. Long launches fit. Check: the shell tool's timeout is at least the launcher's -MaxSeconds.
  12. Runs are silent. Check: a headless game run's log says Using Audio Hardware Device Non-realtime Renderer, never a real device.

14. Test-driven porting

Who this is for: the porting developer. After it you know which test proves what in a port and in which order to run them, and you can test one newly ported rule from the first lookup to the cycle.

A port has something most software never gets: a finished specification that runs. The Unity game already does everything the port must do, so every test in a port asks one question - does the port do, here, what Unity does here - and every expected value can be READ from the game's files or MEASURED from Unity. This chapter turns that into a method, and ends with the procedure for one newly ported rule.

It points to other chapters instead of repeating them: Chapter 9 for the verification procedures (the gates, proving a route offline, conformance over every key, looking at photos), Chapter 12 for the headless Unity tools in full, Chapter 8 for measuring a Unity rule, and Chapter 5 for the game-code method these tests serve.

What makes a test a port's test

  • Its expected value comes from Unity. It is READ (from the game's code or data, with the file and line) or MEASURED (from a Unity run, with the run named). A value typed from memory tests the memory; a value copied from the port's own output tests the port against itself.
  • It can fail. It has been seen to fail on a planted wrong answer. Until then a green result says nothing: a check that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off.
  • It says what it examined. A test that judged nothing reports that it judged nothing, and that report is a failure, not a pass.

The Unity Test Runner is not a layer

Run from outside, Unity's Test Runner launches a second, full Unity Editor that imports assets, takes the foreground window on every assembly reload and throws modal progress dialogs. On the reference port its owner could not use the machine while one ran. A subset run starts the same Editor, so a smaller run is no safer.

So the toolkit's Unity test command (my_unity.py) refuses, exit 3, while .UNITY_TESTS_DISABLED exists at the toolkit root, and pillar 10 of the cycle (u2ue cycle, the toolkit's recurring self-check; "The cycle", below) checks on every run that the file is still there. A test that truly needs a live Editor - a real scene, AssetDatabase, UnityEditor.* - stays unrun, the report says so, and the owner decides. "Compile-verified headlessly, suite not run" is an honest report; "it works", from a test that did not run, is not.

The layers, cheapest first

flowchart LR
  A["dotnet test: the model's rules"] --> B["headless_nunit: Editor-folder tests"]
  B --> C["typecheck: Unity still compiles"]
  C --> D["parity + digest: the same bits on every runtime"]
  D --> E["conform: every key on numbers"]
  E --> F["photo: LOOKED at, last"]
layer command a pass proves it cannot prove
pure rules dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests a moved rule gives Unity's value on CoreCLR Mono's bits; that Unity still compiles
Editor-folder tests py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <file> the test passes on the project's freshly compiled code, no Editor anything that needs UnityEditor, AssetDatabase or a scene
typecheck py typecheck.py the Unity project compiles as Unity would compile it that anything behaves
parity py -m u2ue --project <game> parity every runtime agrees by the bit, or differs only where characterised that the rule is right - only that it is the same
Unity's Mono py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run ... Unity's own runtime gave these bits, no Editor that the Editor would, until digest faithful measured it
conformance py -m u2ue --project <game> conform ... each key's built asset computes what Unity's does, per emitter how it looks; what the probe was blind to
photos py -m u2ue --project <game> photo once LOOKED at, the frames confirm the numbers anything, on their own

Pure rules: dotnet test

The game's rules move into an engine-free model (Chapter 5), and a moved rule is first tested in the model's own test project, <Model>.Core.Tests: written by u2ue scaffold, NUnit on net8.0, one test per moved rule, its expected value the one the Unity build gives. Nothing opens, and the model's gates (u2ue check --only model) have already kept the engine out, so the test tests the rule.

The toolkit's runtime library is tested the same way, and its tests show the shape to copy:

dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests

TrailLawTests replays the TrailRenderer law against Unity's play-mode bake (72 frames, 15 baked meshes, every point and vertex compared), and the same file carries the replay's plant: A_Wrong_Time_Fails_The_Replay runs the frames with a trail time of 0.45 instead of 0.5 and requires a mismatch. Without the plant, the replay would pass a law that ignored its time.

A version trap: the scaffolded tests use NUnit 4 (4.0.1), but Unity's NUnit is 3.x, and NUnit 4 moved Assert.IsNotNull and its family to ClassicAssert. Write a test that must also compile inside Unity to NUnit 3; that is why the headless runner pins 3.14.0.

Editor-folder tests: headless_nunit.py

Many Unity projects keep NUnit tests in an Editor folder, and most of them exercise data and logic, not the Editor. headless_nunit.py compiles the project from Unity's own compiler command line and runs those tests with no Unity process:

py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <Assets/.../Editor/XTests.cs>
py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test A.cs --test B.cs --filter "FullyQualifiedName~Resolver"

Exit 0 all passed, 1 a test failed, 2 nothing ran or the filter matched nothing, 3 an environment or compile failure. What it cannot run fails loudly: TypeLoadException, MissingMethodException or FileNotFoundException, naming the member. A pure member is added to headless_nunit/UnityShimCore/Shim.cs; anything else needs a live Editor, and the test is left unrun and said so. "It lives in an Editor folder" is never by itself a reason to reach for the Unity runner.

The tool names its Unity project and install folder in its own constants (it predates the project file), so on another project you edit them first. Chapter 12 has how it works, what it cannot run and the traps it absorbs, including the one that lets a mutation "pass": read the printed MVID line every time.

Does it compile: typecheck.py

Unity has already written complete compiler command lines to disk, the Bee .rsp files. typecheck.py reuses them with Unity's bundled Roslyn and compiles both assemblies, the Editor one against the runtime assembly it has just built, so the answer is Unity's own, with no Editor:

py typecheck.py                         # both assemblies
py typecheck.py --as-head [--keep <path>]
py typecheck.py --model-from-source     # against the model's source, not its installed DLLs

Exit 0 clean, 1 compile errors, 2 could not run the check, and the tool says in as many words that 2 is not a pass. --as-head asks whether a fresh checkout would compile: a working copy can compile while a checkout does not, when code references files never checked in. Use --model-from-source when the Unity project uses the model's built DLLs. It proves the code builds, not that it behaves, and its last line says so. Chapter 12 has every option and the traps it handles.

The same bits on every runtime: u2ue parity

A rule that passes on CoreCLR can still answer differently on Unity's Mono. Chapter 5, step 7 is the method, with the reference port's real output. Each runtime writes a digest, one key=value row per case with every float as its bit pattern, and u2ue parity compares every row across every runtime found:

py -m u2ue --project <game> parity                       # exit 0 agree, 1 a row differs, 2 refused
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --require Unreal      # refuse unless Unreal's digest is there
py -m u2ue --project <game> parity --characterise        # write the allowance from the digests on disk

Bits, not text: Mono and .NET spell identical bits two ways, and as text, an early pilot of the reference port reported 230 mismatches that did not exist. The allowance, <parity.dir>/logic-allowance.json, keeps parity a test, not a list of excuses: a differing row is red unless the allowance pins that row to its exact bits and to one ULP, so a new row, a moved value or a wider gap stays red, and --characterise refuses any gap wider than one ULP (logic_diff.py's selftest proves all four refusals). Characterising needs a measured cause and never turns a gate green; a fix that moves Unity's own values is the owner's decision.

The trap that costs most: the cases' inputs must be exact on every runtime - integer arithmetic, each written to the sheet (the digest, which records every input as an _in row too). Inputs made with float maths measure their own drift (Chapter 5, step 7).

Unity's answer with no Unity: u2ue digest

Parity needs Unity's digest, and the Editor is the expensive place to get it. u2ue digest gets it from Unity's own runtime, with nothing opening and nothing taking focus:

py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs> [--refs X.dll ...] [--dir DIR]
py -m u2ue --project <game> digest faithful

run compiles the cases twice, for CoreCLR (logic-Headless.txt) and with that Unity version's own compiler and Mono (logic-UnityMono.txt). logic-UnityMono.provenance.json names the Mono and whether it is MEASURED faithful to the Editor for this Unity. That label is the point: Unity's Mono is Unity's runtime, not the Editor. digest faithful measures it against a digest the Editor wrote (Chapter 12); on a Unity with no such measurement the provenance reads UNMEASURED. The selftest proves the standalone Mono both ways: standalone Mono must reproduce the Editor's digest AND must NOT match the CoreCLR one, or the comparison could not tell the runtimes apart.

Every key on numbers: u2ue conform

For assets that simulate - effects, today - this layer compares Unity's state with what the built Unreal asset computes, over every key, on numbers; Chapter 9 has the procedure. It comes after parity because it spends both shared resources (a window in the owner's editor and the one headless Unreal), and its diff is heavy (on the reference port: 673 keys, a 1.7 GB read-back), so the cycle reads the newest stamped report instead (conform latest) and refuses as STALE a report another judge made.

It comes before photos because it sees what a photo cannot: on the reference port one class-wide read found every non-prewarmed burst born one warm-up tick late, 121 of 121, after nights of per-effect photos had not. Its selftest includes a planted 0.03 s late birth and an emitter missing on one side, which must be named, never dropped.

The picture, last: u2ue photo

py -m u2ue --project <game> photo [--tag TAG] [--times 0.1,0.3,0.6,1.0]

Photos run last, and are never skipped. Last, because a metric over pictures can reward the wrong thing (Chapter 9, rule 3: a render that went black scored better). Never skipped, because data can be right about a worthless result: a generated level once passed every file-level check while carrying the same 145 prefab instances as an empty level, where the hand-made level it was meant to match carried 1722.

A photo run is judged by its capture (u2ue/capture.py), never its exit: judged by its exit alone, a photo step could read "ok" for a run that drew nothing. A sheet is evidence only once LOOKED at.

Why the order matters

  • Cost. The first three layers need only the machine (the second and third read Unity's install and the project's last Unity compile, with no Editor running); conformance needs the owner's editor and the one headless Unreal; photos need the Unreal and a person's eyes. A rule that would have failed dotnet test in seconds must never be what fails a conformance run hours later.
  • Trust. Numbers before pictures: a look covers one draw, and data that proved itself says what the picture should show. A skipped layer is not a passed layer.

Determinism across runtimes: what the field knows

A port that runs the same C# on Unity's Mono and on CoreCLR (an UnrealSharp host, a headless test run) meets this directly: parity compares the runtimes' answers by float bits. This section says which differences to expect, which to audit for, and how far byte identity can be relied on. It was read as raw text from the standards, the .NET runtime's GitHub issues and the vendors' own documentation; where a point rests on one author, or was not checked against Unity's own build, the text says so.

What the standards allow

ECMA-334, the C# language standard, section 8.3.7 "Floating-point types", says floating-point operations may be performed with higher precision than the operation's result type, and that an explicit cast forces a value to its type's exact precision. Its own example of the hazard is an expression of the form x * y / z, where the multiplication leaves the double range and the division brings it back: the wider evaluation can give a finite result instead of an infinity (standard, Microsoft's copy).

ECMA-335, the CLI standard, Partition I section 12.1.3, says the size of the internal floating-point representation is implementation-dependent, as long as it is at least as precise as the value it represents; that freedom ends at an explicit conversion (conv.r4 or conv.r8), after which the value must be exactly representable in its type (PDF).

So a one-ULP difference between runtimes is not a bug: both specifications license it. Byte identity across Mono, CoreCLR and a headless run is an observed property of today's builds, not a guarantee; it can break on a Unity or .NET upgrade with no change to the game's code.

Fused multiply-add, and Mono's float32

A natural first suspect for cross-runtime float drift is the JIT fusing a multiply and an add. The .NET team ruled that out on purpose:

  • dotnet/runtime#64591 proposed emitting fmadd for x * y + z. The owner of System.Numerics closed it: a fused operation returns a different result for many inputs, so it is a value-changing optimisation, not IEEE 754 compliant, and not a safe or legal default. Clang and MSVC allow it only under ffast-math and fp:fast; GCC defaults to -ffp-contract=fast.
  • dotnet/runtime#64604 then set -ffp-contract=off for GCC builds of the runtime itself.
  • dotnet/runtime#12753, a configurable fast-math mode, was closed unimplemented. .NET has no fast-math mode.

The better suspect is Mono. Mono's creator wrote (2018-04-11) that Mono, decades earlier, performed all 32-bit float computation as 64-bit while storing the data in 32-bit locations, and later added an opt-in "float32" mode, --O=float32, to do 32-bit float operations in 32 bits (link). That is a one-ULP generator on a float multiply-divide: Mono computing a*b/c at double precision and rounding once at the store, CoreCLR rounding to float32 after each operation, both legal under ECMA-335 section 12.1.3. Which Mono build and which float32 setting a given Unity version ships was not verified.

The experiment. ECMA-335 says extra precision is discarded at an explicit conversion, so compare (float)((float)(a * b) / c) against a * b / c in a differential harness: if the casts close the gap, the fix is explicit float locals. On the reference port they did (Chapter 5), but that result fits both suspects, so it could not tell them apart; the toolkit's first diagnosis read it backwards (logic_diff.py records the correction). What settled it was which runtime differed: on all 35 characterised rows Unity's Mono was the odd one out, and the two CoreCLR runs agreed on every row. A fusing CoreCLR would have made them the outliers.

Two divergences that are not rounding

Float-to-int casts differ between Mono and CoreCLR, and the difference is open. dotnet/runtime#119821, filed 2025-09-17, shows (int)(float)int.MaxValue giving 7fffffff on CoreCLR and 80000000 on Mono. A .NET architect replied that since .NET 9 float-to-integer conversions saturate on CoreCLR on every architecture, that this was not fixed on Mono, and that these conversions are undefined behaviour there. dotnet/runtime#100368 tracks it (the .NET 9 change).

System.Math transcendentals call into the platform's C runtime, and one .NET build was measured to differ between operating systems (dotnet/runtime#12753, a .NET 3.0 preview):

call Windows macOS
MathF.Asinh(0.48549962f) 0.46820483 0.46820486
MathF.Acos(0.57316583f) 0.96043230 0.96043223
MathF.Log2(1/3.0f) -1.5849625 -1.5849624

dotnet/runtime#9001, which asks for System.Math and System.MathF to be implemented in managed code, is still open. Only Math.Sqrt is IEEE-guaranteed. One author's Unity harness, run on Windows (Intel and AMD), Mac, Android, iOS and WebGL, agrees on the shape: only the trigonometric functions gave non-deterministic results; arithmetic, comparisons and int / float casts matched (link).

Both divergences are likelier, larger and cheaper to find than a ULP.

Fixed point

For bit identity across arbitrary hardware, fixed point is the standard answer in the vendors' own documentation: Photon Quantum (Q48.16 in one long; it warns that converting from a float inside the simulation desyncs, link), mas-bandwidth/fixed (which names fused multiply-add, libm transcendentals and -ffp-contract as what differs across compilers and architectures, link), Klotho (32.32, explicitly targeting Mono and IL2CPP, Unity's C#-to-C++ build backend, link), and Factorio's MapPosition (a 32-bit integer with 8 fraction bits, link). The canonical 2010 article "Floating Point Determinism" made float determinism conditional on the same compiler and the same architecture (link), and its author's company now ships the fixed-point library above. Two JITs are two compilers, so byte identity across Mono and CoreCLR is outside what anyone claims to rely on.

What fixed point costs

Quantum's documentation names the costs: the fraction is limited, never as accurate as a double; two parsing routes can disagree on one machine (FP.FromFloat_UNSAFE(1.1f).RawValue != FP.FromString("1.1").RawValue); FP.UseableMax, 32767.9999847412, is the largest value that can be squared without overflowing; precision holds in about 0.01 to 1000 and is lost multiplying very large or very small numbers and dividing back; and FP cannot be a C# constant, so a constant is written as its raw long with the decimal in a comment. A shipped RTS that moved to 64-bit fixed point adds that no third-party library can then be used (link). Quantum's own worst case is multiply-then-divide, the C# standard's float hazard: fixed point turns that one-ULP disagreement into a bounded precision loss both runtimes agree on, an improvement, not the problem gone.

What desynced shipped games

Every shipped lockstep success in this literature (lockstep: every player's machine runs the same simulation from the same inputs, so all must compute the same result) is one binary on one architecture: Supreme Commander and Demigod, quoted in the 2010 article, set the FPU's (the floating-point unit's) precision and rounding at start-up (_controlfp(_PC_24, _MCW_PC), _controlfp(_RC_NEAR, _MCW_RC)) and asserted both every tick; MotoGP, quoted there too, could not share replays between Xbox and PC. And the published desync causes are overwhelmingly not floating point:

  • memory bugs: uninitialised variables, dangling pointers, a reused address (Supreme Commander, link);
  • an ambiguous sort comparator that different compilers' sorts order differently (Factorio FFF #52, link);
  • printf formatting: gcc printing 1e-05 where VS2013 printed 1e-005 (FFF #108, link);
  • serialisation: nil as a placeholder for a cyclic reference deletes the key and changes the iteration order; a cached value recomputed instead of saved (FFF #340, link);
  • random-call counts that must match inside the simulation (Age of Empires, link).

Not needing bit identity at all

The modern alternative is not to need it. Valorant's server is authoritative and some divergence from a client's prediction is accepted; its fixed 128 Hz step makes the comparison like for like, not the bits equal (link). Rocket League's networked physics is server-authoritative too, and corrects a large difference by reverting and re-simulating; the words determinism, float, double, precision and bitwise appear nowhere in its 182 GDC slides (link). That is a tolerance test, not an equality test.

The line for a port: a byte-identical event log across runtimes is a stronger oracle (the source a test's expected answer comes from) than any shipped game in this literature attempted, and it is worth keeping as an instrument, but no specification backs it. The cheap moves, in order: run the explicit-cast experiment; audit for float-to-int casts and for System.Math calls other than Sqrt; then decide deliberately whether the contract is byte identity or logical parity with an ordering-and-tolerance comparison, because the first will one day break on a toolchain upgrade that the second would survive.

Write the test first

The judge before its trial

A judge (u2ue/judge.py) holds a record - a read-back, a capture, a case record - to a measured rule or to Unity, and must fail on its plant. Chapter 8 gives the order for a measurement: the judge, its plants, then the bake. A converter route's trial keeps the same order, because a judge written after the data is fitted to the data and passes whatever happened.

Judges are read off the trial specs' judge steps (<lane>/trials/**/*.json), never listed by hand, so the list cannot drift from what runs:

py -m u2ue --project <game> judge             # each judge, the trials that run it, how its plant is proven
py -m u2ue --project <game> judge --prove     # runs each judge's --selftest; exit 1 when one fails or has no plant

--prove reads PLANTS (its --selftest refused its planted faults), DECLARED (a trial declares a plant for it), NO PLANT (it has only ever passed) or FAIL. A trial step declares a plant beside its judge:

{"judge": {"argv": ["{lane}/<route>/<route>_check.py", "{dir}/<read>.json"],
           "plant": {"argv": ["{lane}/<route>/<route>_check.py", "{dir}/<route-off read>.json", "--plant"]}}}

u2ue trial runs the judge, then the same judge on the record it must refuse - the route-OFF read, a planted shift - and a plant that passes FAILS the step by name. A plant the judge's own verdict already requires refused is declared with in_run. When this became a cycle check on the reference port (2026-10-16), three of its judges had only ever passed.

A gate that has only ever passed

Every gate carries planted defects in its own --selftest, and the null case: an unperturbed input must PASS, or a gate that refused everything would pass its own plants. The headless NUnit runner's selftest is the pattern: a planted passing test exits 0, a planted failing test 1, a filter that matches nothing 2.

The most expensive failure is a check that passes without examining anything, because it turns "unknown" into "verified". On the reference port a test command printed None/None passed ... no regressions and exited 0 for a reply it could not parse; a read got 0 of 150 frames for all six systems of a trial, exited 0, and two judges then reported "0 judged" as if they had looked, which is why every read now writes a capture summary (u2ue/readback.py). The repair was never more checking. It was making each check state what it examined, so an empty examination reads as empty. An empty selection is a refusal, never a quiet skip.

Prefer an oracle from what the thing must do over a threshold. An ON/OFF comparison of a light-scattering effect once differed in 315k pixels; but that effect only ever adds light, and the signed difference was brighter in 152,782 pixels and darker in 155,186 - an even split, which is scene motion between two renders.

A plant must move what is judged

A plant proves something only if it changes the input the judge judges. On the reference port plants proved nothing in four ways:

  • the check read its default file instead of the planted one - check which file it opened;
  • the planted value equalled the measured one in every case of the trial - a plant acts on what the judge actually found;
  • the code refused the plant's input before any engine call, so it tested the refusal, not the route;
