  • a patch was proven against a stub, while at run time a cache wrapper over the called function kept its old signature - run the selftest of whatever is installed over the callee.

Widening a gate, and proving it still fails

A gate that walks one folder stops seeing what the port moves out of it ("Rules that keep tests honest", below). When a gate's scope is widened, its plants are re-run and one is added inside the new scope; otherwise the widened gate has only ever passed where it now claims to look.

A selftest on synthetic input proves the matcher, not the aim. A gate that refuses engine primitives standing in for real assets plants primitives in temporary folders, so a second proof copies the game's real engine-side code folder, plants one offender in the copy and scans it, proving the gate still walks the files that matter. A selftest of a gate is not a run of it, either: run the gate itself too.

A new gate that refuses content also runs offline over the whole existing corpus before a long build relies on it. On the reference port a mesh-import gate proven on two files went into a build of about two hours and refused 3 of 46 meshes it should have passed; 7 emitters vanished from three effects. Checking all 46 offline took about two minutes. A refusal of content that drew correctly yesterday is the gate's bug until shown otherwise.

Mutation: does any test notice?

py -m u2ue --project <game> uml tests <Name> separates called inside a test, merely mentioned in a test file, and not present - and still says only mutation answers whether a test would notice a change. The package ships no mutation harness yet; the reference port's shows what one must do:

  • It copies the current rule files and their tests fresh into an isolated test project on every run, so no open Editor sees a mutant.
  • Each mutation is a row: the file, a label, the exact old text (its anchor), the new text, and the claim the tests protect. It applies one row at a time, runs dotnet test, restores, and reports each as FAILED (caught), PASSED (survived), COMPILE-BREAK, NO-RESULT or ANCHOR-MISS, ending MUTANTS NOT CAUGHT n of m with each survivor's unchecked claim.
  • The suite runs before any mutation and after restoring; both must pass, or the verdicts between mean nothing.
  • A rename is not a mutation: it only breaks the build, which every test "catches" for free. Every row changes behaviour and still compiles.
  • An anchor that matches zero times or twice is an ANCHOR-MISS, counted as not caught: the harness refuses to guess. It can mean the source moved under the row (measured on the reference port, 2026-09-07: a timeline that had grown from 11 beats to 13), and then the fix is the anchor, not the harness.

Add a row whenever you add a rule.

The console is the headless test

A compiler proves the code builds; the console proves it ran. On the reference port three faults in one session passed every other instrument and were obvious in Unity's console within one frame (Chapter 12 lists them). console_check.py reads a running Editor's console through the editor's HTTP bridge (Chapter 12; the bridge does not ship yet, so your project needs its own) and reports only what is NEW. Use it as a gate:

py console_check.py --reset                      # mark everything seen, before the action
py console_check.py --label "what I just did"    # after it: exit 1 when NEW errors appeared

New errors stop the work. Exit 2 means the bridge was unreachable or refused - not a pass. Pair it with a Play cycle when a change touches rendering. Reading the console starts nothing and takes no focus, but it needs an Editor already running. Chapter 12 has its watermark, how it collapses repeated rows and counts Unity's own noise apart, and a known gap on a long console.

A fresh record is not a fresh build. On the reference port a Unity-side recording was triggered after a model change, before the Editor's domain reload had settled. Unity re-recorded 17 s later on the OLD assembly: the recompile had failed on one access error (CS0122), so the Editor kept the old code. The record was newer than the DLL, every timestamp check passed, and the tests failed identically. console_check showed the compile error. So the order is: typecheck.py before anything that recompiles, wait until the reload has finished, record, console_check, then the tests.

The cycle

Pillars and verdicts

u2ue cycle holds the toolkit to its promises when a work cycle ends or a report is about to be written. A pillar is one promise the product makes; a check is one command the toolkit already runs, and the rule that reads its output as a verdict.

py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle                 # every pillar; exit 1 when any pillar is FAIL
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --pillar 2 3    # only these; a partial run never becomes the baseline
py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle --dry           # list the pillars and checks; nothing runs
pillar the promise
1 AUTO-PORT every asset family that is not logic ports with no human step
2 AI LOGIC PORT Opus, pointed at a game through the skill, ports its logic
3 HUMAN ERGONOMICS every concept a named class; diagrams generated from the code and gated
4 AUTOMATION TOOLS SHIPPED the Unity and Unreal automation a port needs ships in the package
5 PROOF AND CONFORMANCE every judge has a plant that fails; conformance read from data
6 MEASURED KNOWLEDGE every Unity rule measured by a probe case, stored per Unity version
7 GENERIC, NOT ONE GAME adapters and project files, no hard-wired paths in the core
8 PACKAGING AND RELEASE a UPM (Unity Package Manager) package that installs into a fresh Unity and a fresh Unreal project
9 SPEED AND PROOF OF VALUE the porting speed and the percent-identical family, from records
10 SAFE OPERATION the toolkit never disturbs the person using the machine
11 RUN INFRASTRUCTURE pinned, resumable runs from data, stoppable between steps
verdict meaning
PASS the check ran and its rule holds
FAIL the check ran and its rule does not hold - red stops the cycle
HELD it fails ONLY in the way a recorded open decision of the owner's says it must; failing any other way is FAIL
ABSENT no check exists yet; never counted as PASS - it names the work that would build it

A pillar is FAIL if any check is FAIL, ABSENT if no check of it ran, otherwise PASS, with HELD checks shown beside it. Red stops the cycle with exit 1, and the record keeps 40 lines of the failing check's output - the lines saying FAIL, REFUSED, ERROR or Traceback first, then the end - so it says why without a re-run.

A HELD check names its decision and the failing lines it explains; one more failing line, or a failure that prints none, is FAIL, so a new failure can never hide behind an old decision. A trend check reads a number and a direction it must not move in (the share of conforming emitters must not fall); the first cycle is the baseline, and a number not read is FAIL.

The record and the baseline

Each run writes <work.records>/cycle/cycle-<stamp>.json; a full run also writes cycle-latest.json, which the next cycle trends against. A trend that FAILED keeps the previous value as its baseline, marked baseline_held: writing the regressed value would make the regression the new bar.

Read a record by its FAIL rows first, then its HELD rows, then its ABSENT rows. A HELD row waits on the game's owner, not on the toolkit: for example, a scene fidelity gate held while whether to keep an imported level's deliberately changed lighting is still undecided.

What the cycle does not run

The cycle checks the toolkit against a project; it does not run your game's own tests. dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests and the project's parity are not cycle checks (pillar 2 runs the project's model gates, the runtime library's tests and the parity tool's selftest). Run them yourself; py -m u2ue --project <game> logic reads where the logic port stands, runs check --only model and parity, and names each test run it does not start as NOT RUN, with its command.

u2ue check: the selftests and the gates

py -m u2ue --project <game> check                      # all four parts
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only selftests [--tool console_check.py ...]
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only gates         # the field gates over this project's IR
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only facts         # the measured rules' Unity versions against the project's
py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model         # layer_gate and host_gate on the engine-free model

The selftests run with every U2UE_, U1E_ or VFXPORT_ variable left in your shell dropped and the project's own U2UE_ paths set, so a switch you exported once cannot change what a plant meets. They run below normal priority, launching neither Unity nor Unreal; exit 1 when any fails. Each tool's last run, its exit and its seconds are in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.json. A selftest that is not run says its measured reason: the package skips one that corrupts and restores a plugin DLL an open Unity editor loads, and a project file can name its own (the reference port's skips one that launches Unreal). Selftests nobody runs rot: the first survey found three broken unseen and both field gates red. Chapter 21 lists every selftest; Chapter 18 has how a tool's selftest is registered.

Rules that keep tests honest

Never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green. A baseline, an allowance or a fingerprint is re-recorded only when the change it records is intended, with the reason committed beside it. The cycle enforces it for trends, parity for allowances; this rule does everywhere else.

A miss is UNKNOWN, never ABSENT. The toolkit's code readers are lexical: a call through an interface, a delegate, reflection or a UnityEvent wired in a prefab is invisible to them, and uml callers and uml tests print UNKNOWN when they find nothing. An ABSENT you write needs the level above: name the search that would prove it, and check the container (a field missing on a record may live on the group holding it), a second rule of the same shape, whether you actually ran the tool, and whether a later pass writes more.

Check whether the code moved before believing a red gate. A gate that walks only the Unity tree reports what the port moved into the model as ABSENT. On the reference port (2026-09-29) three gates did so in one day: the class-model gate said a method did not exist while it sat in the model (both of its channels walked one directory), another reported four abilities no longer called whose calls had moved one hop, and the requirements checker silently covered less each time an annotation moved. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name> walks the code roots and the model together. Then widen the gate and re-run its plants.

A call site is not coverage. A test can call a method in setup and assert on something else. Say "called from N test files", never "covered".

Re-run a red test in a file another worker just wrote. Compare its modification time with the clock and re-run before investigating. On the reference port a test failed identically three runs in a row while its owner had fixed the line a minute earlier; the next run was green. Never patch a live worker's file: record the finding with its file and line, and let the owner land it.

Snapshot suites when work lands concurrently. A suite that reads expectations from data at run time and compares them with code compiled earlier straddles any landing that changes both, so compare the failing area's sources and data with the compiled assembly's time before diagnosing. On the reference port twelve such failures were diagnosed as drift; an hour later the suite was green with no action taken. A compile break in a file saved a minute ago is the same: poll the build until it settles.

Test an agent, or a skill, by running it. u2ue/survey/skill_gate.py checks that every command a skill names exists and each step has a RUN and one DONE WHEN; it cannot see what a model does with the text. On the reference port a static audit of six generated agent definitions found two defects; running one on a bounded, read-only item found five. Grade the run's report against the definition, fix the generator, run it again.

An instrument that answers anyway is worse than one that will not answer. Make an instrument refuse when its input is stale: exit 2 when a coverage report is older than the source it describes, and exit 1 when a to-do list was made from a tree that has since changed. On the reference port a stale coverage report said 15 of 100 files at 18.3 percent where a fresh one said 90 of 101 at 74.1 percent: the opposite conclusion.

Requirements and tests

// REQ: annotations

Every feature traces to a requirement through a // REQ: comment on the rule, and a checker scans the files or folders it is given and checks that each citation resolves. The package has no checker yet: the reference port's names its own requirement documents in its constants. This is what it checks, so you can write yours against your own documents:

  • A citation names a requirements file and line (which must exist and be substantive), a design document, or a spreadsheet tab, resolved against its cached copy.
  • Engineer-owned tags (plumbing, feedback, implementation-only and their kin) pass, and so does an explicit statement that no requirement exists - the ABSENT half of READ-or-ABSENT, written down.
  • An engineer tag citing a line now blank passes marked STALE and counted; a strict mode fails it.
  • An unresolved citation goes to the designer, with a stub line written for them to flesh out.
  • Exit 0 when every citation resolves, 1 when one does not.

Two warnings, both measured on the reference port. A checker that reads only the paths you hand it covers less each time annotations move with the rules into the model, so hand it the model's folders too. And if it reads an indexed copy of the requirements before the file, re-sync the index after every edit to the file.

The discipline it serves: every new feature gets a test, linked to the commit that adds it and to its requirement; a feature with no requirement gets a stub, marked for the designer, before it merges.

The class model gates

The class model comes first: a new concept gets a named class before code is written around it, and diagrams are generated from the code and gated, never hand-drawn and trusted.

  • The class-model gate, py -m u2ue --project <game> uml check --doc <use case model .md>, looks up every identifier the document names in the class model of the game's code roots and the model; a name the extractor lacks is asked of an independent text scan first. When the channels disagree it ABSTAINS and says where to settle it; it FAILS a name written as a call only when both agree it is absent. It also refuses a document with no PROBLEM STORY section (the problem told in words, which the use cases are drawn from), no primary actor or no EPIC, and an epic of fewer than 3 or more than 11 steps. The key case of its selftest is CAN-THE-GATE-FAIL: a fabricated name must be refused.
  • The concept gate, u2ue/survey/concepts_gate.py, holds the toolkit's own concept model (u2ue/CONCEPTS.md) to its code: a row marked EXISTS must name path.py:Class, and that class must be in that file. Chapter 22 has the model it checks.

Procedure: a test for a newly ported rule

Scope: one rule of the game, moved into the engine-free model. Precondition: the model is scaffolded (u2ue scaffold) and its gates pass. Minimal guarantee: a step that cannot run is reported as not run, never as passed. Success guarantee: the rule has a test that was seen to fail, gives Unity's value by the bit on every runtime, cites its requirement, and the cycle reads PASS or HELD by a named decision. Trigger: a rule is about to move out of the Unity tree.

  1. Find the rule. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name> names its type, file and line - proof that the name exists. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml callers <Name> lists its candidate call sites; a miss is UNKNOWN.
  2. Read its inputs and Unity's answer. Constants from the code, with file and line; serialized values from the asset, py -m u2ue --project <game> data --from <Assets/...prefab> --script <ClassName>, never the C# initializer. The expected value is the one the Unity build gives, read from a record or measured (Chapter 8); if neither, stop and measure it.
  3. Write the test before the move. One NUnit test in <Model>.Core.Tests, its expected value from step 2, its source in a comment.
  4. Move the rule unchanged, and gate the model. A behaviour change is a separate, named decision. py -m u2ue --project <game> check --only model proves no engine namespace or platform member came with it.
  5. Run the test. dotnet test <Model>.Core.Tests - green proves the moved rule gives Unity's value on CoreCLR. Not trusted yet.
  6. Make it fail on purpose. Change the rule's behaviour so it still compiles - a constant off by one, a comparison turned round - and rerun step 5: the test must fail with an assertion naming the value. Restore. For a standing proof, keep the change as a row in a mutation harness that applies each change to a fresh copy of the rule and its tests and reports MUTANTS NOT CAUGHT 0 of n (the package has none yet; the section "Mutation: does any test notice?" above says what one does). A failure that is only a compile error proves nothing.
  7. Prove Unity still compiles. py typecheck.py (with --model-from-source when the Unity project uses the model's built DLLs) - exit 0 proves the Unity project still builds around the moved rule. Exit 2 is not a pass.
  8. Run its Editor-folder test, if it has one. py headless_nunit/headless_nunit.py --test <Editor test.cs> - exit 0 proves it passes on the freshly compiled assembly; exit 2 means nothing ran.
  9. Answer the rule on both runtimes. Add its cases to the digest's case file, inputs exact and written to the sheet, and bump the digest's version. py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Cases.Build> --cases <Cases.cs> writes the CoreCLR and Unity Mono sheets with no Editor; the provenance says whether that Mono is MEASURED faithful.
  10. Compare them by the bit. py -m u2ue --project <game> parity - exit 0 proves every runtime agrees on every row. A one-ULP row is diagnosed and its cause measured; only then, by the owner's decision, parity --characterise pins it.
  11. Check the console, when an editor is running. py console_check.py --reset before the Unity side recompiles, then py console_check.py --label "<rule> moved" - exit 0 proves the Unity build ran with nothing new in its console. With no editor running, the step is reported as not run.
  12. Cite the requirement. A // REQ: comment on the rule, then your requirement checker over the model's folder (the section "// REQ: annotations" above says what it checks) - exit 0 proves the citation resolves; exit 1 goes to the designer.
  13. Draw the slice. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <Type> draws it from the code, every member real; py -m u2ue --project <game> uml check --doc <use case model .md> proves every name the use cases use exists.
  14. See where the port stands. py -m u2ue --project <game> logic - each logic skill step DONE, NOT YET, JUDGED or NOT RUN, read from the records now.
  15. Close the cycle. py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle - every pillar PASS, or HELD by a named decision. A FAIL stops the work until it is fixed; it is never re-baselined.

Steps 1 to 8 spend no shared resource, steps 9 and 10 need no Editor, and step 11 only reads one that is already running.

15. Porting with Opus 5.5

Who this is for: the porting developer who runs the port with an AI model - which skills to load, how to keep a long session going, how to keep its tokens down, and how to check its work.

u2ue is built to be driven by an AI model: you point Opus 5.5 at the game's logic through the toolkit's skills, and the verbs carry the other asset families (Chapter 2 lists each family and its commands). This chapter also covers what running several agents at once was measured to cost. The model is never trusted on its own word.

What carries a port from session to session

The reference port was done by AI models working in Claude Code (Anthropic's command-line coding agent) over many sessions (u2ue/basis/tokens.json names the models each measured rate came from). Four things carried it from session to session, and a port of your own needs the same four.

  • A project rules file, read at the start of every session. It holds the iron law written as working rules (no guessing, no fallbacks, no toys, verify with both the data and the picture), the safety rules (never the Unity Test Runner, never the live editor someone is working in, one headless Unreal at a time), "fix the class, not the instance" (fix what produced a fault, not the one case seen; a one-off fix carries its reason), and the rule that UML class diagrams steer the work. Keep it short: every agent pays for it (below).
  • One task list on disk. Every item is a line with an observable a stranger could re-check (DONE WHEN: ...). The session reads it at the start of every item, because a session cannot see its own context being compacted (summarised to make room as it fills).
  • Memory notes, one fact per file. A trap is written down once, with its fix, so that the next session does not pay for it again. Two examples: a shell that rewrote the PATH so Unreal could not find .NET, and a heredoc (a shell's inline block of text) that ate backslashes.
  • Skills. A skill is a packaged procedure that the model loads when the task matches it. Besides the toolkit's two porting skills, the port used three general ones:
  • a long-run skill: finish the list, never stop at a turn boundary, verify before reporting, and when blocked, solve it or ask, never drift sideways;
  • a senior-dev loop for backlogs: waves of work, one driver for a shared editor, and an assessment after each wave;
  • a use-case skill: use cases from the problem story, and a class model from the source, gated so that a name the code lacks fails.

The package ships the long-run habit and the lookup order as skills of their own (below). The senior-dev loop and the use-case skill are not in the package.

Keeping a long port going

A model in a session does not keep going on its own. In the owner's experience, a session stopped after an hour or two whatever the list still held: it wrote a summary at a natural pause and waited. A port's logic is days of work, so two things keep it running, and the default path uses both.

  • In a session: the long-run skill (u2ue/skill/u2ue-long-run/SKILL.md). The list lives on disk, each item with an observable, and the session re-reads it at the top of every item. A summary is the last thing in a run, never a habit at the end of a turn: before writing one, the session checks whether an item is still open and takes it instead. When it is blocked it solves the blocker or asks one question, and it never drifts to an easier task next door. Ask for it in plain words ("finish it all") or load it by name.
  • Across many agents: a workflow. A script, not the model, decides what runs next, so nothing stops at a turn boundary. The reference port's extraction ran that way: one agent per coupled file, four gates per file, in order. Its record shows 81 agents in one run of close to sixteen hours.

u2ue port hands the AI stage over with both in mind. Its stop names the u2ue-logic skill to run with u2ue-long-run, and u2ue logic says the step it resumes from, so a new session picks up from the records instead of re-deriving the state.

The five skills the package ships

skill what it is for read it when
u2ue/skill/u2ue/SKILL.md the entry point: price the port (estimate), run every stage a verb can (port), and take each stop to the skill or the person it needs "port this game to Unreal", with the Unity project open - the default way in
u2ue/skill/u2ue-logic/SKILL.md port a game's C# into an engine-free model behind seams, slice by slice, each step with its command and its DONE WHEN the logic port (Chapter 5)
u2ue/skill/u2ue-port/SKILL.md port an effect gap by the route protocol: census, a switch that starts OFF, proof, trial, LOOK, flip with evidence an effect the converter refuses (Chapter 7, Chapter 11)
u2ue/skill/u2ue-lookup/SKILL.md answer code questions from the index and the class model, read the file last; choose the agent before starting one before reading any file to find something; before fanning out
u2ue/skill/u2ue-long-run/SKILL.md finish a long list: one list on disk, an observable per item, a re-check before any report "finish it all", and any time a session is about to report with items open

The skill gate (u2ue/survey/skill_gate.py, pillar 2 of the cycle) holds all five to the toolkit: a command a skill names must exist, and a step written as ### Step N. must carry at least one RUN: line and exactly one DONE WHEN: line. A skill that sends the model hunting for a command that is not there fails the cycle.

Directing the model at a game

A session opens on where the port stands, never on a re-derivation:

py -m u2ue --project <game> logic          each step of the logic skill, judged by its own DONE WHEN; the step to take next
py -m u2ue --project <game> info           every path the project names, opened

What makes a prompt work, as it was learned on the reference port:

  • Name the observable. "Port this slice" ends when the model thinks it looks done. "Port this slice so that py -m u2ue --project <game> parity exits 0 and the slice's diagram resolves" ends when it does.
  • Give it the diagram, not a description. The logic skill's step 2 draws the class model of one slice before anything moves (py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>). The target diagram is the prompt: the model is asked to make it true, and the gate checks every name in it against the code. A prompt that carries a diagram cannot drift into a design you never saw.
  • Quote the acceptance sentence (the game owner's own words for done) at the top of the list. Then every item answers one question: does this move that line? Progress is measured against those words, never against the model's own plan.
  • Forbid the plausible constant. A value that is not read is ABSENT, with the reason. The iron law is in the rules file because a model, when stuck, will otherwise supply a number that looks right.

Saving tokens: ask the index, read the file last

Anthropic's own guidance names the constraint: the context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills (Best practices for Claude Code, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices). Every file the model reads to answer a question is context it cannot use for the port. The toolkit holds three indexes that answer such questions instead:

  • The catalogue: py -m u2ue find <words> searches the concepts, verbs, adapters, tools, documents, measured Unity rules, converter stages and routes, and prints each hit as path:line. Its selftest (py -m u2ue find --selftest) checks every source it reads.
  • The game's class model: py -m u2ue --project <game> uml extract, then uml where | ask | callers | tests <Name>. It is built from the game's own code roots, and from its engine-free model once one is scaffolded. A project with no code roots is refused, never pointed at a guessed folder (py -m u2ue.verbs.uml --selftest).
  • The requirements model's triples: every use-case step in Chapter 17 is a set of subject-relation-object facts, each citing the page it was read from. The traceability in Appendix E is a walk over them.

The rule that matters most about any index was measured on the reference port, which also searched a compiler-grade index of the game's Unity assembly. A fresh rebuild, minutes old, held no rows at all for five symbols that had moved into the engine-free model, because it indexed one assembly and the port had moved code out of it on purpose. A miss is UNKNOWN, never ABSENT. Before you trust a miss, check what the index read and when.

The lookup skill (u2ue-lookup) is the order to ask in: the catalogue, then the class model, then a text search for an exact name, then the file - and only the lines named.

Several agents, or one: measured

A common belief: several agents work faster but spend more tokens. It was tested on this toolkit with an exact answer key (u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py). The task is to find where each named function or class is defined. Python's own parser builds the key, so an answer is right or wrong by construction. The same task ran in each condition below, and every run was judged.

The lookup task (seed 1017): 12 names, each to be found where it is defined, the answer key built by Python's own parser over the toolkit's code, every run judged against it by survey/agent_bench.py. One run per condition.

condition agents right tokens tokens a name wall-clock (slowest agent)
one agent, text search 1 12 of 12 90,998 7,583 16 s
one agent, the toolkit's index 1 12 of 12 92,099 7,674 67 s
three agents in parallel, text search 3 12 of 12 271,002 22,583 14 s
three agents in parallel, the index 3 12 of 12 272,270 22,689 37 s
one lean agent (no project rules file), text search 1 12 of 12 48,228 4,019 9 s

What the runs measured:

  • Every condition was right on every name (12 of 12 each): the task was easy for all of them.
  • Three agents cost 3.0 times the tokens of one (text search: 271,002 against 90,998), and the wall-clock moved from 16 s to 14 s.
  • Most of an agent's cost is its starting context: a lean agent that does not load the project's rules file did the same task for 48,228 tokens against 90,998 - 47 % less - before any work differs.
  • The index did not save tokens on exact names (92,099 against 90,998) and was slower (67 s against 16 s): a single text search per unique name is already cheap.

The manual's writers: six writer agents drafting the u2ue manual's new chapters in parallel (2026-10-17, launched 11:3x), each a general-purpose agent with the project's rules file loaded. Source: the agent platform's usage report for each agent (tokens, wall-clock), copied from each agent's completion notice.

writer tokens minutes words written
a1 Shuriken to Niagara 573,684 26 10,786
a2 the Unity tools 482,178 24 7,992
a3 the Unreal tools 477,652 26 6,971
a4 test-driven porting 433,857 24 7,000
a5 folding eight documents in 588,767 39 25,617
a6 prior art (Appendix D) 265,493 12 9,653
  • 2,821,631 tokens for 68,019 words (41 a word); the slowest writer took 39 minutes, the six together 2.5 agent-hours: in parallel the work finished 3.9 times sooner than the same six runs one after another.
  • Not measured: what one agent would have spent doing all six in turn. Its context would have grown with every chapter, so its tokens are not the sum above, and no record says which way that goes.

What this means for a port, read with the caution that each condition ran once:

  • Fan out for big work that splits cleanly, not for small work. The writers' work was large, and each writer owned its own files, so parallel agents bought real time. The lookup task was small, so three agents bought almost none and paid three starting contexts for it.
  • The rules file is a tax every agent pays. The lean agent's saving is the project rules file it did not load. Anthropic's guidance says the same from the other side: keep the rules file short, because a bloated one makes the model ignore the rules that matter. Move what is not needed every time into skills, which load on demand, and give lookups to a lean read-only agent.
  • For exact names, a text search is as good as an index. The index earns its place as a refuser of fabrications, not yet as a token saver: the class-model gate refuses a method name the code lacks (Chapter 14).
  • Not measured yet: questions a text search answers badly, such as who calls a function through an interface, which measured rule applies to an emitter, or which use-case step a verb proves. That is the next task family for the benchmark. Until it is run, the toolkit makes no token claim for the index on such questions.

To run the benchmark on your own machine and your own rules file:

py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py task --seed <S>
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py prompt --seed <S> --slice 1/1 --tools grep
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py add --seed <S> --condition one-grep --tokens <N> --ms <M> --answers <file>
py u2ue/survey/agent_bench.py report --seed <S>

Reviewing AI-written code

Anthropic publishes how it reviews work done by Claude (Best practices for Claude Code, the same page). In short:

  • Give the model a check it can run - a test suite, a build, a script that diffs against a fixture, a screenshot to compare. A model stops when the work looks done, and without a check, "looks done" is the only signal.
  • Have it show evidence rather than assert success: the command it ran, and what that command returned.
  • Explore, plan, then code.
  • Review in a fresh context. A reviewer in a separate subagent (an agent another agent starts, with a context of its own) sees only the diff and the criteria, not the reasoning that produced the change. One instance can write the tests and another the code.
  • Scope the reviewer. A reviewer asked to find gaps will report some. Tell it to flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements.
  • Mind the trust-then-verify gap: a plausible implementation that misses its edge cases. If it cannot be verified, do not ship it.

u2ue builds each of these in, and adds UML at both ends: to steer the work, and to review it.

  1. Checks it can run, everywhere. Every step of a skill written in steps has a RUN: and a DONE WHEN: (the skill gate). Every pillar of the product has recurring checks (py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle), and red stops the cycle.
  2. Checks that can fail. A judge with no plant proves nothing, so every judge has one (py -m u2ue --project <game> judge --prove), and a gate that is widened is re-proven against its plants (Chapter 14).
  3. Evidence, not claims. Every number names its record (u2ue metrics). A task line is ticked with its evidence, never with "done".
  4. Fresh-context reviewers. A reviewer gets the diff and the criteria, never the reasoning that produced the change. Measured while this manual was written: agents held to gates rather than their own word, reading the tools' code with fresh eyes, found defects in the tools themselves - a console check that can miss new errors, a recovery script that acts on every editor on the machine, a field gate blind to a module family. Each finding went onto the task list with its file, instead of being patched quietly.
  5. UML for the prompt. A slice's diagram is drawn before its code moves (the logic skill's step 2). The model is asked to make the diagram true, and the diagram is checked against the code. The toolkit itself was moved under its own concept model the same way (Chapter 22).
  6. UML for the review. A reviewer reads the slice's generated diagram before the diff line by line, and uml check --doc fails a name the diagram or the use cases use and the code lacks, so the model cannot be out of date with the code (Chapter 14). Between sessions, the class model's snapshot and diff (uml snapshot, uml diff) show what changed in structure. Chapter 22 shows the same review applied to the toolkit.
  7. Scoped review. The acceptance sentence sits at the top of the list, and reviews report gaps against it, not style.

A session, start to finish

  1. Find where the port stands. py -m u2ue --project <game> logic names the next step.
  2. Look things up before reading. py -m u2ue find <words>, then py -m u2ue --project <game> uml where <Name>; read only the lines named.
  3. Draw the slice. py -m u2ue --project <game> uml mermaid --focus <TypeA> <TypeB>, then the target diagram the slice must become.
  4. Move the slice and prove it. Move it, then run py -m u2ue --project <game> digest run --entry <Ns.Class.Method> --cases <Cases.cs> and py -m u2ue --project <game> parity until they exit 0.
  5. Check the toolkit and the project. py -m u2ue --project <game> check.
  6. Review in a fresh context. Give a separate agent the diff and the slice's diagram, and ask only for gaps against the acceptance sentence.
  7. Run the cycle before any report. py -m u2ue --project <game> cycle; red stops the session's report, not the session.
  8. Write the evidence onto the list, take the next item, and report only at the end of the run.

16. Troubleshooting

Who this is for: the porting developer whose port has stopped or looks wrong - each symptom, its cause and what to do, with where the full answer is.

Every entry was met on the reference port, so each is a trap your port can meet too. The symptom comes first, then the cause, then what to do. Each section names the procedure step it branches from, so you can return to where you were; an entry that branches from another step names its own.

Finding your problem

Start from what you see; each row names where its answer is.

what you see where the answer is
a command printed REFUSED: ... that verb's refusals, every message with its line, are in Chapter 19; the message names its cause, so fix the input it names and run it again
a command says the project is missing a path or a key py -m u2ue --project <game> info opens every path the project file names; Chapter 3, the project file
a headless Unreal hangs, its log grows without end, or a long build stops half way Unreal runs, below; Chapter 13, headless Unreal runs
Unreal plays sound through the speakers, or records silence Unreal runs, below; Chapter 13, audio
a Niagara system draws nothing in an editor script Unreal runs, below; Chapter 13, editor scripting limits
a managed C# editor wedges, or shows compile errors for code that builds Unreal runs, below; Chapter 13, managed C# in Unreal
the converter writes a value but the effect ignores it Chapter 11, the traps (Unreal's Python API: a failed write returns false)
an emitter is born late, counts differ, or a child never fires Chapter 11, the traps (events, sub-emitters and trails); Chapter 9 for the conformance diff
a texture, a blend or a material looks different though the file is the same Reading Unity files, below; Chapter 11, materials and textures
the YAML reader refuses a prefab or a scene Reading Unity files, below; Chapter 6, prefab YAML
Unity crashes or a probe never runs Measuring in Unity, below; Chapter 12, never disturb the owner
the Unity bridge stops answering, or an editor sits behind a modal dialog Chapter 12, recovery
two agents trample one editor Chapter 12, several agents at once
a float or a printed number differs between Unity and the port Comparing runtimes, below; Chapter 14, determinism across runtimes
a patch script left a file empty, or two patches fight Writing tools, below
a gate says something is ABSENT that you know exists, or a test is red in a file someone else just wrote Gates and reports, below; Chapter 14, rules that keep tests honest
a photo differs from Unity's but the numbers agree Gates and reports, below; Chapter 11, proof
u2ue metrics prints STALE or ABSENT Gates and reports, below; Chapter 10

Unreal runs

Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

A headless Unreal never finishes and its log grows to hundreds of megabytes. UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with the trailing backslash. Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without it, so UnrealSharp reports ".NET SDK can't be found" and, under -unattended, raises the dialog again forever (measured: a 634 MB log, nothing built). Run every Unreal verb from native PowerShell. The verbs refuse up front when they are launched from Git Bash.

A long build stops at exactly the shell tool's timeout, leaving the content half old and half new. Stopping a background task kills its children, including UnrealEditor-Cmd. Before a long launch, compare the tool's timeout with the script's own watchdog and give the tool the larger one.

Two Unreal runs at once. One headless Unreal at a time. Every verb that starts Unreal (build, read, photo, scene, host) asks the adapter's host_busy and refuses while an Unreal, or a build queue the game's adapter names, holds the host. --dry on build, read, photo or scene shows the host's state.

Niagara draws nothing in an editor script. -run=pythonscript asserts, and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. The editor world never ticks actors, so Niagara simulates only inside Simulate or Play-In-Editor unless something advances it. The read-back advances each system itself: NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary's immediate capture with bAdvanceSimulation (effects_tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py, which u2ue read runs).

A headless run plays sound through the user's speakers, or records silence. Pass -DeterministicAudio (the non-realtime renderer: nothing reaches a device, and each tick renders its own delta) and -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 (an unfocused application otherwise mixes at volume 0).

An UnrealSharp editor wedges while files are being generated. With automatic hot reload on, the editor recompiles a managed file the instant it is written, mid-write, fails, and can stop responding. Set AutomaticHotReloading=Off in the host's DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini, or keep the editor closed while a tool writes managed C#.

Reading Unity files

Branches from Chapter 4, step 5.

The reader refuses a scene with m_AddedGameObjects or m_AddedComponents. A prefab instance that adds an object or a component to its source prefab is not ported yet, and the nested-prefab expander refuses it by name. Removals are applied: m_RemovedComponents and m_RemovedGameObjects take the component, or the object with its child subtree, out of the instance. u2ue data --no-expand reads the scene's own components without expanding instances. Branches from Chapter 4, step 4.

A nested prefab's object cannot be found by its fileID. A nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's id, with the top bit cleared.

A material's values look like its shader's defaults. A material variant stores only what it overrides; the rest comes through m_Parent. Read the chain.

An effect's blend mode is wrong. The blend mode is a number in the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never the shader's name.

A texture looks different in Unreal although the file is the same. Unity samples its imported texture (mip chain, alpha fill, size caps), not the source file. The import is in Library/Artifacts and can be read offline (effects_tools/unity_tex_artifact.py); validate the match against the source, since the artifact index can point at a neighbouring asset. Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

Measuring in Unity

Branches from Chapter 8, step 7.

Unity crashes in native code during a probe. ParticleSystem.Particle.GetMeshIndex on a renderer that is not a Mesh renderer with meshes kills the editor; a managed try/catch does not see it. Check the renderer before any renderer-dependent query, and write the field ABSENT otherwise.

A probe's work never runs while the editor is in the background. EditorApplication.delayCall does not fire for an unfocused editor. Poll from EditorApplication.update.

The first case a probe renders is wrong, and only that one. The first render after a probe sets up its scene can come out incomplete (measured: without the scene's ambient, so an ON - OFF difference read the ambient as light). Throw one or two renders away before the first case, and have the judge compare every OFF render of a surface against the others, so an incomplete one is refused by name instead of read as data.

A measurement right after a recompile reproduces the old numbers. Entering Play while a compile is pending runs the old assembly. Wait until the editor assembly's timestamp is newer than the source and isCompiling reads false, then Play. Branches from Chapter 8, step 6.

Comparing runtimes

Branches from Chapter 5, step 7.

Text built from floats differs between Unity and .NET. Unity's Mono rounds float text to seven significant digits first, rounds halves away from zero, and prints a value that rounds to zero without a sign. Any number a player reads, or a stream compared against Unity, goes through one formatter that reproduces Mono's rules.

Float results differ by one ULP. Mono may keep a float expression at higher precision. u2ue parity names every such row; an allowance pins the exact row and bits, and the fix (explicit float locals) moves Unity's own value, so it is the owner's call. Chapter 14 has what the standards allow and the two differences that are not rounding.

System.Text.Json writes {} for a Unity data class. Unity's JsonUtility serializes public fields; System.Text.Json ignores fields unless IncludeFields = true.

Writing tools

Branches from Chapter 18, A converter route, step 2.

A patch that refused left the file it patches empty. A patch script changes a tool's source by finding an anchor (an exact piece of its text) and replacing it. open(path, "w").write(patch(text)) opens - and truncates - the file before patch runs, so when patch refuses (an anchor moved, already patched) the file is left at 0 bytes. Build the new text first, then open the file. Give the patch a plant too: pointed at a copy that already carries its mark, it must refuse and leave the copy byte-identical.

Two patches to one file, each proven on its own copy. That proves each, not both: an anchor the first one moves would make the second refuse at landing time (when it is applied to the live file). Apply them in landing order to one copy and compile it before either lands; when the order is not fixed, prove both orders.

Gates and reports

Branches from Chapter 4, step 6.

A gate reports a symbol ABSENT that you know exists. Check whether the port moved it (into the model, for example) before believing the gate. Widen the gate to follow the move, then re-run its plants.

The photo of an effect differs from Unity's in a way the data does not. A photo is one draw of a random process, and a frame can catch a capture artefact. u2ue metrics counts the flagged frames labelled RANDDRAW (one draw) or GRIDTICK apart, as the capture's difference, not the port's. Compare several frames and the read-back data before calling a route wrong. Branches from Chapter 4, step 7.

u2ue metrics prints STALE. An input is older than the newest build. Re-run the step that writes it (the read-back sweep, the photo pass); the number is never presented as current until then. ABSENT means the record a number needs is not on disk, and names it. Branches from Chapter 4, step 8.

Questions and answers

Who this is for: the porting developer - short answers to the questions asked before and during a port, and the reasons behind the toolkit's design, each with the chapter that has the detail.

The first two sections answer what a porter asks before and during a port. The rest give the reasons for the toolkit's design, most of them answers to "why didn't you just...".

Before you start

What do I need installed? Windows 11 with native PowerShell for the Unreal runs, Python 3.13 with PyYAML, the .NET SDK 8 or later, Unreal Engine 5.7, and the game's own Unity Editor for measurement windows and reference photos. The full table, with what needs each, is in Chapter 3.

Does my Unity project have to be set up in a particular way? One setting: asset serialization must be Force Text, so prefabs, scenes, materials and .meta files are YAML the toolkit can read. The toolkit reads the project and writes nothing into it. The one exception is a measurement window: it drops its probe files into the project for the run, removes them after, and never replaces a file (Chapter 8; "Measuring Unity", below).

Does the Unity Editor have to be open? No, for almost everything. Reading prefabs, scenes, materials and data, the inventory, the extraction, the Unreal build, parity and Unity's own Mono runtime all run with no editor. An editor is needed only to measure a behaviour (a window), to take Unity's reference photos, to export a scene and to capture a UI screen (Chapter 12).

Which Unity and Unreal versions does it work with? It was built on Unity 6000.3 with Unreal Engine 5.7, and exercised on a second game on Unity 2021.3. Every measured rule records the Unity version it was measured on. On any other version, u2ue check names the rule as UNVERIFIED: the build still uses it, but no report calls it measured. Re-measuring is the owner's decision; the probes and judges are the means (Chapter 8).

Do I need an AI model to use it? No. Every verb is a command a person can run. The package's skills are written so that an AI model can do the porter's work step by step and have each step checked (Chapter 5, Chapter 15).

What does it not port? Animation and physics are not covered (Chapter 6, Appendix B). On the effects side, VFX Graph assets and particle systems authored directly in scenes are not covered either, and the extraction lists them with their counts (Chapter 4, step 5).

Can I port only the effects? Yes. Part one of the tutorial (Chapter 4) takes a game's effects to a first report with no code port at all. The logic, the scenes and the UI are separate procedures you can run later, or never.

During a port

Where do the results go? Into the work folders your project file names (work.effects, work.records and the rest): the IR, the build records, the read-backs, the photos and the reports. Nothing is written into the Unity project (Chapter 3).

Can I run several things at once? Headless work, yes. Unreal, no: one headless Unreal at a time, and the verbs that need it refuse while it is busy (Chapter 13). A live Unity Editor has one driver at a time, and the other agents work headless or on a second editor instance (Chapter 12).

How do I know the port is right? Four numbers, never one combined figure: coverage (does it draw), measured (drawn by a measured rule), data (do its particles follow Unity's numbers) and image (do the frames agree, with capture artefacts labelled and counted apart). u2ue metrics prints each with its denominator (Chapter 10). u2ue conform holds every emitter to Unity's own particle state (Chapter 9), and u2ue parity holds the game's rules to every runtime by float bits (Chapter 14).

What happens when the toolkit cannot read or convert something? It says so. A value that cannot be read is ABSENT, with the reason. An effect the reader cannot follow is REFUSED by key. An emitter the converter cannot port carries its named gap on the acceptance page. Nothing is dropped silently, and nothing is replaced by a plausible default (Chapter 1, Chapter 7).

My game chooses its effects in code, not by placing prefabs. What then? Write an adapter. It answers the few questions that depend on a game, and the first of them is which effects the game fires (effect_keys()). Chapter 18 has the recipe.

A gate went red, but I know the code is right. First check whether the code moved. A gate that walks one folder reports a symbol it cannot see as absent. Widen the gate to follow the move, then prove that it can still fail (Chapter 14, Chapter 16). Never re-record a baseline to make a red gate green.

How long does a port take? Before you start, py -m u2ue estimate --unity <project> says what the port will cost in tokens, with no editor and no project file. It gives no time, because no time per line has been measured yet (What a port costs). During the port the toolkit measures time rather than estimating it: u2ue tempo times each converter route from its first code to its verified flip, read off git, and u2ue metrics reports the machine time of the builds (Chapter 10). For scale, measured on the reference port (2026-10-15): building 673 effect keys took 31.8 hours of headless machine time, summed over the keys, a median of 98 s a key (Appendix A).

After the port

The game keeps changing in Unity. How does the port keep up? It depends on what changed. The logic lives in one engine-free model that Unity and Unreal both run (Chapter 5), so a rule changes once, in the model, and u2ue parity proves the engines still agree bit for bit. Content authored in Unity is ported again by the verb for that part: u2ue scene for a level, checked against that scene's own baseline (Chapter 6); u2ue extract and u2ue build for effects (Chapter 7); u2ue ui convert for screens (Chapter 6). Running u2ue port again re-reads every stage from its records (Chapter 4). What is not built yet is a step that finds which assets changed since the last port: after a change, rerun the verb for that part yourself.

After the port, is Unity or Unreal the source? That is the owner's decision, and the toolkit does not make it. The verbs read the Unity project, so they serve a team that keeps authoring levels, effects and screens in Unity and ports them again. A team that moves its authoring into Unreal stops porting content; the shared model still keeps the rules in one place for both engines, for as long as both ship.

The approach

Why not just translate the MonoBehaviours into Actors? Because then nothing can be compared. Two engines running two hand-translated copies of the rules disagree in ways no one can locate: every difference is an argument. Moving the rules into one engine-free model, run by both engines, turns every difference into a row in a digest that u2ue parity compares bit for bit (Chapter 5). It is also less code: the hosts are thin, and the rules are written once.

Why doesn't a verb move the game's code for me? Because where the seams go is a design decision about your game, and a tool that guessed them would produce a model nobody chose. The logic skill has the porter, or an AI model, make that decision one slice at a time (Chapter 5), and the toolkit does everything around it: the inventory says what each type touches, the runtime library gives the moved code Unity's rules, the gates keep the model engine-free, parity proves the result.

Why is there no off-the-shelf Shuriken to Niagara converter in here? There is not one to use. Unreal ships a converter from Cascade, its own legacy particle system, to Niagara, and the toolkit uses its library (FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary) to write Niagara stacks, but what to write - Shuriken's semantics, module by module - is the toolkit's own work, measured against Unity where Unity does not document it (Chapter 11).

Why read Unity's YAML instead of exporting through the Unity editor? Reading text needs no editor, so it runs on any machine, in any order, as often as wanted, and leaves the game owner's editor alone. It is deterministic and diffable. The editor is used only for what cannot be read from files: measuring behaviour, and reference photos. The price is that the project must be serialized as text, and that every corner of the format must be handled - which is why an unhandled case is refused by name rather than half-read.

Why Python for the tools, and C# for the runtime? The converter has to run inside Unreal's editor, whose scripting language is Python, so the readers and the converter share one language and one set of tests. The runtime library is C# because it ships into the game, beside the game's own C#.

Measuring Unity

Why measure Unity at all? Read the documentation. The documentation does not say most of what a port must reproduce: the frame a sub-emitter's particle is born in, the order a mesh particle's rotation and a non-uniform scale apply in, how a TrailRenderer drops its points, what a Timeline does before a clip starts. Unity's native engine code is not public, so where the documentation is silent, the behaviour is measured.

Why write the judge before the measurement? A judge written after the data is fitted to the data and passes whatever Unity happened to do. Written first, with planted wrong answers it must refuse, it can be wrong in a way the measurement exposes - which is the point (Chapter 8 has a bake the judge refused, and what it taught).

Why run probes in the owner's own editor, and only after ten idle minutes? Because a second Unity editor on the same machine was measured to take the owner's machine away: it steals window focus on every assembly reload and saturates the processor for many minutes. A probe needs a real compile and sometimes Play mode, which interrupts whoever is working. So a window waits for ten minutes without a key or a mouse movement, stops at its next step when the owner returns, and never answers a modal dialog. A dedicated measurement machine is the better setup when there is one; the protocol is the same.

Why are the probes temporary files dropped into the project, not a permanent editor package? So the game's project carries nothing it did not ask for. The release is to ship them as the package's Editor assembly (Appendix B): the same code, installed once, by the project owner's decision.

Converting and building

Why is every new behaviour behind a switch that defaults to off? Because a converter change that is wrong silently changes hundreds of effects. Behind a switch, the change is proven to alter nothing while off (whole_trace replays the converter over every emitter), then to alter exactly the emitters it names while on, then trialled, read back, photographed and looked at - and only then flipped, with an evidence row. Every switch that reads ON in Chapter 21's table was flipped that way, and the table counts its evidence rows. The cost is the number of switches, which is why retiring the permanently-on ones is on the roadmap (Appendix B).

Why are changes written as patch scripts that land after the build? A full rebuild runs for many hours and loads the converter afresh for each chunk of effects. Editing the converter mid-build would make the build two builds, half old and half new, and its numbers would describe neither. So a change to the live tree is proven on a copy (--prove) and applied (--land) when the build ends; the landing step refuses when an anchor moved or the file already carries the patch. u2ue trial avoids the problem another way: it runs from a snapshot of the code, so an edit to the live converter cannot change a trial that is already running (Chapter 20).

Why only one Unreal process at a time? Two engines contend for memory, the derived-data cache and the project's packages, and an open editor locks packages another process needs to save. So a verb that needs Unreal refuses while another holds the host, naming what holds it, instead of racing it (Chapter 13).

Why headless Unreal, and not a running editor? A headless run is reproducible, unattended and owns nothing anyone else is using. The cost is that the editor world does not tick actors, so Niagara does not simulate by itself; the read-back advances each system explicitly (Chapter 13).

Why does the YAML reader refuse a scene that edits an object inside a model? A model (an FBX) is binary, so the scene's YAML holds only the edit, not the object it edits. Reading FBX in Python to rebuild that object's transform would re-derive what Unity has already resolved: the scene's glTF export walks Unity's live hierarchy and writes every node's own transform, model nodes included. So such a scene is refused by name on the YAML route, and u2ue shear --gltf and u2ue scene read the export instead.

Why one-ULP differences? Surely nobody can see them. Nobody can see them, but a turn-based game can feel them: a damage value one unit in the last place lower can leave a unit alive that should have died. The toolkit pins each such row to its exact bits and reports which runtime is the odd one out, and leaves the fix - which moves the shipped game's own numbers - to the owner (Chapter 14).

Rendering, lighting and UI

Why do lit effects compute Unity's lighting inside the Unreal material instead of using Unreal's lights? Because the goal is Unity's look, and URP and Unreal light a surface differently: a different BRDF, a different ambient (URP's spherical harmonics), a different reflection decode. Evaluating URP's own Lit, transcribed from its source, with the scene's measured sun, ambient and reflection cube, reproduces Unity's result. The trade-off is named: those materials follow the lighting that was measured, not lighting that changes at run time, and they draw no fog or shadows (Chapter 7).

Why is a Unity point light of intensity 1 an Unreal light of pi candelas? Read from both engines' source: URP's diffuse term has no 1 / pi and Unreal's Lambert does, and Unreal's candela unit is 1e4 internal units per candela at 100 cm per metre. pi x I candelas makes the two equal. The Unity side was measured on lit pixels to confirm the formula; the remaining 4 % (URP's diffuse carries a 0.96 that Unreal's does not) is measured and named, not hidden.

Why is the UI painted in one widget instead of built as UMG? Two measured reasons. uGUI's layout (anchors, layout groups, TextMeshPro's glyph placement) does not map onto UMG's, so a UMG rebuild lays out differently; a port of uGUI's own solver lays out as Unity does, and its tests hold it to Unity's captures. And from C#, UnrealSharp exposes a widget tree's root as read-only, so a UMG tree cannot be assembled from the game's code at all.

Why does Unity's reference photo of an effect have no lights? Most effects are unlit and additive: lights do not change them, and an empty scene makes the frame comparable. For lit materials the photo probe has a lit mode that opens the scene and copies its sun, because a lit material photographed in the dark compares nothing.

Why are the Unreal hosts C# and not Blueprints or C++? The game's code is C#. With UnrealSharp the moved model runs unchanged in Unreal, and the host is a thin C# layer. C++ is used only where the managed bindings do not reach (handing raw PCM to Unreal's mixer).

Numbers and reports

Why does every number come with a denominator and a date? Because a percentage without them cannot be checked or compared, and an old number quoted as current is how a project believes it is further along than it is. A coverage figure is quoted as N of the M emitters Unity draws, on <date>: the reader can then find the records it came from, and see when they are older than the newest build.

Why print STALE or ABSENT instead of the last known value? A last known value describes builds that no longer exist. Printing it would be a substitute, which is the one thing the toolkit does not do anywhere.

Why isn't an effect Unity does not draw counted as a gap? Because porting it would make Unreal draw something Unity does not. On the reference port, the first acceptance pages charged 348 such emitters as gaps; each is now classified by a rule (never fired, never started, draws nothing in Unity), and only what Unity draws and Unreal does not is a gap.

Why look at the pictures if the numbers pass? Numbers and pictures fail differently. One render where the whole scene went black scored better on a pixel metric, because dark geometry stopped hiding a bright backdrop. The data proves itself first; then the numbers and the pictures confirm it, and a picture counts only once someone has opened it (Chapter 9).

17. Use cases

Who this is for: the toolkit developer and the reviewer - every use case of u2ue, step by step, each step cited to the page it was read from and to the command that proves it. After it you can follow any step of a port back to its source and its check.

This chapter is the toolkit's requirements model: what each kind of user does with it, step by step. It is generated, not written. The requirements engine is a separate tool, not one of the toolkit's parts, that builds a chained use case model out of documents. It reads the toolkit's own documents (the procedures of this manual, the toolkit's skills, the stakeholder requirements in u2ue/USECASES.md, the verb registry, and the pillars in u2ue/pillars.py), chains each procedure into a use case, and cites every step to the page it was read from. When a page changes, the model changes with it, and a step with no source is printed as INFERRED, a requirement nobody wrote (Reading UML and use cases, "The chain").

How to read a use case

Reading UML and use cases explains the form and its fields; what follows is how this chapter applies it.

  • The level follows Cockburn: kite is a summary goal that spans many sittings (the epic), sea is one user goal achieved in one sitting (most cases), fish is a sub-function.
  • Fully dressed: each case states its primary actor, its trigger, its scope, the precondition that must hold before it starts, the minimal guarantee that holds even when it fails, and the success guarantee that holds when it succeeds.
  • The main success scenario is three to eleven steps. Each step's postcondition (what it leaves true) is the next step's precondition, so a step that needs what nothing before it guarantees shows a gap.
  • Extensions are where the chain breaks. Each is numbered by the step it branches from (3a branches from step 3; * from any step), and each one was read where its document says it starts. Chapter 16 is part of the model, not a page beside it.
  • Include and extend point opposite ways. An include runs from the base case to the case it includes (the epic includes the quick start). An extend runs from the extension to the base it extends.
  • Proven by names the command that checks a step. That command is the test, and it must fail on a planted defect before it is trusted (Chapter 14).

Regenerating the model

py u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py --check      # what the harvest would read, procedure by procedure
py u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py --write      # the harvest files the requirements engine reads
py u2ue/manual/build.py                    # this chapter, from the engine's model

Between the last two, the requirements engine is run over the harvest: its trace, its epic builder, and its checker, which refuses a case without a dressed field, a scenario outside three to eleven steps, or a citation that does not resolve.

21 use cases - one summary-level epic and 20 user-goal cases - with 135 steps and 41 extensions, every step read from the page named beside it. The requirements engine's checker verifies the citation of every numbered row: 174 (the 2 extension(s) that branch from any step carry no row number). The model holds 1752 facts of this domain.

Level kite (summary)
Primary actor porter - porting a game
Trigger a studio decides to move a Unity game to Unreal
Scope u2ue and the porter's two projects.
Precondition the Unity project is on disk serialized as text (YAML prefabs, .meta files); an Unreal project to build into.
Stakeholders the porter wants it to run and to look the same; the game owner wants every difference named and only their decisions asked; a reviewer wants the method to make sense (Q7).
Minimal guarantee everything not ported is NAMED with its reason - never dropped, never stood in for silently (Q11).
Success guarantee the game runs on Unreal from the same rules; the page says, per effect and per system, what draws as Unity draws it, and the numbers (identical, speed) come from records (Q4).
Read from u2ue/USECASES.md

Main success scenario (each step's postcondition is the next step's precondition):

  1. The porter finds what the toolkit holds for their question (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  2. The porter describes the project: Unity root and version, the Unreal project, the work folder, the adapter (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11, UC-17
  3. The tool inventories the game: every MonoBehaviour, the Unity APIs it calls, the scenes and prefabs, the effects (u2ue/USECASES.md)

    • carried by UC-11, UC-14, UC-15
  5. The porter implements the Unreal adapters for those seams: view, input, camera, effects player, platform services (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11, UC-14, UC-15, UC-16
  6. The tool converts the transform chain and the scenes: axes, units, rotation order, scale, hierarchy (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11, UC-14, UC-12
  7. The tool ports the effects (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11, UC-17, UC-13, UC-19
  8. The tool proves parity and reports it (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11, UC-17, UC-15, UC-07
  9. The game owner answers the decisions the page asks, and only theirs (u2ue/USECASES.md)
    • carried by UC-11

Extensions (where the chain breaks, numbered by the step they branch from):

  • 3a The game's effects are chosen by its code, not by its prefabs - the porter writes an adapter that overrides effect_keys() (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  • 4a A MonoBehaviour WAITS (coroutines, Invoke, yield) - the model never waits; the wait becomes a turn / tick step. Stated (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  • 6a A node has a non-uniform scale under a rotation - Unity draws a shear Unreal's transform cannot hold; it must be refused and (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  • 7a A rule the conversion needs is not measured - UC-8 extends here. (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  • 8a The project's Unity version differs from the one the rules were measured on - versions() names them unverified (HAVE). (u2ue/USECASES.md)
  • 8b A frame differs only because one engine drew one random sample - labelled, never counted (HAVE: the RANDDRAW census). (u2ue/USECASES.md)

Extensions (where the chain breaks, numbered by the step they branch from):

  • 2a A patch that refused left the file it patches empty - open(path, "w").write(patch(text)) opens - and truncates - the file before patch runs, so when patch refuses (an anchor moved, already patched) the file is left at 0 bytes. Build the new text first, then open the file. Give the patch a plant too: pointed at a copy that already carries its mark, it must refuse and leave the copy byte-identical. (Chapter 16)
  • 2b Two patches to one file, each proven on its own copy - That proves each, not both: an anchor the first one moves would make the second refuse at landing time (when it is applied to the live file). Apply them in landing order to one copy and compile it before either lands; when the order is not fixed, prove both orders. (Chapter 16)

  • 7a A headless Unreal never finishes and its log grows to hundreds of megabytes - UnrealSharp finds dotnet by the PATH entry Program Files\dotnet\ with the trailing backslash. Git Bash hands PowerShell a PATH without it, so UnrealSharp reports ".NET SDK can't be found" and, under -unattended, raises the dialog again forever (measured: a 634 MB log, nothing built). Run every Unreal verb from native PowerShell. The verbs refuse up front when they are launched from Git Bash. (Chapter 16)
  • 5a An effect's blend mode is wrong - The blend mode is a number in the material (_DstBlend == 1 is additive), never the shader's name. (Chapter 16)
  • 7b A texture looks different in Unreal although the file is the same - Unity samples its imported texture (mip chain, alpha fill, size caps), not the source file. The import is in Library/Artifacts and can be read offline (effects_tools/unity_tex_artifact.py); validate the match against the source, since the artifact index can point at a neighbouring asset. (Chapter 16)
  • 6a A gate reports a symbol ABSENT that you know exists - Check whether the port moved it (into the model, for example) before believing the gate. Widen the gate to follow the move, then re-run its plants. (Chapter 16)
  • 7c The photo of an effect differs from Unity's in a way the data does not - A photo is one draw of a random process, and a frame can catch a capture artefact. u2ue metrics counts the flagged frames labelled RANDDRAW (one draw) or GRIDTICK apart, as the capture's difference, not the port's. Compare several frames and the read-back data before calling a route wrong. (Chapter 16)
  • 8a u2ue metrics prints STALE - An input is older than the newest build. Re-run the step that writes it (the read-back sweep, the photo pass); the number is never presented as current until then. ABSENT means the record a number needs is not on disk, and names it. (Chapter 16)
  • 7d A long build stops at exactly the shell tool's timeout, leaving the content half old and half new - Stopping a background task kills its children, including UnrealEditor-Cmd. Before a long launch, compare the tool's timeout with the script's own watchdog and give the tool the larger one. (Chapter 16)
  • 7e Two Unreal runs at once - One headless Unreal at a time. Every verb that starts Unreal (build, read, photo, scene, host) asks the adapter's host_busy and refuses while an Unreal, or a build queue the game's adapter names, holds the host. --dry on build, read, photo or scene shows the host's state. (Chapter 16)
  • 7f Niagara draws nothing in an editor script - -run=pythonscript asserts, and -ExecutePythonScript quits before the tick loop runs. The editor world never ticks actors, so Niagara simulates only inside Simulate or Play-In-Editor unless something advances it. The read-back advances each system itself: NiagaraSimCacheFunctionLibrary's immediate capture with bAdvanceSimulation (effects_tools/u1e_color_size_readback.py, which u2ue read runs). (Chapter 16)
  • 7g A headless run plays sound through the user's speakers, or records silence - Pass -DeterministicAudio (the non-realtime renderer: nothing reaches a device, and each tick renders its own delta) and -ini:Engine:[Audio]:UnfocusedVolumeMultiplier=1.0 (an unfocused application otherwise mixes at volume 0). (Chapter 16)
  • 7h An UnrealSharp editor wedges while files are being generated - With automatic hot reload on, the editor recompiles a managed file the instant it is written, mid-write, fails, and can stop responding. Set AutomaticHotReloading=Off in the host's DefaultEditorPerProjectUserSettings.ini, or keep the editor closed while a tool writes managed C#. (Chapter 16)
  • 4a The reader refuses a scene with m_AddedGameObjects or m_AddedComponents - A prefab instance that adds an object or a component to its source prefab is not ported yet, and the nested-prefab expander refuses it by name. Removals are applied: m_RemovedComponents and m_RemovedGameObjects take the component, or the object with its child subtree, out of the instance. u2ue data --no-expand reads the scene's own components without expanding instances. (Chapter 16)
  • 5b A nested prefab's object cannot be found by its fileID - A nested object's id is the instance's id XOR the source object's id, with the top bit cleared. (Chapter 16)
  • 5c A material's values look like its shader's defaults - A material variant stores only what it overrides; the rest comes through m_Parent. Read the chain. (Chapter 16)

  2. Assemble it (Chapter 18)
    • proven by py -m u2ue release --to <DIR>
  3. Prove it is current (Chapter 18)
    • proven by py -m u2ue release --check --to <DIR>
  4. Prove it runs from a fresh clone (Chapter 18)
    • proven by dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests
    • proven by py -m u2ue.verbs.release --selftest
  5. Leave the history to the owner (Chapter 18)

Main success scenario (each step's postcondition is the next step's precondition):

    • proven by py -m u2ue --project <game> build --dry
  5. read: the built systems read back frame by frame -> the read-back checks, each with a plant (the u2ue-port skill)
