18. Extending the toolkit

Who this is for: the toolkit developer adding to u2ue, and the reviewer checking it - one recipe per kind of addition, and which tool does what. After it you can add any of them and name the check that proves it.

The toolkit grows in six ways: a game adapter, a verb, a converter route, a material family, a measured rule and a selftest. Two more sections move a concept into a class and an older tool onto the project file. Each recipe names one place to edit and one check that proves the addition works. A recipe with numbered steps opens with its dressed fields (scope, precondition, the two guarantees and the trigger, as Reading UML and use cases defines them), because Chapter 17 reads each such recipe as a use case. The second half of the chapter lists the tools a port runs, by work package (one group of tools per part of a port), for anyone changing or reviewing them.

A game adapter

Scope: one game-specific answer the default adapter gets wrong. Precondition: a project file that info opens. Minimal guarantee: a question the adapter does not override keeps Unity's own answer. Success guarantee: info names the adapter it loaded, and extract holds the key list to the adapter's spawn rules. Trigger: a default answer is wrong for the game.

Most games need none. The default adapter, unity_project, answers the three game-specific questions with Unity's own rules:

question the default answer
effect_keys(p, env, resolve) - which prefabs are the game's effects every prefab under effects.key_source.roots holding a ParticleSystem
spawn_rules - what starts when the game spawns an effect "unity": the systems marked Play On Awake (Unity starts them when the effect is spawned) and their sub-emitters
host_busy(p) - why the Unreal host is not free any Unreal editor process running (one headless Unreal at a time)

In each signature p is the loaded project; resolve is the file the key list is written to, which the IR reader then reads.

# u2ue/adapters/mygame.py - discovered by name; no edit to the core
from . import UnityProject

class MyGame(UnityProject):
    name = "mygame"
    def effect_keys(self, p, env, resolve):
        ...   # write {"keys": [...]} to `resolve`; return 0, or non-zero with the reason printed

ADAPTER = MyGame
  1. Find the question. Read the default answers above against the game; an adapter overrides only a question whose default answer is wrong for it.
  2. Write the adapter. u2ue/adapters/<game>.py: a subclass of UnityProject that overrides that question alone, and ADAPTER = <the class>. It is discovered by name; nothing in the core is edited.
  3. Name it. Set "adapter": "<game>" in the project file.
  4. See it load. py -m u2ue --project <name> info names the adapter it loaded.
  5. See it hold. py -m u2ue --project <name> extract refuses a key list that contradicts the adapter's spawn_rules (keys read with Unity's rule carry a unity. prefix).

The reference port's adapter overrides all three: its keys are the effects its battles actually fire, resolved the way the game's own code resolves them; its spawn rule is the game's own ("game"); and its host also reads busy while its own build queues run.

A verb

Scope: one command of the facade. Precondition: the work it runs exists as a module or a tool on disk. Minimal guarantee: a verb that wraps a tool which is not on disk stops, by name; it never skips. Success guarantee: the command line, find and Chapter 20 all show the verb, from its one registry row. Trigger: a step of a port has no command.

  1. Write the module. u2ue/verbs/<name>.py: a docstring, which becomes the verb's page in Chapter 20, and run(p, argv), where p is the project, or None for a verb that needs none.
  2. Register it. One row in VERBS in u2ue/verbs/__init__.py, in the order a port runs the verbs. The command line, the verb list, find and this manual all read that registry; a verb added anywhere else is invisible.
  3. Find it. py -m u2ue find <name> lists it under verb, with the file it lives in.
  4. Rebuild the manual. py u2ue/manual/build.py writes its page into Chapter 20; py u2ue/manual/build.py --check exits 1 until it has.

A verb that wraps a tool runs it as a subprocess through u2ue.tools, with the project's U2UE_* environment, below normal priority.

A converter route

Scope: one Unity behaviour the converter did not port before (Chapter 7). Precondition: the behaviour is measured or read. Minimal guarantee: until the route is flipped, it changes no call the converter makes. Success guarantee: the route is on by default, with its evidence in the flip table. Trigger: the acceptance page names a gap no route ports.

  1. Measure or read the behaviour (Chapter 8).
  2. Write the route behind VFXPORT_<NAME>, read default OFF.
  3. Prove it offline with whole_trace.py: off, identical calls everywhere; on, exactly the predicted emitters change.
  4. Trial it: build, read, judge, photograph and LOOK.
  5. Flip it: one row in vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py's table with its evidence. u2ue tempo and u2ue metrics read that table.

A material family

Scope: one Unity shader and every material that uses it. Precondition: the shader's .shadergraph can be read. Minimal guarantee: every surface the shader exposes is accounted for; none is dropped silently. Success guarantee: every material of the family is an instance of one authored parent, its values read from its .mat. Trigger: an effect material's shader has no Unreal parent.

Unity effect materials use custom shaders, so each distinct shader needs one Unreal parent material, authored once:

  1. Author the parent by a script, never by hand (the reference port's vm1_author.py, for its largest family, a vendor's uber shader graph: one Shader Graph whose many features are switched by its keywords and properties).
  2. Account for every surface. vm1_read_shadergraph.py reads every property, keyword and node the shader graph exposes off the .shadergraph file, never typed; vm1_account.py marks each APPLIED (the Unreal material carries it), INERT with the arithmetic that shows it changes nothing, or ABSENT with the reason. The count of unaccounted surfaces must be 0.
  3. Instance it. Every material of the family becomes an instance of the parent, with its values read from its .mat.

A measured rule

Scope: one rule the converter uses, measured in Unity. Precondition: the rule cannot be read from Unity's data or its source. Minimal guarantee: a bake the judge cannot read the rule from is refused, with its numbers. Success guarantee: the converter re-derives the rule from the fact file at every build. Trigger: the converter needs a rule Unity's files do not state.

  1. Write the judge first, with planted wrong answers it must refuse (Chapter 8).
  2. Write the probe: an Editor script that bakes the behaviour, placing a real prefab only through ProbeSpawn.
  3. Run it in a window: py -m u2ue --project <name> window run <spec.json> waits until the editor's owner is away (no cursor move and no key for 600 s).
  4. Keep the fact file the judge reads off the bake, with the Unity version it was measured on.
  5. Re-derive it at build time. The converter reads the rule from the fact file when it builds, so the build stops if the rule stops holding.

A selftest

Scope: one tool that can be wrong. Precondition: the tool runs offline, or the reason it cannot is measured. Minimal guarantee: a tool whose selftest cannot run offline is listed with that reason, never skipped silently. Success guarantee: u2ue check runs the selftest and Chapter 21 lists it. Trigger: a tool that can be wrong is written.

  1. Plant the defects. The tool carries --selftest with planted defects, and must refuse each one.
  2. Register it in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py (RUNS: the tool, its folder, its exact command). A tool whose selftest cannot run offline goes in NOT_RUN with the measured reason. A gate written against one game's own model, adapter or HUD goes in that game's project file instead, under selftests (runs and not_run), so the package never lists a tool it does not ship.
  3. Run it with the rest. py -m u2ue --project <name> check --only selftests runs it.
  4. See it listed. py u2ue/manual/build.py writes it into Chapter 21's selftest list.

A concept

A concept is a row of u2ue/CONCEPTS.md, drawn in Chapter 22's concept model. One that is only functions or data (PARTIAL) moves to a class (EXISTS) in four moves: its class is drawn in u2ue/CONCEPTS.md first, with the members it needs and the concepts it talks to; the class is written, and the existing functions move under it as methods, one at a time; each move is proven output-identical (the tool's own selftest, whole_trace.py for the converter, the records it writes); and only then its row says EXISTS with the class path. u2ue/survey/concepts_gate.py checks that row against the code, and the count it prints rises.

Every rule traced to its probe

A fact file records the format its probe writes, and the probe's source holds that literal. u2ue/survey/rule_probes.py reads both as text and attributes each fact file: ATTRIBUTED when exactly one writer holds its format (a Unity probe first, then the toolkit's own Python, then the scripts of the lane part), AMBIGUOUS when several do, ORPHAN when none does (its probe is gone), UNFORMATTED when the file names no format. A run over the toolkit's facts (2026-10-17):

py u2ue/survey/rule_probes.py
RULES ATTRIBUTED 189 of 220 (orphan 0, ambiguous 3, unformatted 28)

An orphan is a measured rule nobody can re-measure.

Where the toolkit's parts live

The facade is the u2ue/ package (Chapter 22 maps its modules). u2ue/tools.py names each part's folder once (PARTS). Setting U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT=<root> resolves every part to <root>/<part>, which is the layout of the release package. A tool never names another part's absolute path; it asks tools.part(name).

The first three of Chapter 1's five layers (the product), by module:

  • Unity readers, offline. u1e_ir and t1_guid_index (the YAML prefab reader: nested, variant and legacy prefabs, m_RemovedComponents); unity_tex_artifact (Unity's own imported textures off Library/Artifacts, every mip); u1e_builtin_names (the built-in resources in unity_builtin_extra); u1e_alpha and u1e_alphadilate (alpha derivations); u1e_psdtex (a PSD inside a PNG).
  • Shuriken to Niagara. build_niagara and shuriken_size; the flip table patch_flip_defaults.TABLE and the OFF list in flip_audit; the measured facts in shared/conformance/*.json.
  • The proof machinery. u1e_color_size_readback and its sweep checks, the judges and their plants, the photo pairs and sheets, the acceptance report, and u2ue metrics.

A tool that still names one game's folder instead of reading the facade's U2UE_* variables is converted by the recipe below, Converting a tool, and Appendix B tracks the ones left. u2ue check runs every tool's own selftest.

Where a tool finds the project

A tool reads the project only through u2ue/env.py. need("U2UE_<NAME>") returns the project's value, or REFUSES by name when it is not set: there is no default, because a default is some other game's folder. part(name) gives the toolkit's own folders. The facade exports the project's values to every tool it runs (Project.env(): the project's folders as U2UE_*, the toolkit's as U2UE_PART_*), and u2ue check hands them to every selftest. To run one tool by hand, run it through the facade:

py -m u2ue --project <name> tool <file> [its own options]

A tool kept in another tree finds the toolkit through U2UE_HOME, or refuses.

Converting a tool

Scope: one tool that still names a game's folders. Precondition: the tool has a selftest, or one is written first. Minimal guarantee: run without the facade, the converted tool refuses by name. Success guarantee: the tool reads the project only through u2ue/env.py, and does what it did before. Trigger: a tool names a game's folder.

Converting a tool is a patch, proven like a route:

  1. Replace each literal with need("U2UE_<NAME>") for a project folder and part(name) for a toolkit folder.
  2. Prove the values. Under the project the tool was written for, every literal it replaced resolves to the same value.
  3. Prove the refusal. The converted copy refuses, by name, when it runs without the facade.
  4. Prove the behaviour. Its selftest prints the same output before and after.
  5. Run it through the facade: py -m u2ue --project <name> tool <file>.

A release

Scope: the toolkit's own trees, assembled into one repository by the manifest in u2ue/release.py. Precondition: the target folder is empty, or a checkout an earlier release wrote. Minimal guarantee: a secret in a shipped file refuses the whole release, and every file left out is named with its reason. Success guarantee: the repository holds exactly what the manifest ships, and release --check says it is current. Trigger: the owner wants the toolkit's current state in its repository.

  1. See what would ship. py -m u2ue release --to <DIR> --dry prints what would be written and deleted, what is left out and why, and the public-readiness count (shipped files that still name a game, a person or a machine path). It writes nothing.
  2. Assemble it. py -m u2ue release --to <DIR> writes the repository. A secret refuses it (exit 2), and so does a folder that an earlier release did not write.
  3. Prove it is current. py -m u2ue release --check --to <DIR> exits 1 when the folder differs from what the manifest writes.
  4. Prove it runs from a fresh clone. Clone the repository, point U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT at the clone, and run dotnet test u2ue/runtime/U2ue.Runtime.Tests and py -m u2ue.verbs.release --selftest there.
  5. Leave the history to the owner. The verb commits and pushes nothing: the repository's history, its remote and whether it is public are the owner's decisions.

The work packages: every tool a port runs

Every tool a port runs belongs to one of fifteen work packages, by the part of the port it serves. The packages come from a survey of the tools on the reference port's disk (u2ue/README.md): each tool's entry point, its own selftest's result, and its bindings (the paths and names a second game would have to change). The facade WRAPS these tools and never rewrites them, so each still runs by hand. Each package's tools are listed in the chapter that uses them:

# package where they are described
1 the game model and its seams Chapter 5, "The model's tools"
2 Unity IR extraction (effects) Chapter 6, "The effect readers: the IR extraction tools"
3 the effect converter this chapter, "The converter's tools"
4 materials and shader parents this chapter, "Material parents: the tools"
5 meshes, textures and sprite art Chapter 6, "Meshes, textures and sprite art: the tools"
6 scenes and maps Chapter 6, "The scene tools"
7 UI and HUD Chapter 6, "The UI tools"
8 measurement: the Unity windows and the Niagara probes Chapter 8, "The measurement tools"
9 Unreal runs Chapter 3, "The Unreal-run tools"
10 queues and the pause protocol Chapter 3, "Unattended queues and the pause protocol"
11 read-back and checks Chapter 10, "Read-back and checks: the tools"
12 proofs and flips this chapter, "Proofs and flips: the tools"
13 photos and contact sheets Chapter 10, "Photos and contact sheets: the tools"
14 game integration: the effect ledger Chapter 5, "Game integration: the effect ledger"
15 the acceptance report Chapter 10, "The acceptance report: the tools"

How the survey was measured

Three tools in u2ue/survey/ make the survey. Re-run them when the tools change:

  • Inventory: pt1_inventory.py opens every tool file in the toolkit's tool folders and the model gates, and records each one's first docstring line, its usage lines and its bindings. A binding is found by one regular expression per kind over the file's source, so it counts the files that NAME a path or a name; it does not prove that every use is a dependency.
  • The core: pt1_callgraph.py follows what the drivers call (the queues, the trial chain, the Unity window and its launcher, the report builder), then what those call, until a pass names nothing new: the core chain a port runs. The packages are that core plus the model gates, the UI converter and the art steps, which the effect drivers do not call.
  • Selftests: pt1_selftests.py runs every core tool's OWN selftest (only the ones its file defines - none invented), offline, at below-normal priority. A selftest whose body writes was read first, and writes only to a temporary folder. It is also the registry u2ue check --only selftests runs (the selftest recipe above). The ones deliberately not run are listed below, each with its reason.

What the survey found

Measured on the reference port's tools (2026-10-13). Each finding is a trap any port's tooling can fall into:

  • A selftest no driver runs rots unseen. No driver ran any selftest, and three were broken: shuriken_size.py, v4_msg_gate.py (which reads the writes Unreal refused the converter, as saved inside each package; a bare --selftest compared a package with itself) and the port's adapter gate (below). u2ue check --only selftests runs them all, your project file's own included.
  • Orchestration kept in a temporary folder is one clean-up from gone. 123 of 143 driver-shaped files lived only in a session's temporary folder, with no copy in any repository. Keep every driver in a repository; the reference port keeps its drivers in the lane part.
  • A zero is believed only when the instrument finds the known positive. v4_msg_gate.py --dir read 0 refused converter writes over all 672 saved effect systems. The zero was trusted because the same reader parsed 1,992,662 exports there (none unreadable) and finds the 80 refusals of a package known to hold them.
  • A gate that cannot reach a verdict must say so. The adapter gate could not reach one for eleven days, and nothing said so. One leg held copies another change had removed, so it could only answer BLOCKED; another built a check project missing two references the real project had gained (210 false errors). Both were repaired with plants; the gate then ran, and was red on one real thing.
  • Tools spread over several repositories need one place that names them: u2ue/tools.py names each part's folder once (above, "Where the toolkit's parts live").

Which tool each verb runs

The facade runs each tool with the project's U2UE_* variables (project.py, tools.py), read from the project's JSON file in u2ue/projects/. The Unreal verbs share u2ue/verbs/_ue.py: host_busy, native_path_ok, run_ps (one effect-tools PowerShell script with the project's environment, below normal priority), build_record and built_systems (the record <records>/u1e-build-<tag>.json and its BUILT systems), and clean_env: the project's environment with every inherited U1E_* and VFXPORT_* variable removed and named, so a verb runs the project's defaults, never a switch left over in the shell. The effect verbs run these tools:

  • extract (verbs/extract.py): the guid index (t1_guid_index.py), then the keys - the reference port's own resolver (u1e_resolve.py), or the generic particle_prefabs source in keys.py (every prefab holding a ParticleSystem in its own file or through a nested instance or variant, each keyed unity.prefab.<guid>) - then u1e_ir.py. It strips any inherited U1E_* or VFXPORT_* switch first, and exits 1 unless every READ key came out as an IR file or a NAMED refusal, every IR parses, and every Assets/... path an IR names exists in THAT project's tree. A unity. key is read with Unity's own spawn rules (playOnAwake; a sub-emitter's parent) and no game timing - ABSENT, and named - and its scripts are listed as not read.
  • check (verbs/check.py): every tool's own selftest, the two field gates for the project (yaml_field_gate over its IR, ir_field_gate for the reader against the converter), the measured rules' Unity versions (facts) and the model's layer and host gates (model) - a gate nobody runs goes red unseen.
  • report (verbs/report.py): report_build.py over the project's records (U2UE_EFFECTS_DIR, U2UE_RECORDS_DIR). Proven on the reference port: the patched tools with no facade give the same page byte for byte (bar its generation time), and through the facade the same page plus its title.
  • build, read, photo (verbs/build.py, verbs/read.py, verbs/photo.py, sharing verbs/_ue.py): the asset-name table and fx17_build.ps1 (record <records>/u1e-build-<tag>.json); u1e_color_size_readback per frame (<records>/rb_<tag>_<N>.json); u1e_fx_photo then u1e_photo_sheet. Each refuses while the Unreal host is busy (the adapter's host_busy) and refuses a Git Bash launch (Chapter 13).

The effect tools read the project's paths through one patch, pt23_chain_patch.py in the lane part, proven like a route (the tool-conversion recipe above): every binding equals the old literal with no facade variables set and under the reference project, and a sample built through the facade equals its records.

What a second project found in the readers

Measured 2026-10-13 (u2ue/README.md). A second, unrelated game is the test that the readers are not tuned to one project:

  • The reference project through the facade is byte-identical: a 21-key sample covering every kind of prefab the reader handles gave 20 IR files equal to a direct run and to the live IR; the summary rows were equal, and the one refusal the same.
  • The second game (Unity 2021.3.21f1): 3,229 prefabs, 60 keys (52 hold a ParticleSystem, 8 only through nesting), 56 IR files with 189 emitters, 4 refused by name, 0 dropped, 0 foreign paths; 3 more prefabs UNKNOWN (they nest assets the project lacks). It found three reader gaps the reference port never exercised, and each was fixed with a selftest case and a mutant that must break it: the 2018.1-2018.2 legacy Prefab record (m_SourcePrefab {fileID: 0}, m_IsPrefabAsset), nested MODEL instances (an imported model file, such as an FBX, placed inside a prefab: left out and named, refused when a ParticleSystem depends on one) and m_RemovedComponents (applied). Of the 4 refused, 3 are modifications aimed at objects inside a model that was left out (Unity derives a model's object ids internally, which cannot be proven from the files) and 1 is a script field the source's data lacks.
  • Every shader a project's effects use is named. The guid index covers a project's PACKAGES too: after Assets, its embedded Packages/, then Library/PackageCache, pruning a folder starting . or ending ~ as Unity's importer does. So URP's particle and lit shaders resolve. Unity's BUILT-IN shaders (guid 0000000000000000f000000000000000, which are not files) are named off the project's own Editor's Resources/unity_builtin_extra by u1e_builtin_names.py, which walks that SerializedFile by its own type trees. A project opts in with unity.editor.
  • An older format meets no silent default. A census of every field emitter_ir looks for and does not find, over both projects, found two kinds of new miss: field renames, now read from the other name, and Unity 5-era documents whose newer fields reach the IR as None. Those are ABSENT, and the converter then has to name them.
  • yaml_field_gate runs on any project (U2UE_UNITY_ROOT, U2UE_IR_DIR). It found the second game's unread light-module fields. It also found the reference port's own whole-game corpus RED: three excuses written on a sample of 51 prefabs ("0 on every fired emitter") were false on 655 (ring buffers, unscaled time, renderer priority). The reader reads all of them now and the gate passes on both projects; what is left is held by ir_field_gate, which names the fields the converter must port or name. An excuse measured on a sample is a claim about the sample.

Not run, and why

  • plugin_sync_gate.py --selftest corrupts and restores the INSTALLED plugin DLL in the game's live Unity project, and a DLL change under an open editor is a domain reload nobody asked for. Run it by hand when that editor is closed.
  • A project's own not_run rows (the selftests block of its project file) each print their measured reason. A publish gate whose selftest launches Unreal belongs there, because one headless Unreal runs at a time.
  • Read-dependent plants (--plant* on the read-back checks) need a trial's own read pair. The trial chain runs each one in every trial, never against an older read (Chapter 10).

The tools no driver reaches

A tool outside the core chain stays where it is, because each finished step's tools are its evidence. Chapter 21's generated inventory counts every folder's tools, how many are in the core chain a port runs, and how many carry a selftest.

The converter's tools

In this chapter's tables, "check" says whether u2ue check --only selftests runs the tool's own selftest; "a plant per trial" means the trial's judges hold the tool's output and must refuse their plants.

tool part what it does check
build_niagara.py vfxport the converter: one IR emitter into Niagara stack writes, imported by u1e_build.py inside a headless Unreal run a plant per trial
shuriken_size.py vfxport the Shuriken to Niagara SIZE rule, with no engine in it yes
subframe_rule.py vfxport the frame a Birth or Death sub-emitter child emits its shape in, re-derived from its bake at build time (Chapter 8) yes
cube_remap.py vfxport Unity's cube faces onto the faces of an Unreal TextureCube that samples, along the converted direction, the texel Unity samples yes
u1e_slots.py effects_tools which material slots of an emitter Unity DRAWS, and which of them point at an asset the project lacks yes

Every value the converter cannot read is named SUBSTITUTED or ABSENT in the build record, never defaulted. A second game brings nothing project-specific to the rules themselves, only its content root and its IR folder.

Inside the converter

vfxport/build_niagara.py turns one IR emitter into Niagara stack writes through Unreal's FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary. build_emitter is the loop over the twenty stages (Chapter 7 lists them, in the order Unity's own modules run); each stage is a _stage_* function. The state one stage hands to a later one lives on ONE object, _EmitterBuild; everything else is a local of its stage. Each stage calls a family of helpers named for what they write (build_frame_shape, build_frame_mesh_renderer, write_collision, sub_emitter_plan, ...), and a rule measured in Unity is re-derived from its bake at build time by its judge (alignmesh_rule(), ringbuffer_check.rules()), so a rule that stops holding stops the build instead of drawing wrongly.

Prove any refactor of the converter with whole_trace.py. The stages were split out of one 1,430-line function with 221 locals by vfxport/split_build_emitter.py. It finds the locals a stage reads but an earlier stage set, and only those go on the state object. whole_trace.py proved the split: 0 calls differ, 0 exceptions. A new route lands in one stage, behind its switch, and its offline proof ("Proofs and flips", below) names exactly the emitters it touches.

Material parents: the tools

Each Unity material becomes an Unreal material instance over a HAND-PORTED parent, one parent per distinct Unity shader family. The blend is read as a NUMBER from the .mat, textures are imported with Unity's own alpha and settings, and anything built is reused only when nothing it was built from changed. The families below are vendor asset packs (the ones the reference port used), so their parents are reusable by any game that uses those packs.

The largest family, a vendor's uber shader graph, done in full (scene_tools):

tool what it does check
vm1_read_shadergraph.py reads the .shadergraph (one JSON record per object, no Unity) and emits its complete surface: every property a .mat overrides, every node type the parent must reproduce -
vm1_read_materials.py the REAL numbers off every .mat that uses the shader - the set the game fires, and the superset on disk, both reported, because the difference matters for an INERT claim yes
vm1_hlsl.py the graph's arithmetic as the HLSL of the parent's Custom node (an Unreal material node that runs shader code written by hand): every line names the ShaderGraph node it came from, and every formula is the one Unity's own node source generates -
vm1_hlsl2.py the same arithmetic split across three Custom nodes, so that no texture is sampled inside a Custom node -
vm1_tex3.py the eleventh null case on a texture-override blocker, and the first whose control could FAIL -
vm1_author.py builds the parent, and one material instance per Unity .mat with the numbers READ off it -
vm1_account.py every surface the graph exposes marked APPLIED, INERT with the arithmetic that makes it inert, or ABSENT with the reason; exits 1 unless the unaccounted count is 0 (the material-family recipe above) yes

A null result is evidence only when its control could have come out the other way: the ten null cases before vm1_tex3.py had ruled out a cause against a control that could not fail.

Proofs and flips: the tools

These are the tools behind the converter-route recipe above: the trace proof, the flip and the audit. u2ue/routes.py reads the flip table and flip_audit's list into Route objects: ON when EVERY file that reads the switch reads it default on, DELIBERATELY OFF when flip_audit names what it waits on, OFF otherwise. Pillar 3 fails a cycle in which the converter's line count went up (a trend check, Chapter 14), which is why a flip adds no line to it.

tool part what it does check
whole_trace.py vfxport the WHOLE engine-call trace of every active emitter of all IRs, one converter file against another (Chapter 9) yes
burst_trace.py vfxport the same trace for every emitter whose emission carries a burst, the committed converter against the working one yes
converter_trace_gate.py vfxport does the working converter still write EXACTLY what a committed one wrote, for every existing route yes
unreachable_gate.py vfxport refuses Python source with a statement that can never run (one after a return, raise, continue or break in the same block): deleting one if line once left a block silently dead yes
absentdraw_proof.py lane a route's offline proof written as a script: the reference converter at a commit, the working copy with the switch OFF and ON, and the changed emitters PREDICTED before the working copy runs -
patch_flip_defaults.py vfxport flips VERIFIED switches to default ON - each os.environ.get("NAME", "0") == "1" becomes os.environ.get("NAME", "1") != "0", so NAME=0 still switches it off - with the evidence held once, as a row of its TABLE -
flip_audit.py lane every switch a trial set by hand: flipped, or named DELIBERATE_OFF with its reason -
fx9_space_gate.py effects_tools a sub-emitter's space cases on a moved and turned component, each child taken on its first frame against its parent's world point - 
py -m u2ue --project <name> tool whole_trace.py REF.py WORK.py [--on VFXPORT_X --expect-only KEY:PSFILEID]   # the trace proof
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py --list      # the flip table
py vfxport/patch_flip_defaults.py <ROUTE>     # the flip, with its TABLE row

A second game supplies nothing here: the proofs are the converter's.

19. The facade: detailed requirements

Who this is for: the reviewer checking what a verb promises, and the toolkit developer changing one - every verb as a requirement, with the options it takes, the refusals it can give, its exit values and the checks that hold it. After it you can check a verb's behaviour against its code without reading the code first.

The facade is the toolkit's one entry point, py -m u2ue. Each verb it answers is one requirement on the toolkit. This chapter states each requirement and everything the code says about it, read from the verb's own source on every build, so the page and the code cannot drift apart.

How each requirement is read

  • Requirement: the verb's row in the registry (u2ue/verbs/__init__.py), the single list the command line, find, the verb list and this manual all read. A verb added anywhere else would be invisible, which is why there is only one list.
  • Implemented by: the verb's module and its public functions. Every verb module exposes run(p, argv), where p is the loaded project (or nothing, for a verb that needs none).
  • Inputs: every option the module's argument parser declares, with its help text, read from the code. A verb that reads its arguments by hand lists the options it compares.
  • Refuses: every refusal message the module can print or raise, with its line. A refusal is the toolkit's answer when an input is missing or wrong: it names the cause and stops, and never substitutes a default. A message that names a machine path or the reference game is shown with that part replaced by <path> or <game>. Those are hard-wired sites the core is shedding (pillar 7, Chapter 14).
  • Exits: the literal exit values in the module. Across the facade, 0 is success, and 2 is a refusal before any work starts (an unknown verb, a project that does not load, or a verb that needs a project run without one). Each verb's own meaning of 1 is in its usage text (Chapter 20).
  • Verified by: the verb's selftest in the selftest registry (u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.py), with the verdict of its last run. ABSENT means the registry runs no selftest for that verb. The gap is listed here instead of being hidden. Each run's date is in u2ue/survey/pt1_selftests.json. This page carries only the verdict, so a cycle that re-runs the selftests leaves it current, and a verdict that changes makes it stale.
  • Exercised by: the use-case steps (Chapter 17) whose proof command runs the verb. A verb that no step runs is still a requirement, just one the model does not exercise yet.

30 verbs, each read from its module's own source: 22 with a selftest in the registry, 30 run as the proof of a use-case step. A requirement is numbered FR-<verb>; its inputs, refusals and exits are the code's, line by line.
