The review, finding by finding

The class model was reviewed on 2026-10-15 against one question: is the way the toolkit ports logical, efficient and as simple as possible to grasp? Each finding names its module. A refactor counted as done only when the outputs it touched were proven unchanged (the full review, with each proof: u2ue/ARCHITECTURE.md, "The review"). A developer extending the toolkit keeps to what the DONE rows established: no verb imports a verb, no literal tool path in the facade, one registry, and a core that knows no game.

# where what was wrong what is better status, and the proof
1 adapters and the reference port's adapter a CYCLE: the ports imported one game's adapter adapters discovered by name (a module that declares ADAPTER); the core knows no game DONE: outputs byte-identical; the old queue guard, planted, fails the adapter's selftest
2 verbs.metrics -> verbs.check, verbs.tempo a verb imported verbs for shared logic that logic moved into facts and routes DONE: metrics, tempo, info and check --only facts byte-identical
3 verbs._ue the effect tools named by a literal path tools.part("effects_tools") DONE
4 cli an if/elif chain of verbs, with the usage text kept separately one registry that dispatch, the usage and find read DONE: every verb dispatches as before
5 build_niagara.build_emitter one 1,430-line function with 221 locals twenty stages in Unity's module order, the state handed on one object (_EmitterBuild) DONE: whole_trace.py shows 0 calls differ, 0 exceptions
6 uml.py, the reviewer's own instrument every package __init__ merged into one type; check blind to Python; nested functions drawn as members each fixed, each with a selftest case that fails on the old behaviour DONE
7 the flip switches the switches now permanently ON still carry OFF branches that are dead code retire them in one pass that whole_trace.py proves OPEN (Appendix B)
8 measuring a new rule elsewhere the reference port's editor is driven through its own bridge the probes as a package's Editor assembly, triggered by a file OPEN: it waits on the package's name and on installing the package into a project (Appendix B)
9 scope the toolkit ported effects; the rest of a game had a written route only a topic-by-topic route (BASICS.md, now Chapter 5) and tooling for the code inventory, the transforms and shear, and game-rule parity PARTLY DONE: u2ue inventory, u2ue shear with u2ue.transform, u2ue parity and the runtime library, each with plants; since then the host templates, u2ue host, u2ue scene, u2ue ui and the audio plugin. Animation and physics are not covered (Appendix B)
10 layer_gate.py, host_gate.py the two gates that keep a model engine-free ran on one game's tree (host_gate took no root) a root argument each, run by check DONE: --layer and --root --scan --hosting; the old defaults byte-identical; u2ue check --only model; two planted project files FAIL

What a senior will ask

Why convert through an IR instead of reading Unity and writing Unreal in one pass? The IR is the seam between the two engines. It is plain JSON, testable offline without either editor, diffable between runs, and the only thing a different Unity version changes is the reader. The converter never opens a Unity file.

Why Python inside Unreal and not C++? The stack-writing API (FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary) is exposed to Python, runs headless (UnrealEditor-Cmd) and needs no engine rebuild. whole_trace.py can replay the same Python against a recording stub outside Unreal, which is what makes every change provable in about 100 seconds. What runs in the game at run time (spawning the systems) is the game's own code, not the tool's.

Why so many switches? Each route shipped as a staged rollout: OFF until its trial held, then ON, with VFXPORT_<NAME>=0 still able to switch it off for an A/B against the old behaviour (Chapter 21 counts them, generated). The cost is the dead OFF branches of review finding 7, to be retired in one pass that whole_trace.py proves (the trace with the flipped set ON must not move).

Why does the lane hold so many queue scripts? They are the reference port's job history: each trial's exact orchestration, kept so any result can be re-run. They are not the tool. A new project runs a trial as data with u2ue trial (Chapter 3).

What is not general yet? Measuring a new rule in another studio's Unity editor (review finding 8, and I7 below). A measurement window drives the editor through a bridge that is the reference port's own; the plan is the probes as a package's Editor assembly, triggered by a file, so no recompile runs per measurement (Appendix B). Until then, a measurement in another project is a set of steps its owner runs (Chapter 8).

Reading order for a reviewer

When the diagrams have been followed and it is time to open the toolkit's own documents and code, in this order:

  • u2ue/GUIDE.md - the route for a second project's effects, its rules and its traps (Chapter 7).
  • u2ue/BASICS.md - the rest of the game, topic by topic (Chapter 5).
  • u2ue/USECASES.md - the use case model, its epic, and the requirements it inferred (below).
  • u2ue/adapters/__init__.py - the ports.
  • vfxport/build_niagara.py - build_emitter and its _stage_* functions (Chapter 18, "Inside the converter").
  • vfxport/whole_trace.py - how any converter change is proven (Chapter 9).
  • u2ue/README.md - every tool, by work package (Chapter 18).

The use case model in full

Chapter 17 is the use case model, generated by the requirements engine from the toolkit's own documents (the manual's procedures, the toolkit's skills, u2ue/USECASES.md, the verb registry and the pillars). u2ue/USECASES.md is the hand-written model: the problem story, the stakeholder requirements in the owner's words, the epic EPIC-1 ("port a Unity game to Unreal and show how identical it is"), and the requirements the chain inferred that nobody had written. uml.py check gates it: a class or method it names must exist in the code ("Verifying the model", below). This section keeps what the hand-written model adds to Chapter 17: how it was made, the code behind each epic step, four cases of its own (UC-1 finding, UC-6 the transform chain, UC-10 review, UC-11 speed), and the inferred requirements. The UC numbers here are the hand-written model's own; Chapter 17 numbers its generated cases separately (its UC-01 is a converter route).

How the model was made

The model's mode is clone-and-change: the reference product is one whole Unity game running on Unreal (its rules, scenes, UI and effects), and u2ue is the tool extracted from it for OTHER games. The model says what a porter must be able to do with the toolkit, and which of those steps the toolkit does today (HAVE, with the symbol) or nobody had built or specified (INFERRED). Its one rule of authority: the only authored requirements are the toolkit owner's own words, quoted with their dates in u2ue/USECASES.md. The toolkit's own documents were written by the agents doing the work, so they describe and do not require; nothing in the model cites one as a requirement.

EPIC-1 Port a Unity game to Unreal and show how identical it is

Chapter 17 draws the epic's flow and dresses it (scope, actors, trigger, guarantees), generated from u2ue/USECASES.md. This section adds what the generated page leaves out: the code each step runs today. The supporting actors are the owner's Unity editor, the Unreal host and the game owner.

The main success scenario (each step's result is the next step's precondition):

# step what it needs the code that does it
1 the porter finds what the toolkit holds for their question one entry point search() behind py -m u2ue find
2 the porter describes the project: the Unity root and version, the Unreal project, the work folder, the adapter a project file load() of Project, for_project()
3 the tool inventories the game: every MonoBehaviour, the Unity APIs it calls, the scenes and prefabs, the effects a reader of the game's C# and scenes inventory() behind py -m u2ue inventory (kinds, the Unity API by family including value types, pure rules, frame order); the effects through particle_prefabs()
4 the porter, or an agent through the logic skill, moves the rules out of the MonoBehaviours into an engine-free model, behind a platform seam and a view seam the lifecycle mapping, and a gate that the model knows no engine scaffold() (the Core, its tests, the model block), model() of check (the layer and host gates on any project), the runtime library (UnityFrame, Coroutines, PlaybackQueue); the skill (Chapter 5)
5 the porter implements the Unreal adapters for those seams: view, input, camera, effect player, platform services the seams' interfaces and a worked example the toolkit's templates (u2ue/templates/unreal/U2ue.Unreal); the reference port's own hosts are the worked example, found through find
6 the tool converts the transform chain and the scenes: axes, units, rotation order, scale, hierarchy one stated conversion, and a refusal where Unreal cannot hold Unity's matrix inside the effect converter (shape_rotation_writes(), motion_scale(), build_frame_mesh_renderer()); for scenes u2ue.transform, u2ue shear and u2ue scene (Chapter 6)
7 the tool ports the effects the IR, the converter, a build build_emitter() and its twenty stages; the verbs extract, check, build, read and photo
8 the tool proves parity and reports it records, a read of the result, photos; for game rules the same model run on every engine measure() (tempo), the metrics verb, the acceptance page; for game rules run_cases() of digest (CoreCLR and the Unity version's own Mono, no Editor) and the parity verb
9 the game owner answers the decisions the page asks, and only those the report's decision list the report's decisions

Which procedure carries each step is Chapter 17's use case diagram (each include is labelled with its steps); the procedures are read from the manual and the skills by u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py.

Extensions:

  • 3a. The game's effects are chosen by its code, not by its prefabs: the porter writes an adapter that overrides effect_keys() (HAVE: a game adapter is the worked example, Chapter 18).
  • 4a. A MonoBehaviour WAITS (a coroutine, Invoke, yield): the model never waits, and the wait becomes a step of a turn or a tick. HAVE: Coroutines and PlaybackQueue in the runtime library (Chapter 5).
  • 6a. A node has a non-uniform scale under a rotation: Unity draws a shear Unreal's transform cannot hold, and it must be refused and named, never averaged. HAVE for particles (the converter refuses it) and measured for scenes (u2ue shear; the owner decides).
  • 7a. A rule the conversion needs is not measured: UC-8, the hand-written model's "Measure a Unity behaviour", extends here.
  • 8a. The project's Unity version differs from the one the rules were measured on: versions() names them unverified (HAVE).
  • 8b. A frame differs only because one engine drew one random sample: labelled, never counted (HAVE: the random-draw census, u1e_randdraw_census, which names those keys from the IR alone; Chapter 11).

UC-1 Find what the toolkit holds

  • Primary actors: the porter, an AI agent, a reviewer. Trigger: a question ("how is a hemisphere ported?"). Precondition: none (no project is needed). Success guarantee: every hit says where it lives (file and line).
  • The actor runs py -m u2ue find <words>; everything() reads the sources from disk; search() ranks every entry holding all the words; the actor opens the place named.
  • Extension: a source reads nothing - the search stops, because a silent empty source would answer wrongly.

UC-6 Convert the transform chain and the scenes

  • Primary actor: the porter. Precondition: the inventory (UC-3, "Inventory the game"). Success guarantee: every node's world transform in Unreal equals Unity's, or the node is named with why it cannot.
  • The tool reads each node's local position, rotation and scale; composes the chain as Unity does; converts the axes, the units and the rotation (Unity's Euler order to a quaternion to Unreal's rotator); refuses a node whose chain carries a shear Unreal's transform cannot hold; and places the actor. In the effect converter for particles (shape_rotation_writes(), motion_scale()); for scenes, Chapter 6.

UC-10 Review how it is ported

  • Primary actor: a reviewer. Success guarantee: the reviewer can follow every step from a diagram to the code.
  • The reviewer reads this chapter (found by find), the class diagram drawn from the code, the use cases, and the review's findings and what was changed.

UC-11 Measure the porting speed

  • Primary actors: the game owner, an AI agent. measure() reads each route's first code and its flip off git; the metrics verb reads the build records' machine time; both print with their definitions (Chapter 10). HAVE.

The requirements the chain inferred

What the chain NEEDS that no authored requirement states. Each was checked by a case-insensitive search of the owner's quoted words for its key term, with every hit inspected (a hit inside another word is not a hit); py -X utf8 u2ue/survey/usecase_absence.py re-runs the search, and a term that starts to hit leaves this table.

id inferred requirement needed at today
I1 an inventory of a game's code: each class's Unity API calls by family, which are pure rules EPIC-1 step 3, UC-3 HAVE: inventory(), value types a family of their own
I2 the MonoBehaviour lifecycle mapped to Unreal (Awake, Start, Update, FixedUpdate, OnEnable, OnDestroy to constructor, BeginPlay, Tick, EndPlay) with a worked example step 4 HAVE: UnityFrame and the Unreal template AU2ueFrameActor; the logic skill's step 8
I3 ONE stated conversion of a transform: axes, units, rotation order, handedness step 6, UC-6 HAVE: u2ue.transform (Chapter 6)
I4 a non-uniform scale under a rotation refused and named for scenes, as the converter does for particles 6a particles: refused and named; scenes: measured by u2ue shear, the owner decides
I5 game-rule parity provable for another game (the same model on both engines, compared) step 8 HAVE: run_cases() of digest and the parity verb; proven on a second game's first slice (green, with 2 characterised 1-ULP rows)
I6 a waiting MonoBehaviour (coroutine, Invoke, yield) mapped to a step of a model that never waits 4a HAVE: Coroutines and PlaybackQueue (the model emits events; the host replays them)
I7 a Unity measurement in another studio's editor without the reference port's bridge UC-8 OPEN (review finding 8; Appendix B)
I8 prefab overrides, ScriptableObjects and inspector values carried as DATA, read not retyped step 4 HAVE: u2ue data (Chapter 5)
I9 the per-frame order (Unity's script execution order) kept on Unreal step 4 HAVE: inventory() reads each .cs.meta execution order; UnityFrame runs it
I10 time and randomness made deterministic for parity (float32 time sums, seeded randoms) step 8 HAVE: UnityClock, SeededRandom and Digest; the generic particle probe pins every seed

Verifying the model

py uml.py --lang py --root . check --doc u2ue/USECASES.md    # every backticked call the model names resolves in the toolkit's code
py -X utf8 u2ue/survey/usecase_absence.py                    # the inferred requirements' key terms, against the owner's words

The use-case model tests the documents

The toolkit's use-case model is read from its manuals, not written beside them, and measured against the code. Both tools are pillar 3 checks:

  • u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py builds the model from the manuals, skills, use cases, verb registry and pillars, each procedure parsed from its source (a skill's ### Step N. with DO, RUN and DONE WHEN; a chapter's numbered steps); a document it cannot read is refused, never guessed around. Its --selftest refuses a step with no DONE WHEN, an epic include that names no procedure, a procedure with no stated trigger, and a branch naming a step its procedure lacks - which is why this manual's procedures state their Trigger in the text.
  • u2ue/survey/usecase_gaps.py measures against two denominators. Against its own list a model always looks nearly complete. Against the source - every verb, project field, public runtime type, manual page, skill and pillar, READ from the code and files - it lists what no use case owns and prints USECASE COVERAGE n of m, which the cycle holds as a trend. Its --selftest plants a verb no step runs and a chapter never read; both must come back UNOWNED.

Appendix A. A worked example: the reference port

Who this is for: the evaluator - the reference port in numbers: what was ported and how each part was proven, what its effect numbers say, and what the port taught.

The toolkit was built while porting one game, the reference port. This appendix puts that port in one place. Every number is as measured on the date given. It is evidence for the method, not a target for your port.

The game. A turn-based tactics game on Unity 6000.3: painted card units on tiled battle maps, a uGUI battle HUD, and 674 particle effects. All but 7 of them come from three asset-store vendors' packs, which use their own custom shaders. Ported to Unreal Engine 5.7 with UnrealSharp C# hosts.

What was ported, and how

part how the proof
the game's rules moved out of MonoBehaviours into two engine-free assemblies: the rules, and the per-frame presentation layer_gate and host_gate PASS (u2ue check --only model)
the Unreal side thin UnrealSharp C# hosts over the same model three scripted battles on the first battle map - a win, a loss, and a win with a deployed roster - write battle event logs byte-identical to the headless run's (cmp exit 0 on every pair, 2026-09-30)
floats across runtimes the model's digests from Unity (Mono), the Unreal host (CoreCLR) and the headless tests u2ue parity: 383 rows agree, except 35 one-ULP rows in one function where Mono is the odd one out on every row, characterised
the HUD the uGUI canvas captured and laid out by a port of uGUI's solver, painted in one widget held to Unity's own pixels on every captured state (Chapter 6)
sound voice and gain chosen by the model; procedural clips played as PCM through a C++ bridge Chapter 6
levels glTFast export, Interchange import, a fidelity gate Chapter 6; the rope bridge's shear accepted with its number (63.46 / 55.89 cm)
effects the full pipeline of Chapter 7 below

The effects, in numbers

The current headline numbers are the measured tiles on Why u2ue, printed from their record on every build. What they are made of, as u2ue metrics recorded it on 2026-10-15 and u2ue tempo on 2026-10-14, read as a sample of what the two verbs say (Chapter 10 has the definitions):

  • 674 effect keys: 673 built, 1 refused by the IR reader with its reason. 197 of the built keys carry a named gap. Every key is accounted for: built, or refused with its reason.
  • 7,810 emitters drawn. 374 more are absent exactly as they are in Unity (267 Unity never fires; 72 the game does not start; 35 draw or emit nothing in Unity itself) - these are not gaps. 642 are gaps: Unity draws them and Unreal does not, each named and charged to its root.
  • Coverage 92.4 %: of the 8,452 emitters Unity draws, Unreal draws 7,810.
  • 85.6 % measured: 6,689 of the drawn emitters use only rules measured against Unity; 1,121 carry a named stand-in.
  • The read-back: 20,378 emitter-checks over 22 checks, 17 failures (99.92 % hold), printed STALE because the sweep was older than the newest build: a number that describes builds that are gone is never quoted as current.
  • 31.0 hours of headless build time over 673 keys, a median of 97 s a key.
  • 86 converter routes flipped from off to verified on, median 36.2 h from first code to flip; the 33 flipped alone or in a set of fewer than five took a median of 2.4 h.

Every measured Unity bake behind the converter's rules was taken on Unity 6000.3.16f1, so on any other Unity version u2ue check names those rules UNVERIFIED (S11 of the short version shows it on the second game).

The gaps are the work list. Each gap is charged to its root, so the roots sorted by count say which route brings back the most. On the acceptance page of 2026-10-17 the largest was an enabled shape under non-uniform scale (31 emitters over 20 keys), then the children of a few sub-emitter parents whose routes were not ported, then a vendor shader with no Unreal parent (17 emitters). The converter's side of that list is in Appendix B.

What it taught

  • Move the rules out first. Comparing two engines only became possible once both ran the same model. Before that, every difference was an argument; afterwards each one was a row in a digest.
  • Measure, don't recall. Most of the converter's hard cases (sub-emitter frames, ring buffers, sheared nodes, mesh alignment, trails) behaved differently from what the documentation and intuition said. Each became a probe, a judge and a bake.
  • Count what Unity does not draw. The first acceptance pages charged 348 emitters as gaps that Unity itself never draws.
  • A gate can lie by looking at nothing. Several of the toolkit's own instruments passed while reading an empty set or the wrong folder. Every gate now carries plants, and a check that looked at nothing fails.
  • The look is checked by eye. A metric once improved while the whole scene went black.

Release

The package plan is u2ue/PACKAGE.md: a Unity package installed in the source project, with the parts Unity must not import in folders ending ~ (Tools~/u2ue the facade and tools, Data~/conformance the measured rules, Unreal~/U2UE the Unreal-side builders, Skills~ the agent playbook, Documentation~ the documentation), and the measurement probes as its Editor assembly.

Whose call each item is: the toolkit's, or its owner's (the person who ships u2ue, not the owner of a game being ported).

item plan whose call
No absolute paths the facade and the toolkit's own parts resolve through u2ue/tools.py (U2UE_TOOLKIT_ROOT); many effect, scene and lane tools still hard-wire the reference port's folders as their defaults (PACKAGE.md counts them). Each moves onto the project file's U2UE_* variables, proven by its selftest and an unchanged output the toolkit
The other documents this manual names no game (its build refuses a page that does); the documents it points to - BASICS.md, GUIDE.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, USECASES.md, PACKAGE.md - still use the reference port's names and paths as their examples. Each goes through the same naming gate when it is packaged the toolkit
Probes as an Editor assembly the probes and the window driver ship in the package's Editor/ folder, triggered by a file, with no dependency on the reference port's editor bridge the toolkit's owner: it means installing the package into a project
A second game end to end a second, unrelated game through the whole toolkit: its effects' build, read-back, photos and report, timed from extract onward, are the speed benchmark the toolkit
Packaging package.json, the ~ folders, an install script for the Unreal plugin, a versioned release the toolkit
A player-compile check the headless typecheck never compiles a player, so runtime code calling a member inside #if UNITY_EDITOR passes it and fails in a player build; compile the development player's Assembly-CSharp.rsp the way the typecheck compiles the editor's, its output redirected to a work folder (Chapter 12) the toolkit
The bridge in the package split the reference port's editor bridge into a generic server, the generic routes (Chapter 12's table) and a registration table where a game adds its own routes, which /capabilities lists, so the advert cannot drift from the dispatch. Until then a window and the console gate need a bridge in your project (Chapter 12) the toolkit
Name and licence the package's name, vendor and licence the toolkit's owner
Python or .NET Python stays a dependency of the readers and the facade, or they move to .NET beside the runtime library (the converter runs in Unreal's own Python either way) the toolkit's owner
One package or two whether the game-code part (the runtime library and the method of Chapter 5) ships in the same package as the effects toolkit the toolkit's owner

Two choices are settled, and a port meets both: each game gets its OWN new .uproject, made by u2ue host the way a customer would make one (Chapter 3) - which tests project creation, the plugin install and the host template - and lit effect materials transcribe URP's Lit model rather than being named and left (Chapter 7, "Lit materials").

Appendix C. Glossary

Who this is for: every reader - each term the manual uses, defined in a sentence or two, with the chapter that explains it where one does.

ABSENT - a value the toolkit proved does not exist in the source, or could not read, named with the reason. Never replaced by a default.

acceptance page - the page u2ue report builds from a project's records: every effect key, every gap and every decision the game owner owes; a key never built reads "never built" (Chapter 10).

actor - a role that wants something from the system: a person, the AI model, or the toolkit's own runners (the scripts that, for example, measure Unity in an idle editor: Chapter 17, UC-10); one person can play several roles (Reading UML and use cases).

adapter - the object that answers the three game-specific questions (which prefabs are effects, what starts on spawn, when the host is busy). unity_project is the default (Chapter 18).

aggregate - the one engine-free class that holds an entity's state and rules; the engine's object holds one and forwards to it, so state has one home (Chapter 5).

anchor - the exact text a patch script, or a mutation row, looks for before it replaces it; the patch refuses when an anchor moved or the file already carries the patch (Chapter 14, Chapter 16).

asset family - one kind of asset that ports itself through the same five steps: extract, build, read, judge, photo (Chapter 2).

bake - one run of a probe in Unity, saved as a fact file.

billboard - a particle drawn as a flat quad that faces the camera; Unity drops the camera's roll, Niagara's facing modes keep it (Chapter 11).

bridge - the HTTP server inside the Unity editor that agents and the toolkit's tools call; the reference port's does not ship yet, so a project needs its own (Chapter 12).

capability seam - the optional interfaces an engine implements when it draws more of the game than the base view calls say; a view without one gets the base call instead (Chapter 5).

capture artefact - a photo frame whose difference comes from the capture, not the port (a black frame, a missing texture stream, one random draw); labelled, and never counted for or against the port (Chapter 9).

Cascade - Unreal's older particle system. Epic's CascadeToNiagaraConverter plugin converts it to Niagara; the toolkit uses only that plugin's Python library, FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary (Chapter 3, Appendix D).

census - an offline count over the whole IR, run with today's converter, of the emitters a new route would gain and of what refuses them next (Chapter 11).

class model - which classes a body of code holds and how they use one another, read from the code itself: the game's (u2ue uml, Chapter 5) or the toolkit's (Chapter 22; how to read one: Reading UML and use cases).

Claude Code - the Anthropic tool the AI model works in during a port; it serves most of a session's tokens from the prompt cache (the cost page, Chapter 15).

concept model - the toolkit's main ideas, each held by one named class, drawn in u2ue/CONCEPTS.md before the code; every cycle, concepts_gate.py checks that each class it names exists (Chapter 22).

conformance - the effects held to Unity on numbers: Unity's own particle state, read by one generic probe, against Niagara's read-back, emitter by emitter (u2ue conform, Chapter 9).

Core - <Model>.Core, the engine-free model's C# project, made by u2ue scaffold, whose only reference is U2ue.Runtime (Chapter 5).

CoreCLR - the runtime of modern .NET: the Unreal hosts and the headless runs execute the model on it, and it can round a float expression differently from Mono (Chapter 5).

coupled and pure lines - the two kinds of C# line u2ue estimate counts: coupled code uses a Unity API, a lifecycle method or a Unity base class; pure code is plain C# (the cost page).

coverage - of the emitters Unity draws, the share Unreal draws: drawn / (drawn + gap).

cycle - u2ue cycle, the toolkit's recurring self-check: every pillar's checks run, each read as PASS, FAIL, HELD or ABSENT, and a FAIL stops the cycle (Chapter 14).

digest - a runtime's per-case output of the game's model, floats as bit patterns, compared by u2ue parity.

domain host - a host interface (I*Host) through which the model asks a question only the game can answer, or makes an announcement only the game can render; it declares domain callbacks only (Chapter 5).

domain reload - Unity reloading the scripts' assemblies after a compile; Unity defers it while in Play (Chapter 12).

DONE WHEN - the observable that ends one step of the logic skill; u2ue logic judges each step by its own (Chapter 5, Chapter 15).

effect key - one effect the game can spawn, usually one prefab; the unit the IR, the build and the report count in.

emitter - one Unity ParticleSystem, and the Niagara emitter built from it.

engine adapter - one engine's implementation of the model's seams: the entity view, camera director, effect player and input source, and the six platform services. Not the project's adapter (Chapter 5).

engine-free model - the game's rules as plain C# that references no engine, run by both engines' hosts.

epic - the summary-level use case that strings the others together; EPIC-1 is the whole port, and each of its steps names the cases that carry it (Chapter 17).

event stream - the ordered, append-only list of events the model writes as it resolves an action; an engine draws only what it says, so everything a player must see is said once (Chapter 5).

evidence row - a switch's row in the flip table: the trial, the Unity measurement and the check that held; a switch is flipped on only with one (Chapter 21).

facade - py -m u2ue, the single entry point; every verb is one row of its registry.

fact file - a probe's output in shared/conformance, with the Unity version that produced it.

file id - the number after & on an object's header line in a Unity YAML file, by which other objects reference it; the IR and every later record pair an emitter by its ParticleSystem's file id (Chapter 11).

flip - turning a converter switch's default from OFF to ON, with an evidence row naming the trial.

gap - an emitter Unity draws and Unreal does not, named with the converter's reason.

gap root - the emitter a gap is charged to: an absent parent's children count against the ancestor that is absent for its own reason, so a root's count is what porting it brings back.

gate - a check that refuses a result breaking one rule (a field gate, the model gates, a scene's fidelity gate) and carries plants it must refuse (Chapter 9).

HAVE / NOT YET - whether the toolkit provides something today; NOT YET is followed by the plan that delivers it (About this manual, Appendix B).

headless - run with no window open and no one needed to answer it, so nothing takes the screen's focus; for Unreal, UnrealEditor-Cmd with -unattended, launched only through ue_headless.ps1 (Chapter 13).

HELD - a cycle verdict: the check fails only in the way a recorded open decision says it must; failing any other way is FAIL (Chapter 14).

host - the engine-side code that runs the model in one engine: Unity's MonoBehaviours, or UnrealSharp actors. Not the Unreal host (below).

hosting folder - model.hosting, the one folder of the model where platform services may be declared (<Model>.Core/Hosting as scaffold writes it); host_gate.py refuses them anywhere else (Chapter 5).

include and extend - the two ways one use case uses another: an include always runs as part of its base (the arrow runs from the base to it); an extend runs only when a condition at one step holds (the arrow runs from the extension to the base) (Reading UML and use cases).

IR - the engine-neutral intermediate representation of an effect: one JSON file per key, read from Unity's YAML.

iron law - u2ue's one principle: propose from a fixed space, verify by execution, report a measured confidence, refuse rather than invent (Why u2ue). Written as working rules for a session: no guessing, no fallbacks, no toys, verify with both the data and the picture (Chapter 15).

judge - a script that holds a record (a fact file, a read-back, a capture) to a rule and refuses it when the rule does not hold. It carries planted defects it must refuse, and is written before the data it judges (Chapter 8, Chapter 14).

land - apply a change already proven on copies (--prove) to the live file (--land); the landing refuses a moved anchor, a file already patched, or a running queue (FAQ).

LOOKED - a picture actually opened and examined by a person or agent. A file that was written has not been looked at.

MEASURED - a value or rule taken from Unity itself by a probe, with the run that measured it.

min-max value - a Shuriken field held in one of four modes (a constant, a curve, a random value between two constants, or one between two curves); the IR keeps it as an object whose readAs says how it was read (Chapter 11, Chapter 21).

miss - in conformance, an emitter judged LATE or EARLY (first drawn on a different frame from Unity's) or COUNT (its live particle count more than max(1, 5 %) from Unity's at a probe time) (u2ue conform, Chapter 9).

Mono - the runtime Unity's editor runs C# on; u2ue digest runs the game's rule cases on the project's Unity version's own Mono, with no editor (Chapter 5).

mutation run - the code under test changed on purpose, one change at a time, to see whether any test notices; the package ships no harness yet (Chapter 14).

MVID - the module version id in a .NET assembly's metadata; the publish proof compares the loaded model's with the one the source just built, to know which build an engine ran (Chapter 5).

owner - the game owner: the person a port is for, who works in the Unity editor a window measures in and answers the report's decisions; a tool that needs that editor waits until the owner is away (Chapter 8, Chapter 12). Not the toolkit's owner, the person who ships u2ue (Appendix B).

pair sheet - one contact sheet per effect, Unity's frames above Unreal's at the same sample times, LOOKED at before a route is called done (Chapter 9, Chapter 10).

parity - the same rule cases answered on every runtime and compared float bit by float bit; a difference is red unless that exact row is characterised, pinned to its bits and to one ULP (u2ue parity, Chapter 5).

pillar - one promise of the product, checked every cycle by u2ue cycle (Chapter 14).

plant - a deliberate defect a selftest feeds a gate or tool; the tool must refuse it.

platform seam - the six services every engine provides and the model never calls directly: the log, text assets, a key-value store, a file store, a JSON codec and a random source (U2ue.Runtime.Platform).

PlaybackQueue - the host's replay of the event stream: one event per frame, only while the views are idle; input waits until it is caught up (Chapter 5).

probe - an Editor C# script that sets up a case in Unity, steps it and writes a fact file.

processed and new tokens - the two token counts u2ue estimate prints: processed is every token a call reads or writes, cache reads included; new is the uncached input, the cache writes and the output (the cost page).

project file - the one JSON file per game, u2ue/projects/<game>.json, naming its Unity tree, its Unreal host and where the work goes; no field is defaulted, so a missing one is an error (Chapter 21).

prompt cache - what serves the part of a model call the model has read before; on Opus 5.5 a cache read costs a twentieth of an uncached input token, so most processed tokens cost little (the cost page).

READ - a value taken from a file, with where it came from.

read-back - the built Niagara systems simulated headless in Unreal, their particles recorded per 1/60 s frame.

requirements engine - the separate tool, not one of the toolkit's parts, that builds Chapter 17's chained use case model from the toolkit's own documents, which u2ue/survey/req_harvest.py turns into its input (Chapter 17).

requirements model - the toolkit's use cases and requirements held as subject-relation-object facts, each citing the page it was read from; Chapter 17, Chapter 19's "Exercised by" lines and Appendix E are generated from it.

resolve - the list of effect keys an adapter writes (work.resolve), which the IR reader reads; extract refuses one whose keys disagree with the adapter's spawn rule (Chapter 18).

route - the converter's handling of one Unity behaviour, behind its own switch.

seam - an interface the model calls instead of an engine API; each host implements it.

selftest - a tool's own check of itself, with plants, run by u2ue check --only selftests.

shear - the skew a rotated child gets under a non-uniformly scaled parent in Unity. Unreal's transform cannot represent it.

shim - a library that declares Unity's value types in namespace UnityEngine, so Unity-shaped code compiles without Unity; not the architecture to build a model on (Chapter 5).

Shuriken and Niagara - Unity's built-in particle system, and Unreal's; the converter turns the first into the second.

sim cache - a recording of a Niagara system's particle attributes, which u2ue read captures frame by frame (Chapter 13).

skill - a packaged procedure an AI model loads when its task matches it; the package ships five under u2ue/skill/, and each ### Step N. carries at least one RUN line and exactly one DONE WHEN (Chapter 15).

slice - one feature's rules, moved into the model at a time, smallest first, and proven by parity before the next is taken (Chapter 5).

STALE - printed beside a number whose input is older than the newest build: it describes builds that are gone and is never quoted as current (Chapter 10).

stand-in - a value or asset the converter used in place of the real one, marked SUBSTITUTED and never counted as measured.

sub-emitter - a child particle system its parent's particles start (at their birth or death, for example); in Niagara the child is an event-spawned emitter (Chapter 11).

sweep - the read-back sweep: every read-back check run over every built system's read, with emitters checked and failures summed per check (Chapter 10).

switch - an environment variable (VFXPORT_<NAME>, U1E_<NAME>) that turns one route on or off.

trend - a pillar check that reads a number and the direction it must not move in; a cycle where it moves the wrong way against the last cycle's value fails, and the first cycle sets the baseline (Chapter 14).

trial - a route tried on real keys in its own content root before its switch flips: built, read back, judged and photographed, from a data file run by u2ue trial (Chapter 7, Chapter 11).

trigger - in a use case, what starts it (Reading UML and use cases); in a window, the file dropped into the Unity project to start a probe or an export, such as .RUN_SCENE_EXPORT, whose one line is the output folder (Chapter 8).

ULP - unit in the last place: the gap between two neighbouring floats. A one-ULP difference is the smallest a float can differ by.

UML - the Unified Modeling Language, a standard set of diagram kinds for software; this manual uses class, use case and flow diagrams (Reading UML and use cases).

UNKNOWN - an answer the toolkit could not reach either way: a lookup that found nothing, or a prefab that nests an asset the project lacks. Never read as ABSENT (Chapter 15).

Unreal host - the Unreal host project the verbs that run Unreal (build, read, photo, host) work in, and the one Unreal slot they share: one headless Unreal at a time, so they refuse while another runs (Chapter 3). u2ue host makes a game its own host project (Chapter 13). Not the same as a host, the code that runs the model.

UnrealSharp - the plugin that runs C# inside Unreal; the Unreal hosts run the model's C# through it (Chapter 3, Appendix D).

URP - Unity's Universal Render Pipeline; the lit-material route evaluates its Lit lighting inside the Unreal material (Chapter 7).

use case - one goal of one actor, told as three to eleven numbered steps that end with the goal reached, plus the ways it can go wrong (its extensions) (Reading UML and use cases).

verb - one command of the facade (extract, build, metrics, ...).

view seam - the interfaces through which the presentation asks an engine to draw; every method is a game verb, never an engine primitive (Chapter 5).

whole_trace - the offline proof of a route: the converter run against a recording stub at two versions, and every engine call compared.

window - a short, guarded session in the game owner's Unity editor, started only once the owner is idle, that runs its probes and removes them (Chapter 8).

work package - one group of the toolkit's tools that does one part of a port; Chapter 18 indexes the fifteen.

workflow - a script that runs many AI agents and decides what runs next, so nothing stops at a turn boundary (Chapter 15).

Appendix D. Prior art: other ways to port a Unity game

Who this is for: the evaluator comparing u2ue with the other ways to move a Unity game to Unreal - what each route moves and what it leaves to you, the risks of running C# inside Unreal, the strongest case against an engine-free core, and where u2ue sits.

It covers Epic's own guidance and tools, the community converter, the plugins that run C# inside Unreal, the engine-free cores that middleware and networking products ship, what studios have published about changing engine, and the strongest arguments against the approach u2ue takes. The last section says where u2ue sits among them.

How to read this appendix

The research behind it was read-only and ran in two passes: a search for effect converters on 2026-08-22 (its record is vfxport/README.md), and a wider pass on 2026-09-30, whose second half read the language standards and the .NET runtime's issues as raw text rather than through a summarising reader. Every claim below was read from the source it names, with its link, or is marked ABSENT with what was searched for.

  • Each finding carries a confidence and the reason for it (VERY HIGH, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, as the research labelled it), because one blog post and the same answer in three shipped systems are not the same evidence.
  • Products move. Star counts, open issues, supported platforms, versions and last-push dates are as measured on the date given. Any of them may have changed since; read the source again before relying on one.
  • Sources were read as data. Their wording is paraphrased here, with the link to the original.

The routes at a glance

route what it moves what it leaves to you read
Epic's migration guidance assets exported from Unity all code (rebuilt in C++ or Blueprints), Shader Graphs, Timeline and Cinemachine, particle systems 2026-08-22, 2026-09-30
ProjectExodus (community) assets all C# game logic, prefabs as Blueprints, custom shaders, particles 2026-08-22, 2026-09-30
Epic's CascadeToNiagaraConverter Unreal's own legacy Cascade effects everything that comes from Unity 2026-08-22
C# inside Unreal (UnrealSharp) lets moved C# run in Unreal the hosts; anything not exposed to reflection needs C++ 2026-09-30
an engine-free core with a layer per engine (the Spine and Quantum shape) the rules, written once every engine-side object, made again in each engine 2026-09-30
a separate process and a protocol (the chess-engine shape) the core, behind a process boundary the boundary becomes serialisation, and state ownership can split 2026-09-30
change engine and rewrite nothing automatically everything 2026-09-30
u2ue effects converted; scenes, UI and transforms by tools; the code by a method with a runtime, gates and an AI skill moving the code (you, or an AI model with the logic skill), writing the hosts, animation, physics this manual

The 2026-08-22 search covered Fab and the UE Marketplace, the Unity Asset Store, GitHub and Epic's documentation. It found no tool that converts Shuriken effects to Niagara, and named ProjectExodus as the only Unity-to-Unreal project converter. A product may have appeared since.

What Epic and the community converters move

Epic's migration guidance

Epic's page "Migrating assets from Unity to Unreal Engine", read on 2026-09-30, sets the baseline (link):

  • Unity C# scripts and Bolt visual-scripting files cannot be exported from Unity and imported; the functionality is built again in C++ or Blueprints.
  • A Shader Graph cannot be converted to a Material graph. The textures can be exported and the node network rebuilt in the Material Editor.
  • Camera animation and behaviour made with Timeline and Cinemachine cannot be exported; they are recreated with Sequencer.
  • Particle systems are recreated by hand (the 2026-08-22 search, vfxport/README.md).

Confidence VERY HIGH: first-party, read directly.

Read it two ways, because both are true. Epic's baseline assumes the code does not come across at all, and a route that moves the rules into plain C# and runs that C# inside Unreal beats it, and that is a real advantage. But it makes a community plugin the load-bearing beam of the code half of the port, and that plugin's limits are in "C# inside Unreal" below.

ProjectExodus

The leading community migration tool works on assets only and ignores all of the game's C#. It does not turn prefabs into Blueprints and does not support custom shaders (its README, read 2026-09-30, link). The 2026-08-22 search found that it targets Unity 2018.3 and UE 4.25 and does not convert particles. It agrees with Epic about where the work is.

Epic's Cascade converter

CascadeToNiagaraConverter is Epic's plugin for converting Unreal's own older Cascade particle systems to Niagara; it does not read Unity. Its library is still useful to a Unity port: FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary is a Python API that writes Niagara emitter stacks, and it exists only while the plugin is enabled in the project (vfxport/README.md). u2ue's converter writes through it (Chapter 7).

Why engine independence is not paranoia

EA acquired Criterion in October 2004 and later withdrew Criterion's RenderWare engine from the commercial market, stranding its licensees (link). An engine can be taken away. That is a named precedent for keeping a game's rules free of any one engine.

Keeping one game core under two engines

The shipped shape is almost never one core under two engines. It is one core, one engine and one headless server; and where a product really does span engines, it keeps a separate layer per engine, often over a separate core per language, not one binary.

One core, one engine, one headless server

Photon Quantum is the closest commercial product to the engine-free-core architecture. Its documentation credits the split between the simulation (Quantum) and the view (Unity) for the product's modularity. The simulation is a pure C# assembly with no Unity types, Unity is the view, and the same assembly runs on the server as a Quantum plugin. Its events even carry client and server keywords to scope which side raises them, which only exists because one build runs on both. Confidence HIGH: the vendor's current documentation for a product with paying customers, read directly (events, DSL, frames).

SharedMeta (CoreGameIO) does the same for another server stack: one C# game-logic assembly that runs on a server built with Microsoft Orleans and replays on a Unity or .NET client, with optimistic execution, rollback and desync detection; 25 stars, version 0.12.x (link). Confidence LOW as proof that anything works (a tiny project, no shipped title, its README read but not its code), MEDIUM as evidence that the same shape keeps being arrived at.

Middleware keeps two cores, not one binary

Spine (Esoteric Software) is animation middleware shipped in many games on both Unity and Unreal; open source, 5,305 stars on 2026-09-30. Its per-runtime READMEs on the 4.2 branch say:

  • spine-cpp loads and manipulates skeletal animation data in C++ and does no rendering: the engine-free core.
  • spine-ue is built on spine-cpp.
  • spine-unity is built on spine-csharp.

So the Unity path and the Unreal path share neither a binary nor a language. They are two hand-maintained implementations of one documented model, held together by a version rule the repository states: freeze the Spine editor version to the runtime source in use and update the two in lock step.

The presentation layers do not reach parity either. spine-unity claims every Spine feature; spine-ue lists what it lacks: multiply and screen blending, pre-multiplied alpha atlases and two-colour tinting.

Measured from the repository tree on the 4.2 branch, counting only .cs, .cpp, .h, .c and .hpp files and leaving out example, sample, test and demo paths:

part files bytes
spine-csharp (core) 48 599,469
spine-unity (engine layer) 132 1,527,046
spine-cpp (core) 160 1,131,900
spine-ue (engine layer) 39 180,585

On the Unity side the engine layer is about two and a half times the size of the engine-free core. Confidence HIGH: four READMEs read, sizes computed from the tree, not estimated (repository, spine-ue, spine-unity, spine-cpp).

What it means for a port: moving the core is the part the field agrees works. A presentation layer that lags on the second engine is the documented, normal outcome for a mature example of exactly this pattern, and its maintainers' answer was to write the gap down in the README rather than close it.

A separate process and a text protocol

Chess has run one simulation core behind many unrelated front ends since November 2000 through UCI (the Universal Chess Interface), which puts the GUI and the engine in separate processes talking over stdin and stdout (link).

The caveat cuts against a naive reading: under UCI the GUI keeps the board state and decides who wins, and the engine only picks moves. Even the canonical decades-old example splits state ownership, and that split is exactly what makes engine and GUI disagreements a known class of bug there. Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: the Chessprogramming wiki is a reliable community reference, not a vendor's primary source.

What was not found

No shipped game was found that runs one shared gameplay core inside both Unity and Unreal. Searched: "shared game simulation core across Unity and Unreal engine-agnostic postmortem", "game logic library separate from engine Unity Unreal same C# core adapter interfaces open source", "github engine agnostic game logic C# dll Unity Unreal both adapters netstandard shared simulation", and "we abandoned/we stopped engine abstraction layer game shared core two engines postmortem". The results were patents for simulation-industry middleware, generic engine comparisons and machine-written blogs; nothing primary.

The nearest real thing is Photon itself: Fusion ships for Unity, Unreal and Godot over a shared Photon Realtime C++ core, with a separate SDK per engine (Fusion, Realtime core). That is the Spine shape again: a shared core and separate per-engine layers, not one binary everywhere.

The absence is itself a finding. One artifact under two engines is something the field mostly does not attempt, and where it does (middleware), it maintains parallel code per engine rather than one artifact.

What published engine changes say

  • Slay the Spire 2. Mega Crit built it in Unity for over two years, moved it to Godot after the runtime-fee episode, and stayed moved after Unity backed down. No shared core is reported as extracted; the work was a move, not a bridge. Confidence MEDIUM: press reporting of the developer's statements, not an engineering write-up (link).

The line for a port: moving the core matches what Quantum and Spine do. One artifact running inside both Unity and Unreal has no published precedent, so treat a shared binary as a convenience you happen to get, not as the thing the architecture depends on.

Determinism across runtimes

A port that runs the same C# on Unity's Mono and on CoreCLR (an UnrealSharp host, a headless test run) meets this directly: u2ue compares the runtimes' answers by float bits (Chapter 5, Chapter 14). What the research found, in short:

  • No standard promises bit identity. ECMA-334, the C# language standard (section 8.3.7), says floating-point operations may be performed with higher precision than the operation's result type; ECMA-335, the CLI standard (Partition I, section 12.1.3), says the internal representation may vary until an explicit conversion. A one-ULP difference between runtimes is not a bug, and byte identity across Mono, CoreCLR and a headless run is an observed property of today's builds, not a guarantee: it can break on a Unity or .NET upgrade with no change to the game's code. Confidence VERY HIGH: both read as raw text from the standards' own sources.
  • Two divergences are not rounding, and both are likelier, larger and cheaper to find than a ULP: float-to-int casts, which differ between Mono and CoreCLR, and System.Math transcendentals, which call into the platform's C runtime. Confidence VERY HIGH.
  • Every shipped lockstep success in this literature is one binary on one architecture, and the published desync causes are overwhelmingly not floating point: iteration order, sort stability, serialisation, string formatting, random-call counts, caching. Confidence HIGH.
  • For bit identity across arbitrary hardware, fixed point is the standard answer, at a cost in precision and an overflow ceiling. The modern alternative is not to need it: server-authoritative games compare to a tolerance, not for equality.

So a byte-identical event log across runtimes is a stronger oracle than any shipped game in this literature attempted, and no specification backs it. u2ue keeps it as an instrument and does not assume it ("How u2ue differs", below). The sources, and the checks they suggest for a port's model, are in Chapter 14.

C# inside Unreal

A game whose rules are C# can keep them only if C# runs inside Unreal. All figures here were measured on 2026-09-30 from the GitHub API and the projects' own sites; any of them may have changed since.

UnrealSharp

  • UnrealSharp/UnrealSharp: MIT licence, 1,942 stars, 33 open issues, last push 2026-09-29. Active.
  • It requires Unreal Engine 5.6 to 5.8 and .NET 10.0.5 or newer, and strongly recommends a C++ project (repository, site).
  • It ships games and disclaims production readiness at the same time, and both statements are current. Its homepage lists three Steam titles made with it (Ballistic Brews, Forged: Reconquest, Prompt Crisis); its FAQ still says the plugin is not production ready yet, though the plan is that it will be (FAQ). The FAQ also says up-to-date binary builds are not released consistently, because of the pace of change, so it is compiled from source.

Read that as: it works well enough for small PC titles, its maintainers will not promise more, and its API is still moving. u2ue's Unreal hosts are UnrealSharp C# (Chapter 5), so this is the toolkit's dependency too.

Platforms

From the site's supported-platforms section: Windows and macOS are supported; Linux, iOS and Android are planned; no console appears at all, neither as supported nor as planned. Console and mobile builds are an open feature request, "NativeAOT (Console, mobile)" (issues). A community fork for native C++ transpilation and AOT (ahead-of-time: compiled to native code before the game ships) builds exists, takuma-komatsu/UnrealSharp-dn2cpp, pushed 2026-09-23 with 0 stars: an experiment, not a route. Confidence HIGH: the project's own platform table and the open issue, both read on the day.

If consoles are in scope, the arrangement that runs the model's assembly inside Unreal through this plugin has an expiry date, and the model's boundary should stay serialisable, so that a separate process or a reimplementation could drive it one day. If they are not in scope, this costs nothing.

The trap class

The recent open issues are almost all interop lifetime and marshalling (how long an object lives, and how data is passed, across the line between C# and Unreal's C++) - what you would predict of a managed layer over UObject memory, and a class of bug a logic-parity test does not see. UnrealSharp also reaches only what is exposed to reflection, the same restriction Blueprint has, so anything else needs C++ written by you. The issues as read on 2026-09-30, and the traps a port meets with it and their fixes, are in Chapter 13 and Chapter 16.

The alternatives

option its state on 2026-09-30
UnrealCLR (nxrighthere) 3,305 stars, last push 2023-06-07: over three years dormant. Asked about this exact use, "all game logic in C#, Unreal used as UI only", its maintainer said the plugin accepts compiled assemblies whatever the project's structure, but that interop with managed code from widgets is the biggest problem, that only desktop is supported, and that the project depends on Microsoft and Epic (discussion)
USharp (pixeltris) archived, last push 2020-05-16; its own README said it was not usable for most use cases
Mono-UE a personal side project of several Microsoft employees, supported by neither Microsoft nor Epic (link)
a native core plus a layer per engine the Spine shape: proven, expensive, two implementations kept in lock step
a separate process plus a protocol the UCI shape: proven for decades, but the boundary moves out to serialisation and, in the chess case, state ownership splits between the two sides
reimplement the presentation per engine, keep only the model portable what Spine actually does

Confidence HIGH on the repository facts (measured through the API on the day), MEDIUM on the maintainer's words (read through summaries of the linked discussion, not the raw thread).

The line for a port: UnrealSharp is the only live option, and it is good enough to prove logic parity today. With no console path and no production promise from its maintainers, treat its CoreCLR run as a very good test instrument rather than a shipping commitment. The engine-free model is what keeps the options open if the plugin stalls; callbacks from the model into the engine are what close them.

The case against an engine-free core

This part of the research was told to find the case against. It found one, and not the one expected: it is not "do not separate the core". It is about the motive. The arguments about where the seam is drawn (how many ports, interfaces with one implementor, pass-through layers) are in Chapter 5, for the developer drawing it.

Test the motive

Fowler's YAGNI ("You Aren't Gonna Need It") page names four costs of a presumptive feature: building it, the delay, carrying it, and repairing it. Then it exempts the case that decides this one: YAGNI applies only to capabilities built for a presumptive feature, not to effort that makes the software easier to modify (link).

Run that over the work. Determinism, replay, save-game integrity and tests that need no editor all make the software easier to modify, and they pay this month, on the engine the game already runs on: exempt. A set of adapters for a second engine is a presumptive feature, and it pays build, delay, carry and repair every week until the second engine is real.

So the test: if taking the second engine off the roadmap would kill the appetite for extracting the model, the extraction was never about testability, and the literature will not back it. If it survives that question, it is exempt and the argument is closed. Confidence HIGH on Fowler's text; the test is the research's own framing of it.

The one measured study

BinSubaih and Maddock, "G-factor Portability in Game Development Using Game Engines", CyberGames 2007, University of Sheffield (PDF), built a "Game Space Architecture" - an engine-free game state with an adapter per engine - and ported it between Torque and a second engine. They measured:

  • a CPU overhead of 1.51 % and a memory overhead of 16.49 MB;
  • frames per second down 11.6 % at 55.49 messages per second, with the warning that the game space becomes the bottleneck;
  • data integrity across the different game states at risk: initial tests found no problems, but more were needed;
  • that the approach plainly requires extra work;
  • and, from their own port checklist, the finding that matters most: the game logic is not affected, but while the game objects in the game space stay intact, the ones in the engine have to be created again, and so does the object model.

Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: peer-reviewed and actually measured, which is rare here, but on a small Torque demo, not a shipped commercial game, so the numbers are indicative rather than transferable.

What it says: the shared core saves the logic, and every engine-side object still has to be created again. The part the architecture protects is not the part the port costs.

The rule of three

Robert Glass, Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering: Fact 16, reuse-in-the-large (components) remains a mostly unsolved problem, though everyone agrees it matters; Fact 18 restates Biggerstaff's rules of three - a reusable component is three times as hard to build as a single-use one, and should be tried in three different applications before it is general enough to accept into a reuse library (link, restated independently at Coding Horror).

A model extracted from one game has been exercised in one application. By this rule it is two short of known-general, and the three-fold cost is being paid now. Confidence HIGH: a published book, a named researcher, cited independently.

Why studios separate a core

  • BIT.GAMES. Pavel Schevaev, its CTO, on a shipped match-3 with a deterministic C# core split out of Unity, gives five motives: replays, determinism, testing, scripted logic and bot validation. Engine portability is not among them, and he says the overhead may not make sense in small projects (link).
  • Hearthstone runs its rules engine on the server, off the Unity client, for server authority, not portability.
  • Age of Empires separated simulation from rendering because 28.8 kbit bandwidth forced it, and got replays and anti-cheat free as a side effect.
  • Factorio's separation exists for lockstep.

The pattern across every real case in this research: people separate the core for determinism, testing and server authority. In the sources reached, nobody separated it in order to change engines. Confidence MEDIUM-HIGH: four independent cases, but "nobody" is bounded by what was found, not by what exists.

What nobody has published

  • No published case was found of an engine-agnostic core making a real engine port cheap. Searched across Unity to Godot, Unity to Unreal, Unreal to Unity, studio engineering blogs and the academic literature. The one measured study found the port still recreates every engine-side object. That is the hole in the justification for an engine-free core as a porting strategy, and it is stated here rather than papered over.
  • No published breakdown was found of a real engine port's work by part - game code against assets, effects, UI and tools. Epic's documentation answers it qualitatively (code does not transfer; everything visual is rebuilt), but nobody published percentages.
  • Not read, flagged rather than asserted: Casey Yano's Godot evaluation (Medium, 403), the Road to Vostok devlogs (Patreon, 403) and Reddit (unreachable by the search tool). The research spent its search budget part way through and fetched sources directly after that, which is why a few are cited through a secondary restatement rather than their primary.

The Unity MCP server, and what this package adds

A Unity MCP server is the off-the-shelf way to let an AI model drive a Unity editor. It runs inside the editor, so it does what only an editor can, the Unity Test Runner included (its tests-run tool), and this package's second-instance route, my_unity.py, drives it on a clone of the project. Every call needs an open editor, though: the owner's, or a second full editor that takes window focus. Chapter 12 ("Compared with the open-source Unity MCP server") has what was measured against it.

What this package adds:

  • Tests without an editor: the headless NUnit runner, the typecheck, Unity's own Mono through u2ue digest.
  • An editor the owner is not using: idle gating on the cursor and keys, a presence watch, the editor lock, md5-held records.
  • The console as a test: a watermark, collapsed rows, noise counted apart, an exit code.
  • A real editor that is not the owner's: a clone on its own port with the traps of Chapter 12 absorbed, behind a kill switch.
  • Tools that can be trusted: selftests with planted faults, from the runner's planted pass, fail and empty filter to the window runner's simulated editor and every probe judge's plants (Chapter 8).

The window and the console gate still reach the editor through the reference port's editor bridge, which does not ship yet; until it does, a new project needs a bridge of its own (Chapter 12, Appendix B).

How u2ue differs

Measured against the routes above, using only this appendix's sources and the manual's own measured claims:

  • The shape is not new, and that is the point. An engine-free simulation that resolves a step and hands the view an ordered list of events is what Photon Quantum sells and what Epic's Gameplay Ability System does inside Unreal. u2ue's runtime library ships that split as PlaybackQueue<TEvent>: the model resolves an action at once and appends ordered events, and the host shows one per frame and takes input only when it has caught up (Chapter 5). As with Quantum's commands, nothing in the model waits on the view.
  • The model owns the state, the unanimous answer of every source this research read (Chapter 5 has them), and u2ue holds it with gates rather than advice: u2ue check --only model refuses an engine reference in the model and a platform member outside the hosting folder (Chapter 5, Chapter 9).
  • Logic parity is the contract for the code, and it is measured. On the reference port, three scripted battles write event logs that are byte-identical between the headless run and the Unreal host, and u2ue parity compares 383 rows across three runtimes (Unity on Mono, the Unreal host on CoreCLR, a headless test run): all agree except 35 one-ULP rows, each characterised and pinned to its exact bits (Chapter 5, Appendix A). No source in this research had a byte-comparable log across three runtimes; the Age of Empires post-mortem is an account of not having one. Because the standards do not promise bit identity, u2ue does not assume it: a difference is red unless that exact row is characterised, pinned to its bits and to one ULP.
  • It beats Epic's baseline for the code, and does not automate it. Epic's guidance assumes the code does not come across, and ProjectExodus ignores it. u2ue gives the code a method instead - an inventory, an engine-free model, Unity's frame, clock and coroutine rules in a runtime library, gates and parity - and thin UnrealSharp C# hosts. It does not move the code or write the hosts for you (Chapter 1, Chapter 5).
  • It converts the part an engine-free core does not protect. The one measured study found that every engine-side object has to be created again, and that is where u2ue's content tools are. No off-the-shelf Shuriken converter was found on 2026-08-22; u2ue converts Shuriken effects to Niagara through Epic's own FXConverterUtilitiesLibrary, and on the reference port (measured 2026-10-15) Unreal draws 7,810 of the 8,452 emitters Unity draws, 92.4 % (Chapter 7, Appendix A). Scenes are imported and graded by a fidelity gate of 45 checks against the scene's own baseline (on 2026-10-17 the reference port's first map failed 3 of them, each named), and uGUI screens are laid out by a port of uGUI's own solver (Chapter 6).
  • Gaps are written down, as Spine writes its gaps down. Every emitter Unity draws and the port does not is a gap, named and charged to its root, and an emitter one side lacks is named UNPAIRED, never dropped (Chapter 7, Chapter 9, Chapter 10).
  • Its gates can fail. mas-bandwidth/fixed, the fixed-point library of Chapter 14, hashes every result against a constant frozen into its source and ships deliberately broken targets, so that a suite which goes blind says so instead of passing quietly. Every u2ue gate carries planted defects it must refuse, because a gate that has only ever passed cannot be told apart from one that is switched off (Chapter 9).

And what the prior art says u2ue has not answered:

  • UnrealSharp is load-bearing for the Unreal hosts. On 2026-09-30 it had no console path, supported or planned, and its maintainers did not call it production ready.
  • Two games are one short of the rule of three. u2ue has run on the reference port and on a second, unrelated game, whose own Unreal host went from nothing to parity --require Unreal passing in 9 minutes (Chapter 3).
  • There is still no independent published case of an engine-free core making a real port cheap. The reference port is one case, documented in this manual (Appendix A), not an independent one.
  • Animation and physics are not covered (Chapter 1).

Appendix E. Traceability

Who this is for: the reviewer checking that what the toolkit's owner asked for is proven - one table to follow each of the owner's requirements to the selftests that hold it, and to see which ones nothing traces yet.

The chain from what the toolkit's owner asked for to what proves it was delivered: each stakeholder requirement, the steps of the epic that cite it, the use cases that carry those steps (Chapter 17), the verbs those cases prove with (Chapter 19), and each verb's selftest with its last verdict. Everything here is generated from u2ue/USECASES.md, the requirements engine's model and the selftest registry. A requirement that the epic does not cite is listed as untraced, not as met.
